entries.title: Bluff One Bigger Silhouette
entries.objective: Use posture, clothing, or a harmless prop to create a larger scorpion-like or warning silhouette for a theatrical photo, without approaching or targeting anyone.
entries.animalRule: The bluff must be visual only: no weapon, threat, chase, or interaction with an unsuspecting person is allowed.
entries.userBenefit: Develops theatrical visual communication by showing how shape alone can trigger a strong interpretation before any real capability is tested.
entries.mechanismConnection: Devil's Coach Horse Beetle uses this mode by presents a shape that triggers an avoidance response in anything that has encountered a scorpion, which is a visual bluff with no weapon behind it

entries.title: Bold Wins Some Years, Cautious Wins Others
entries.objective: Great tits differ consistently and heritably in how fast they approach something new, and the Wytham Woods population showed what follows: in some years the bold birds survive better and in others the cautious ones do, depending on food supply and competition, and sometimes differently for males and females in the same year. Neither strategy is correct; the environment decides. Its principle is Milk-Top Learning. The metaphor? Work out which year you are in before choosing bold or cautious, because neither is right in general.
entries.animalRule: The evidence for which conditions apply must be stated during the attempt, and the choice has to follow it rather than habit.
entries.userBenefit: Always being the bold one or always the careful one means you are right about half the time and never know which. Reading the conditions first turns that into a decision.
entries.mechanismConnection: Parus major exploration behaviour is heritable and under fluctuating selection, with bold and cautious phenotypes favoured in different years according to food supply and competition.

entries.title: Bolt Three Times at the Three-Metre Line
entries.objective: Hold still while someone walks toward you, then bolt the instant they cross a three-metre line, three times from three different approaches.
entries.animalRule: Still until the critical distance, then all-out: moving before the walker crosses the line, or still standing when they take their next step, spoils the run.
entries.userBenefit: A few seconds of all-out speed with a real reaction test and a big grin at the end.
entries.mechanismConnection: Black-tailed Jackrabbit — Explosive • Zigzag • Escape: Lepus californicus sits still in a shallow form, relying on camouflage and wide sightlines, and holds until a predator closes to a critical distance before exploding into a high-speed zigzag sprint. This Trial translates that hold-then-bolt at a critical distance into three still stands, each broken by an all-out sprint with a sharp cut the instant a walker crosses three metres.

entries.title: Boom in Turn From Taped Mat Squares
entries.objective: Share one display ground with at least one other person, each stamping and booming only from their own taped square, in turn.
entries.animalRule: Every display stays inside its own square, and each person booms only on their turn.
entries.userBenefit: A ridiculous, loud, bonding few minutes that nobody forgets.
entries.mechanismConnection: Greater Prairie-Chicken — Rhythmic • Lek • Signaling: Tympanuchus cupido males gather at the same open booming ground each spring, each defending its own small patch while stamping its feet rapidly, raising its pinnae and inflating orange air sacs to boom. This Trial translates that crowd of separate claims displayed on one shared ground into stamp-and-boom turns from taped squares on one mat.

entries.title: Boom Three Low Hoots From a Bottle
entries.objective: Blow across the mouth of an empty bottle to produce three clear, low hoots within ten seconds.
entries.animalRule: The sound must come from the bottle resonating: no humming or voice.
entries.userBenefit: A goofy, surprising burst of sound that is harder than it looks.
entries.mechanismConnection: Bare-necked Umbrellabird — Focused • Resonant • Displayer: Male Cephalopterus glabricollis inflate a bare red throat sac and lean forward to give short, deep booming calls, using an air-filled chamber to amplify a low resonant note in brief courtship bouts. This Trial translates that air-filled chamber that turns breath into a deep boom into three low bottle hoots within ten seconds.

entries.title: Bore Five Burrows in the Mix That Holds
entries.objective: Find the one sand mix that is soft enough to dig yet firm enough to keep a tunnel open, then fill it with doorways.
entries.animalRule: Burrows are made only with the pencil tip, and the winner is chosen by which hole stays open, not by guessing.
entries.userBenefit: A quick hands-on lesson in why builders care so much about getting the mix right.
entries.mechanismConnection: Burrowing Parakeet — Digging tunnels • Flying out to feed • Returning to the wall: the parrot digs its nest tunnel with its bill, which works only in sedimentary rock within a narrow band of hardness, soft enough to excavate and firm enough not to collapse, so the colony crowds thousands of tunnels into the few walls that qualify. This Trial translates that narrow soft-but-firm band and the crowded colony wall into testing three sand mixes and boring five burrows into the one that holds.

entries.title: Born Bright Orange
entries.objective: The gut here is the same solution its relatives use, a chambered forepart where microbes break down leaves ahead of stomach acid, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. What sets this species apart is happening outside the body. Its newborns are bright orange, a colour no adult in the group carries, and the effect on the other females is immediate: they crowd to handle, carry and groom the infant. Its principle is Dietary Fit. The metaphor? Make what is new unmistakably different and the group will come to it.
entries.animalRule: The difference must be immediately visible rather than explained, and no request for attention may be made during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: New things that look like everything else get ignored and you end up asking for attention. Making it unmistakably different brings the group to it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Trachypithecus cristatus neonates are bright orange, a colour absent in adults, which elicits intense allomaternal handling and carrying from other group females.

entries.title: Born Walking, No Nest Stage
entries.objective: A guinea pig has no defence at all: it cannot climb, jump, run fast or fight. What it has instead is a group and a newborn that needs no protecting. Gestation runs about sixty-eight days, extraordinary for a rodent this size, and the young arrive fully furred with eyes open, walking within hours. That removes the vulnerable nest stage entirely, because the litter travels with the group from the start. Its principle is Gentle Herding. The metaphor? Spend longer in preparation so that nothing you launch has a helpless phase.
entries.animalRule: The extra preparation must remove a specific vulnerability rather than merely improve quality, and that vulnerability has to be named during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Launching early means you spend weeks nursing something that cannot stand on its own. Extra preparation removes that phase from your work completely.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cavia porcellus has a ~68-day gestation exceptionally long for its body size, producing precocial young that are furred, open-eyed and mobile within hours, eliminating the altricial nest stage.

entries.title: Borrow a Reputation Early
entries.objective: Ants are avoided by an enormous range of predators because they bite, sting, taste of formic acid and summon others, and many insects have converged on looking like them. The Ant Mimic Mantis does it for the first part of its life only: early nymphs are black, narrow-waisted, ant-sized and move with the jerky gait of an ant. Later it stops, because by then it no longer needs the borrowed protection. Its principle is Trail-Worker Disguise. The metaphor? Early on, borrow someone else's standing. Drop it when you have your own.
entries.animalRule: The thing borrowed must be genuinely relevant and truthfully described rather than implied falsely, and it has to be used in a real introduction during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: A new thing standing entirely alone has to earn attention from zero, which mostly means being ignored. Attaching yours truthfully to something already trusted gets it looked at while it is still new.
entries.mechanismConnection: Odontomantis planiceps nymphs are myrmecomorphic, matching ant size, colouration, waist proportion and jerky gait, and lose the mimicry at later instars when size alone provides defence.

entries.title: Borrow One Light to Find Three Things
entries.objective: Borrow One Light to Find Three Things.
entries.animalRule: The light must be carried to each gap rather than the gap brought to the light.
entries.userBenefit: A borrowed light turns inaccessible darkness into searchable space.
entries.mechanismConnection: Produces light by housing colonies of luminous bacteria in jaw organs and feeding them, so the fish rents the chemistry it cannot perform and uses the output to hunt in caves and at night

entries.title: Borrow One Warning Color Without Words
entries.objective: Borrow One Warning Color Without Words.
entries.animalRule: No text or hazard impersonation; use it only for a harmless household pause cue.
entries.userBenefit: You turn spring glow into one concrete experience with a visible finish.
entries.mechanismConnection: Red Salamander — Red • Borrowed • Cold-spring: Bright red skin closely resembles the genuinely toxic red eft stage of the eastern newt, so predators that have learned to avoid efts avoid this animal too. This Trial translates that mechanism into one warning using borrowed red color.

entries.title: Borrow the Body of a Coursing Mammal
entries.objective: A patas monkey lives on open savanna with almost no trees, which for a primate removes the usual answer to everything. What replaced it is anatomy borrowed from a coursing mammal: long limbs, a narrow deep chest, short digits and a gait that makes it the fastest primate on the ground. It did not adapt its climbing; it adopted a completely different body plan. Its principle is Ground Speed. The metaphor? When your usual escape does not exist, adopt a different category's method entirely.
entries.animalRule: The method must come from a different field rather than being a variation of your own, and it has to be actually used during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Adapting your usual method when it does not apply gets you a worse version of something that already failed. A different field's method often just works.
entries.mechanismConnection: Erythrocebus patas has elongated limbs, a narrow deep thorax and short digits characteristic of cursorial mammals rather than arboreal primates, making it the fastest primate on the ground.

entries.title: Borrow the View, Lend the Nose
entries.objective: Chital outsource half their senses to another species. They feed under Hanuman langur troops routinely and both sides gain: the monkeys drop fruit and leaves, and more importantly they sit high with a clear view and call when they see a predator, while the deer contribute a sense of smell nothing in the canopy has. Naturalists track tigers through Indian reserves by listening to chital barks. Its principle is Herd Alertness. The metaphor? Pair with someone whose blind spot is your strength, and say so out loud.
entries.animalRule: The complementary blind spots must be named explicitly, and what each party reports has to be agreed during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: You cannot see your own blind spot, which is why you keep walking into the same thing. One explicit arrangement with the right person covers it permanently.
entries.mechanismConnection: Axis axis forages beneath Semnopithecus troops in a mutual alarm network, gaining elevated visual detection from the langurs while contributing olfactory detection unavailable in the canopy.

entries.title: Borrowed Colour Does Not Keep
entries.objective: Green is difficult for an insect, and most green in the animal world is structural because green pigments are hard to make and harder to keep stable. Emerald moths went the other way: they use an actual pigment derived from the chlorophyll in the plants the larvae ate. It works beautifully and it fades, in life and especially in collections, because it was borrowed rather than built. Its principle is Camouflage Mastery. The metaphor? Anything you took rather than made will fade. Plan for it.
entries.animalRule: The advantage must be genuinely borrowed from circumstance rather than built, and the conversion step has to be concrete rather than an intention.
entries.userBenefit: Advantages that came from circumstance feel like yours right up until the circumstance changes. Converting one into something you actually own is the difference between a good year and a good decade.
entries.mechanismConnection: Geometrinae produce green using geoverdin, a pigment derived from larval dietary chlorophyll rather than from structural colour, and it degrades over time both in life and in preserved specimens.

entries.title: Both Birds, the Whole Way
entries.objective: The red-breasted goose's borrowed-protection tactic only works because the pair stays together through it: both birds hold the site inside the raptor's radius, both watch, and both escort the young, because the protection is incidental rather than guaranteed and anything that does get through has to be met. Borrowed cover is not the same as safety. Its principle is Pairwatch. The metaphor? Borrowed protection is incidental, so do not reduce your own watch because of it.
entries.animalRule: The own watch must not be reduced during the attempt, and the gap in the borrowed cover has to be named.
entries.userBenefit: Reducing your own watch because you are inside someone else's perimeter means the thing that gets through finds you unguarded. Naming the gap keeps you ready.
entries.mechanismConnection: Branta ruficollis pairs maintain joint nest attendance and brood escorting within raptor-protected areas, since the protection is incidental and incomplete.

entries.title: Both Display, Both Judge
entries.objective: In most ornamented birds one sex displays and the other judges. Grebes do both at the same time. Males and females are almost identical, both carrying the head ruff and crest, and the courtship is a series of shared routines in which the two birds face each other and perform the same movements together. Neither is auditioning; both are assessing while being assessed. Its principle is Grace Display. The metaphor? Make the assessment mutual and simultaneous, rather than one of you performing.
entries.animalRule: Both sides must perform the same actions simultaneously during the attempt, and neither may be solely assessing.
entries.userBenefit: One side presenting to the other means you learn nothing about them while they learn everything about you. Mutual assessment is fairer and faster.
entries.mechanismConnection: Podiceps cristatus is sexually monomorphic with both sexes bearing the ruff and crest, performing mutual synchronised courtship ceremonies rather than unilateral display.

entries.title: Both Do Everything
entries.objective: In most ducks the male's contribution ends at fertilisation: the plumage is dimorphic, he displays, and the female incubates and raises the brood alone. Whistling ducks do none of this. Male and female are identical, with no plumage difference and no division of labour, and both incubate, both brood and both lead the ducklings. The pair bond lasts years. Its principle is Coordinated Flight. The metaphor? Dividing by role means each of you is a single point of failure. Both learn to do everything.
entries.animalRule: The person who normally does it may watch but must not take over or guide step by step, and the other has to complete it themselves.
entries.userBenefit: A job only one of you can do means that person can never be ill or away without it stopping. One handover where they actually do it removes a fragility you have been living with for years.
entries.mechanismConnection: Dendrocygna javanica is monomorphic with no sexual plumage difference, and both sexes share incubation, brooding and care of ducklings within long-term pair bonds, without division of parental roles.

entries.title: Both Give and Both Receive
entries.objective: Both animals in a snail mating are hermaphrodites and both will give and receive sperm, which makes the encounter a negotiation rather than a courtship. Many land snails settle it with a dart: a hardened calcareous spear driven through the partner's body wall during an extended preliminary, and what matters is not the wound but the mucus coating it carries. Its principle is Slow Progress Strategy. The metaphor? When both sides are giving and receiving the same thing, the exchange is a negotiation; treat it as one.
entries.animalRule: The two-way nature must be named during the attempt, and what each side gets has to be stated explicitly.
entries.userBenefit: Treating a two-way exchange as a favour you are doing means you give more than you get and resent it. Naming both sides balances it immediately.
entries.mechanismConnection: Land snails are simultaneous hermaphrodites in which both partners donate and receive sperm, and many deploy a mucus-coated calcareous love dart during a prolonged preliminary.

entries.title: Both Shield and Signal
entries.objective: A jewel beetle has a hard compact exoskeleton and a metallic iridescent cuticle that reflects different colours as light and viewing angle change. On bark the armour is both shield and signal: in one posture the colours blend with sunlit leaves, while a small shift flashes metallic hues that make the animal look hard and inedible. The same surface does protection and advertising. Its principle is Metallic Warning. The metaphor? Build one surface that protects you and signals, and switch between them by angle.
entries.animalRule: The same surface must do both during the attempt, and the switch has to come from presentation rather than alteration.
entries.userBenefit: Maintaining separate things for protection and for signalling costs you twice. One surface doing both means the angle you hold it at is the whole decision.
entries.mechanismConnection: Chrysochroa fulgidissima has a hard elytral cuticle with multilayer structural iridescence, functioning as both physical armour and an angle-dependent visual signal.

entries.title: Bound Up One Grassy Bank Before the Tag
entries.objective: Escape a chasing friend by whistling and bounding up a grassy slope to a marker before they tag you.
entries.animalRule: You must whistle before your first bound and flash the white cloth at your back all the way up the slope.
entries.userBenefit: A short, laughing hill sprint that turns a slope into your advantage.
entries.mechanismConnection: Mountain Reedbuck — Whistling • Bounding • Uphill: Redunca fulvorufula answers disturbance with a sharp alarm whistle and a rocking-horse bounding gait that carries it across or up the slope, flashing the white underside of its bushy tail. This Trial translates that whistled, bounding escape uphill into a race up a grassy bank ahead of a chasing friend.

entries.title: Bound Where They Have to Wade
entries.objective: Where a waterbuck uses water as somewhere to stand, a lechwe uses it as a surface to run on. Its hooves are unusually long and splay widely, spreading weight across soft mud, and the lower legs carry a water-repellent substance. Its gait in shallow flood is a series of bounds, inefficient on dry land and very effective in water, where a pursuing predator is wading while the lechwe is leaping. Its principle is Wetland Footing. The metaphor? Fight on the ground where your movement works and theirs does not.
entries.animalRule: The advantageous ground must be named before moving, and the contest has to actually relocate during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Fighting on ground that suits them means losing while doing everything right. Naming your own ground and moving there usually settles it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Kobus leche has elongated splayed hooves distributing load on soft substrate and water-repellent leg secretions, and uses a bounding gait in shallow flood that outpaces wading predators.

entries.title: Bound, Do Not Scurry
entries.objective: The Baluchistan pygmy jerboa crosses open desert on two legs, hind limbs long for its body, forelimbs held against the chest, a tail much longer than head and body balancing each bound. For an animal this size each hop covers a long distance and keeps it upright with a clear view around, which is what makes crossing bare ground between scattered plants survivable. Its principle is Tiny Desert Spring. The metaphor? Cross exposed ground in long deliberate bounds with your head up, rather than scurrying.
entries.animalRule: The crossing must be made in few long moves during the attempt, and the number has to be counted rather than estimated.
entries.userBenefit: Crossing something exposed in lots of small anxious moves means you are out there far longer and see less. A few long ones with your head up gets you across.
entries.mechanismConnection: Salpingotulus michaelis crosses open ground by bipedal saltation on elongated hindlimbs with a long balancing tail, covering large distances per bound while maintaining visual vigilance.

entries.title: Brace and Raise Your Eyeline
entries.objective: The argus monitor's distinctive behaviour is standing up. It rears onto its hind legs and uses a thick heavy tail as a third leg, forming a tripod that lifts the head well above grass height, and holds the position while scanning. In flat open country where a lizard at ground level can see perhaps a metre, that is what makes the difference between blind and informed. Its principle is Scanning Readiness. The metaphor? A third support buys the height.
entries.animalRule: A genuine third support has to take part of your weight, the raised position is held two minutes, and the thing looked at must be one you usually see from below.
entries.userBenefit: Looking at a problem from the same level you always do means you keep seeing the same metre of it. Two minutes higher usually shows you the obvious thing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Varanus panoptes adopts a tripodal stance using its heavy tail as a third limb to elevate the head above grass height for extended visual scanning.

entries.title: Brace Flat Then Snap Upright
entries.objective: Store tension on your back, then release into one clean upright flip.
entries.animalRule: Use a soft mat and stop if your neck or back complains.
entries.userBenefit: You practice a stored-tension escape that rights you when you are stuck on your back.
entries.mechanismConnection: Click Beetle — Latching • Snapping • Flipping: A threatened or overturned adult arches, braces a thoracic peg in a groove, then lets it slip so the body jack-knifes with a click and flings into the air. This Trial stores brace tension on the back and releases it into upright snaps.

entries.title: Brace on the Spines
entries.objective: The white-throated needletail is named for its tail: the feather shafts project beyond the vanes as short bare spines, and the bird presses them against a tree trunk or a rock face to brace itself when it clings. An animal built almost entirely for the air still needed one small hard point of contact for the rare moment it stops. Its principle is Needleline. The metaphor? Keep one hard point to brace against.
entries.animalRule: The brace point must be specific and already existing, and one pause has to actually be taken against it.
entries.userBenefit: Improvising where to stop means your pauses happen wherever you collapse and do not restore anything. One named hard point gives every pause somewhere to take your weight.
entries.mechanismConnection: Hirundapus caudacutus bears projecting bare rectrix shafts that it presses against vertical surfaces to brace while clinging.

entries.title: Brace the Web Across the Middle
entries.objective: Two things about the wasp spider are widely misread. The banding resembles a wasp closely enough that birds treat it as one, though the spider has no sting worth the name. The second is the zigzag band of thick silk running through the middle of the web, long argued to be a lure or a warning, and most likely structural: it braces and stabilises an otherwise flimsy orb. Its principle is Strategic Bluffing. The metaphor? The decorative-looking thing may be holding the structure together. Find out before removing it.
entries.animalRule: Its actual function must be established before removal rather than assumed, and the removal has to be reversible if attempted.
entries.userBenefit: Removing things that look redundant is how working systems break in ways nobody can trace. One check before removal costs minutes and saves you a week of confusion.
entries.mechanismConnection: Argiope bruennichi constructs a stabilimentum of thick zigzag silk through the orb web, which evidence indicates primarily provides structural reinforcement rather than prey attraction or predator warning.

entries.title: Break Cover and Zigzag Home Untagged
entries.objective: Stay hidden until you are spotted, then burst out and zigzag to base before a seeker can tag you.
entries.animalRule: Stay still in cover until you are seen, then run only in sharp zigzags: a straight dash to base does not count.
entries.userBenefit: A burst of play that gets your heart going and your reflexes sharp.
entries.mechanismConnection: Snowshoe Hare — Explosive • Evasive • Escape: Lepus americanus relies on a coat and cover matched to the season, and when a lynx or owl breaks that concealment it bursts out in sudden zigzag sprints on broad, furred feet. This Trial translates that burst from broken camouflage into zigzag escape into a dash from a discovered hiding place to base with three sharp turns.

entries.title: Break Off and Look at the Face
entries.objective: What separates a dog from a wolf is not tameness but where its attention points. Hand-reared wolves given the same upbringing do not reliably follow a human finger, and dogs do it untrained as puppies; faced with a problem they cannot solve, dogs break off and look at the human face while wolves keep working at the box. The anatomy followed the behaviour. Its principle is Companion Readiness. The metaphor? When you are stuck, break off and look at a person rather than continuing to work the problem.
entries.animalRule: The break-off must happen within a minute of being stuck during the attempt, and a person has to be actually looked to.
entries.userBenefit: Continuing to work at something you are stuck on burns your afternoon and the answer was in the room. Breaking off within a minute costs you nothing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Canis familiaris spontaneously follows human pointing and breaks off unsolvable tasks to gaze at the human face, unlike identically reared wolves.

entries.title: Break the Circle of the Eye
entries.objective: Most camouflage fails at the eye. Everything else can be broken up by pattern, but a round dark pupil is a shape nothing in leaf litter produces, and visual predators are very good at finding it. This frog's answer is the pointed projections above each eye and at the snout, which extend the outline into sharp points and carry the leaf's false midrib line directly across the eye, so the circle is interrupted. Its principle is Leaf Ambush. The metaphor? Find the one feature your disguise cannot hide and run the pattern straight through it.
entries.animalRule: The undisguisable element must be identified explicitly, and the pattern has to be extended across it during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Working around the one thing you cannot disguise is exactly what makes it visible. Running the pattern through it is what finally hides it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Megophrys nasuta bears supraocular and rostral projections that extend the body outline and carry a false midrib line across the eye, disrupting the circular pupil outline predators detect.

entries.title: Break the Outline, Not the Colour
entries.objective: The bongo is one of the largest forest antelopes and survives by not presenting a shape. A chestnut coat crossed by ten to fifteen narrow white vertical stripes works against the vertical stems and hanging light of dense African forest: the pattern breaks the body's outline rather than matching any background colour, which is why the animal can be metres away and unresolved. Its principle is Broken Outline. The metaphor? Break up your outline rather than matching the colour, because shape is what gets recognised.
entries.animalRule: The change must disrupt outline rather than match colour during the attempt, and it has to be checked from a few metres.
entries.userBenefit: Matching the colour still leaves your shape recognisable from a few metres. Breaking the outline is what makes you genuinely hard to resolve.
entries.mechanismConnection: Tragelaphus eurycerus bears narrow white vertical striping that disrupts body outline against vertical forest stems rather than providing background colour matching.

entries.title: Break the Plates Into Flecks
entries.objective: A mirror spider's silver patches are guanine crystals over cells that can expand or contract, so the bright plates can be broken within seconds into small scattered flecks. Expanded, the abdomen looks like a cluster of shining droplets; broken up, the outline softens and the spider disappears into leaves. Visibility is a dial, not a fixed trait. Its principle is Reflective Adaptation. The metaphor? Be able to turn your visibility down in seconds, rather than being stuck at one setting.
entries.animalRule: The change must be achieved by breaking the thing up rather than covering it during the attempt, and it has to be reversible within seconds.
entries.userBenefit: Being stuck at one level of visibility means you are either exposed when you need quiet or invisible when you need to be seen. A dial you can turn in seconds solves both.
entries.mechanismConnection: Thwaitesia argentiolus adjusts abdominal guanine-crystal reflectance by expanding or contracting underlying tissue, fragmenting bright plates into scattered specks.

entries.title: Break the Shape, Not the Colour
entries.objective: This river stingray carries a reticulated net of pale rings over a dark ground, and the pattern does not match any particular riverbed. It works by disruption: the high-contrast net breaks the continuous disc outline into fragments so the eye does not assemble a ray-shaped object at all. Not blending, fragmenting. Its principle is Patterned Concealment. The metaphor? Matching the background is hard and fragile. Break your outline instead and nothing has to match.
entries.animalRule: The breaking must disrupt how it reads as a single thing rather than hiding or disguising it, and the parts have to stay in plain view.
entries.userBenefit: Trying to make something blend in requires you to match a background that keeps changing. Breaking how it reads as one object works everywhere and needs no upkeep from you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Potamotrygon falkneri bears a high-contrast reticulated pattern that functions as disruptive colouration, fragmenting the continuous outline of the disc rather than matching any specific substrate.

entries.title: Break Up One Card Bird's Outline With Bars
entries.objective: Show how bold barring hides a shape by laying a barred card bird and a plain one side by side on leaf litter.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may cover either shape: no burying or tucking under leaves, so only the barring can break up the outline.
entries.userBenefit: A slow outdoor puzzle that trains your eye for pattern and outline.
entries.mechanismConnection: European Nightjar — Camouflaged • Dayground • Still: Caprimulgus europaeus spends the day lying flat and still on the ground or along a branch, its grey-brown barred and streaked plumage breaking up its outline so completely against leaf litter and bark that it is almost impossible to spot. This Trial translates that disruptive barring that dissolves a still bird's outline on leaf litter into a barred card bird compared with a plain one on open litter.

entries.title: Breathe Through the Skin Instead
entries.objective: Amphibian skin is permeable, which is a frog's great vulnerability on land and its solution in winter. Many common frogs spend months at the bottom of a pond without surfacing, not breathing with their lungs at all; oxygen is taken up entirely across the skin. That is only possible because metabolism has dropped far enough for skin exchange to supply the whole demand. Its principle is Leap Courage. The metaphor? Lower what you need until the cheap, passive supply is enough.
entries.animalRule: The demand must be genuinely reduced rather than the supply increased, and the passive source has to actually cover it during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Hunting for a bigger supply is why everything you run needs you. Lowering the demand until something passive covers it means it keeps going without you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Rana temporaria overwinters submerged with lungs unused, relying entirely on cutaneous gas exchange, which is sufficient only because metabolic rate has dropped to match its low capacity.

entries.title: Breathe Through the Wrong End
entries.objective: A Mary River turtle can stay underwater for up to three days, and it manages that by breathing through the wrong end. Its cloaca contains highly vascularised sac-like structures, effectively gills, which extract dissolved oxygen directly from the water, so the animal does not have to break the surface. That removes the single most dangerous and most energetically costly thing a freshwater turtle does. Its principle is Aquatic Oddity. The metaphor? Find another route for the one requirement that keeps forcing you into the open.
entries.animalRule: The requirement that forces exposure must be named, and an alternative route for it has to be found during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: One requirement that forces you into the open is where everything goes wrong, repeatedly. Finding another route for it lets you stay hidden indefinitely.
entries.mechanismConnection: Elusor macrurus has highly vascularised cloacal bursae permitting direct aquatic oxygen uptake, allowing submergence for up to three days without surfacing.

entries.title: Breathe While You Move
entries.objective: Most lizards cannot breathe properly while walking, because the side-to-side bending that drives the stride squeezes the lungs, so a dash runs on no oxygen and is repaid with a long stop. A Water Monitor pumps air with the floor of its mouth and throat while the trunk is still flexing, so oxygen keeps arriving. That buys hours of activity instead of bursts. Its principle is Sustained Range. The metaphor? Stop sprinting and collapsing. Breathe while you move.
entries.animalRule: You must stay able to speak a full sentence throughout the ten minutes, and the pace must be deliberately below your sprint. If you cannot talk, the pace is wrong and the attempt restarts.
entries.userBenefit: Sprinting then collapsing means most of your day is recovery. A pace you can hold while still breathing easily finishes more by the evening and leaves you able to do it again tomorrow.
entries.mechanismConnection: Varanus salvator supplements costal breathing with gular pumping, drawing air using the throat floor while axial bending constrains the ribcage, and a well-divided ventricle maintains systemic pressure, together supporting sustained aerobic activity rather than anaerobic bursts.

entries.title: Breathing Pore Moved to the Rear
entries.objective: Land slugs have generally lost their shells and kept everything else; the veronicellids went further. The whole upper surface is a thick tough leathery mantle with no shell beneath it and no mantle cavity on the flank, the breathing pore sits at the rear of the body instead of on the right side, and the animal is flattened rather than rounded. Everything was rearranged, not just removed. Its principle is Sole-Ripple Glide. The metaphor? Removing a structure is only half of it; move what depended on it somewhere that still works.
entries.animalRule: The dependent thing must be actually relocated during the attempt, and leaving it in place is not sufficient.
entries.userBenefit: Removing a structure and leaving what depended on it in place means that thing now fails quietly on you. Relocating it is the half of the job people skip.
entries.mechanismConnection: Veronicellid slugs have a thick leathery dorsal mantle without shell or lateral mantle cavity, with the pneumostome relocated to the posterior body.

entries.title: Breed Early on Last Year's Store
entries.objective: The spotted nutcracker breeds unusually early, while the mountains are still under snow and nothing fresh is growing. It can do that because it feeds its young almost entirely on seeds it buried the previous autumn. The store is not insurance against a bad year; it is what makes an early start possible at all. Its principle is Mountain Seed Memory. The metaphor? Spend the store to start early.
entries.animalRule: The reserve must actually be spent rather than reallocated, and what it bought has to be named before the day ends.
entries.userBenefit: A reserve you never spend is not safety, it is a start you keep postponing until the chance has gone. Spending part of it now buys you a head start nothing else can.
entries.mechanismConnection: Nucifraga caryocatactes breeds in late winter and provisions its nestlings largely from seeds cached the previous autumn, decoupling breeding from current food availability.

entries.title: Breed on the Rimu's Schedule
entries.objective: A kakapo does not breed on its own schedule; it breeds on the rimu tree's. Rimu fruits heavily only every two to four years, and in those mast years the kakapo breeds, because nothing else in the forest can supply a chick with enough of the right food. In every other year it simply does not. Its principle is Grounded Uniqueness. The metaphor? Take your schedule from whatever actually supplies you, not from your own calendar.
entries.animalRule: The supplying thing's schedule must be established during the attempt, and your own calendar has to be set aside.
entries.userBenefit: Setting your timing from your own calendar means arriving when the supply is not there. Taking it from the supply means every attempt lands.
entries.mechanismConnection: Strigops habroptilus breeds only in rimu mast years occurring every two to four years, because no other food source can support chick development.

entries.title: Breed Small Rather Than Not At All
entries.objective: A Nile tilapia does not have a fixed size at maturity; it has a rule. In open water with food and space it grows large before breeding and holds a nest pit. Crowd the same fish, or give it poor water, and it simply breeds much smaller and much earlier, producing a dense population of stunted individuals instead. Nothing fails; the output changes shape. Its principle is Adaptive Hardiness. The metaphor? In poor conditions, produce smaller rather than waiting for conditions that may not come.
entries.animalRule: The smaller version must be genuinely produced during the attempt, and no waiting for better conditions is permitted.
entries.userBenefit: Waiting for conditions good enough for the full version often means you produce nothing at all. A smaller one now is real and those conditions may never arrive.
entries.mechanismConnection: Oreochromis niloticus exhibits plastic size at maturity, reproducing at much smaller body size and younger age under crowding or poor water quality.

entries.title: Breed to the Water, Not the Calendar
entries.objective: In Australia water is not seasonal, it is episodic. Inland wetlands can be dry for several years and then fill over a few weeks when rain falls in a distant catchment, and a duck that bred to a calendar would miss it entirely. This species breeds to the water instead: birds move to newly flooded country, come into condition within weeks, and raise broods on the invertebrate flush. Its principle is Adaptive Foraging. The metaphor? Hold yourself ready to come into condition within weeks, and go when the thing actually appears.
entries.animalRule: The triggering condition must be named rather than a date during the attempt, and readiness has to be actually arranged.
entries.userBenefit: Committing to a date for something that depends on an episodic condition means you miss it entirely. Being ready to start on the signal catches every one.
entries.mechanismConnection: Anas superciliosa breeds opportunistically in response to episodic inland flooding rather than to season, attaining breeding condition within weeks of water arrival.

entries.title: Breed Twice as the Crop Ripens North
entries.objective: Every other European gamebird stays put. This one crosses the Sahara. Quail winter in the Sahel and move north through spring, and the movement does not stop on arrival: cereal and hay fields are suitable for only a few weeks before they are cut, so quail breed early in North Africa or Iberia, then move north as the crop ripens behind them and breed again. Its principle is Low Covey. The metaphor? Follow the ripening window north rather than staying with one field through its whole cycle.
entries.animalRule: The move must follow an advancing window during the attempt, and a full cycle has to be completed before moving.
entries.userBenefit: Staying with one source through its decline means your second half produces nothing. Following the window gets you two full cycles in a season.
entries.mechanismConnection: Coturnix coturnix breeds successively northward through the season, tracking the advancing suitability window of cereal and hay crops before each is harvested.

entries.title: Breed Twice, Hundreds of Miles Apart
entries.objective: A sedge wren differs from most songbirds decisively: it does not commit to a place. A wet meadow is usable only in a narrow window, tall enough to hide a nest and wet enough for insects but not flooded or dried, and which meadows qualify shifts month to month. So the bird breeds early in one region and again hundreds of kilometres away later in the same summer. Its principle is Grass Weaving. The metaphor? If the window is narrow and moves, run the whole cycle twice in different places.
entries.animalRule: The first cycle must be completed rather than extended, and a second run elsewhere has to be planned during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Extending one run past its window means the second half returns nothing. Two complete runs in different places gets you twice the result for the same season.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cistothorus platensis is itinerant, nesting early in one region and again hundreds of kilometres away later the same season, tracking the shifting narrow suitability window of wet meadow.

entries.title: Breed When the Desert Floods
entries.objective: Most birds breed on a seasonal schedule. The Australian Pelican breeds when the desert floods. Monsoon rain drains south through ephemeral channels and in some years fills Lake Eyre, turning the driest salt pan on the continent into a shallow inland sea swarming with fish within weeks. Pelicans arrive from hundreds of kilometres away. The trigger is the event, not the calendar. Its principle is Patient Foraging. The metaphor? Stop running on the calendar. Move when the conditions actually arrive.
entries.animalRule: The trigger must be an observable event rather than another date, and the arbitrary date has to be actually cancelled rather than kept as a backup.
entries.userBenefit: Scheduling something for a date that has nothing to do with readiness means it arrives and you postpone it. Tying it to the real trigger means it happens the moment it can actually work.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pelecanus conspicillatus breeds opportunistically when monsoon runoff fills Lake Eyre, with birds converging from hundreds of kilometres to exploit the ephemeral fish population rather than following an annual breeding schedule.

entries.title: Brief Runs, Then Back Into the Crack
entries.objective: A silverfish is flattened and wingless and lives in the gaps. It sits out the day in a humid crevice, comes out at night for short quick runs after starch, and is back in a crack before anything can lock onto it. Its energy goes out in small amounts across hundreds of nights rather than in any single push. Its principle is Hidden Persistence. The metaphor? Make each exposure brief and go back under, and you can repeat it indefinitely.
entries.animalRule: The exposed run must be brief enough to repeat during the attempt, and the return to cover has to happen immediately rather than after a pause.
entries.userBenefit: Long exposed pushes mean you need to recover afterwards and do not go back out for a week. Brief runs with an immediate return are the only ones you keep making.
entries.mechanismConnection: Lepisma saccharina shelters in humid crevices by day and forages nocturnally in brief rapid excursions for starch-rich material, minimising exposure duration.

entries.title: Bright Blocks on a Mossy Floor
entries.objective: A rhinoceros viper carries some of the brightest markings of any African snake, blue, green, crimson and black in sharp geometric blocks, and is almost impossible to see. The pattern works because its habitat is not dry brown litter but the wet mossy light-dappled floor of swamp forest, where strong contrasting shapes read as scattered vegetation and reflected light rather than as an animal. Its principle is Ornamental Camouflage. The metaphor? Loud and contrasting can be invisible, if the background is loud and contrasting too.
entries.animalRule: The contrast level must be matched rather than the colour during the attempt, and loudness has to be permitted where the background is loud.
entries.userBenefit: Toning something down to be unobtrusive in a loud environment makes it the only quiet thing there, and that is what draws your audience's eye. Match the contrast instead.
entries.mechanismConnection: Bitis nasicornis bears high-contrast geometric blocks that read as scattered vegetation and reflected light against the wet mossy dappled floor of West African swamp forest.

entries.title: Bright Far Off, Intricate Close Up
entries.objective: A display has to work at the distance it will be seen from, and a forest floor offers two of them. The male silver pheasant's upperparts are white, which against dim mottled ground reads as a bright shape visible a long way off, and each of those white feathers is finely ruled with black lines, which at close range resolves into an intricate pattern. One surface works at both distances. Its principle is Confident Display. The metaphor? Build something that reads as one thing from across the room and as another in the hand.
entries.animalRule: The thing must work at both distances during the attempt, and it has to be checked at each.
entries.userBenefit: Something built for one distance looks wrong at the other, and you will be seen at both. One surface that works at each means you never have to choose.
entries.mechanismConnection: Lophura nycthemera males have white upperparts reading as a high-contrast shape at distance, with fine black vermiculation on each feather resolving into detail at close range.

entries.title: Bright Only in the Short Window
entries.objective: A male ladybird spider is red and black and very visible, which on open ground is close to suicidal. He gets away with it because the exposure is brief and targeted: he leaves the silk-lined burrow for short periods only to find females and court, and the rest of the time he is underground. The colour is affordable only because the window is small. Its principle is Hidden Brilliance. The metaphor? Be conspicuous only inside a narrow window you chose, and the risk stays priced.
entries.animalRule: The window must be fixed before the attempt begins, and the return out of sight has to happen the moment it closes rather than drifting on.
entries.userBenefit: Being visible all the time means paying the risk continuously for the few moments it helps. A short fixed window gets you the same benefit at a fraction of the exposure.
entries.mechanismConnection: Eresus kollari males leave their silk-lined burrows displaying conspicuous red-and-black coloration only during brief mate-searching excursions.

entries.title: Bring Back the Predator
entries.objective: An oil palm plantation is a rodent's ideal landscape: continuous food, dense nesting, no cover for predators. Rats reach damaging densities, and poisoning works briefly then fails because they breed faster than baiting removes them. What holds them down is barn owls, given somewhere to nest. The lasting fix was structural, not chemical. Its principle is Palm-Row Pantry. The metaphor? Stop treating the symptom on a schedule. Restore the thing that keeps it in check.
entries.animalRule: The mechanism must work without you once in place, and the manual clearing has to actually stop rather than continuing alongside it.
entries.userBenefit: Clearing the same thing every week is a job you gave yourself and never finish. One mechanism that holds it down by itself removes the task permanently for an afternoon of setup.
entries.mechanismConnection: Rattus tiomanicus reaches damaging densities in oil palm where baiting fails against its reproductive rate, and sustained control is achieved by installing nest boxes to support barn owl populations as a structural predator.

entries.title: Bring Up What Is Buried
entries.objective: Darwin spent his last years on earthworms and concluded they shaped the land surface more than almost anything else. An anecic worm swallows soil at depth, grinds it with ingested grit, passes it through a gut that adds mucus, calcium carbonate, enzymes and an enormous microbial load, and voids it at the surface. Material from below is brought up and improved on the way. Its principle is Soil Renewal. The metaphor? The good stuff is buried. Bring it up and work it as it comes.
entries.animalRule: The thing must come from genuinely old or deep storage rather than recent material, and it has to be improved on the way up rather than simply relocated.
entries.userBenefit: Old material sits buried because nothing ever surfaces it, so you keep remaking things you already had. Bringing one thing up and improving it as you go turns dead storage into something you use this week.
entries.mechanismConnection: Anecic earthworms such as Pheretima posthuma ingest subsoil at depth, grind it in a muscular gizzard with ingested grit, enrich it with mucus, calcium carbonate, enzymes and gut microbes, and deposit the processed cast at the surface.

entries.title: Broad Hooves With Rough Pads
entries.objective: A bighorn's everyday business is not fighting but moving across broken ground where a slip can be fatal. Broad hooves with rough pads, strong leg muscles and good balance let it graze and travel in a steady mid-intensity rhythm on terrain that would stop most animals. The footing is what makes the territory usable at all. Its principle is Horned Contest. The metaphor? Fix the footing before anything else, because everything you do happens on it.
entries.animalRule: The footing must be addressed first during the attempt, and what it enables has to be named.
entries.userBenefit: Working on anything while your footing is poor means every step costs you attention. Fixing it first makes all of the rest straightforward.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ovis canadensis has broad hooves with rough textured pads and strong limb musculature providing secure purchase on steep broken terrain.

entries.title: Broadcast One Message Without Leaving Seat
entries.objective: Broadcast One Message Without Leaving Seat.
entries.animalRule: You must remain seated until all three recipients have received the same message.
entries.userBenefit: You turn canopy resonance into one concrete, visible experience instead of an abstract idea.
entries.mechanismConnection: Black Howler Monkey — Leaf-fed • Still • Broadcasting: A gut built for slow fermentation of leaves keeps the animal sitting for most of the day, and the territorial work that other primates do by travelling is done instead by a dawn call thrown across kilometres of forest. This Trial translates that low-frequency mechanism into one message without leaving seat.

entries.title: Brood Six Sock Eggs in a Quiet Nook
entries.objective: Sit tight in an enclosed nook for ten still minutes, keeping a clutch of six sock eggs covered and warm on your lap.
entries.animalRule: Stay in the nook for the whole ten minutes with the clutch covered at all times: no getting up, no screens.
entries.userBenefit: Ten minutes of genuine stillness in a sheltered spot, with a simple job that keeps you there.
entries.mechanismConnection: Bufflehead — Sheltered • Stationary • Recovering: Bucephala albeola nests in tree cavities, often old flicker holes, and the incubating female sits tight inside for long stretches, keeping still and conserving heat so the eggs stay warm, leaving only briefly to feed. This Trial translates that still, heat-saving incubation inside a familiar cavity into ten still minutes in a nook with a sock clutch kept covered on your lap.

entries.title: Brush Pollen Through Six Paper Flower Cups
entries.objective: Visit six paper flower cups in turn with one small brush and carry each cup's coloured powder into the next.
entries.animalRule: Use one brush that is never cleaned, visit the cups in order, and let only the brush tip, standing in for the snout, enter each cup.
entries.userBenefit: A tiny, colourful experiment that shows how pollination really moves between flowers.
entries.mechanismConnection: Honey Possum — Clambering • Licking • Pollinating: Tarsipes rostratus pushes its long, pointed snout into banksia and heath flowers and licks up nectar and pollen with a bristle-tipped tongue, and pollen that sticks to the fur of its snout and head is carried to the next flower it probes, making it an important pollinator. This Trial translates that pollen carried on the snout from one flower to the next into one brush tip, standing in for the snout, carrying colour through six cups in order.

entries.title: Brush the Hairs Into the Air
entries.objective: The goliath birdeater is the heaviest spider in the world and its main defence involves no contact at all. The abdomen carries urticating hairs with microscopic barbs, and when threatened the spider brushes them off with its hind legs into the air toward the attacker, where they lodge in eyes, nose and airways and cause intense irritation, a deterrent that works on a mammal far too large to bite effectively. Its principle is Intimidation. The metaphor? Build a defence that works at a distance on things far too large for you to engage directly.
entries.animalRule: The defence must work without contact during the attempt, and the oversized threat it addresses has to be named.
entries.userBenefit: Having only contact defences means anything much larger than you simply wins. One distance deterrent makes those threats stop bothering with you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Theraphosa blondi flicks barbed urticating setae from its abdomen with the hind legs toward threats, lodging them in the attacker's mucous membranes without physical contact.

entries.title: Brush Twelve Paper Tents Without Toppling One
entries.objective: Brush a pipe-cleaner tip across twelve standing paper tents in fifteen seconds so each sways but none falls.
entries.animalRule: Every tent must be touched and seen to move, and a single toppled tent ends the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: A tense little test of speed against control.
entries.mechanismConnection: Twelve-wired Bird-of-paradise — Focused • Rapid • Contact-led: Seleucidis melanoleucus males have twelve bare, wire-like plume shafts on their flanks, and in short, intense display bouts they swivel to brush those wires precisely across the female's face and body. This Trial translates that fast, precise contact display into brushing twelve paper tents so each sways and none falls.

entries.title: Buckle the Ribs One by One
entries.objective: A cicada does not rub anything together. On each side of the abdomen sits a tymbal, a curved membrane stiffened by a series of ribs, and a large muscle pulls it sharply inward until the ribs buckle one after another, each buckle producing a distinct click. The muscle fires once; the ribs convert that into a train of clicks loud enough to carry hundreds of metres. Its principle is Seasonal Emergence. The metaphor? One effort can produce many outputs if the structure is ribbed for it. Build the ribs.
entries.animalRule: The structure must be set before the work begins rather than salvaged afterwards, and at least three outputs have to come from the single effort.
entries.userBenefit: One effort producing one output is why you never have anything to show for a busy week. Structuring it first so three things fall out costs no extra time at all.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cicada tymbals are ribbed membranes buckled inward by a single large muscle contraction, with each rib collapsing sequentially to produce a separate click, converting one muscular effort into a rapid train of pulses.

entries.title: Build a Borrowed Nest Beside a Cache
entries.objective: Make a resting nest from things you already own, lined with the softest fabric, with a small cache of water and snack within reach.
entries.animalRule: Nothing new is bought: the nest is taken over from things you already have, and the cache must be reachable while curled up.
entries.userBenefit: A cosy, well-stocked place to recover in.
entries.mechanismConnection: Least Weasel — Resting • Caching • Recovering: Between hunts the Least Weasel rests curled in a nest taken over from a rodent, often lining it with fur from its prey, and stores surplus kills close by. This Trial translates that borrowed nest lined with soft material and a cache stored nearby into a repurposed, soft-lined nest with water and a snack within arm's reach.

entries.title: Build a Box Periscope for Sofa Peeking
entries.objective: Make a simple periscope from a long box and two small mirrors, then use it to see over a sofa back while staying hidden behind it.
entries.animalRule: Your head must stay hidden below the edge: only the periscope may show above it.
entries.userBenefit: A classic, satisfying build that actually works.
entries.mechanismConnection: Wonderpus Octopus — Burrowed • Watching • Sheltered: Wunderpus photogenicus spends much of the day inside a burrow in sand or rubble, often with only its raised, stalked eyes showing, so it can watch the reef while its body stays hidden. This Trial translates that concealed body with raised eyes into a periscope that lets you watch a room from behind cover.

entries.title: Build a Drill, Not a Straw
entries.objective: Most moths carry a proboscis built for one job: a flexible tube for drawing nectar from a flower that is offering it. The fruit-piercing moths carry a different one, stiffened, barbed, ridged and reinforced, and they use it as a drill, working it through intact fruit skin to reach what is inside. The same organ, redesigned for taking rather than receiving. Its principle is Understory-Shade Wings. The metaphor? Your tool is built for things that are offered. Build one that opens what is closed.
entries.animalRule: The tool must open something genuinely closed rather than speed up something already available, and something has to be extracted during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Your tools only work on things already being handed to you, so you are limited to what people volunteer. One tool that opens closed things changes what is available to you permanently.
entries.mechanismConnection: Fruit-piercing noctuids including Cyclodes omma have a stiffened proboscis armed with barbs and cutting ridges, reinforced along its length, which pierces intact fruit skin rather than drawing offered nectar.

entries.title: Build a Peephole Box Hiding a Vivid Pattern
entries.objective: Make a box that looks plain from outside but reveals a vivid pattern only to someone who peers in close.
entries.animalRule: The outside stays plain: all colour lives inside where only a close look finds it.
entries.userBenefit: A small making project with a delightful reveal to show others.
entries.mechanismConnection: Splendid Toadfish — Sheltered • Local • Revealing: Sanopus splendidus lives tucked into crevices under reef ledges with most of its body hidden, and its vivid facial stripes and yellow fins show fully only to a viewer peering into its shelter. This Trial translates that vivid pattern hidden in a crevice and revealed at close range into a plain box whose bright interior shows only through a peephole.

entries.title: Build a Spined Beak That Holds Six Fish
entries.objective: Make a beak that keeps hold of each catch while it opens to take the next.
entries.animalRule: Each new catch is taken with earlier ones still inside, and nothing may be held in place by your fingers.
entries.userBenefit: A clever little build that shows how a small design detail changes what a tool can do.
entries.mechanismConnection: Atlantic Puffin — Whirring • Diving • Carrying back: backward-pointing spines on the palate and tongue pin each sand eel in place while the bird opens its bill for the next, so a beak already full keeps hunting. This Trial translates that backward-spined bill that keeps hold while it opens again into a card beak with angled teeth that holds six catches.

entries.title: Build a Two-Wall Twig Avenue With Ornaments
entries.objective: Build a small avenue of two parallel twig walls on a tray and arrange five collected ornaments at its entrance.
entries.animalRule: Build the avenue first, then curate five ornaments at its entrance.
entries.userBenefit: A small, strangely pleasing sculpture made from found bits.
entries.mechanismConnection: Fire-maned Bowerbird — Rhythmic • Curating • Persuasive: Male Sericulus bakeri build an avenue bower of two parallel stick walls and keep collecting and arranging objects around it, then display there to persuade visiting females. This Trial translates that avenue of stick walls with a curated court into one twig avenue with five ornaments at its entrance.

entries.title: Build for the Thing Nobody Takes
entries.objective: A woodlouse is a crustacean in a segmented calcareous shell that rolls or clamps down when touched, and the overwhelming majority of spiders leave them alone because there is nowhere to bite. The Woodlouse Hunter is built for exactly this: chelicerae enormous relative to the body, projecting forward rather than down, opening to an unusually wide angle, with fangs long enough to reach past the plates. An abundant prey nobody else can open. Its principle is Plate-Piercing Fangs. The metaphor? Find what is abundant and untouched, then build the one tool that opens it.
entries.animalRule: The resource must be genuinely abundant and genuinely unused by others, and the tool has to be specific to it rather than general capability.
entries.userBenefit: Abundant things sit untouched because of one awkward barrier, not because they are worthless. Building the single tool that opens them gives you a supply with no competition at all.
entries.mechanismConnection: Dysdera crocata has greatly enlarged forward-projecting chelicerae that open to a wide gape with fangs long enough to penetrate or straddle the calcareous plates of woodlice, a prey most spiders cannot handle.

entries.title: Build From What Weighs Nothing
entries.objective: A yellowjacket colony starts with one queen who survived winter and ends the year dead, and everything it builds is sized to exactly that. The nest is paper: workers rasp fibre from weathered timber, chew it with saliva and lay it in sheets, so the supply is effectively unlimited, costs only flying time and weighs almost nothing. The material choice is what makes a whole season's construction affordable. Its principle is Architectural Ingenuity. The metaphor? Pick the material that costs you nothing to get.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be bought or ordered, and the material used has to be genuinely abundant and free to you. The first version must actually work rather than being a sketch.
entries.userBenefit: Waiting on a purchase is usually waiting on a decision you have not made. Building the first working version from free material tells you within an hour whether the idea is worth spending anything on.
entries.mechanismConnection: Vespula germanica workers rasp weathered wood fibre and mix it with saliva to lay down paper sheets, building horizontal combs inside a multi-layered envelope from a material that is effectively unlimited and costs only foraging time.

entries.title: Build It Before Anything Is Wrong
entries.objective: Pan paniscus lives south of the Congo River, and female alliance is what makes it what it is. Unrelated females form strong bonds and act together, and because a coalition of females outweighs any single male, no male can dominate the group by force. That runs through everything: tension at a fruiting tree is resolved by grooming and contact rather than escalating, infanticide is effectively absent, and lethal aggression between groups has never been documented in the wild. Its principle is Affiliation. The metaphor? Build the alliance before the conflict.
entries.animalRule: The thing done is concrete work rather than words, nothing is asked in return, and the commitment is stated plainly to them.
entries.userBenefit: Alliances built during a crisis are weak and everyone can tell. One real favour done for someone when nothing is wrong is what you will actually be able to draw on later.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pan paniscus females form coalitions with unrelated females that collectively outweigh any individual male, so dominance by force does not arise in their groups.

entries.title: Build It Knowing It Ends
entries.objective: A yellowjacket nest is an annual construction that ends in total loss: the colony dies entirely each autumn and the structure is abandoned, never reused. It is built at full effort anyway, because the point was never permanence. The next queen starts from nothing somewhere else. Its principle is Paper-Nest Roster. The metaphor? Knowing it is temporary is not a reason to build it badly. Build it properly and let it end.
entries.animalRule: The thing must be genuinely temporary with a known end, and it has to be brought to a proper finished standard rather than left adequate.
entries.userBenefit: Doing temporary things badly because they will not last means most of your work is bad, since most things are temporary. Building it properly costs a little more and the whole season runs better.
entries.mechanismConnection: Vespula nests are annual: the colony dies entirely in autumn and the paper structure is abandoned rather than reused, yet is constructed to full architectural standard during the single season of use.

entries.title: Build One Branching Basket That Catches Confetti
entries.objective: Make a many-forked pipe-cleaner basket and use it to catch drifting paper confetti in a fan's airflow.
entries.animalRule: The basket stays curled shut until the fan is running and opens only into the flow: food comes to the net, the net never chases it.
entries.userBenefit: A satisfying build that makes branching structure and flow easy to see.
entries.mechanismConnection: Northern Basket Star — Unfurled • Rhythmic • Filter-feeding: Gorgonocephalus eucnemis unfurls arms that branch again and again into a fine three-dimensional basket at night when currents run, intercepting plankton carried to it and curling each tendril around what it catches. This Trial translates that unfurling a repeatedly branching arm net only once the current is running into a forked basket that opens only once the fan runs and catches drifting confetti.

entries.title: Build One Cardboard Den With a Single Doorway
entries.objective: Enclose one fragile work in progress in a cardboard den whose only access is one narrow doorway.
entries.animalRule: There must be exactly one entrance, narrow enough to guard, and the fragile work must sit fully inside.
entries.userBenefit: An unfinished project that pets, children and elbows can no longer wreck.
entries.mechanismConnection: Threadfin Acara — Focused • Defended • Gateway-led: Acarichthys heckelii digs a nest chamber into soft river bottom and leaves only a small entrance, so every approach to its eggs and fry has to pass one narrow point that the parents can patrol and defend. This Trial translates that excavated chamber with one guarded entrance into a cardboard den with a single hand-sized doorway over your fragile work.

entries.title: Build One Chain From Eighteen Identical Links
entries.objective: Build One Chain From Eighteen Identical Links.
entries.animalRule: Use exactly eighteen same-sized links; every link must connect into the same chain.
entries.userBenefit: You turn wetland build into one concrete experience with a visible finish.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pere David's Deer — Recovered • Bottlenecked • Identical: Extinct in the wild and reduced to a single European herd, the entire world population descends from about eighteen animals, so every individual alive is closely related to every other. This Trial translates that mechanism into eighteen identical paper links into one chain.

entries.title: Build One Complete Microbase
entries.objective: Choose one small desk, bag, or activity station and arrange everything needed for one recurring task inside that single bounded area.
entries.animalRule: The task must be completable from the microbase without fetching an essential item from another location.
entries.userBenefit: One recurring activity stops needing a setup phase, because everything is already together.
entries.mechanismConnection: Mottled Duck's relevant mechanism is: Completes its entire annual cycle within a single marsh system rather than migrating, so everything it needs must be present in one place and any change there reaches the whole population at once

entries.title: Build One Curved Safe Entrance
entries.objective: Make a small cardboard or paper enclosure whose inner chamber cannot be reached by a straight line from the entrance.
entries.animalRule: The entrance path must turn at least once before reaching the chamber; no direct line of sight may connect opening to chamber.
entries.userBenefit: You learn why a bend in the entrance protects a chamber better than a longer straight one.
entries.mechanismConnection: Rufous Hornero uses this mode by builds a closed clay dome with an internal partition forming a curved corridor, so the chamber cannot be reached in a straight line and the structure hardens into a shell no predator can open

entries.title: Build One Domed Nest Inside a Sideways Flowerpot
entries.objective: Turn an empty flowerpot on its side into a nook and build a bulky domed nest inside it with a small side entrance and a soft lining.
entries.animalRule: The nest is built into a human-made nook, domed over, entered from the side only, and softly lined inside.
entries.userBenefit: A cosy, tactile build that shows how much shelter fits in an ordinary household nook.
entries.mechanismConnection: Carolina Wren — Rhythmic • Guarded • Site-led: Thryothorus ludovicianus often nests in human-made nooks such as flowerpots, boots and mailboxes, filling the cavity with a bulky nest of leaves, bark strips and grass, often domed over with a side entrance and lined with softer material. This Trial translates that bulky, domed, side-entered nest built into a household nook into a lined, domed nest built inside a sideways flowerpot.

entries.title: Build One Mixed Menu
entries.objective: Choose four ordinary items from at least three categories and arrange them into one usable snack, toolkit, or work set.
entries.animalRule: No category may supply more than two items; the finished set has to work without depending on one repeated type.
entries.userBenefit: A real snack from four unrelated things, and no shopping trip.
entries.mechanismConnection: Green Chafer Beetle uses this mode by feeds on the foliage of a very wide range of unrelated plants rather than specialising, so no single host failing affects it and it can build up in any vegetation rather than tracking one species

entries.title: Build One Passive Warning
entries.objective: Make a small tactile or visual warning that alerts someone before they touch a harmless object, without requiring you to operate it.
entries.animalRule: The warning has to function while you do nothing and must sit before the object rather than on the far side of it.
entries.userBenefit: Practises preventative design: making the environment communicate a boundary before contact happens.
entries.mechanismConnection: Eupterote Moth uses this mode by sheds brittle irritant hairs on contact and into the air around it, so anything that touches or approaches the larva is affected without the caterpillar having to do anything at all

entries.title: Build One Pencil Avenue to Frame a Treasure
entries.objective: Build two upright walls of pencils or twigs into an avenue, and arrange five objects so it frames one treasure.
entries.animalRule: The walls must stand upright on their own, and the treasure must be seen through the avenue from its entrance.
entries.userBenefit: A charming small build that trains an eye for composition.
entries.mechanismConnection: Flame Bowerbird — Rhythmic • Site-focused • Display: Sericulus aureus males build an avenue bower of two parallel walls of upright sticks on a cleared court and keep rearranging objects and returning to perform there, so the structure frames them for a visiting female. This Trial translates that stick avenue built and arranged to frame a display into a pencil avenue arranged to frame one treasure.

entries.title: Build One Plate From Only End Bits
entries.objective: Assemble one snack plate entirely from ends and leftovers that would otherwise be thrown away, with no cooking.
entries.animalRule: Scavenge only: every item is an end or leftover already there, and no energy goes into cooking.
entries.userBenefit: A free snack and a fridge with less waste in it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pacific Hagfish — Burrowed • Scavenging • Low-cost: Pacific Hagfish live as slow, low-metabolism scavengers on the seafloor, feeding on carrion and fallen remains with minimal effort and able to go months between meals. This Trial translates that thrifty, low-cost scavenging of what has already fallen into one no-cook plate built from kitchen end bits.

entries.title: Build One Ridiculous Presentation Corner
entries.objective: Transform one small corner you actually use into a deliberately striking display using things you already own.
entries.animalRule: Constructs and repairs a stick avenue daily and paints its walls with a saliva-and-plant mixture. Keep that true for the whole attempt.
entries.userBenefit: One corner you use becomes one you actually enjoy looking at, using only what was already there.
entries.mechanismConnection: Regent Bowerbird expresses Preparation through this mode: Regent Bowerbird — Painted Avenue Bower — Building • Maintaining • Seasonal: Constructs and repairs a stick avenue daily and paints its walls with a saliva-and-plant mixture. The Trial carries that same limiting structure into one concrete human action.

entries.title: Build One Sparse Intercept Frame
entries.objective: Intercept traffic with the lightest frame that still covers the path.
entries.animalRule: Keep the frame light and open-centred; do not build a dense barrier.
entries.userBenefit: You learn to solve a catch problem with minimal structure instead of overbuilding.
entries.mechanismConnection: Long-jawed Orb Weaver — Spinning • Intercepting • Renewing: Most species spin a light orb with an open hub, often inclined or horizontal over water or among vegetation, and take midges, mosquitoes and other small flying insects that blunder in, often renewing the web daily. Long-jawed orb weavers stretch slender bodies along supports and build sparse orb webs across insect flight paths near water. This Trial translates that mechanism into intercept traffic with the lightest frame that still covers the path.

entries.title: Build One Stretch-and-Strength Test
entries.objective: Make a simple strip or bridge from ordinary material and test it once for stretch and once for load.
entries.animalRule: Use the same piece for both tests; it must flex without immediately failing and still support the chosen light load.
entries.userBenefit: Teaches the difference between stiffness and toughness through a tangible object that must combine give with strength.
entries.mechanismConnection: Giant Golden Orb-weaver uses this mode by spins a fibre combining stiff crystalline regions with a flexible matrix, which gives it both strength and stretch and therefore a toughness that absorbs the energy of a large insect striking it at speed

entries.title: Build Outward Without Opening It
entries.objective: A hornet nest's envelope is not one shell but several loose paper layers with air gaps between them, which is why the inside holds a workable temperature through nights the insects could not survive directly. Building outward as the colony grows means the comb inside can be enlarged without the nest ever being opened. Growth without exposure. Its principle is Defensive Architecture. The metaphor? Do not tear the thing open to make it bigger. Add a layer outside.
entries.animalRule: The existing working part must not be opened, moved or reorganised at all, and the extension has to be added entirely from outside it.
entries.userBenefit: Rebuilding something that works means days of it not working. Adding a layer outside gets you the extra capacity today and the thing never stops running.
entries.mechanismConnection: Dolichovespula maculata builds a multi-layered paper envelope with insulating air gaps and expands it outward as the colony grows, allowing internal combs to be enlarged without breaching the nest.

entries.title: Build the Ball Before the Cold
entries.objective: The monito del monte is a mouse-sized marsupial in the cool rainforests of southern Chile, and its winters are cold with little food. By day it sleeps in a round nest it weaves from moss and bamboo leaves, a tight insulated ball built before it is needed. That nest is what makes the cold season survivable for an animal that small. Its principle is Ancestral Night Nest. The metaphor? Build the shelter before you need it.
entries.animalRule: The shelter must be built before the lean stretch arrives, and it has to be left in place rather than used now.
entries.userBenefit: Meeting a hard stretch empty-handed means every small problem inside it becomes a crisis you improvise through. One piece of shelter built in advance absorbs the first hit for you.
