entries.mechanismConnection: Dromiciops gliroides constructs an insulated spherical nest of moss and bamboo leaves and enters torpor in it through the cold southern winter.

entries.title: Build the Cell Before You Hunt
entries.objective: A Mud Dauber does everything in what looks like the wrong order and it works. She collects mud, flies it back and shapes a tubular cell against a sheltered wall, often several side by side. Only then does she hunt. The prey is spiders and the sting paralyses rather than kills, so the provisions stay fresh. The container exists before there is anything to put in it. Its principle is Thread-Thin Waist. The metaphor? Stop gathering with nowhere to put it. Build the container first.
entries.animalRule: The container must be completed while still entirely empty, and only then may the first item go in. Nothing may be gathered beforehand.
entries.userBenefit: Gathering before you have somewhere to put things is why it all ends up in one pile. Building the empty container first takes ten minutes and everything after it lands in the right place automatically.
entries.mechanismConnection: Sceliphron constructs mud cells first and provisions them afterwards with paralysed rather than killed spiders, so each completed cell receives living prey that remains fresh for the developing larva.

entries.title: Build the Fix Before You Launch
entries.objective: A wood owl hunts in darkness where prey is heard long before it is seen. Most of the night is spent perched and still, which costs almost nothing and lets the bird build an accurate fix on a rustle below. The attack is then short and quiet, with fringed flight feathers breaking up the airflow that would otherwise warn the target. Nothing is spent chasing, because a strike is only launched on a fix. Its principle is Discernment. The metaphor? Build the fix cheaply from stillness, and only then commit.
entries.animalRule: The fix must be built from stillness during the attempt, and no commitment may happen before it is accurate.
entries.userBenefit: Committing before you have a fix means repeated attempts that each warn the target. Building the fix from stillness costs nothing and one attempt lands.
entries.mechanismConnection: Strix seloputo localises prey acoustically from a static perch at near-resting cost, launching a silenced attack only once an accurate fix is established.

entries.title: Build the Gap So You Can Close
entries.objective: Most armadillos have armour that covers them; this one has armour that encloses them. Almost everything about its build exists to make the ball possible: the carapace is deliberately loose, with a gap between shell and body, and the animal walks on the tips of its front claws rather than flat-footed, because a tight shell and a normal gait would leave no room to tuck into. The head and tail plates plug the openings exactly. Its principle is Closure. The metaphor? Leave slack on purpose, because without it you cannot close at all.
entries.animalRule: The slack must be left deliberately and named as such, and the closing capability it preserves has to be stated during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Running everything tight means you cannot shut anything down when you need to. Deliberate slack is what gives you that option at almost no cost.
entries.mechanismConnection: Tolypeutes matacus has a deliberately loose carapace and digitigrade forelimb posture that create the internal volume required for complete conglobation, with head and tail plates sealing the aperture.

entries.title: Build the Gland for the Bad Water
entries.objective: A bird's kidney cannot concentrate urine much beyond the salinity of its own blood, so a duck on a salt pan drinking that water takes in more salt than it can excrete and dehydrates surrounded by liquid. The Cape Teal is not limited that way: it has supraorbital salt glands above the eyes that secrete concentrated brine, which runs off the bill. It drinks what would kill others. Its principle is Adaptive Strategy. The metaphor? The resource everyone else cannot use is still a resource. Build the organ for it.
entries.animalRule: The filter must be built or set up during the attempt rather than wished for, and the previously unusable source has to actually be used afterwards.
entries.userBenefit: Writing a source off for one contaminant leaves a large supply unused while you compete for clean ones. One filter built once turns it into something only you can draw on.
entries.mechanismConnection: Anas capensis possesses supraorbital salt glands that actively secrete hypertonic brine excreted via the nares, allowing it to drink hypersaline water that other ducks cannot process.

entries.title: Build the Heat, Then Stay
entries.objective: Every other tortoise digs a hole, drops the eggs in, covers it and walks away. Manouria emys does something no other tortoise does: the female rakes leaf litter backwards into a mound a metre or more across, lays inside it, and then stays. The decomposing litter generates its own heat, and she guards the mound for weeks. She built a system that works and then remained with it. Its principle is Steady Progress Pattern. The metaphor? Setting it up is not the end. Build the thing that self-sustains, then stay with it.
entries.animalRule: The thing must be something you previously set up and left, and you have to remain with it for a stated period during the attempt rather than tending it and leaving immediately.
entries.userBenefit: Setting things up and walking away is why you have a trail of half-alive projects. Going back to one and staying with it briefly is usually all it needed to start running on its own.
entries.mechanismConnection: Manouria emys constructs a mound nest from raked leaf litter whose decomposition generates heat for incubation, and uniquely among tortoises the female remains to guard the mound for weeks after laying.

entries.title: Build the Organs for the Meal
entries.objective: A python's physiology is something it builds and dismantles. Between meals the gut lining thins, the heart and liver lose mass, and metabolism falls so low that a huge animal costs almost nothing to maintain. Then it swallows something enormous and within a day or two the intestine, heart and liver all grow substantially to process it. Nothing is kept running that is not being used. Its principle is Giant Pressure. The metaphor? Stop maintaining capacity you are not using. Build it when the meal arrives.
entries.animalRule: The thing must be genuinely stood down rather than merely flagged, and you must write the specific route to rebuilding it before shutting it off.
entries.userBenefit: Standing capacity you are not using drains money and attention quietly all year. Shutting it down with a written route back costs nothing and you can rebuild in days if the need returns.
entries.mechanismConnection: Python bivittatus downregulates its digestive system between meals, with intestinal mucosa, heart and liver all losing mass and metabolic rate falling sharply, then rapidly upregulates all of them within days of ingesting a large prey item.

entries.title: Build the Place Slowness Needs
entries.objective: A common wombat runs one of the lowest metabolic rates of any mammal its size and holds food in its gut for up to a fortnight, extracting nearly all the water and nutrient from poor dry grass. That slowness is only survivable because of the burrow: a tunnel system that stays cool and humid, removing most of the thermal cost of an Australian summer. Its principle is Shelter. The metaphor? Make the slowness affordable somewhere.
entries.animalRule: Light, noise and temperature all have to be dealt with before the work starts, and the twenty minutes inside must be genuinely slow.
entries.userBenefit: Trying to work slowly in a bright, loud, hot room means you speed up to escape it and lose the quality. A place built for slowness lets you keep it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Vombatus ursinus survives on poor forage with an exceptionally low metabolic rate and fortnight-long gut retention, which depends on the stable cool humidity of its burrow.

entries.title: Build the Structure, Then Do Nothing
entries.objective: The harp sponge has given up the filter feeding its whole phylum does. Anchored by root-like rhizoids on deep Pacific mud, it holds its body out as flat vanes carrying rows of evenly spaced upright branches tipped with swollen balls, and microscopic hooked spicules snag drifting crustaceans as they pass. It does not pump, chase or search. The geometry does the catching. Its principle is Passive Net. The metaphor? Build the geometry and stop working.
entries.animalRule: The structure must catch without any further action from you, and the active effort has to stop once it is built.
entries.userBenefit: Getting something by repeated active effort means you pay for it every time and lose it the week you are busy. One structure catches the same thing while you do nothing at all.
entries.mechanismConnection: Chondrocladia lyra captures small crustaceans passively on hooked spicules arranged along evenly spaced vertical branches, having abandoned filter feeding entirely.

entries.title: Built for Reach, Not Force
entries.objective: A banded linsang weighs under a kilogram and is built almost entirely for reach rather than force. The body is long and narrow, the limbs short, and the tail is as long as the animal itself and carries the balance, which lets it work out along branches too slender to support a marten or a civet. That opens a hunting layer in the thin outer canopy. Its principle is Shadow Lightness. The metaphor? Trade force for reach and the thin outer edge becomes yours.
entries.animalRule: No force may be applied during the attempt, and the reach has to extend beyond where force would be usable.
entries.userBenefit: Pushing harder on the solid part puts you against everyone strong enough to be there. Going further out on the thin edge leaves you uncontested.
entries.mechanismConnection: Prionodon linsang has a very long body and tail with short limbs, trading mass and power for access to terminal branches too slender to bear larger arboreal carnivores.

entries.title: Built for Straight, Not for Turning
entries.objective: The white-throated needletail is a heavy cigar-shaped swift with long powerful wings, built for fast direct flight rather than fluttering manoeuvre. It takes beetles, flying ants, termites and bees high in the air and spends much of the non-breeding year aloft over eastern Australia. It gave up agility for speed in a straight line, and it hunts in a way that only needs the straight line. Its principle is Needleline. The metaphor? Build for the one direction you actually go.
entries.animalRule: No part may be revisited once passed, and the task has to be completed in one continuous pass.
entries.userBenefit: Going back to improve earlier parts is how a one-hour task takes a day and still is not finished. One straight pass gives you something complete that you can then decide whether to improve.
entries.mechanismConnection: Hirundapus caudacutus has a heavy fusiform body and long stiff wings adapted for rapid direct flight rather than manoeuvrability.

entries.title: Built to Climb, Not to Perch
entries.objective: A reedbed is not a small forest. It is a dense stand of vertical stems with almost no horizontal surface, and a bird living in it has to be built for climbing rather than perching. This warbler has long toes and a narrow laterally slim body that slips between stems and grips them directly, so it forages by working up and down the stalks and moves through the stand without ever crossing open space. Its principle is Stealthy Song. The metaphor? Match your equipment to the surfaces that actually exist, not the ones you expect.
entries.animalRule: The actual available surfaces must be established during the attempt, and the approach has to match them rather than convention.
entries.userBenefit: Expecting surfaces that do not exist means your equipment never grips and you blame yourself. Checking what is actually there fixes it immediately.
entries.mechanismConnection: Acrocephalus agricola has elongated toes and a laterally compressed body adapted for gripping vertical reed stems rather than perching on horizontal branches.

entries.title: Bulk From Something Very Thin
entries.objective: The southern right whale feeds by skimming: it swims slowly with its mouth open and lets water pour through long fine baleen, trapping copepods a few millimetres long. The prey is absurdly dilute, so nothing is gained from any single mouthful. Volume moved through the filter is the whole mechanism, and it is what pays for a metre of blubber. Its principle is Southern Slow Return. The metaphor? Move volume through a fine filter.
entries.animalRule: The source must be one whose single units are genuinely too small to matter, and the accumulated total has to be counted.
entries.userBenefit: Dismissing things because each one is too small to matter means you never find out what a concentrated hour of them adds up to. Counting the total once changes what you bother with.
entries.mechanismConnection: Eubalaena australis skim-feeds continuously with its mouth open, filtering millimetre-scale copepods from dilute water through long fine baleen plates.

entries.title: Bulk, Then Hours of Fermenting
entries.objective: A gorilla is built around a diet most animals its size could not live on. Leaves, stems and pith are bulky and low in energy, so it eats for much of the day and ferments the result in a large hindgut over many hours, extracting slowly from material that is abundant and uncontested. Nothing about it is fast, and nothing needs to be. Its principle is Gentle Strength. The metaphor? Rich sources are contested. Take the abundant poor one and give it the time it needs.
entries.animalRule: The source must be abundant and low-value rather than rich, and it has to be processed fully rather than skimmed during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Chasing rich sources puts you against everyone else chasing them. Giving the abundant ignored one real time gets you something nobody else has bothered to extract.
entries.mechanismConnection: Gorilla gorilla gorilla subsists largely on bulky low-energy foliage and pith, feeding for much of the day and fermenting it in an enlarged hindgut over extended retention times.

entries.title: Bunch Up and Go Forward
entries.objective: A banded mongoose pack of ten to thirty spreads across savanna to dig, and when a raptor, snake or jackal appears the usual answer is to run for cover. But some threats are met the other way: the whole group bunches tightly together into a single mass and advances on the predator. A bunched pack is a larger animal than any of them, and that is the only version that works forward. Its principle is Teamwatch. The metaphor? Close up tight before advancing.
entries.animalRule: The group must be physically or visibly gathered before any advance, and the advance has to happen as one.
entries.userBenefit: Advancing on something alone or with your people spread out means it picks off whichever position is weakest, usually yours. Closing the gaps first makes the whole group one thing it has to deal with.
entries.mechanismConnection: Mungos mungo packs form a tightly bunched mass and advance collectively on certain predators rather than scattering for cover.

entries.title: Bunch Up Then Clear The Spot
entries.objective: On one alarm cue, gather tight and move the group to a marked perch zone.
entries.animalRule: Use only people who opted in; keep the run short and on clear ground.
entries.userBenefit: You practice fast coordinated relocation instead of freezing when a cue hits.
entries.mechanismConnection: Domestic Turkey — Alarming • Bunching • Fleeing: A sharp alarm or sudden posture change sends the flock bunching and running, with lighter birds lifting toward perches while bare head skin flushes with arousal. This Trial turns that alarm into a group bunch-and-clear burst.

entries.title: Buried, Eyes Still Up
entries.objective: Eryx jayakari is built to be under the surface rather than on it: a blunt wedge-shaped head for pushing into loose sand, a countersunk lower jaw so grains stay out of the mouth, and eyes on top of the head pointing upward. That arrangement only makes sense for an animal buried with everything but its gaze covered. Its principle is Sand Concealment. The metaphor? Stay hidden with your eyes still up. Watch from under.
entries.animalRule: The hour runs unbroken with zero contributions, and the three observations are written before you speak again.
entries.userBenefit: Constant input makes you miss what is actually happening in a room, including things that affect you directly. An hour of deliberate silence shows you information your own talking was covering up.
entries.mechanismConnection: Eryx jayakari buries in loose sand with a countersunk jaw and dorsally placed upward-facing eyes, so it stays concealed while still watching the surface above it.

entries.title: Burrow Under One Heavy Blanket for Fifteen Minutes
entries.objective: Retreat under a heavy blanket with your limbs tucked in and let fifteen quiet minutes recharge you.
entries.animalRule: Limbs stay drawn in under the cover and no one and nothing is attended to until the fifteen minutes are over.
entries.userBenefit: A proper, guilt-free recharge when the day has been too much.
entries.mechanismConnection: European Pond Terrapin — Sheltered • Withdrawn • Slow-recovering: Emys orbicularis meets harsh conditions by drawing its head and limbs into the shell and settling into soft mud or under vegetation, slowing breathing and movement so it spends as little energy as possible while it waits for stress or cold to pass. This Trial translates that shell-in, buried, slowed-down retreat into fifteen minutes tucked under a heavy blanket.

entries.title: Burst From Flat Into Whistle, Bounds and Dash
entries.objective: Lie flat and hidden until a random signal, then burst up with a whistle, three stiff-legged bounds and a low dash that ends looking back.
entries.animalRule: Stay flat and still until the signal, then whistle, bound and dash in one unbroken sequence with no pause before the final look back.
entries.userBenefit: A thrilling reaction burst that trains you to go from total stillness to full speed.
entries.mechanismConnection: Oribi — Whistling • Stotting • Sprinting: Ourebia ourebi lies pressed flat in the grass until a threat is very close, then switches abruptly to flight with a sharp whistle, a series of stiff-legged stotting bounds and a low, fast run that ends with a stop to look back. This Trial translates that explosive switch from concealment to whistle, stot and sprint into one signalled burst from lying flat.

entries.title: Burst From One Sheet to a Chair Cushion
entries.objective: Lie flat with a light sheet over your head and torso and, on a random cue, burst out and slap a cushion on a chair seat three metres away in under three seconds.
entries.animalRule: You must stay under the sheet until the cue, and the slap must land within three seconds of it.
entries.userBenefit: Three seconds of pure adrenaline in your own living room.
entries.mechanismConnection: Spiny Softshell Turtle — Explosive • Flexible • Escape: Apalone spinifera trades a hard shell for a flat, leathery, flexible body that lets it lie buried in sand and then explode away or strike in an instant, relying on speed rather than armour for protection. This Trial translates that burst from concealment into flinging off a sheet and reaching a chair cushion in under three seconds.

entries.title: Burst, Then Get Out of the Current
entries.objective: The chinook's upstream run is not a steady swim. The fish pushes through fast water and rapids in hard bursts, mostly in daylight, then pulls out of the current entirely and rests in slack water before the next push. Trying to hold against the flow between bursts would burn the reserves the whole journey depends on. Resting out of the current is part of the mechanism. Its principle is King Run Force. The metaphor? Burst hard, then leave the current.
entries.animalRule: The rest must happen outside the working environment rather than beside it, and there must be two separate bursts.
entries.userBenefit: Staying in the current between efforts burns you down without producing anything, which is why long days feel heavy and deliver little. Leaving the environment entirely between bursts is what makes the second one possible.
entries.mechanismConnection: Oncorhynchus tshawytscha ascends rapids in anaerobic burst swimming interspersed with recovery in slack water, since holding against the current would exhaust its finite reserves.

entries.title: Bury the Scent as Well
entries.objective: A steenbok's defence has two halves and the first is unusual. Like many small antelope it lies flat in cover and holds still, which defeats anything hunting by sight. What it adds is removing scent: it digs a small hole with its hooves, deposits dung and urine into it and covers it over, so the ground it has been using carries far less sign that anything lives there. Against a predator working by nose, that is the part that matters. Its principle is Vanish. The metaphor? Hiding is not enough if you leave a trail.
entries.animalRule: The traces must be actively removed after the activity during the attempt, and discretion during it alone is not sufficient.
entries.userBenefit: Being discreet while doing something and leaving your traces behind means it is found anyway, later and worse. Removing them takes you minutes.
entries.mechanismConnection: Raphicerus campestris buries its dung and urine in excavated and covered scrapes, reducing olfactory cues at its home range in addition to relying on immobility and crypsis.

entries.title: Bury Them Before the Heat Does
entries.objective: An Egyptian plover nests on bare sandbar in full sun, and when it leaves or danger appears it buries the eggs in warm sand, fast. The window is narrow in both directions: too long uncovered and they cook or are taken, and the burying has to be complete rather than partial. Everything about the site is exposed, so the response has to be quick. Its principle is Clean Partnership. The metaphor? When you have to leave something exposed, cover it completely and quickly rather than partially.
entries.animalRule: The covering must be complete rather than partial during the attempt, and it has to be finished before you leave rather than returned to.
entries.userBenefit: Half-covering something before you leave is worse than nothing, because you stop worrying about it. One complete quick cover means you can actually go.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pluvianus aegyptius buries its eggs in warm sand when leaving the nest or when disturbed, providing both thermal buffering and concealment on fully exposed sandbars.

entries.title: Bury Yourself and Let It Come Over
entries.objective: The adult turbot is a broad diamond-shaped ambush predator that buries itself in sediment and matches the bottom closely, then takes fish that pass above it. It does not chase, it does not patrol, and its flat shape makes it almost invisible from directly overhead. Being in the right place, covered, is the entire hunting method. Its principle is Hidden Broadness. The metaphor? Position yourself and stop searching.
entries.animalRule: No active chasing may happen for the day, and the position chosen must be a place the thing genuinely passes.
entries.userBenefit: Chasing something tells everyone exactly what you want and raises the price of it. Putting yourself where it already passes gets you the same thing without the pursuit costing you anything.
entries.mechanismConnection: Scophthalmus maximus is an ambush predator that buries in sediment and crypsis-matches the substrate, taking fish that swim overhead.

entries.title: Button a Shirt With Chilled Then Warmed Hands
entries.objective: Time yourself fastening five buttons with cold hands and again with warmed hands to see how temperature limits speed.
entries.animalRule: Same shirt, same five buttons: only your hand temperature changes between runs.
entries.userBenefit: A quick, memorable way to feel why warming up before work matters.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pond Slider — Foraging • Commuting • Composed: Trachemys scripta is ectothermic, so its swimming and foraging speed depends on body temperature and it returns to bask between feeding bouts to restore the warmth that powers its muscles. This Trial translates that temperature-limited activity restored by warming into two timed buttoning runs with chilled then warmed hands.

entries.title: Buy the Height Once
entries.objective: A sea eagle's prey sits at the surface of open water, invisible from the shoreline and obvious from above, so height is the sensing apparatus and the bird buys it once. Broad wings hold it on coastal updrafts with very little work, and the same traditional perches on headlands and dead trees are used for years because of the water they overlook. Nearly the whole day goes into holding that vantage. Its principle is Coastal Vantage. The metaphor? Stop paying for visibility over and over. Buy the high seat once and keep it.
entries.animalRule: The vantage must be permanent and reused rather than rebuilt each time, and the manual checking has to stop once it exists.
entries.userBenefit: Checking several places to work out the state costs you the same ten minutes every single day. One permanent vantage built once removes that for good.
entries.mechanismConnection: Haliaeetus leucogaster uses low-cost soaring on coastal updrafts and returns to the same traditional headland and dead-tree perches across years, maintaining elevated vantage over water where surface prey is visible.

entries.title: Buy the Speed With Height
entries.objective: A peregrine's famous speed is not produced by muscle, it is bought with altitude. Most of a hunt is spent climbing and holding position far above the prey, and only then does the bird fold its wings and let gravity do what no flapping animal could. The whole descent is paid for in advance, slowly, by going up. Its principle is Gravity. The metaphor? Stop trying to generate the force. Spend the time getting into the position that supplies it.
entries.animalRule: No attempt at the move may be made during the attempt, and the time has to go into a position that will supply the force later.
entries.userBenefit: Forcing a move from a weak position costs you everything and usually fails anyway. Time spent getting above it means the same move takes almost nothing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Falco peregrinus gains potential energy by climbing to altitude and converts it in a folded-wing stoop, achieving velocities unattainable by muscular flapping flight.

entries.title: Buzz One Trill a Blindfolded Friend Calls Insect
entries.objective: Voice a rising buzzing trill convincing enough that a blindfolded friend picks it as the insect in a blind test.
entries.animalRule: The friend stays blindfolded throughout and hears both sounds from the same spot, at the same distance and height.
entries.userBenefit: A silly, surprisingly tricky vocal challenge that is fun for everyone listening.
entries.mechanismConnection: Fire-tufted Barbet — A call consisting of a rising buzzing trill that closely resembles the sound of a cicada rather than of a bird • That call delivered from high in the canopy where the bird itself is invisible among leaves • Listeners including rivals, mates and observers frequently mistaking it for an insect, so the bird is present and unremarked: Psilopogon pyrolophus calls with a rising buzzing trill that sounds far more cicada than bird, delivered unseen from high canopy, so listeners repeatedly take a loud territorial signal for part of the insect background. This Trial translates that insect-like trill that passes as part of the background into a voiced trill tested blind against a real insect recording.

entries.title: Cache and Recover Five Snacks Along One Route
entries.objective: Hide five wrapped snacks along a route through your home, wait ten minutes, then collect all five in one run.
entries.animalRule: One pass along the route only: no backtracking and no checking spots twice.
entries.userBenefit: A quick memory game that shows how well you already know your own home.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cliff Chipmunk — Route • Cache • Reuse: Neotamias dorsalis scatter-hoards seeds in many small caches along the routes it regularly travels and later relies on spatial memory to recover them, so the food it stored is waiting where it already goes. This Trial translates that route-linked caching and recovery into five snacks hidden along one route and collected in a single pass.

entries.title: Cache Five Small Tools in Five Hidden Spots
entries.objective: Hide five small tools in five different spots in one room, rest, then recover all five from memory in one pass.
entries.animalRule: Scatter, don't pile: every tool gets its own hiding place, and recovery is from memory with no searching or opening wrong drawers.
entries.userBenefit: A calm memory workout that leaves five handy tools gathered and ready.
entries.mechanismConnection: Carrion Crow — Caching • Remembering • Reusing: Corvus corone spends quiet stretches hiding surplus food in separate chosen spots and later relocates each cache from memory. This Trial translates that scatter-caching and remembered recovery into five small tools hidden in five places and retrieved in one straight pass.

entries.title: Cache Five Snacks and Recover Them All
entries.objective: Split a surplus snack into five hidden caches around your home, then recover all five from memory in one run.
entries.animalRule: Every cache is hidden out of sight and no record is kept: recovery within two minutes depends only on remembering where you put each one.
entries.userBenefit: A fun memory test that ends with a snack you have properly earned.
entries.mechanismConnection: Arctic Fox — Rhythmic • Opportunistic • Foraging: Arctic Foxes cache surplus food such as lemmings and seabird eggs in many small scattered stores while it is plentiful, and return to them when the season turns lean. This Trial translates that scatter-caching of surplus and later recovery into five hidden snack caches recovered from memory in one run.

entries.title: Call From Inside the Hole
entries.objective: An Amazon milk frog breeds in water-filled tree holes, a resource both safe and closed: no fish, few predators, but no inflow, so whatever it holds is all there will be. The whole system is about finding one and holding it, and the male calls from inside the cavity, which acts as a resonator and carries a deep note far through the canopy. Its principle is Canopy Vigilance. The metaphor? Broadcast from inside the thing you are holding.
entries.animalRule: The broadcast must originate from within the held thing during the attempt, and the position may not be left to do it.
entries.userBenefit: Leaving a position to advertise it means someone takes it while you are gone. Broadcasting from inside means you hold it and advertise it at once.
entries.mechanismConnection: Trachycephalus resinifictrix males call from within water-filled tree cavities, the cavity acting as an acoustic resonator that projects the call while the male retains occupancy.

entries.title: Call From the Exposed Perch
entries.objective: The male King of Saxony spends much of the day calling from exposed high perches in New Guinea's montane forest, where he can be seen and heard across the valley. Females choose among displaying males and raise the young entirely alone, so being found is the whole of his contribution. Hiding would cost him everything he has to gain. Its principle is Banner-Wire Display. The metaphor? Be findable from a long way off.
entries.animalRule: The statement must be public rather than sent to individuals, and it has to be left up.
entries.userBenefit: Telling individuals what you can do means you reach only the people you already thought of, and you repeat yourself forever. One public statement left up works while you are asleep.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pteridophora alberti males advertise from exposed high canopy perches for much of the day, since female choice and sole female care make detectability their only contribution.

entries.title: Call It for Someone
entries.objective: Junglefowl give one alarm call for a hawk overhead and a different one for a predator on the ground, and listeners look up or run for cover accordingly. What makes it more than reflex is the audience: a male with a hen nearby calls readily, and the same male alone or with only a rival barely calls at all. The call is aimed, not emitted. Its principle is Alertness. The metaphor? Noticing is not the job. Tell the person it is for.
entries.animalRule: It must go to a specific named person rather than a group broadcast, and the message has to say what kind of problem it is, not only that something is wrong.
entries.userBenefit: Noticing something and saying nothing leaves the risk exactly where it was. Telling the one person it affects, with enough detail to act, is the step that converts your attention into something useful.
entries.mechanismConnection: Gallus gallus produces functionally distinct aerial and ground alarm calls that elicit different escape responses, and calling rate depends strongly on audience, rising when a hen is present and falling when the male is alone or with only a rival male.

entries.title: Call Softly From Under Cover
entries.objective: The Sunda Scops Owl hunts at night from low perches, relying heavily on hearing, and it calls with a soft repeated note from inside canopy cover rather than from an exposed perch. A loud call from the open would reach more listeners and also reach the larger owls that would take it. Quiet, from cover, reaching exactly the intended radius. Its principle is Nighttime Whisper. The metaphor? Reaching everyone is not the goal. Reach exactly who you meant and no further.
entries.animalRule: The distribution must be the narrowest that reaches everyone who needs it, and you have to actively remove anyone who does not.
entries.userBenefit: Wide distribution feels safer and means everything you send is skimmed by people it was not for. Narrow distribution gets a real response and nothing comes back to bite you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Otus lempiji calls with a soft, repeated, low-amplitude note from within canopy cover, limiting broadcast range to conspecifics while avoiding detection by larger owl predators.

entries.title: Calls Hold the Family Together
entries.objective: Whooper swans form long-term pairs and cygnets travel with their parents through the first autumn and winter, so the family is the unit that feeds, migrates and learns the route. Calling is what keeps that unit together in flocks, in poor visibility and in flight, and paired birds greet each other vocally. The voice is maintenance, not display. Its principle is Trumpet Fidelity. The metaphor? Use regular contact to hold a group together through the stretches where you cannot see each other.
entries.animalRule: The contact must continue through the whole stretch during the attempt, and it may not wait for something to report.
entries.userBenefit: Going quiet through the stretch where nobody can see each other is when your group comes apart. Regular contact through it costs seconds and holds everyone.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cygnus cygnus families maintain cohesion through continual vocal contact in flocks, in flight and in low visibility, with paired birds performing greeting calls.

entries.title: Camouflage One Shoebox in Two Different Spots
entries.objective: Disguise a shoebox with material from one spot until it blends in, then move it and redress it for a second spot.
entries.animalRule: Every piece of disguise must come from the spot where the box is sitting, and the old disguise must come off before the new one goes on.
entries.userBenefit: A playful design challenge that trains you to read a space before you fit into it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Decorator Crab — Rhythmic • Context-tuned • Masking: Camposcia retusa snips pieces of sponge, algae and other reef material and fixes them onto hooked setae that cover its shell, and it keeps adding and replacing pieces so the living coat matches the patch where it is sitting. This Trial translates that living disguise rebuilt from whatever surrounds the crab into one box disguised twice with materials from each spot in turn.

entries.title: Canids Do Not Climb
entries.objective: Canids do not climb. The gray fox does, because its forearms rotate further than any other dog's and its claws are hooked and only partly retractile, so it grips a trunk, works up by hugging and pushing with the hind feet, and moves along branches. The consequence is that a pursuing coyote hits a wall: the fox goes vertical and the chase is over. One departure from the family pattern opened a whole dimension. Its principle is Rule-Breaking. The metaphor? One thing your group does not do, done well, ends most contests.
entries.animalRule: The thing must be one your category is assumed not to do, and it has to actually resolve the situation during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Playing a contest the way your category plays it means losing to whoever is better at that. One unexpected move ends it without you being better at anything.
entries.mechanismConnection: Urocyon cinereoargenteus has exceptional forearm rotation and hooked semi-retractile claws permitting true arboreal climbing, unique among canids, which terminates terrestrial pursuit.

entries.title: Capillary, Not Injection
entries.objective: Heloderma horridum delivers venom in a way almost no other reptile does. It has no hollow fangs; grooved teeth in the lower jaw sit beside glands, and the animal bites and then chews, working its jaws so venom runs down the grooves into the wound by capillary action rather than being injected. That is slow, which is what makes it right for an animal not trying to bring down large prey but to defend itself and subdue eggs and nestlings. Its principle is Beaded Slow Venom. The metaphor? Slow and permanent beats fast and shallow.
entries.animalRule: The change has to be physical or irreversible rather than a reminder, and it must hold without any daily effort from you.
entries.userBenefit: Changes that rely on you remembering them fail the first bad week, every time, and you lose the ground again. One slow permanent change holds while you are not paying attention.
entries.mechanismConnection: Heloderma horridum has grooved lower-jaw teeth beside venom glands and chews to let venom run into the wound by capillary action rather than injecting it.

entries.title: Capillary, Not Suction
entries.objective: A red-legged honeycreeper works the flowering canopy with a fine downcurved bill and a tongue frayed at the tip into a brush, which draws nectar up by capillary action rather than by sucking. Each flower holds very little, so the bird moves constantly between blossoms and tops up with fruit and insects when flowering is thin. The whole design favours frequent small returns. Its principle is Nectar Specialism. The metaphor? Build for many tiny returns taken passively rather than few large ones taken by force.
entries.animalRule: The collection must be passive and repeated rather than a single effort, and it has to be actually running during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: One big collection effort is exhausting and gives you a number you cannot repeat. Something small and passive running constantly adds up past it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cyanerpes cyaneus has a fine decurved bill and brush-tipped tongue that draws nectar by capillarity rather than suction, suited to many low-volume flowers visited in rapid succession.

entries.title: Carol One Layered Chorus With Two People
entries.objective: Sing a short layered chorus with at least two other people, each voice entering at a different time.
entries.animalRule: Each voice must enter at a different moment, and all voices must be singing together for the closing line.
entries.userBenefit: A daft, joyful few minutes that bonds a household quickly.
entries.mechanismConnection: Australian Magpie — Vocal • Patrol • Networked: Gymnorhina tibicen groups carol together, layering complex warbled phrases from several birds into one chorus that announces and holds their shared territory. This Trial translates that layered group carolling into a three-voice chorus where each singer enters in turn.

entries.title: Carried All Year, Used for Weeks
entries.objective: For most of the year fallow deer graze in quiet separate herds, palmate antlers carried but entirely unused. In autumn the system inverts: bucks hold small trampled patches of ground, groan almost continuously for weeks, fight when challenged, and eat so little that they lose a large share of their body weight. Females move between stands and choose. Its principle is Elegance. The metaphor? Carry it quietly for months, then spend it completely in the window that counts.
entries.animalRule: The deciding window must be identified explicitly, and the effort put in has to be disproportionate rather than evenly spread during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Spreading effort evenly across a year where a few weeks decide everything means you are tired and unremarkable in both. Loading the window is how the whole year pays.
entries.mechanismConnection: Dama dama carries palmate antlers year-round but concentrates all reproductive effort into a weeks-long rut of continuous groaning and stand defence, during which bucks lose a substantial proportion of body mass.

entries.title: Carry a Poison You Did Not Make
entries.objective: Three of the four living horseshoe crabs are simply armoured animals that lay eggs in sand. This one is different, and the difference is chemical: individuals from parts of Southeast Asia carry tetrodotoxin and saxitoxin in their eggs, almost certainly acquired from their diet and the bacteria in it rather than synthesised. The protection was accumulated, not built. Its principle is Tidal Persistence. The metaphor? Some of your protection comes from where you have been. Know which parts you did not make.
entries.animalRule: Each protection must be marked as built or acquired, and one acquired one has to get a concrete securing action during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Protections you did not build can disappear without you doing anything wrong, and you will not see it coming. Marking which are which takes ten minutes and tells you exactly what to shore up.
entries.mechanismConnection: Carcinoscorpius rotundicauda from some Southeast Asian populations carries tetrodotoxin and saxitoxin in its eggs, apparently of dietary and bacterial origin rather than endogenous synthesis.

entries.title: Carry a Two-Kilo Load Along a Rope Branch
entries.objective: Walk the length of a rope branch laid on the floor while hugging a two-kilo load, plucking three paper leaves on the way without stepping off.
entries.animalRule: Plant each foot fully on the rope before lifting the other, keep the load hugged to your chest the whole way, and never step off the rope.
entries.userBenefit: A calm, loaded balance drill that steadies the ankles and the core.
entries.mechanismConnection: Northern Luzon Giant Cloud Rat — Climbing • Leaf-eating • Nocturnal: At around two kilograms Phloeomys pallidus is one of the heaviest rats in the world, and it climbs slowly and deliberately through the trees at night to browse young leaves and buds. This Trial translates that slow, deliberate climbing of a heavy body to reach leaves into carrying a two-kilo load along a rope branch and plucking three paper leaves without stepping off.

entries.title: Carry Both Cups While Walking Finger-Linked
entries.objective: Walk one slow lap with a partner as a linked pair, with one of you doing all the carrying.
entries.animalRule: The carrier holds both cups the whole way and hands one over only at the finish, for drinking; fingers stay linked until then.
entries.userBenefit: A slow, silly, careful minute together that nobody spills if you get the pace right.
entries.mechanismConnection: Red-bellied Titi — Duetting at dawn • Sitting tails twined • The father carrying: In titi monkeys the male carries the infant almost all the time and passes it to the mother only to nurse, and the young are more distressed by separation from the father, so the pair moves and works as one unit. This Trial translates that father-carrying with handover only for feeding into one linked lap where the carrier holds everything until the drink.

entries.title: Carry Coloured Pollen Between Three Paper Flowers
entries.objective: Deliver bright pollen from one deep paper flower to two others on a snout.
entries.animalRule: The snout must reach the nectar at the bottom of every flower, and you may not dust the other flowers directly.
entries.userBenefit: A tidy little experiment that makes an unusual island partnership easy to see.
entries.mechanismConnection: Giant Day Gecko — Carrying Pollen on Its Face: It pushes its whole face into flowers to lick nectar, picking up pollen on its snout and throat and carrying it to the next flower. This Trial translates that face-borne pollen transfer into carrying bright pollen on a snout pushed deep into successive paper flowers.

entries.title: Carry It Fifty Kilometres
entries.objective: A Large Flying Fox has a wingspan approaching a metre and a half and commutes from its roost to feeding trees up to fifty kilometres away, returning before dawn. What matters is what travels with it: seeds passing through the gut over hours, and pollen from durian and other night-flowering trees carried on its fur. The distance is the service. Its principle is Strategic Foraging. The metaphor? What you carry between two places is worth more than what you do in either.
entries.animalRule: The two settings must be genuinely unrelated, and the thing has to be actually applied in the second rather than merely mentioned. Its origin must be named.
entries.userBenefit: You keep what you know in separate boxes, so the same problem gets solved badly twice. Carrying a method across is free and it is usually the fastest improvement available to you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pteropus vampyrus commutes up to fifty kilometres between colonial roosts and feeding trees nightly, dispersing seeds through hours-long gut passage and carrying pollen from night-flowering species including durian and petai on its fur.

entries.title: Carry It Home, Do Not Eat It There
entries.objective: Ord's kangaroo rat has the widest range of any kangaroo rat, from southern Canada to central Mexico, and the thing that makes that range work is carrying food home. It gathers grass and herb seeds into fur-lined cheek pouches and takes them back to burrow stores and shallow caches nearby rather than eating where it finds them. Transport, not consumption. Its principle is Pouch-Filled Return. The metaphor? Carry it back to the store instead of using it where you found it, and your range stops limiting you.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be used where it was found during the attempt, and everything gathered has to reach the store before you stop.
entries.userBenefit: Using things where you find them means nothing accumulates and every lean week starts you at zero. Carrying it all back is what turns ordinary days into a reserve.
entries.mechanismConnection: Dipodomys ordii transports seeds in fur-lined external cheek pouches to burrow larders and shallow satellite caches rather than consuming them in situ.

entries.title: Carry It in the Pouch
entries.objective: The little auk is starling-sized and lives on plankton, diving for fat-rich Calanus copepods and other small crustaceans. Because each item is tiny, it stores the catch in a pouch under its tongue and brings the whole accumulated load back at once, nesting deep among boulder scree where the rocks keep the chick safe. Many small things, carried in one go. Its principle is Smallsea. The metaphor? Accumulate the small things, deliver once.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be sent during the day, and the entire accumulated batch has to be delivered in one go.
entries.userBenefit: Passing small things on the moment you have them interrupts the other person constantly and makes each item feel urgent. One accumulated delivery costs them a single interruption for all of it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Alle alle accumulates copepods in a sublingual pouch and delivers the whole load in a single visit to a chick nested deep in boulder scree.

entries.title: Carry It Instead of Leaving It
entries.objective: An egg laid in a nest develops at whatever temperature the nest happens to be. A reptile that retains its embryos develops them at whatever temperature the mother chooses, and a basking lizard chooses well. The Common Sun Skink goes further: the embryos are not just retained but supplied through a placental connection, with substantial nutrient transfer. Keeping it with you means controlling its conditions. Its principle is Sunbathing Strategy. The metaphor? Leave it somewhere and it gets whatever that place gives. Carry it and choose.
entries.animalRule: You must take back something genuinely out of your control and move it yourself, telling whoever held it rather than quietly retrieving it.
entries.userBenefit: Things you hand off too early develop at whatever pace that queue runs, which is rarely yours. Taking one back and moving it yourself costs an hour and unsticks what had been waiting weeks.
entries.mechanismConnection: Eutropis multifasciata is viviparous with placental nutrient transfer, retaining embryos internally so development occurs at the temperature the basking female selects rather than at ambient nest temperature.

entries.title: Carry It Where Your Hands Are Free
entries.objective: A parrot's bill is a climbing tool, a third limb used constantly to move through branches, and filling it with a load of leaf strips makes that impossible. The Blue-crowned Hanging Parrot does not fill it. The female cuts strips and tucks them in among the feathers of her rump and flanks, working them in until they hold, and flies to the nest with her bill free. Its principle is Upside-down Rest. The metaphor? Carrying it in your hands stops you using them. Find somewhere else to put the load.
entries.animalRule: The load must move off your hands or out of your head into something that holds it for you, and you have to use the freed capacity during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Holding things in your hands or your head uses the exact capacity you need for the work. Moving the load somewhere that holds it gives that capacity straight back.
entries.mechanismConnection: Female Loriculus galgulus tuck cut strips of leaf and bark into the feathers of the rump and flanks to transport nest material, leaving the bill free for climbing rather than carrying.

entries.title: Carry It With You
entries.objective: A spider that lays eggs and walks away has put everything in one place, and whatever finds that place takes all of it. A Carolina Wolf Spider attaches the egg sac to her spinnerets and drags it everywhere, through burrows, across sand, while hunting, abdomen raised to keep it clear, and retrieves it aggressively if it detaches. Carrying it is what keeps it safe. Its principle is Grounded Pursuit. The metaphor? Stop leaving it somewhere safe. Take it with you.
entries.animalRule: The thing must end up physically attached to something you always carry, not just placed inside it, and you show it staying attached while you move around.
entries.userBenefit: Anything kept in a safe place is only there when you are. Attaching it to what you always carry means you stop rediscovering that you need it when you are somewhere else.
entries.mechanismConnection: Hogna carolinensis attaches her egg sac directly to her spinnerets and transports it continuously while burrowing and hunting with the abdomen raised, retrieving it aggressively if detached, and later carries the emerged spiderlings on her abdomen.

entries.title: Carry One Awkward Thing Gracefully
entries.objective: Choose one bulky but manageable object that genuinely needs moving and carry it across the room with deliberately smooth posture.
entries.animalRule: Moves constantly through open woodland, using horns to pull branches within reach of the tongue. Keep that true for the whole attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Combines useful work with posture, composure and control under an awkward load.
entries.mechanismConnection: Giant Eland expresses Gentle Grandeur through this mode: Giant Eland — Horn-Hooked Branch Browse — Nomadic • Browsing • Wary: Moves constantly through open woodland, using horns to pull branches within reach of the tongue. The Trial carries that same limiting structure into one concrete human action.

entries.title: Carry One Bagged Egg Inside Your Top
entries.objective: Carry a raw egg sealed in a zip bag inside your top through five slow laps and two sit-downs without it cracking or slipping out.
entries.animalRule: Your hands stay at your sides from tuck-in to take-out: only your own body and top may hold the egg.
entries.userBenefit: A few slow, careful minutes that sharpen balance and body awareness.
entries.mechanismConnection: Darwin's Frog — Sheltering • Selective • Carried: Rhinoderma darwinii males take the hatching tadpoles into the mouth and keep them inside the enlarged vocal sac, carrying them through ordinary movement on the forest floor until the young emerge as froglets. This Trial translates that fragile brood carried inside the father's own body while he goes about his day into a raw egg carried inside your own top, hands off, through slow laps and sit-downs.

entries.title: Carry One Coin Across Four Supports
entries.objective: Carry One Coin Across Four Supports.
entries.animalRule: The coin may not touch the table between the first and fourth support.
entries.userBenefit: You turn floating balance into one concrete, visible experience instead of an abstract idea.
entries.mechanismConnection: Purple Gallinule — Deliberate • Spread-footed • Climbing: Every step is placed on a chosen leaf by enormously long unwebbed toes that divide the bird's load across a wide patch of surface, and the same toes grip stems and hold food up to the bill. This Trial translates that mid-frequency mechanism into one coin across four supports.

entries.title: Carry One Heavy Bag Ten Steps
entries.objective: Carry one safely manageable heavy bag or loaded backpack for ten deliberate steps, then set it down under control.
entries.animalRule: A legless body works grass and sandy ground where limbs would be an obstacle, and most of its length is a tail with built-in fracture planes that can be thrown off in pieces while the animal that matters goes on. Keep that true for the whole attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Provides a short strength challenge with a concrete finish and controlled effort.
entries.mechanismConnection: Eastern Glass Lizard expresses Category Escape through this mode: Eastern Glass Lizard — Two Thirds Detachable Tail — Slipping • Hunting • Shedding: A legless body works grass and sandy ground where limbs would be an obstacle, and most of its length is a tail with built-in fracture planes that can be thrown off in pieces while the animal that matters goes on. The Trial carries that same limiting structure into one concrete human action.

entries.title: Carry One Loaded Pack an Even Kilometre
entries.objective: Walk one kilometre at a steady, unhurried pace with a comfortably loaded backpack.
entries.animalRule: The load stays on your back for the whole kilometre and the pace stays calm: no stops, no bursts to catch up.
entries.userBenefit: A calm, weighted walk that shows how steadily you can carry a load.
entries.mechanismConnection: Common Eland — Calm • Enduring • Heavy-step: Taurotragus oryx, among the largest antelopes, covers long distances at a steady walk or easy trot, moving its heavy frame economically between browse and water and saving bursts, including standing jumps of over two metres, for the rare moments that need them. This Trial translates that steady, economical travel of a large, heavy body without urgency into one kilometre walked at an even, calm pace carrying a loaded pack.

entries.title: Carry One Packed Lunch Out to Open Grass
entries.objective: Pack a lunch at home, take it out to open public grass away from home to eat, and bring everything back.
entries.animalRule: Packed at home, eaten out on open ground away from home, and every scrap carried back to base.
entries.userBenefit: A lunch break outside instead of at a desk, and a short walk each way.
entries.mechanismConnection: Common Wood Pigeon — Rhythmic • Commuting • Forager: Columba palumbus roosts and rests in the safety of woodland trees but flies out daily to feed in open fields and parks, returning to cover to rest and digest. This Trial translates that shuttle from a safe base out to open feeding ground and back into carrying a packed lunch from home out to open grass and back.

entries.title: Carry One Sheet Between Shoulders Around Three Chairs
entries.objective: Weave a figure-eight around three chairs with a partner while holding a sheet of paper between your shoulders.
entries.animalRule: You move as a pair side by side the whole way: if the paper drops, restart the course.
entries.userBenefit: A giggly coordination game that makes two people move as one.
entries.mechanismConnection: Blue-winged Macaw — Flocks that on close inspection consist of pairs flying side by side rather than a uniform mass • Each pair maintaining position relative to one another rather than to the flock as a whole • The bond persisting across years and outside the breeding season entirely: Primolius maracana flocks are really sets of mated pairs flying wing to wing, each pair keeping position relative to its partner rather than to the flock, and the bond persists across years and seasons. This Trial translates that pairs holding station side by side within a moving flock into a figure-eight walked shoulder to shoulder with a sheet trapped between two partners.

entries.title: Carry One Thing Without Your Hands
entries.objective: Move one small useful object across a room using your body or clothing but not your hands.
entries.animalRule: Uses a gripping tail as a load-bearing fifth limb to work fruit at the ends of branches across a large range. Keep that true for the whole attempt.
entries.userBenefit: You discover how much your body can carry when your hands are not allowed to.
entries.mechanismConnection: Woolly Monkey expresses Soft Strength through this mode: Woolly Monkey — Fifth-Limb Tail Reach — Ranging • Suspended • Frugivorous: Uses a gripping tail as a load-bearing fifth limb to work fruit at the ends of branches across a large range. The Trial carries that same limiting structure into one concrete human action.

entries.title: Carry One Wrapped Bundle for Ten Minutes
entries.objective: Carry One Wrapped Bundle for Ten Minutes.
entries.animalRule: The bundle must stay with you and remain wrapped for the whole interval.
entries.userBenefit: You turn paternal care into one concrete, visible experience instead of an abstract idea.
entries.mechanismConnection: Common Midwife Toad — Loaded • Damp-bound • Slow: A male spends weeks at a time with egg strings wound around his hind legs, feeding quietly in crevices and damp cover while the clutch develops on land, and enters water only to moisten the eggs and release the tadpoles. This Trial translates that low-frequency mechanism into one wrapped bundle for ten minutes.

entries.title: Carry Ten Nest Strips Tucked at Your Back
entries.objective: Build a small nest cup from strips you carried tucked into your waistband at the back, not in your hands.
entries.animalRule: Your hands stay empty on the walk: every strip travels tucked in at the back.
entries.userBenefit: A calm little build that ends with something cosy to look at.
entries.mechanismConnection: Peach-faced Lovebird — Nesting • Pair-bound • Sheltered: Female peach-faced lovebirds carry nesting material, strips of bark or grass, tucked into the feathers of the rump and lower back rather than in the bill, and bring it back to chambers in sociable weaver nests, rock crevices or buildings. This Trial translates that rump-tucked carrying of nest strips into carrying ten strips tucked at the back and weaving them into a nest cup.

entries.title: Carry the Air With You
entries.objective: A backswimmer stays submerged for long periods without surfacing because it carries its own atmosphere: a silvery store of air held along the belly and under the wings, drawn on while it hangs motionless under the film. It did not adapt to breathing water; it brought the air down. Its principle is Upside-Down Oar. The metaphor? Bring the thing you cannot get locally with you, and the hostile place becomes somewhere you can simply stay.
entries.animalRule: The thing must be brought in before entering during the attempt, and no trip out to resupply may occur.
entries.userBenefit: Going back out for the thing a place does not have means you never settle into it and lose the time twice. Bringing it with you lets you simply stay.
entries.mechanismConnection: Notonecta glauca retains a ventral and subalar air store that functions as a physical gill, allowing extended submergence without surfacing.

entries.title: Carry the Big Seed
entries.objective: A large fruit with a large seed has a problem: almost nothing can swallow it. On Sulawesi the Knobbed Hornbill can, and that makes it the principal disperser for a substantial part of the forest. It takes fruits whole, holds the seeds in the gut and then commutes several kilometres, depositing them far from the parent tree. Being one of the few that can handle the big item is the whole role. Its principle is Sealed Trust. The metaphor? The oversized thing nobody else can carry is the one worth carrying.
entries.animalRule: The item must be one genuinely nobody else is taking on, and it has to be moved a stated distance rather than merely claimed or planned.
entries.userBenefit: The oversized item sits untouched for months blocking everything behind it, because everyone takes the small ones. Moving it a real distance makes you the person who unblocked the thing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Rhyticeros cassidix swallows large fruits whole and passes big seeds intact after commuting several kilometres between feeding and roosting sites, making it the principal disperser of large-seeded trees on Sulawesi.

entries.title: Carry the Bundle With the Tail
entries.objective: An eastern bettong does two jobs every night with the same body plan. It digs underground fungi across a range of a kilometre or more, turning over soil at a rate that makes it one of the most important diggers in dry Tasmanian forest, and it maintains several domed grass nests hidden under fallen timber. The nesting material is carried with the tail, curled into a prehensile loop. Its principle is Busy Shelter. The metaphor? Use a part you were not counting on so your hands stay free for the main job.
entries.animalRule: The carrying must use a secondary capacity during the attempt, and the main capacity has to stay free.
entries.userBenefit: Using your main capacity to carry things means it is unavailable for the work. One secondary capacity frees it entirely.
entries.mechanismConnection: Bettongia gaimardi carries nesting material in a prehensile tail loop while using the forelimbs for excavating hypogeal fungi across a home range of over a kilometre.

entries.title: Carry the Defence in the Skin
entries.objective: A mimic octopus lives on open sand and mud where most octopuses would be far too exposed. Instead of a burrow or a reef to retreat into, it carries its defence in its skin and arms: colour cells, texture and posture can be reorganised in seconds, and observers have recorded it flattening into a banded flatfish, trailing arms like a lionfish's spines, and tucking into a hole with two arms out as a sea snake. Its principle is Shape Mimicry. The metaphor? With no refuge available, carry several presentations and switch between them in seconds.
entries.animalRule: At least two presentations must be prepared and actually switched between during the attempt, with no retreat used.
entries.userBenefit: One presentation in a situation with no retreat means being read and cornered. Two or three switched between keeps you workable wherever it goes.
entries.mechanismConnection: Thaumoctopus mimicus reorganises chromatophores, skin texture and arm posture within seconds to impersonate flatfish, lionfish and sea snakes on open substrate lacking refuge.

entries.title: Carry the Seeds Away From the Parent
entries.objective: Through summer and autumn the Japanese marten eats insects and soft fruits, swallowing the seeds of vines such as wild kiwi and akebia, and it later passes them far from the plant they came from. In winter, when fruit is scarce, it switches to small mammals and birds. The flexibility feeds it, and a side effect of the fruit half is that it moves those seeds somewhere the parent plant could never reach. Its principle is Marten Edgecraft. The metaphor? Carry what you took somewhere new.
entries.animalRule: The destination must be genuinely distant from the source, and both have to be named.
entries.userBenefit: Using what you learn only where you learned it means it adds nothing, because that place already has it. Carrying it somewhere distant is where the same thing becomes genuinely valuable.
entries.mechanismConnection: Martes melampus ingests the seeds of vines such as Actinidia and Akebia in summer and autumn and deposits them at distance from the parent plants.

entries.title: Carry the Shell Away
entries.objective: Tinbergen's experiment with Black-headed Gulls is one of the cleanest in behavioural biology. They nest on open ground in dense colonies, the eggs are camouflaged, and a hatched shell has a conspicuous white inner surface. Parents carry it away within minutes. Laid out on dunes, camouflaged eggs beside broken shells were found by crows far more often. The evidence of success is what gives away the hiding place. Its principle is Adaptive Foraging Strategy. The metaphor? Clear the evidence of what you just did. The debris is what gets you found.
entries.animalRule: The clearing must happen as part of finishing rather than being deferred, and every piece of debris produced has to go rather than the obvious ones only.
entries.userBenefit: Debris left behind is what makes the next task start in a mess and what tells everyone what you were doing. Clearing it as the last step costs two minutes and the next start is clean.
entries.mechanismConnection: Chroicocephalus ridibundus removes hatched eggshells from the nest within minutes, and Tinbergen demonstrated experimentally that camouflaged eggs adjacent to broken shells suffer markedly higher predation.

entries.title: Carry the Water to the Nest
entries.objective: On an open sandbar in full sun an Egyptian plover cannot shade its chicks for long, so it soaks its belly feathers in the river and walks back to wet them directly. The water is brought to the nest rather than the chicks taken to water, because moving them across open ground is what gets them taken. Its principle is Clean Partnership. The metaphor? Carry the resource to the thing that cannot move, instead of moving the thing.
entries.animalRule: The thing may not be moved during the attempt, and the resource has to be carried to it in a trip you make.
entries.userBenefit: Moving something fragile to where the resource is exposes it for the whole journey. Making the trip yourself and bringing the resource keeps it where it was safe.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pluvianus aegyptius soaks its ventral feathers in river water and returns to the nest to wet eggs and chicks directly, avoiding any movement of the brood.

entries.title: Carry the Water With You
entries.objective: Every crustacean group but this one is tied to water to breed, because the eggs need it. A woodlouse solved that without going back: overlapping plates on the female's underside meet to form a sealed chamber filled with fluid, the eggs develop in that fluid through the stages that would otherwise need standing water, and out comes a miniature adult. The aquatic phase travels inside a walking animal. Its principle is Moisture Seeking. The metaphor? Stop going back for the conditions. Carry them.
entries.animalRule: The kit must be fully self-contained and physically closable, and you must complete the task somewhere you could not do it before, using only what is inside.
entries.userBenefit: If a task needs a particular place, it only happens when you are there. Making the conditions portable means it happens in the gaps, and the gaps are where most of your time actually is.
entries.mechanismConnection: Terrestrial isopods brood their eggs in a marsupium formed from overlapping ventral plates filled with fluid, where embryos pass through the stages that would otherwise require standing water, emerging as miniature adults, so the aquatic phase is carried inside the mother.

entries.title: Carry Them Across Altitude Bands
entries.objective: A dwarf cassowary is the smallest cassowary and works mountain forest rather than lowland, which changes what its seed dispersal means. Like its relatives it swallows fruit whole and passes large seeds intact in a pile of dung that acts as a fertilised seedbed, but because it moves up and down steep New Guinea slopes those seeds are carried across altitude bands as well as distance, moving plants between climates. Its principle is Hidden Seedwork. The metaphor? Moving something across a boundary matters more than moving it far.
entries.animalRule: The movement must cross a genuine boundary during the attempt, and distance within one band is not sufficient.
entries.userBenefit: Moving something further within its own band changes nothing about who sees it. Crossing one boundary puts your work in front of people who never would have.
entries.mechanismConnection: Casuarius bennetti disperses large intact seeds in nutrient-rich dung while moving across steep montane altitude gradients, transporting plants between climatic bands.

entries.title: Carry Twenty Handfuls to One Sheltered Leaf Pile
entries.objective: Build a leaf pile under shelter by making twenty separate trips, carrying one handful each time.
entries.animalRule: One handful per trip, no bags, rakes or armfuls; the pile grows only by repeated trips.
entries.userBenefit: A brisk garden job with a satisfying heap at the end.
entries.mechanismConnection: American Pika — Haying • Territorial • Industrious: Through the short alpine summer Ochotona princeps makes many trips a day from the talus into nearby meadow, clipping grasses, sedges and flowers and carrying each mouthful back to a haypile under the rocks, calling to defend the store. This Trial translates that many-trip carry of single mouthfuls into a haypile into twenty single-handful trips building one sheltered leaf pile.

entries.title: Carry Twenty Torn Scraps Down One Taped Trail
entries.objective: Tear scrap paper into twenty carry-size pieces and carry them one at a time along a single taped trail to build a layered pile.
entries.animalRule: One piece per trip, always on the taped trail, and every piece must be laid flat to build even layers.
entries.userBenefit: A gently rhythmic job that clears scrap paper and shows how small repeats add up.
entries.mechanismConnection: Leafcutter Ant — Rhythmic • Networked • Layered: Atta cephalotes workers cut leaves into fragments sized for carrying and haul them one by one along cleared, reused trails to the nest, where the pieces are worked into layered fungus gardens. This Trial translates those countless single-load trips on one cleared trail into twenty torn scraps carried one at a time and layered in a box.

entries.title: Carry What Nobody Else Can
entries.objective: The Southern Cassowary is the most important seed disperser in Australian tropical rainforest, and the mechanism is simply gut volume. It swallows fruit whole, including species whose seeds are far too large for any other animal there, passes them through a short tract that strips the flesh without damaging the seed, and leaves them kilometres away in a fertilised pile. Over seventy plant species depend on it. Its principle is Seed Bearing. The metaphor? Your advantage is the load others cannot take. Carry the big one.
entries.animalRule: The task must be one genuinely nobody else can take on, not simply one nobody wants, and it must be moved a visible distance rather than merely claimed.
entries.userBenefit: Everyone picks up the small tasks, so the big awkward one sits for months blocking things behind it. Taking the load only you can carry moves what nobody else could.
entries.mechanismConnection: Casuarius casuarius swallows large fruits whole and passes seeds too big for any other local frugivore through a short digestive tract that removes pulp without damaging them, depositing them kilometres away in nutrient-rich dung.

entries.title: Carry What Nothing Else Can Swallow
entries.objective: The Hawaiian crow was one of the largest native fruit-eating birds on its island, and it probably dispersed the seeds of native plants whose fruit few other birds could swallow. When it disappeared from the wild, those plants lost the only carrier they had. Being the one thing large enough to do a job makes that job yours alone. Its principle is Crow Comeback Mind. The metaphor? Move what only you can move.
entries.animalRule: The thing chosen must genuinely have no other carrier, and the step taken has to be concrete rather than planned.
entries.userBenefit: Spending your day on work others could also do means the one thing only you can move never moves at all. Finding it and taking a step is the part of your effort nobody can replace.
entries.mechanismConnection: Corvus hawaiiensis, among the largest native frugivores on Hawaii Island, dispersed large-seeded native fruits that smaller birds could not swallow.

entries.title: Carry What Others Cannot Survive
entries.objective: The Red Swamp Crayfish is on every continent except Australia and Antarctica, and it is usually described as outcompeting native crayfish. The decisive mechanism is different: it carries crayfish plague, a pathogen it survives and which is lethal to European species. It does not need to win any contest. It only needs to arrive. Its principle is Resourceful Tools Pattern. The metaphor? Tolerance for something that stops others is worth more than beating them at anything.
entries.animalRule: The thing must be available precisely because others will not tolerate the condition, and it has to be taken on during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Competing on ability puts you against everyone good at the same things. Taking the work that sits in a condition others will not tolerate means it is simply yours.
entries.mechanismConnection: Procambarus clarkii is a tolerant carrier of Aphanomyces astaci, the crayfish plague oomycete, which is lethal to European crayfish species, so displacement occurs via disease rather than competition.

entries.title: Carve One Useful Slot From Scrap
entries.objective: Make a small functional cavity in soft disposable material.
entries.animalRule: Use only soft craft material and make the cavity for one specific object.
entries.userBenefit: You turn scrap into a custom holder and give one loose object a permanent home.
entries.mechanismConnection: Willow Tit — Excavates a fresh nest cavity each year in standing dead wood that has rotted to the point where a small bird's bill can remove it, which means the species needs decaying timber of a specific softness rather than simply a hole. The Trial compresses that mechanism into one immediate, proofable human session.

entries.title: Cascade Twenty Cards Face Up in One Wave
entries.objective: Spread twenty cards face down in an overlapping line and turn the whole line face up in one continuous cascade.
entries.animalRule: One lift starts the flush: after the first card, no card may be touched as the wave runs.
entries.userBenefit: A slick little card flourish that feels brilliant when the whole line goes.
entries.mechanismConnection: Snow Bunting — Alert • Flaring • Evasion: A foraging flock of Plectrophenax nivalis bursts into the air together when a predator appears, the sudden simultaneous flash of white wings making it hard for a hunter to single out one bird. This Trial translates that whole flock flushing at once into twenty cards turned face up in one continuous cascade.

entries.title: Catch Five Tossed Tissues From a Seated Start
entries.objective: Sally up from a chair to catch five tossed tissue balls before they land, sitting back down between each, within thirty seconds.
entries.animalRule: Every catch starts and ends seated: a dropped tissue must be tossed again.
entries.userBenefit: A quick, bouncy burst that wakes up your legs and reflexes.
entries.mechanismConnection: Common Poorwill — Brief • Aerial • Foraging: Phalaenoptilus nuttallii waits on the ground at night and launches in short, fast sallies to snap up passing moths and beetles, dropping straight back to its spot to conserve energy. This Trial translates that short sallies from a resting spot to snatch flying insects into five seated-start tissue catches in thirty seconds.

entries.title: Catch One Jug of Warm-Up Tap Water
entries.objective: Save the cold water that runs before a hot tap warms up and put it to use.
entries.animalRule: Not a drop of the warm-up water goes down the drain, and the saved water must be used, not poured away.
entries.userBenefit: Water saved without effort and a jug of plant water ready to use.
entries.mechanismConnection: Mongolian Gerbil — Stored • Sheltered • Timed: Meriones unguiculatus survives in the dry steppes of Mongolia by conserving water: it produces very concentrated urine, gets much of its water from seeds and plants, and sits out the hottest and coldest hours in its burrow. This Trial translates that water-sparing life that wastes almost nothing into one jug of warm-up water caught and reused.

entries.title: Catch One Thing Seated With Both Hands
entries.objective: Take something out of the air without standing up.
entries.animalRule: Both hands must make the catch and your seat may not leave the chair.
entries.userBenefit: A quick burst that is genuinely fun to land and takes under two minutes to set up.
entries.mechanismConnection: Spectral Tarsier — Immobile-Eye Head Swivel — Launched • Seizing • Instant: Fires from the perch on elongated ankle bones and takes the insect in the air with both hands. This Trial converts that high mechanism into five falling objects. This Trial translates that ankle-launched seizure taken in both hands into a two-handed catch made without leaving the seat.

entries.title: Catch Only Balls That Roll Into Your Nook
entries.objective: Sit tucked in one nook while a helper rolls ten soft balls past you, and grab only the ones that come within reach.
entries.animalRule: You may never lean or reach past the tape line: let the chances come to you.
entries.userBenefit: A calm patience game that is surprisingly hard to resist.
