entries.mechanismConnection: Acanthurus xanthopterus grazes damselfish algal territories by entering in large shoals, overwhelming the resident's capacity to repel individuals one at a time.

entries.title: Cross-Flow, So It Never Clogs
entries.objective: A whale shark is the largest fish alive and feeds on some of the smallest food in the sea, which only works because of how the filtering is arranged. Water entering the mouth passes across twenty filter pads rather than into them, so plankton is deflected toward the throat while the flow continues out through the gills, a cross-flow arrangement that keeps the mesh from clogging and lets the animal feed continuously. Its principle is Gentle Scale. The metaphor? Run the flow across your filter rather than into it, and it never blocks.
entries.animalRule: The flow must pass across rather than into the filter during the attempt, and no clearing step may be required.
entries.userBenefit: A filter that material passes into needs clearing constantly and blocks when you are busy. Running the flow across it means it never stops.
entries.mechanismConnection: Rhincodon typus uses cross-flow filtration, water passing tangentially across twenty filter pads so particles are deflected rearward without accumulating on the mesh.

entries.title: Crowd by Day, Feed After Dark
entries.objective: Unlike most stick insects, this large flightless New Guinea species does not rely on looking like a twig. Groups pack together by day in tree hollows, under bark or among roots, out of sight entirely, and come out after dark to feed on leaves in low shrubs and saplings rather than the canopy. Crowding in cover and feeding low are both refusals to be exposed. Its principle is Defensive Texture. The metaphor? Stay low and go out late.
entries.animalRule: The busy hours must be spent out of view, and the task has to happen at the quietest hour at reduced scale.
entries.userBenefit: Doing your work in the busiest window means you compete for every bit of attention and get interrupted through all of it. The quiet hour costs you visibility and gives you the whole thing done.
entries.mechanismConnection: Eurycantha calcarata aggregates diurnally in tree hollows and under bark, emerging nocturnally to feed in low shrubs rather than the canopy.

entries.title: Crown One Snack Bowl With Its Own Heat
entries.objective: Make one bowl of snacks whose warning colour and whose heat come from the same chilli, beside a plain, uncoloured bowl of the same snack.
entries.animalRule: The signal and the sting are the same borrowed ingredient: only the chilli may colour the hot bowl, and the plain bowl stays uncoloured.
entries.userBenefit: A snack for sharing where the heat announces itself, so nobody gets an unwelcome surprise.
entries.mechanismConnection: Spanish Shawl Nudibranch — Flow-led • Signalling • Forager: Flabellinopsis iodinea eats Eudendrium hydroids, stores their unfired stinging cells in the tips of its cerata, and takes its vivid colour from pigment in the same hydroid diet, so the food that arms it also paints its warning. This Trial translates that defence and warning colour taken from the same food into one bowl coloured red-orange and armed by the same chilli, with whole chillies standing up like cerata.

entries.title: Cruise Quietly, Then Act Fast
entries.objective: Domestic cats spend much of their time in controlled routines: resting, grooming, watching, patrolling and stalking, a steady rhythm that costs little. Hunting then compresses attention and movement into a short precise pounce. The animal is bimodal, and the two modes are not blended at any point; the cruise is genuinely cheap and the burst is genuinely brief. Its principle is Self-chosen Rhythm. The metaphor? Keep the cruise genuinely cheap and the burst genuinely brief, and never blend them.
entries.animalRule: The baseline must be genuinely low-cost during the attempt, and intensity has to be confined to one short burst.
entries.userBenefit: Blending your cruise and your burst means a baseline that tires you and a burst with nothing behind it. Keeping them separate gets you both.
entries.mechanismConnection: Felis catus alternates a low-cost maintenance rhythm of resting, grooming and patrolling with brief high-intensity predatory bursts, without intermediate states.

entries.title: Crush It With Broad Flat Jaws
entries.objective: For most of its life Kemp's ridley is a crab specialist, working shallow sandy and muddy bottoms in the Gulf of Mexico and crushing blue crabs and other shellfish with broad, powerful jaws. It is the smallest sea turtle and it eats armoured prey, which works only because the jaw is built wide and blunt for force rather than for grip or speed. Its principle is Mass Beach Landing. The metaphor? Build for force where the food is armoured.
entries.animalRule: The item chosen must be the most defended one available, and no softer item may be worked on today.
entries.userBenefit: Leaving the armoured item for later means it accumulates and starts blocking everything behind it. Spending one day applying blunt force to it is how it finally stops being on your list.
entries.mechanismConnection: Lepidochelys kempii crushes blue crabs and other hard-shelled prey with broad, heavily muscled jaws adapted for force rather than grasping.

entries.title: Crush One Carton of Eggshells Into Garden Grit
entries.objective: Pick up clean eggshells with tongs and crush them to fine grit for the garden, seizing at the front and grinding at the back.
entries.animalRule: The tongs only seize and the pin only crushes: fingers never break the shells.
entries.userBenefit: A quiet, useful job that gives your garden plants a mineral top-up.
entries.mechanismConnection: Wolf Eel — Den-bound • Slow • Crushing: A Wolf Eel lives in one rock crevice for years and eats hard-shelled prey such as crabs, clams and sea urchins, seizing them with canine teeth at the front of the jaws and crushing them on broad molars further back and on the palate. This Trial translates that front teeth that seize and back teeth that crush shell into eggshells seized with tongs and ground to grit with a pin.

entries.title: Crush One Hard Problem Into Parts
entries.objective: Crush One Hard Problem Into Parts.
entries.animalRule: Exactly three pieces, and the easiest must be finished before you stop.
entries.userBenefit: A hard problem becomes penetrable instead of intimidating.
entries.mechanismConnection: Overcomes hard-shelled prey by crushing it with massive forward-striking jaws rather than relying on venom to penetrate, which opens snails and armoured beetles that soft-bodied specialists cannot use at all

entries.title: Crush One Soft Core Without Tearing
entries.objective: Crush One Soft Core Without Tearing.
entries.animalRule: The outer bag must remain closed and intact while the contents visibly change.
entries.userBenefit: You turn ambush grip into one concrete, visible experience instead of an abstract idea.
entries.mechanismConnection: Giant Water Bug — Seizing • Piercing • Dissolving: The strike closes in milliseconds and a short stout rostrum injects paralytic saliva and digestive enzymes, so tissue is liquefied inside the prey's own skin and drawn out without anything being torn apart. This Trial translates that high-frequency mechanism into one soft core inside its skin.

entries.title: Cryptic and Cautious Alone
entries.objective: At low density a desert locust develops the solitary form: cryptic green colouring that matches vegetation, less robust hind legs, a smaller brain, and cautious dispersive behaviour that actively avoids other locusts. That is not an immature version of the swarming form; it is the correct configuration for being alone, and it is actively maintained. Its principle is Changed By Company. The metaphor? Being alone has its own correct configuration, which is cautious and inconspicuous rather than diminished.
entries.animalRule: The configuration must be purpose-built for solitary work during the attempt, and no reduced group setup may be used.
entries.userBenefit: Running a stripped-down version of the group setup alone means it fits badly and you feel diminished. A purpose-built solitary configuration works properly.
entries.mechanismConnection: Schistocerca gregaria solitarious phase individuals are cryptically coloured, mutually avoidant and dispersive, a distinct configuration rather than an immature gregarious form.

entries.title: Curdle One Cup of Milk Into Fresh Cheese
entries.objective: Use lemon juice or vinegar to turn one cup of warm milk into soft fresh cheese.
entries.animalRule: Acid does the work: no rennet, starter or shop cheese.
entries.userBenefit: Fresh cheese in fifteen minutes from one cup of milk.
entries.mechanismConnection: Vulture Bee — Foraging • Processing • Commuting: Trigona necrophaga collects carrion instead of pollen, and its gut holds acid-loving microbes that break down meat protein so foragers can carry it home as a processed food. This Trial translates that acid processing that turns raw protein into usable food into one cup of milk curdled into fresh cheese with lemon or vinegar.

entries.title: Cure It in the Sun First
entries.objective: Ochotona iliensis lives on bare Tianshan rock above three thousand metres, where plants grow for a few weeks and winter lasts most of the year. It does not hibernate, which is why it must keep eating through a season that produces nothing. The mechanism is haymaking: it cuts vegetation, carries it to rock crevices and spreads it to cure in the sun before stacking, because green material stored wet would rot and be lost. Its principle is Alpine Preparation. The metaphor? Cure it before you store it.
entries.animalRule: No item enters storage before its keeping step is finished, and skipping the step for one item ends the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Most of what you save is lost because you stored it wet, unlabelled or unportioned, and you pay for that in the lean week. The curing step costs minutes and saves the whole store.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ochotona iliensis cuts alpine vegetation and sun-cures it on rock before stacking it in crevices, because wet-stored green material would rot and leave it without winter food.

entries.title: Curl One Many-Armed Star Into a Mug
entries.objective: Make a many-armed, branching star from pipe cleaners or twisted foil, then curl every arm tight against its centre until the whole star hides inside a mug.
entries.animalRule: Nothing is cut, snapped or untwisted once the star is made: every arm and branch is curled in against the centre, and no tip pokes above the mug's rim.
entries.userBenefit: A quiet, fiddly few minutes that ends in a satisfyingly tiny bundle.
entries.mechanismConnection: Northern Basket Star — Sheltered • Coiled • Hidden: Gorgonocephalus eucnemis spends the day with its many-branched arms rolled into tight coils against the central disc, wedged into cover on the reef or slope, which keeps it low-profile to fish and costs almost no energy. This Trial translates that branched reach curled tight against the body and tucked into a crevice by day into a many-armed star curled in on itself until it hides inside a mug.

entries.title: Curved to Go Under the Stones
entries.objective: An ibisbill is built for one specific surface: the shingle beds of fast cold high-altitude rivers. Its long red bill curves downward at exactly the angle needed to be slid under and around rounded stones, where caddisfly and stonefly larvae shelter out of the current, so the bird feeds in a layer nothing else there can reach. The angle is not approximate. Its principle is River Precision. The metaphor? Shape your tool to the exact geometry of the obstacle and a sheltered layer opens.
entries.animalRule: The geometry must be matched exactly during the attempt, and no general-purpose version may be used.
entries.userBenefit: A general-purpose tool works adequately everywhere and reaches nothing sheltered for you. Shaping it to one exact geometry opens a layer nobody else can enter.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ibidorhyncha struthersii has a decurved bill angled to be inserted beneath and around rounded river cobbles, accessing invertebrates sheltering out of the current.

entries.title: Cut a New One Each Time
entries.objective: Barbets are not woodpeckers and lack the skull to hammer sound timber, but this one has a stout bill and excavates its own nest hole in soft dead wood, which almost no other non-woodpecker manages. It usually cuts a new hole rather than reusing last year's, so cavities accumulate in a wood over time and other species move into the ones it left. Its principle is Canopy-Green Back. The metaphor? Reusing the old one saves a day and costs the thing you would have left behind.
entries.animalRule: The old setup must be left intact and usable rather than dismantled or overwritten, and the new one has to be built rather than copied from it.
entries.userBenefit: Overwriting your old setup saves you an hour and destroys the version someone else could have used. Leaving it intact costs almost nothing and quietly builds a stock of usable things.
entries.mechanismConnection: Psilopogon rubricapillus excavates fresh nest cavities in soft decaying wood each season rather than reusing previous holes, and the abandoned cavities accumulate and are occupied by other cavity-nesting species.

entries.title: Cut In at the Base
entries.objective: A long tubular flower is a mechanism for enforcing a deal: the nectar sits at the bottom, so an insect that wants it must push past the anthers, picking up pollen on the way. A Carpenter Bee does not accept the terms. It lands outside, cuts a slit at the base with heavy mandibles, and takes the nectar without entering. Its principle is Bored Tunnel. The metaphor? Some processes exist to take something from you on the way through. Go in at the base.
entries.animalRule: The direct route must be legitimate rather than a rule breach, and you have to actually obtain the thing rather than simply avoid the process.
entries.userBenefit: Going through the designed route costs you the whole process to get one thing out of it. Asking directly is legitimate, takes a message, and usually gets you the thing the same day.
entries.mechanismConnection: Xylocopa robs nectar by slitting the corolla base with its mandibles and feeding without contacting anthers or stigma, bypassing the floral morphology that otherwise enforces pollen transfer.

entries.title: Cut the Tie to the Sea
entries.objective: Nearly every crab is tied to the sea by its young: eggs hatch into planktonic larvae that need salt water, which is why even land crabs migrate to spawn. Vampire crabs do not. Eggs develop directly into miniature crabs in fresh water, so the species has no obligatory journey and completes its life in one small pool. Its principle is Pocket Territory. The metaphor? One inherited dependency decides where you can be. Remove it and the map changes.
entries.animalRule: The requirement must be genuinely removed or replaced during the attempt rather than scheduled, and it has to be one that constrains where or how you operate.
entries.userBenefit: One inherited requirement quietly decides everything about where and how you work, and you plan around it forever. Removing it once reopens options you stopped considering years ago.
entries.mechanismConnection: Geosesarma undergoes direct development, with eggs hatching into miniature crabs in fresh water rather than planktonic marine larvae, eliminating the obligatory spawning migration typical of brachyurans.

entries.title: Cut Them Before They Establish
entries.objective: A slug grazing a mature leaf takes a small proportion of a plant that survives. This one does something much worse: it works at ground level at night and rasps through the soft stems of germinating seedlings at or just below the soil line. Each cut removes an entire future plant rather than part of an existing one. The timing is what makes small damage total. Its principle is Slow Power. The metaphor? Small interference at the start removes the whole thing. Protect the beginnings, not the mature parts.
entries.animalRule: The protection must go to the newest and least established thing rather than the most important one, and the established things have to be deliberately left unprotected.
entries.userBenefit: Your established work survives neglect and your newest thing dies from one bad week, so protecting the big thing is backwards. Shielding the newest is where the same hour does most good.
entries.mechanismConnection: Sarasinula linguaeformis feeds nocturnally at ground level, rasping through the stems of germinating seedlings at or below the soil surface, killing entire plants at establishment rather than partially damaging mature ones.

entries.title: Cutters Front, Grinders Behind
entries.objective: Hard-shelled prey on a rocky shore presents two separate problems and most fish are equipped for one. Detaching a limpet needs a cutting edge applied at an angle; breaking it open afterwards needs a crushing surface. The White Seabream carries both: chisel-like incisors at the front and flattened molars behind, so one animal performs both operations in sequence. Its principle is Open Coast Opportunism. The metaphor? Two different jobs need two different tools. Carry both and do them in order.
entries.animalRule: The two operations must be named separately and handled with different approaches in sequence rather than one method applied throughout.
entries.userBenefit: Using one approach for a task that is secretly two jobs is why it half-works on you every time. Naming the two and handling each properly usually fixes it first attempt.
entries.mechanismConnection: Diplodus sargus has chisel-shaped incisiform anterior teeth for detaching attached prey and flattened molariform posterior teeth for crushing shells, performing both operations sequentially.

entries.title: Damage Makes It the Most Attractive Plant
entries.objective: Most herbivores disperse as they eat. This one concentrates. Adults chew the tissue between leaf veins, and two signals then work together: the volatiles released by damaged foliage, detectable at a distance, and a sex pheromone released by females. The result is that a plant already being eaten becomes the most attractive plant in the garden, and beetles pile on. Its principle is Garden. The metaphor? Damage advertises itself and attracts more; repair the first break before the signal spreads.
entries.animalRule: The repair must happen before any other work during the attempt, and the break has to be one that is currently visible.
entries.userBenefit: A visible break advertises itself and attracts more of the same to you. Repairing the first one before anything else stops the whole cascade.
entries.mechanismConnection: Popillia japonica aggregates in response to herbivory-induced plant volatiles combined with female sex pheromone, so damaged foliage becomes increasingly attractive to further beetles.

entries.title: Dance One Full Song Like Everyone's Watching
entries.objective: Play one full song and perform it at maximum commitment as if you just walked onto a stage.
entries.animalRule: Erects the cape into a black ellipse around the iridescent breast shield and dances in tight arcs around the female. Keep that true for the whole attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Pushes performance confidence, physical energy and willingness to look ridiculous for something memorable.
entries.mechanismConnection: Superb Bird-of-paradise expresses Stage Transformation through this mode: Superb Bird-of-paradise — Cape-Spread Ellipse Display — Transformed • Snapping • Minutes: Erects the cape into a black ellipse around the iridescent breast shield and dances in tight arcs around the female. The Trial carries that same limiting structure into one concrete human action.

entries.title: Dance Ten Seconds Then Stop
entries.objective: During a normal friendly moment, dance intensely for ten seconds with no announcement, then stop and continue exactly where you left off.
entries.animalRule: The bird holds its wings in a shallow V and rocks from side to side exactly as a turkey vulture does, often circling inside vulture flocks, so ground animals that have learned scavengers are harmless keep feeding while it passes overhead. Keep that true for the whole attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Ten seconds that a room does not see coming, and an immediate return to normal.
entries.mechanismConnection: Zone-tailed Hawk expresses Strategic Disguise through this mode: Zone-tailed Hawk — Borrowed Vulture Silhouette — Soaring • Rocking • Unremarkable: The bird holds its wings in a shallow V and rocks from side to side exactly as a turkey vulture does, often circling inside vulture flocks, so ground animals that have learned scavengers are harmless keep feeding while it passes overhead. The Trial carries that same limiting structure into one concrete human action.

entries.title: Dark, Moving, Warm
entries.objective: A horse fly's adult stage is short and built entirely for finding hosts. The female needs a blood meal to mature her eggs, and she finds large mammals by a very short list of cues: dark colour, movement, warmth and carbon dioxide. Some species find water to lay in by detecting polarised light reflected off its surface. Everything is reduced to a handful of unmistakable signals. Its principle is Persistent Pursuit. The metaphor? Reduce what you are looking for to three cues you cannot mistake, and you will find it anywhere.
entries.animalRule: No more than three cues may be used, they must be written down before searching, and judgement may not be substituted during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Searching on overall judgement means you miss things and cannot say why. Three written cues make the search fast and give you the same answer twice.
entries.mechanismConnection: Tabanid females locate hosts using a restricted cue set of dark colour, motion, thermal gradient and carbon dioxide, and some locate oviposition water by polarised light reflection.

entries.title: Darken Your Card With Every Win
entries.objective: Play a quick knockout game with friends where each win shades your card one step darker, so the ranking is readable at a glance.
entries.animalRule: Nobody announces a score: rank is shown only by how dark each card has become.
entries.userBenefit: A fast, fair little tournament with a scoreboard anyone can read.
entries.mechanismConnection: Blackbuck — Grazing open plain • Holding a small patch • Darkening with rank: A male Blackbuck's coat darkens from fawn towards black as he gains status, so on the lek of tiny adjacent territories every animal's rank can be read across the open ground without a contest. This Trial translates that coat colour that darkens with rank so status is visible from afar into cards shaded darker with each win and lined up from palest to darkest.

entries.title: Dart Out for Scattered Pegs Then Regroup
entries.objective: With at least one partner, burst out to grab a peg each on a clap and re-form a shoulder-to-shoulder line, five rounds in one minute.
entries.animalRule: Each player darts only into their own sector and the group regroups in the same order every time before the next signal.
entries.userBenefit: A fast, cheerful group burst that gets everyone moving together.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cownose Ray — Burst • Strike • Disperse: Rhinoptera bonasus schools break into short, rapid surges to seize exposed prey or dodge a shark, then close back into their travelling formation. This Trial translates that brief surge out of the school and quick re-forming into five dart-and-regroup rounds for scattered pegs.

entries.title: Dart Through Five Sharp Turns
entries.objective: Cover ground with rapid, hard-to-predict direction changes.
entries.animalRule: Every turn must change direction; no coasting in a straight line through the course.
entries.userBenefit: You train burst navigation that corrects course instead of relying on one perfect line.
entries.mechanismConnection: Skipper Butterfly — Darting • Erratic • Rapid: Large flight muscles packed into a stout thorax beat comparatively small wings fast, driving rapid, erratic darts between flowers, perches and host plants with frequent sharp changes of direction that birds find hard to follow. Skippers combine powerful thoracic muscles with rapid darting flight and frequent perching to navigate complex vegetation. This Trial translates that mechanism into cover ground with rapid, hard-to-predict direction changes.

entries.title: Dash to Cover on Three Random Alarms
entries.objective: Reach a chosen hiding spot within three seconds each time a random alarm sounds.
entries.animalRule: You must be fully behind cover within three seconds of each alarm, then count five in cover and step back to the start mark, ready for the next alarm.
entries.userBenefit: A jolt of reaction speed and a cover spot you will remember.
entries.mechanismConnection: Rock Cavy — Explosive • Cliff-Sprint • Hide: Kerodon rupestris lives in groups among boulder piles in north-eastern Brazil, and when one animal gives the alarm the others bolt at once into rock crevices, where their padded feet and quick scrambling get them out of reach. This Trial translates that shared alarm answered with an instant dash into a crevice into three unpredictable alarms each answered by a three-second dash into cover.

entries.title: Dawn, Still Air, Exposed Perch
entries.objective: A magpie-robin holds its territory by singing, not fighting, and it concentrates that singing into dawn and dusk from a perch at the top of a bush. The timing is not habit: the air is still then, so sound carries furthest, and the boundaries between neighbours are maintained by mutual listening rather than patrol. Same song, chosen hour. Its principle is Vocal Mastery. The metaphor? Say it when the air is still and you will not have to say it again.
entries.animalRule: It must be said only once during the attempt, and the timing has to be chosen for when the channel is genuinely quiet.
entries.userBenefit: Repeating something into a noisy hour is why nobody has registered it, and the repetition makes you look difficult. Saying it once when it is quiet usually lands.
entries.mechanismConnection: Copsychus saularis concentrates loud varied territorial song into dawn and dusk from exposed perches, exploiting still-air conditions that maximise acoustic transmission distance.

entries.title: Days of Being Soft
entries.objective: After leaving the old shell a brown crab swells with water so the new one hardens at a larger size, and that hardening takes days to weeks. Through it the animal cannot feed, cannot use the claws that are its entire defence, and is soft enough for almost anything to take, so it hides. The growth is paid for with a window of total vulnerability. Its principle is Shell Hold. The metaphor? Plan for the soft window after a change, and be somewhere protected for the whole of it.
entries.animalRule: The protected arrangement must cover the whole vulnerable period during the attempt, and its expected length has to be stated.
entries.userBenefit: Treating a change as finished the moment you make it ignores the weeks afterwards when you cannot defend it. Planning that window is what stops the change being undone.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cancer pagurus takes up water to expand after ecdysis and remains soft and unable to feed or defend itself for days to weeks while the new cuticle mineralises.

entries.title: Days of Food, Not a Meal
entries.objective: The famous parts are the silence and the snowshoe paws, and the shape of a lynx's life is set by arithmetic. It routinely kills roe deer weighing several times what it does, so one successful hunt yields days of food rather than a meal. That inverts the usual predator schedule: hunting is rare, and the ordinary business of the week is covering the carcass, lying up nearby and returning to it. Its principle is Quiet Focus. The metaphor? Take one thing large enough that most of your time becomes guarding it rather than hunting.
entries.animalRule: The thing must be large enough to occupy a sustained period, and no further searching may happen during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Chasing many small things means your whole week is searching rather than working. One large enough thing turns searching into a rare event.
entries.mechanismConnection: Lynx lynx routinely takes roe deer several times its own mass, so a single kill provides days of food and most activity consists of caching, guarding and returning to the carcass.

entries.title: Days to Change Colour
entries.objective: A crab spider's camouflage is chemical: it secretes yellow pigment into its outer cells to match a yellow flower, or reabsorbs it to return to white, and each change takes days, faster going yellow than coming back. That timescale is the real constraint, because the spider must commit to a flower long before it knows whether the bees will come. Its principle is Flower-edge Ambush. The metaphor? Where adapting takes days, the choice of where to sit has to be made early and then kept.
entries.animalRule: The commitment must genuinely take days to reverse, and it may not be revisited during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Revisiting a slow-to-reverse decision daily means you pay the switching cost without ever getting the benefit. Choosing once and holding is the only way it pays.
entries.mechanismConnection: Misumena vatia shifts between white and yellow by secreting or reabsorbing a pigment into the outer cuticle layer, a process taking days in each direction and slower returning to white.

entries.title: Dead Leaf, Then Four Eyes
entries.objective: Closed, a Peacock Butterfly is a dead leaf: the underwings almost black with fine striations, and a hibernating individual in a shed is effectively invisible. The defence is what happens when that fails. The wings snap open to expose four large eyespots and the animal hisses audibly by rubbing them together. Total concealment, and one loud escalation held in reserve. Its principle is Eyespot Startle. The metaphor? Stay invisible while it works, and keep one loud move for when it stops.
entries.animalRule: The trigger must be named before the period begins, and the escalation may only be used if that specific trigger occurs, not before.
entries.userBenefit: Escalating early spends the move on something small and leaves you nothing later. Naming the trigger first means you stay quiet cheaply and the loud move still works when you need it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Aglais io rests with cryptic near-black underwings resembling dead leaf and, on disturbance, snaps the wings open to display four large eyespots while producing an audible hiss by stridulation.

entries.title: Deadhead Every Spent Flower Along One Border
entries.objective: Work one flower border or row of pots in short passes, picking off every spent bloom.
entries.animalRule: Work the same line from end to end and pick off every spent flower in it, not just the obvious ones.
entries.userBenefit: A tidier border that keeps flowering for longer.
entries.mechanismConnection: Common Bluetail — Rhythmic • Patrol • Circuit: Ischnura senegalensis works a familiar strip along reed edges in short, repeated flights, picking off small insects and returning to perch, rather than roaming widely or waiting in long ambush. This Trial translates that repeated patrol along one edge picking off small targets into deadheading every spent flower along one border.

entries.title: Decades of Slow Grazing
entries.objective: A red sea urchin can live for over a century, and almost nothing about it is fast. Tube feet anchor it to rock, long spines and a hard test make it awkward and costly to attack, and it scrapes algae with its five-part jaw at a rate that grows the animal over decades. Nearly all the energy goes through the digestive engine rather than into movement or active defence. Its principle is Centuries in Spines. The metaphor? Put everything into slow steady intake and passive protection, and time does the growing.
entries.animalRule: The rate must be one sustainable for years during the attempt, and the active defending or accelerating has to be removed.
entries.userBenefit: Running something at a rate you cannot sustain means stopping and losing the accumulated position. A rate you could hold for years gets further than any sprint you can manage.
entries.mechanismConnection: Mesocentrotus franciscanus grazes kelp with its Aristotle's lantern over a century-long lifespan, relying on long spines and a rigid test as permanent passive defence.

entries.title: Dedicated Neurons That Predict
entries.objective: Chasing a moving target means always arriving where it was. Dragonflies solve it the other way. The upper part of each compound eye carries a dense acute zone pointed at the sky where prey appears as a silhouette, and a small set of dedicated neurons tracks a selected target and predicts its future position, steering the body so the interception is already arranged. Its principle is Fast Focus. The metaphor? Dedicate a small permanent capacity to prediction, and you stop chasing.
entries.animalRule: The predictive capacity must be dedicated rather than shared during the attempt, and action has to follow the prediction.
entries.userBenefit: Attention spread across everything leaves nothing predicting, so you always arrive late. A small dedicated slice is enough to put you ahead of it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Odonate dorsal acute zones detect prey silhouettes against the sky while small target motion detector neurons track and extrapolate target trajectory for interception.

entries.title: Deep by Day, Up by Night
entries.objective: A female black dragonfish stays deep through the day and migrates upward at night to feed, lunging at small fish and crustaceans with long jaws and a chin barbel. The vertical commute is daily and substantial, and its whole logic is that the productive layer and the safe layer are not the same place at the same time. Its principle is Blackwater Lantern. The metaphor? Separate where you are safe from where you feed, and commute between them on a schedule.
entries.animalRule: The two places must be genuinely different during the attempt, and the commute has to follow a stated schedule rather than mood.
entries.userBenefit: Working and resting in the same place means neither ever happens properly and you feel on duty constantly. Two places and a schedule separates them without extra effort.
entries.mechanismConnection: Idiacanthus atlanticus females remain at depth by day and undertake nocturnal vertical migration into shallower water to feed on fish and crustaceans.

entries.title: Defence as a Coating, Not a Behaviour
entries.objective: A citrus mealybug barely moves once it has found a feeding site. It pushes mouthparts into the phloem and drinks a sugar-rich stream requiring no searching, and covers itself in a secreted white wax that breaks up its outline, repels water and physically obstructs small predators and sprays. Because feeding is passive and defence is a coating rather than a behaviour, energy goes into reproducing. Its principle is Crevice Wax Coat. The metaphor? Make your defence a coating that needs no attention, and your whole budget goes into output.
entries.animalRule: The replacement must require no attention during the attempt, and the freed attention has to go into output.
entries.userBenefit: A defence that needs your attention takes it from your output every day. A coating that needs none means all of it goes into what you produce.
entries.mechanismConnection: Planococcus citri secretes a hydrophobic waxy coating that disrupts its outline and obstructs predators and contact sprays, replacing behavioural defence entirely.

entries.title: Defend the Granary, Not the Acorns
entries.objective: An acorn woodpecker granary takes years to drill and is used across generations, which means the thing worth fighting for is the structure rather than any season's nuts. Groups defend it hard, because losing the pole loses every winter to come, not just this one. Its principle is Granary Drummer. The metaphor? When something is challenged, work out whether the structure or the contents is at stake, and defend the structure.
entries.animalRule: The structure must be what is defended during the attempt, and the contents have to be conceded if both cannot be held.
entries.userBenefit: Fighting for this season's contents while the structure is taken means you win the argument and lose every year after. Defending the structure is the only version that lasts.
entries.mechanismConnection: Melanerpes formicivorus groups vigorously defend the multi-generational granary tree itself, which represents years of drilling investment beyond any single acorn crop.

entries.title: Defended by Size Alone
entries.objective: The lappet-faced vulture owns one step in a shared process: it makes the first opening in an intact hide, after which everything else present can feed. That position is defended by size alone, because it dominates other vultures at a carcass outright. It does not need to arrive first; it needs to be the only one who can do the step and heavy enough not to be displaced. Its principle is Heavy Opening. The metaphor? Own the step only you can do, and be heavy enough to keep it.
entries.animalRule: The step must be one others genuinely cannot do during the attempt, and your security in it has to be checked first.
entries.userBenefit: Doing the step only you can do without securing your position means being displaced the moment it is open. Checking first is what keeps the value.
entries.mechanismConnection: Torgos tracheliotos opens intact carcass hide with a massive bill and heavy skull and dominates all other African vultures at the carcass by body size.

entries.title: Defined by Where, Not What
entries.objective: Most raptors are defined by what they are good at. The Variable Hawk is defined by where it can be: Pacific coastal desert at sea level, temperate forest, Patagonian grassland, the Falklands, and high Andean puna above four thousand metres. It is not the best hunter in any of those places and it is present in all of them, which is a different kind of success. Its principle is Range Over Specialism. The metaphor? Being the best somewhere is one strategy. Being adequate everywhere is another, and it fails less often.
entries.animalRule: The new area must be one you currently cannot do at all rather than one you are improving, and one real task has to be completed in it.
entries.userBenefit: Deepening what you are already good at has diminishing returns and leaves you fragile if that thing stops being wanted. Becoming adequate at one new thing changes what you can survive.
entries.mechanismConnection: Geranoaetus polyosoma occupies habitats from Pacific coastal desert and temperate forest to Patagonian steppe and high Andean puna above four thousand metres, succeeding by breadth rather than specialisation.

entries.title: Deliver It Still Sticky
entries.objective: Mistletoe cannot grow on the ground. The seed must arrive on a living branch of a suitable host and stick firmly enough to stay, which is a very specific delivery requirement, and this flowerpecker meets it exactly: the gut is short, transit takes minutes, and the seed emerges still coated in viscin, which the bird then wipes onto a branch. Speed and stickiness, not volume. Its principle is Nectar Navigation Pattern. The metaphor? A delivery that arrives late and loose does not take. Pass it on fast and make it stick.
entries.animalRule: It must be passed on within an hour of receiving it, with the original context attached rather than summarised away.
entries.userBenefit: Holding something to tidy it before passing it on means it reaches you late and stripped of what made it useful. Passing it fast with the context attached is what makes it act on.
entries.mechanismConnection: Dicaeum erythrorhynchos has a short gut with minutes-long transit and deposits mistletoe seeds still coated in viscin, wiping them onto branches where the adhesive secures germination on a living host.

entries.title: Deliver It Without Going In
entries.objective: A Bee Fly looks like a small bumblebee, which keeps predators off an insect with no sting at all. Its reproduction is stranger still: the larvae develop inside solitary bee burrows, and the female has to get her eggs in there without entering. She hovers at the entrance and flicks them in from outside. Delivery without exposure. Its principle is Stingless Fuzz Bluff. The metaphor? You do not have to go inside to get it in. Deliver from the entrance.
entries.animalRule: You must not join or enter the group or system, and the thing has to genuinely arrive inside rather than be offered from outside.
entries.userBenefit: Waiting until you are inside a group to contribute means waiting indefinitely. Delivering from the entrance gets the thing used now, and it is usually what gets you invited in.
entries.mechanismConnection: Bombylius major is a Batesian mimic of bumblebees and oviposits by hovering at the entrance of solitary bee burrows and flicking eggs inside, so the parasitoid larvae enter the nest without the adult doing so.

entries.title: Deliver One Message at Speed
entries.objective: Pick a short message, move briskly to its destination, deliver it clearly, and return immediately.
entries.animalRule: You get one delivery run only; the message must arrive intact without stopping to refine it on the way.
entries.userBenefit: Trains decisive delivery under time pressure instead of spending energy perfecting something whose value is in reaching the destination.
entries.mechanismConnection: Luzon Garden Spider uses this mode by operates as a short-lived dispersal and delivery system that invests nothing in growth or capture because it will not live long enough to need either

entries.title: Dense Contact, Then Gone
entries.objective: In spring the sinkholes produce one of the largest reptile aggregations anywhere, with males massing around emerging females in writhing balls, some even mimicking female scent to draw rivals away or to take warmth from them. Then everything disperses for a brief northern summer, which is why the crowd exists only for days. Its principle is Ribbon Motion. The metaphor? A crowd is a phase, not a home.
entries.animalRule: The crowded period is bounded at twenty minutes, you do not return to it, and the rest of the day is spent on solitary work.
entries.userBenefit: Staying in the crowd all day means you get the contact and none of the work. Twenty dense minutes and then leaving gives you both of them.
entries.mechanismConnection: Thamnophis sirtalis parietalis forms enormous spring mating aggregations at hibernacula, with some males employing female pheromone mimicry, before dispersing for the short summer.

entries.title: Deployed and Gone in a Fraction of a Second
entries.objective: The dewlap is a mechanical trick. A rod of cartilage running back from the jaw swings forward when the throat muscles pull on it, stretching a loose fold of skin into a taut coloured fan several times the apparent size of the animal's head, and releasing it lets the whole thing vanish. Because deployment and retraction take a fraction of a second, the lizard can be highly conspicuous and then not. Its principle is Quick. The metaphor? Make the conspicuous version instant to deploy and instant to remove.
entries.animalRule: Deployment and removal must each take seconds during the attempt, and the display may not be left out between uses.
entries.userBenefit: A conspicuous thing that takes effort to put away gets left out and stops meaning anything. One you can remove in seconds keeps all its effect.
entries.mechanismConnection: Anolis sagrei extends the dewlap by protracting the second ceratobranchial cartilage, deploying and retracting a fan several times head size within a fraction of a second.

entries.title: Deposit Five Paper Eggs Across Five Plants Fast
entries.objective: Spend five paper eggs you made beforehand by balancing one on each of five spread-out host spots in fifteen seconds.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be made during the dash: only the five eggs built beforehand are spent, one per plant.
entries.userBenefit: Fifteen seconds of quick, careful movement around your home, powered by preparation you already did.
entries.mechanismConnection: Eupterote Fabia Moth — Brief • Mobile • Reproductive: Eupterote fabia emerges as an adult with little ability to feed and spends the reserves stored by its caterpillar on a short, intense programme of night flight, mate finding and egg-laying across host plants. This Trial translates that brief adult stage spending stored reserves on rapid dispersal into a fifteen-second dash leaving five pre-made eggs on five spread-out host spots.

entries.title: Describe It, Do Not Just Flag It
entries.objective: A prairie dog alarm call is not a single warning but closer to a description. Calls for a hawk and a coyote are acoustically distinct and produce different responses, and recordings show calls vary consistently with the size, shape, colour and speed of the intruder, so a colony reacts differently to two different people. The listener gets enough to choose a response. Its principle is Town Vigilance. The metaphor? Shouting that something is wrong helps nobody decide. Describe it.
entries.animalRule: All four specifics must be present in the first message rather than supplied on request, and it has to go to someone who can actually act on it.
entries.userBenefit: A problem you report without detail turns into three rounds of questions before anyone can move. Four specifics in your first message means the person can act immediately.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cynomys ludovicianus produces acoustically distinct alarm calls for different predator types, and call structure varies consistently with intruder size, shape, colour and speed, eliciting correspondingly different escape responses.

entries.title: Deseed One Pomegranate as a Flock of Three
entries.objective: Harvest every seed from one pomegranate with two other people working side by side over one bowl.
entries.animalRule: All three work the same fruit over the same bowl at the same time.
entries.userBenefit: A shared snack job that goes fast and ends in something good to eat.
entries.mechanismConnection: Nutmeg Mannikin — Rhythmic • Flocking • Forager: Lonchura punctulata feeds in tight flocks on seeding grasses, harvesting many small seeds quickly in short bouts and returning to the same productive patches while they last. This Trial translates that flock harvesting of a rich patch of small seeds into three people clearing every seed from one pomegranate over one bowl.

entries.title: Detect One Held Tray by Tongue Clicks
entries.objective: Use your own echoes to tell whether a tray is held in front of your face with your eyes closed.
entries.animalRule: Only your own clicks may inform the answer, and the tray is always held at short range.
entries.userBenefit: You hear a real echo from a real object, which almost nobody believes they can do.
entries.mechanismConnection: Harbor Porpoise — Clicking • Scanning • Never stopping: It hunts in murky coastal water by narrow-band clicks so high that they are absorbed within tens of metres, which gives a sharp picture only at short range. This Trial translates that short-range echolocation into detect one held tray by tongue clicks.

entries.title: Deter, Do Not Destroy
entries.objective: Polydesmid millipedes make cyanide. The spirobolids, including the American Giant Millipede, make quinones: released from pores along each segment, they irritate, smell strongly and stain skin a persistent purple-brown. The chemistry deters rather than kills, and combined with a heavily calcified shell and the ability to coil tight, it is enough. Nothing has to die for it to work. Its principle is Slow Progress. The metaphor? You do not need to win the confrontation. Make it unpleasant enough that it stops.
entries.animalRule: The friction must be mild and impersonal rather than a confrontation or a block, and it has to be put in place today rather than threatened.
entries.userBenefit: Confronting someone over a small repeated intrusion costs you far more than the intrusion does. One mild friction ends it without a conversation and nobody has to lose.
entries.mechanismConnection: Spirobolid millipedes discharge benzoquinones from repugnatorial pores along each segment, which irritate and stain rather than kill, paired with a calcified exoskeleton and tight coiling as a layered deterrent.

entries.title: Different Alarms for Different Threats
entries.objective: A squirrel monkey troop can number dozens moving quickly through forest where visibility is a few metres, and the thing holding it together is sound. The repertoire is large and used almost continuously: contact calls placing each animal, and crucially specific alarms distinguishing an aerial threat from a ground one, because the right response to each is opposite. One undifferentiated alarm would be useless. Its principle is Canopy Chatter. The metaphor? One alarm for everything is no alarm; name the kind of threat.
entries.animalRule: At least two distinct signals must be defined during the attempt, and the responses to them have to be genuinely different.
entries.userBenefit: One alarm for everything means people guess the response and half of them guess wrong, including you. Two distinct signals make the right reaction automatic.
entries.mechanismConnection: Saimiri sciureus uses structurally distinct alarm calls for aerial and terrestrial predators, which require opposite escape responses, alongside continuous contact calling.

entries.title: Different Room, Different Instrument
entries.objective: Steatornis caripensis runs two separate sensory systems because it lives in two places that share nothing. Echolocation gets it through a lightless cave, but it is useless for finding fruit outside, so the bird switches to a highly developed sense of smell and eyes with the highest rod density recorded in any vertebrate. Keeping both is what makes a nocturnal fruit-eater possible at all. Its principle is Cave Echolocation. The metaphor? Change the instrument when you change the room.
entries.animalRule: The two settings use genuinely different methods, and the swapped method holds for the entire time you are in the second one.
entries.userBenefit: Using one approach everywhere is why it works well in one place and badly in another, and you blame the place. Matching the method to the room removes friction you assumed was unavoidable.
entries.mechanismConnection: Steatornis caripensis echolocates with audible clicks inside lightless caves but switches entirely to olfaction and extremely rod-dense eyes to locate fruit outside them.

entries.title: Dig a Room the Weather Cannot Reach
entries.objective: A Savannah Monitor builds and occupies deep tunnels where air and soil temperature change far more slowly than on the surface and humidity stays higher. Inside that buffered chamber its metabolic rate, water loss and exposure to disturbance all drop at once. It did not learn to tolerate the surface; it built somewhere the surface conditions do not reach. Its principle is Burrow Refuge. The metaphor? Stop enduring the swings. Build one place where they arrive damped.
entries.animalRule: The space must structurally damp the variation rather than depend on you resisting it, and it has to be used during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Enduring the daily swings means every day costs you the same tax and you never get ahead. One buffered space makes a predictable stretch possible without any willpower.
entries.mechanismConnection: Varanus exanthematicus excavates deep burrows where diel temperature and humidity fluctuations are strongly attenuated, reducing metabolic rate, evaporative water loss and predation exposure.

entries.title: Dig Before Anyone Is Watching
entries.objective: Heterocephalus glaber workers dig tunnel networks kilometres long with their incisors, and the design detail matters: the lips seal behind the teeth so soil never enters the mouth while they cut. Nobody above ground sees any of it, and the colony's entire food supply - tubers found blind, underground - is what that invisible digging buys. Its principle is Eusociality. The metaphor? The unseen digging is the actual work.
entries.animalRule: The invisible part is finished before any visible work begins, and it is not mentioned to anyone once done.
entries.userBenefit: Doing the visible work first leaves the invisible part undone, and that is the part everything else rests on. Finishing it before anyone is watching removes the quiet failures you keep being surprised by.
entries.mechanismConnection: Heterocephalus glaber workers excavate kilometres of tunnel with their incisors while the lips seal behind the teeth, locating tubers blind underground.

entries.title: Dig Forwards, Head First
entries.objective: Most burrowing frogs dig backwards with their hind feet, lowering themselves into the ground. The turtle frog does the opposite: it digs forwards, head first, with stout forelimbs, and its small head and rounded body let it push through deep loose sand. Going head first is how it breaks into termite galleries and eats them in large numbers. The whole family's method would not get it there. Its principle is Backward Burrow. The metaphor? Go in head first where everyone reverses.
entries.animalRule: The approach must lead with what you usually keep for last, and it may not revert to the cautious order partway.
entries.userBenefit: Approaching things backwards means you spend most of the encounter on preliminaries and arrive at the real point with no time or nerve left. Leading with it gets a straight answer while you still can act on it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Myobatrachus gouldii burrows forwards head-first using robust forelimbs, unlike the hind-limb backward digging of most burrowing frogs, to reach termite galleries.

entries.title: Dig In Backwards With What You Have
entries.objective: A toad on the Great Plains faces months with no standing water and a surface too dry to survive on. It does not migrate and does not search for shelter. On the heel of each hind foot it carries a hardened tubercle with a sharp edge, and it uses these as blades, shuffling backwards into the soil until it is below the dry layer. Its principle is Adaptive Burrowing. The metaphor? Stop looking for shelter. Dig in where you are.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be bought or fetched from elsewhere, and you must stay in the same place rather than relocating to a better one.
entries.userBenefit: Waiting to relocate somewhere better means putting up with the current conditions indefinitely. Improving where you are with what you have usually takes twenty minutes and you stop noticing the problem.
entries.mechanismConnection: Anaxyrus cognatus bears a sharp keratinised metatarsal tubercle on each hind foot and excavates backwards into soil with them, burying itself below the desiccated surface layer for extended dry periods.

entries.title: Dig In Twice a Year
entries.objective: The marginated tortoise's year divides in two, and both halves involve stopping. From late autumn it digs into loose soil under bushes and hibernates until spring, and in the hottest part of the Greek summer its activity drops right off again. Europe's largest tortoise spends a large fraction of the year deliberately doing nothing, in the two windows that would cost it most. Its principle is Shellflare. The metaphor? Shut down in both bad seasons, not just one.
entries.animalRule: Both bad periods must be named, and the shutdown for the less obvious one has to be dated and told to someone.
entries.userBenefit: Planning around only your obvious bad season means the second one takes you by surprise every year and you treat the collapse as a personal failure. Dating it in advance makes it a rest instead.
entries.mechanismConnection: Testudo marginata hibernates in soil under scrub through winter and undergoes a second activity reduction during peak summer heat.

entries.title: Dig In Where the Food Is
entries.objective: The Humboldt Penguin lives where a cold current meets a desert, and both halves make the problem. The current drives one of the richest upwellings on earth against the coast, putting an enormous fish supply in reach; the same coast is among the hottest and driest on the continent, and a bird insulated for cold water cannot sit in that sun. So it nests underground, digging burrows beside the food. Its principle is Cool Current Loyalty. The metaphor? Do not leave the good supply because the conditions are hard. Dig in beside it.
entries.animalRule: You must stay at the source rather than relocating away from it, and the adjustment has to be to your own setup rather than to the source. It must be used at least once.
entries.userBenefit: You drift away from your best source because sitting near it is uncomfortable, then wonder why the quality dropped. Adjusting your own setup to tolerate it keeps the supply and costs one afternoon.
entries.mechanismConnection: Spheniscus humboldti forages in the highly productive Humboldt Current upwelling while nesting in burrows dug into guano or soil on the adjacent arid coast, using excavated shelter to tolerate heat and aridity without leaving the food supply.

entries.title: Dig Into What Piled Up
entries.objective: A penguin insulated for cold water has a serious problem breeding on a bare island in full African sun. The solution was guano. Centuries of seabird droppings built deposits metres deep, and penguins dug burrows into them: cool, shaded, humid chambers keeping eggs out of the sun and out of reach of gulls. The accumulated waste of generations became the habitat. Its principle is Coastal Pairing. The metaphor? The pile you have been meaning to clear is material. Dig into it.
entries.animalRule: The accumulation must not be cleared or removed, only excavated into, and the space carved out has to be actually used during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Treating a pile as something to clear means it never gets touched because clearing it is a day you do not have. Digging one usable space into it takes an hour and the pile stops blocking you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Spheniscus demersus historically excavated nest burrows into guano deposits metres deep on offshore islands, producing shaded humid chambers that protected eggs and chicks from heat and from kelp gull predation.

entries.title: Dig It So the Sun Cannot Reach
entries.objective: Magellanic penguins breed in huge coastal colonies and dig burrows into the soil, or nest in under bushes, and those burrows do two jobs at once: they shade eggs and chicks from the Patagonian sun and they hide them from gulls and skuas. The same hole answers heat and predators. Pairs come back to the same burrow year after year rather than digging again. Its principle is Burrow-Colony Loyalty. The metaphor? Build one shelter that solves two problems.
entries.animalRule: The one arrangement must genuinely handle both problems, and one of the separate measures has to stop.
entries.userBenefit: Handling two problems with two separate measures means you maintain both forever and neither gets your full attention. One arrangement covering both halves what you have to keep running.
entries.mechanismConnection: Spheniscus magellanicus excavates burrows that simultaneously shade eggs from solar heat and conceal them from gulls and skuas, reusing the same burrow annually.

entries.title: Dig the Bowl, Clear the Tracks
entries.objective: A male kakapo does not just call; he builds the acoustics. He digs bowl-shaped depressions on ridges, connects them with cleared tracks, and booms into them through the night, the bowl acting as a reflector for a very low call that carries kilometres across the valleys. The infrastructure is built before any signalling happens. Its principle is Grounded Uniqueness. The metaphor? Build the structure that amplifies your signal before you start producing it.
entries.animalRule: The amplifying structure must be built before any signalling during the attempt, and it has to be physical or procedural rather than intended.
entries.userBenefit: Producing a signal before building what carries it means repeating yourself and still not reaching anyone. Building the structure first means saying it once.
entries.mechanismConnection: Strigops habroptilus males excavate bowl-shaped depressions connected by cleared tracks on ridgelines, the bowls acting as reflectors for low-frequency booming calls audible over kilometres.

entries.title: Dig the Hole They Will Come To
entries.objective: An alligator's patience is not a temperament, it is engineering. It maintains a gator hole, a depression cleared and deepened over years, which holds water when the surrounding marsh dries, so fish, turtles and everything that comes to drink are concentrated in the one place it is already lying. It did not learn to wait well. It arranged the waiting. Its principle is Patience. The metaphor? Build the thing that brings them to you, then waiting costs nothing.
entries.animalRule: No pursuit may happen during the attempt, and something that draws people in has to be actually built rather than planned.
entries.userBenefit: Chasing each opportunity separately means starting from nothing every time. One thing built that brings them to you keeps working while you do something else.
entries.mechanismConnection: Alligator mississippiensis excavates and maintains gator holes that retain water through dry periods, concentrating prey and drinking animals at a site the alligator already occupies.

entries.title: Dig the Tubers Out of Wet Ground
entries.objective: In the dry season brolgas gather around whatever wetlands remain, and much of the diet is sedge tubers dug out of wet ground with a strong bill. A salt gland lets them use saline wetlands too, which widens the set of places that still count as water. The food is underground and the equipment is for digging, not picking. Its principle is Wetland Dance Bond. The metaphor? Go after the part of the resource that is buried, because that is what is still there when the easy part has gone.
entries.animalRule: Only the buried part may be taken during the attempt, and a tool suited to digging has to be used rather than one for picking.
entries.userBenefit: Taking the surface part means you compete with everyone for what is nearly gone. Going after the buried part is harder once and uncontested for the whole season.
entries.mechanismConnection: Antigone rubicunda excavates sedge tubers from saturated soil with a powerful bill and tolerates saline wetlands via a functional salt gland.

entries.title: Dig Up and Crack Ten Buried Pistachios
entries.objective: Find ten in-shell pistachios buried in a tray of rice by digging, and crack each one open before digging for the next.
entries.animalRule: Dig, crack, then dig: each shell must be open before you search for the next one.
entries.userBenefit: A tactile, rhythmic snack break that rewards patience.
entries.mechanismConnection: Spotted Eagle Ray — Rhythmic • Bottom • Forage: Aetobatus narinari dips to the seabed, digs buried clams and snails out of the sand and crushes their shells between plate-like tooth rows before moving on. This Trial translates that rhythmic dig-and-crush feeding on buried shellfish into a rhythm of digging buried nuts out of rice and cracking each in turn.

entries.title: Dig With Water, Eat With Suction
entries.objective: Two things about a walrus are widely misdescribed. The tusks do not dig and the mouth does not crush. Digging is done with water: it squirts jets from its mouth into the sediment and sweeps its muzzle sideways, exposing buried clams without touching them with anything hard. Then the mouth becomes a pump, sealing around the shell and withdrawing a muscled tongue like a piston. Its principle is Tuned Strength. The metaphor? The obvious hard tool is often not the one doing the work.
entries.animalRule: The obvious hard tool may not be used during the attempt, and the alternative has to actually complete the job.
entries.userBenefit: Reaching for the hard tool first means you apply force where finesse would do, and usually cause damage. Pressure or flow does the same job cleanly for you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Odobenus rosmarus excavates bivalves by hydraulic jetting from the mouth and extracts flesh by piston-like tongue suction rather than using the tusks or crushing dentition.

entries.title: Dig With Your Teeth If That Is What You Have
entries.objective: Most burrowing mammals dig with their claws. The Middle East blind mole-rat digs with its teeth: large incisors that protrude outside closed lips loosen the soil, and a broad flattened head and body shove the spoil back and up into mounds. It is not the obvious tool for the job and it is the one the animal has, used hard. Its principle is Burrowcraft. The metaphor? Use the odd tool you actually have.
entries.animalRule: No proper tool may be acquired first, and a real piece has to be finished with what is already to hand.
entries.userBenefit: Waiting for the right tool is the most respectable way to never start, and you can stay there for years. Doing a real piece with the wrong tool tells you in one afternoon whether the tool was the problem.
entries.mechanismConnection: Nannospalax ehrenbergi excavates with protruding incisors rather than claws, pushing spoil with a broad flattened head and body.

entries.title: Digest It Where It Lies
entries.objective: A ground beetle's mandibles are curved and sharp but not built for crushing, and the prey, slugs and caterpillars, is often larger than the beetle's head. The solution is to digest it where it lies: the beetle seizes the animal, regurgitates digestive enzymes onto and into it, then waits while the tissue is liquefied externally before drinking it back. The processing happens outside the body. Its principle is Quiet Strategy. The metaphor? Apply the solvent, wait, and then take it, rather than trying to break something larger than you.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be moved or broken by force during the attempt, and the waiting period has to be genuinely allowed.
entries.userBenefit: Trying to break something larger than you by force fails and damages your tools. Applying the solvent and waiting takes the same time and works.
entries.mechanismConnection: Carabus regurgitates proteolytic digestive fluid onto prey larger than its own head, liquefying tissue extraorally before ingestion.

entries.title: Digest the Indigestible
entries.objective: Keratin is the protein of hair, wool, feather and horn, cross-linked by disulphide bonds that make it effectively indigestible, which is why a dead bird's feathers persist after everything else is gone. Carpet beetle larvae digest it anyway: the gut maintains strongly reducing conditions that break those bonds. An entire category of material, available to almost nothing else. Its principle is Wool-And-Feather Fare. The metaphor? There is a whole class of thing nobody can use. Build the conditions that break it down.
entries.animalRule: The conversion must be set up so it works on the whole category rather than being done by hand once, and one item has to be actually converted during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: A whole category you cannot read or use is a permanent blind spot that quietly shapes what you know. One conversion set up once opens all of it, not just the item in front of you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Anthrenus larvae maintain strongly reducing conditions in the midgut that cleave the disulphide cross-links of keratin, allowing digestion of hair, wool, feather and horn that virtually no other organism can process.

entries.title: Dimple It, Do Not Break It
entries.objective: A water strider lives on the skin of water. Its legs are covered in thousands of microscopic grooved hairs that trap a layer of air so water cannot wet them, and each foot presses a dimple into the surface film without ever penetrating it, with the upward force supporting the animal many times over. It also reads the ripples other insects make. Its principle is Surface Tension. The metaphor? Rest your weight on the surface without breaking through, and read what disturbs it.
entries.animalRule: No intervention or commitment may be made during the attempt, and what was read from the surface has to be stated.
entries.userBenefit: Breaking into a situation to understand it means you are now part of it and cannot see it. Resting on the surface tells you what is actually moving.
entries.mechanismConnection: Gerridae legs bear grooved microsetae that trap an air layer, making them superhydrophobic so each tarsus deforms the water surface without penetrating it, while surface ripples are used to detect prey.

entries.title: Disappear Into One Still Frame
entries.objective: Arrange yourself or an object against a similar background and hold completely still for 30 seconds. Take one final photo from normal viewing distance.
entries.animalRule: Once positioned, nothing in the subject may move for the full 30 seconds; the disguise must come from placement, not digital editing.
entries.userBenefit: Trains patient visual concealment by making stillness and background match do the work at almost zero ongoing cost.
entries.mechanismConnection: Imperial Fruit-sucking Moth uses this mode by operates as a cryptic object relying entirely on not being distinguished from the branch it lies on, which costs nothing and works until it is found

entries.title: Disappear One Object Into a Brown Scene
entries.objective: Disappear One Object Into a Brown Scene.
entries.animalRule: The object must remain fully visible; it may not be covered.
entries.userBenefit: You turn revelation into one concrete experience with a visible finish.
entries.mechanismConnection: Sunbittern — Narrow • Barred • Streamside: Folded, it is a slim brown bird stepping along a shaded forest stream, its barring breaking up the outline against leaf litter and water. This Trial translates that mechanism into one object in a brown patterned scene.

entries.title: Disappear One Object Into Its Background
entries.objective: Disappear One Object Into Its Background.
entries.animalRule: It must be photographed from normal viewing distance; a close-up does not count.
entries.userBenefit: You create concealment by reducing contrast rather than hiding the object away.
entries.mechanismConnection: Operates as a concealed resting animal whose disrupted pattern hides a sleeping fish that cannot watch for predators or deploy any active defence

entries.title: Discard One Parental Genome
entries.objective: The calling is ordinary and the genetics are not. Where the pool frog overlaps with the marsh frog they produce a hybrid, the edible frog, which does something almost no vertebrate does: before making eggs or sperm it discards one of its two parental genomes entirely and passes on only the other, cloned rather than recombined. In most populations the discarded half is the marsh frog's. Its principle is Small Voice. The metaphor? Carrying both inheritances is not the same as passing both on; choose which one you transmit.
entries.animalRule: Both inheritances must be named and exactly one chosen for transmission during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Passing on everything you inherited means whoever follows you gets the contradiction too. Choosing one to transmit is what makes it usable for them.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pelophylax hybridogenetic hybrids eliminate one parental genome from the germline before gametogenesis, transmitting the remaining genome clonally rather than recombined.

entries.title: Discarded Tools in a Midden
entries.objective: This macaque's reputation for mischief is a single learning system pointed at whatever a place contains. On Thai islands troops select stone hammers and anvils to open shellfish, discarding worn tools in middens archaeologists can excavate, and the technique is acquired by young animals watching adults rather than invented individually. The same capacity in a temple produces something else entirely. Its principle is Adaptive Mischief. The metaphor? One learning capacity aimed at whatever is local produces completely different behaviour in each place.
entries.animalRule: What the current place contains must be surveyed during the attempt, and the habit has to be aimed at that rather than the previous target.
entries.userBenefit: Aiming your learning habit at what worked last place means ignoring what this one offers. One survey redirects the same capacity to something better.
entries.mechanismConnection: Macaca fascicularis acquires stone tool use for shellfish processing by social learning, with worn tools accumulating in excavatable middens, while the same capacity produces different behaviours elsewhere.

entries.title: Disguise One Obvious Feature
entries.objective: Take an everyday object with one visually obvious end or handle and disguise that feature as part of a larger arrangement.
entries.animalRule: The obvious feature must remain functional but may no longer be the first feature the eye notices.
entries.userBenefit: Practises visual integration by making the feature that normally reveals an object's identity blend into the whole.
entries.mechanismConnection: Snout Moth uses this mode by turns its own mouthparts into the stalk of the dead leaf it imitates, so the head, which is the feature a searching predator looks for, becomes part of the disguise rather than the thing that breaks it

entries.title: Disguise the Next Generation Too
entries.objective: The Philippine Leaf Insect copying a leaf is the famous half, and it is thorough: flattened body, vein markings, imitation damage, a rocking motion matching foliage in a breeze. The unfamiliar half is the eggs. They are not glued to a plant in a batch but dropped singly to the forest floor, where each resembles a seed closely enough that ants carry them into their nests. The disguise continues after the animal stops. Its principle is Leaf Mimicry. The metaphor? Protecting yourself is half of it. Protect what comes after you.
entries.animalRule: The handover must be usable by someone who was not there, and it has to be actually given to a person or placed where they will find it rather than written and kept.
entries.userBenefit: Everything you set up well dies with your memory of it, which is why things break the week you are away. One usable handover note means the thing survives you and nobody has to rebuild it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Phyllium eggs are dropped singly to the forest floor and resemble seeds in shape, colour and surface texture, including structures that induce ants to carry them into nests where they are protected until hatching.

entries.title: Disperse Wet, Converge Dry
entries.objective: A giant ibis runs two opposite strategies in one year. Through the wet season, when water is everywhere, the birds disperse widely and probe soft ground wherever they find it; as the dry season advances and water contracts to a few pools, they converge on those. The same animal spreads out and concentrates depending on where the resource is. Its principle is Grand Probing. The metaphor? Disperse when the resource is everywhere and converge when it contracts, rather than keeping one pattern.
entries.animalRule: The current distribution of the resource must be established, and the pattern has to switch to match it during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Keeping one pattern means being spread out when you should concentrate and crowded when you should spread. Switching to match costs nothing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Thaumatibis gigantea disperses across wet-season dry forest where water is ubiquitous and converges on remnant waterholes as the dry season concentrates the resource.

entries.title: Dissolve It Before You Draw It Out
entries.objective: A wheel bug overpowers nothing. It takes hold of a caterpillar, drives in a short curved beak, and pumps in enzymes that break the prey down internally; what it eventually draws back out is liquid. Digestion is done outside the body, before anything is consumed, which is why no jaws, strength or speed are needed. Its principle is Piercing. The metaphor? Break it down where it is instead of trying to take it whole.
entries.animalRule: The breaking down must happen before anything is moved or taken on, and no attempt to handle it whole may be made during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Trying to take something on whole is why it has sat untouched for weeks. Reducing it to parts first means you only ever handle pieces you can actually lift.
entries.mechanismConnection: Arilus cristatus injects proteolytic saliva through its rostrum, liquefying prey tissue extraorally so that only fluid is ingested, removing any need for mandibular force.

entries.title: Dissolve Limescale Off a Showerhead or Tap
entries.objective: Use a mild acid to take apart the crusted scale on one shower head or tap aerator so the water runs clean through every hole.
entries.animalRule: The acid does the work: vinegar on its own, never mixed with any other cleaner, and no scraping at the nozzles with anything hard.
entries.userBenefit: A shower that sprays evenly again, cleaned with something from the kitchen cupboard.
entries.mechanismConnection: White-headed Vulture — Soaring alone • Arriving early • Digesting what would kill anything else: Vulture stomach acid is strong enough to destroy anthrax, botulism toxin and rabies during ordinary digestion, so a carcass that would seed an outbreak is taken apart and removed instead of being left to spread. This Trial translates that acid that breaks down what would otherwise keep spreading into one vinegar soak that dissolves the scale where biofilm lives in a shower head or tap.

entries.title: Distance, Not Terrain
entries.objective: A urial is a wild sheep of dry open mountains rather than sheer cliffs, and that choice shapes everything. Where a markhor escapes by climbing into terrain a predator cannot use, urial live on rolling ridges where the defence is distance: a herd that sees a wolf early and moves off across open ground is rarely caught, so vigilance, spacing and readiness to run are the working parts. Its principle is Ridge Balance. The metaphor? Decide whether your safety comes from terrain or from distance, because they need completely different habits.
entries.animalRule: The source of safety must be decided explicitly, and the matching habit has to be actually built during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Building terrain habits when your safety comes from distance leaves you slow in the open. Deciding which it is tells you what to practise.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ovis vignei occupies rolling open mountain terrain where antipredator defence depends on early detection, spacing and sustained flight rather than inaccessible ground.

entries.title: Distinguished in the 1760s by Listening
entries.objective: Chiffchaff and willow warbler are so similar in the hand that plumage, structure and measurements overlap almost completely, and for a long time they were not separated at all.
