Gilbert White distinguished them in the 1760s by listening: the chiffchaff repeats a simple two-note phrase, the willow warbler sings a descending cadence. The difference the birds themselves use was the one nobody had measured. Its principle is Leafsong. The metaphor? The difference that matters may be in a channel nobody has been measuring.
entries.animalRule: The channel must be one not previously examined during the attempt, and the difference has to be stated.
entries.userBenefit: Measuring the usual dimensions means two different things look identical to you and you treat them the same. One unexamined channel often separates them completely.
entries.mechanismConnection: Phylloscopus collybita and trochilus overlap almost entirely in morphometrics but differ decisively in song, the trait by which the species were first separated.

entries.title: Dive for Buried Buttons in Ten-Second Bouts
entries.objective: Search the bottom of a deep tub of dried rice for five buttons in short, timed dives with a pause between each.
entries.animalRule: Every dive must touch the bottom, last no more than ten seconds and end with a ten-second pause; eyes stay on the ceiling during each dive.
entries.userBenefit: A tactile search game that trains touch and patience.
entries.mechanismConnection: Australian Sea Lion — Diving • Bottom-searching • Repeated: Neophoca cinerea forages over the continental shelf by diving again and again to the seabed and working along the bottom for most of each dive, many of them close to its aerobic limit, with short recoveries at the surface. This Trial translates that chain of bottom-searching dives with recoveries between into timed ten-second hand dives into a tub of rice with ten-second pauses.

entries.title: Divide Six Similar Objects Into Groups
entries.objective: Take six visually similar objects, inspect them closely, and divide them into at least two evidence-based groups using a subtle feature.
entries.animalRule: Group by an observed distinguishing feature rather than by where the objects happened to be placed; write or show the feature in the proof.
entries.userBenefit: Practises revising a broad category when closer evidence reveals meaningful hidden divisions inside something that first looked uniform.
entries.mechanismConnection: Black-capped Bulbul's relevant mechanism is: Was divided into several species when genetic work showed its regional forms to be deeply separate lineages, so a widespread bird of least concern became several narrow endemics overnight without anything changing in the field

entries.title: Divided Lobes Still Make Lift
entries.objective: A plume moth's wings are not solid membranes but divided along their length into narrow feathered lobes, which has two consequences. In flight the fringed lobes still generate lift at the very low Reynolds numbers a tiny insect operates at, where a solid surface offers no particular advantage. At rest the lobes roll tightly against a thin stiff body. Its principle is Delicate Specialization. The metaphor? At your scale a divided version may work as well as a solid one and fold away to nothing.
entries.animalRule: The replacement must work as well at your actual scale during the attempt, and it has to fold away when unused.
entries.userBenefit: A solid structure takes up space the whole time whether you are using it or not. A divided one does the same job and disappears between uses.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pterophorid wings are deeply cleft into fringed lobes that generate lift effectively at low Reynolds numbers and roll compactly against the body at rest.

entries.title: Do Not Chase, Inhale
entries.objective: A leaf scorpionfish does not pursue anything. It holds against rubble rocking gently with the current, and when a fish comes close enough it opens its mouth and expands the buccal cavity so fast that the prey is pulled in by the water itself. The strike covers almost no distance; the water does the travelling. Its principle is Leaf-Still Ambush. The metaphor? Create the conditions that pull it in, rather than covering the distance yourself.
entries.animalRule: No distance may be covered by you during the attempt, and the thing has to arrive through the change in conditions rather than being fetched.
entries.userBenefit: Going to fetch everything yourself means the distance is the whole cost and you cannot scale it. Changing the conditions so it arrives takes the distance out entirely.
entries.mechanismConnection: Taenianotus triacanthus captures prey by rapid suction feeding, expanding the buccal cavity to draw water and prey inward with minimal body displacement.

entries.title: Do Not Circle the Globe
entries.objective: The black-browed albatross is the most numerous albatross and uses the same physics as its larger relatives: long narrow wings, a shoulder lock holding them extended without muscular effort, and dynamic soaring harvesting the wind gradient. What distinguishes it is where that machinery is pointed, because rather than circling the globe it works productive shelf waters close to its colonies. Its principle is Ocean Handling. The metaphor? Having the range to go anywhere does not mean the best use of it is going far.
entries.animalRule: The capability must be genuinely long-range, and it has to be applied close during the attempt with the reason named.
entries.userBenefit: Having the range to go far makes distant options feel like the point. Pointing the same capability at productive nearby ground usually pays you more.
entries.mechanismConnection: Thalassarche melanophris uses the same dynamic-soaring machinery as circumpolar albatrosses but concentrates foraging on productive continental shelf waters near its colonies.

entries.title: Do Not Go Looking
entries.objective: A dead leaf mantis does not hunt by searching. Its body is shaped and coloured as dried foliage, and that only works where it is already standing; walking the forest looking for prey would destroy the one asset it has. So it holds position and lets the forest bring food past, spending almost nothing for days. Its principle is Perfect Stillness. The metaphor? When your advantage is where you are, searching is what loses it.
entries.animalRule: No searching may happen during the attempt, and the position held has to be the one where the advantage already exists.
entries.userBenefit: Going out to look for something destroys the advantage of already being in the right place, and you pay for the search as well. Holding position costs nothing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Deroplatys desiccata depends on cryptic resemblance to leaf litter that functions only while stationary, so it ambushes from a held position rather than foraging actively.

entries.title: Do Not Pick a Depth
entries.objective: Most ducks pick a depth: dabblers work the surface and the first few centimetres, divers go under and stay. A red-crested pochard does not really commit to either, feeding on the surface, upending like a mallard, and making short shallow dives, which puts it across a band of the water column that other species split between them. That breadth is the competence the bright head is attached to. Its principle is Styled Competence. The metaphor? Refuse to specialise to one level and you cover the band others divide.
entries.animalRule: Real work must happen at both levels during the attempt, and neither may be delegated.
entries.userBenefit: Specialising to one level means the band next to it belongs to someone else. Working both yourself means the whole middle is yours.
entries.mechanismConnection: Netta rufina feeds by surface dabbling, upending and short shallow diving, covering a water-column band that dabbling and diving ducks otherwise partition between them.

entries.title: Do Not Present a Shape
entries.objective: The thing a bird searches for is a moth shape: a triangle of wing with a body at the front. Plume moths do not present one. The wings are cleft along their length into narrow lobes fringed with long scales, so each wing is a set of separate feathery plumes rather than a continuous membrane, and at rest they roll tight. There is no outline to match. Its principle is Withered-Stalk Rest. The metaphor? Hiding inside the expected shape still gets you found. Present no shape at all.
entries.animalRule: The thing must be broken into parts that no longer read as one recognisable item, and it must not simply be hidden or moved somewhere less visible.
entries.userBenefit: Hiding something whole means it is still one findable thing the moment anyone looks. Breaking the outline means nothing you own matches the shape people are searching for.
entries.mechanismConnection: Platyptilia carduidactyla has wings deeply cleft into narrow fringed lobes that roll tightly at rest, eliminating the continuous triangular wing outline that visually hunting predators search for.

entries.title: Do Not Start Until Year Twenty
entries.objective: A radiated tortoise plays an extremely long game. It does not begin breeding until somewhere between its fifteenth and twentieth year, and then continues for a very long time; one individual given to a Tongan royal family in the eighteenth century died in 1965 at an age estimated around 188. That strategy works where adult survival is nearly certain, because a late start costs little if the lifetime is long. Its principle is Shell Radiance. The metaphor? A very late start is affordable only if survival until then is close to certain; check that first.
entries.animalRule: Survival to the payoff must be established as near-certain before committing during the attempt, and what secures it has to be named.
entries.userBenefit: A long slow approach is excellent if you are certain to still be there, and ruinous if not. Naming what secures your survival decides which.
entries.mechanismConnection: Astrochelys radiata delays first reproduction to between fifteen and twenty years with extreme longevity, a strategy dependent on very high adult survival probability.

entries.title: Do Not Stir the Water You Are Reading
entries.objective: A Russian desman reads a muddy river through a long touch-sensitive snout and whiskers, because vision is useless there. That only works if the water stays still enough to read, which is why its webbed feet and flattened tail produce smooth controlled swimming with almost no turbulence. The way it moves is designed around not spoiling its own instrument. Its principle is River-Snouted Sensing. The metaphor? Move in a way that does not disturb the thing you are trying to sense.
entries.animalRule: Your approach may not disturb the thing being assessed during the attempt, and the assessment has to happen while it is still undisturbed.
entries.userBenefit: Arriving loudly to find out what is going on changes what is going on, and then you are reading your own effect. A quiet approach shows you the real thing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Desmana moschata probes riverbed substrate with a vibration-sensitive proboscis while swimming smoothly on webbed hindfeet and a laterally flattened tail to avoid generating turbulence.

entries.title: Do One Task at Changing Light
entries.objective: Work at dawn or dusk and notice what the changing light makes easier.
entries.animalRule: It must happen while the light is actually changing; full daylight or full dark ends the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: You discover that one recurring task genuinely belongs at an hour you never do it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Zander — Hunting, twilight and turbid: at dawn, dusk and in coloured water it hunts prey fish that cannot see it coming, holding the sensory advantage entirely to itself. This Trial translates that twilight advantage into one ordinary task moved to the hour the light is turning.

entries.title: Dodge Ten Rolled Sock Balls in Thirty Seconds
entries.objective: Evade ten soft sock balls thrown at you in a thirty-second burst.
entries.animalRule: You may not leave the circle or catch the socks; only dodging counts, and throws stay below the shoulders.
entries.userBenefit: A fast, funny burst of agility that gets the heart going.
entries.mechanismConnection: Tui — Burst • Claim • Evade: Prosthemadera novaeseelandiae defends nectar trees with fast, explosive flights, chasing off rival birds and twisting away from attackers with sudden bursts and loud wingbeats made by a notch in its outer flight feathers. This Trial translates that explosive evasive manoeuvre when rivals dive in into thirty seconds of dodging ten sock balls inside a small circle.

entries.title: Dodge Three Noodle Strikes Then Tag the Head
entries.objective: Draw three strikes from a partner's pool noodle with feints, dodge them all, then close in and tag a sticker on their hat within thirty seconds.
entries.animalRule: The partner's feet stay planted and strikes stay below the shoulders; you must draw and dodge three strikes before closing in, and a hit means you restart.
entries.userBenefit: A fast, laughing reflex duel with nothing sharp involved.
entries.mechanismConnection: Egyptian Mongoose — Feinting • Explosive • Close-quarter: Herpestes ichneumon meets a venomous snake with quick feints and sidesteps that draw strikes and then closes with a bite to the head, relying on speed first and only partial venom resistance second. This Trial translates that feint, dodge and close sequence into drawing three noodle strikes before tagging the partner's hat.

entries.title: Dodge Three Surprise Cues
entries.objective: Ask someone to give three unpredictable visual cues while you stand in a clear area; sidestep immediately on each cue.
entries.animalRule: No countdowns are allowed and each sidestep must begin on the cue, not before it; keep the movement area clear.
entries.userBenefit: Three reactions to things you could not predict, which is the only kind worth training.
entries.mechanismConnection: Long-legged Fly uses this mode by launches within about five thousandths of a second of detecting a looming object by acting on an incomplete early visual signal, so the escape is committed before the image the eye is forming has been finished

entries.title: Dodge Wall Taps With a Blinking Torch Spot
entries.objective: For one minute, keep a torch spot on a wall from being tapped by a helper by switching it off and relighting it somewhere new.
entries.animalRule: The spot may only move while it is off, and the torch always points at the wall: once lit, it stays still until you click it away.
entries.userBenefit: A fast, funny reaction game for two that sharpens anticipation.
entries.mechanismConnection: Flashlight Fish — Sudden • Masked • Evasive: Anomalops katoptron can rotate its light organs out of sight in an instant, vanishing and reappearing elsewhere so a pursuing predator loses track of where it actually is. This Trial translates that light organ shut off and relit to mislead a pursuer into a torch spot switched off and relit elsewhere to dodge a helper's taps.

entries.title: Dormant Most of the Year
entries.objective: A Mourning Cloak emerges in midsummer, flies for a few weeks, then goes dormant in a hollow tree or under loose bark for the rest of the summer and the whole winter, reappearing on the first warm days of spring. It is an adult for most of a year and active for a small fraction of it. The dormancy is not failure, it is the design. Its principle is Seasonal Adaptability Strategy. The metaphor? Being dormant most of the time is a valid shape. Stop treating the quiet months as lost.
entries.animalRule: The thing must be formally parked with a stated wake date rather than abandoned or left open, and the guilt has to be explicitly discharged by saying it is parked.
entries.userBenefit: Things left open but not progressing cost you guilt every week and produce nothing. Formally parking one with a wake date removes the guilt and loses you nothing real.
entries.mechanismConnection: Nymphalis antiopa overwinters as an adult in sheltered cavities and also aestivates through late summer, spending the majority of its long adult life dormant and flying only briefly in summer and early spring.

entries.title: Dormant Today, All of It Later
entries.objective: Heloderma horridum barely operates most of the year. It spends most of its life in burrows and is active for only a few weeks, feeding heavily on eggs and nestlings when they are available and then going quiet, which is what makes a slow venom delivery and a slow body viable at all. Nothing about it is built for frequent effort. Its principle is Beaded Slow Venom. The metaphor? Be dormant on purpose, then take everything.
entries.animalRule: Not one minute goes to the activity today, and the single future window is written down with a date and a time.
entries.userBenefit: Daily nibbling at something keeps it permanently open in your head while never finishing it. Stopping entirely and taking it in one window later frees the attention it has been costing you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Heloderma horridum spends most of the year inactive in burrows, surfacing for only a few weeks to feed heavily on eggs and nestlings.

entries.title: Double the Weight Before the Crossing
entries.objective: A wagtail weighs about twenty grams and crosses the Sahara twice a year, and it cannot feed or drink on the way, so the crossing is funded entirely in advance. At stopover sites either side of the desert the birds feed intensively for days or weeks, laying down fat that can approach their own lean body weight, and only then depart. The preparation is longer than the crossing. Its principle is Trans-Sahara Stopover. The metaphor? The hard stretch is short and cannot be resupplied. Spend much longer loading than crossing.
entries.animalRule: Preparation must take longer than the stretch itself, and nothing may be added once the stretch begins.
entries.userBenefit: Preparing for the same length as the task means you arrive short and improvise through the hard part. Loading for longer than the crossing takes is what makes it uneventful for you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Motacilla flava undergoes hyperphagia at stopover sites either side of the Sahara, accumulating fat reserves approaching lean body mass before non-stop desert crossings during which it cannot feed.

entries.title: Double the Weight on One Aphid
entries.objective: Most small migrants cross Europe and the Sahara in stages, stopping repeatedly to refuel. The sedge warbler does it in one flight, and it pays for that by gorging on a single food: at particular reedbeds in late summer the plum-reed aphid swarms, and the bird feeds on almost nothing else until its weight climbs from about eleven grams to over twenty. One narrow window funds the entire journey. Its principle is Reedweave. The metaphor? Load up completely at the one source.
entries.animalRule: Only the single source may be used today, every other opportunity has to be declined, and the amount accumulated must be recorded.
entries.userBenefit: Grazing across several sources during a narrow rich window means you leave it with nowhere near enough to carry you. Going exclusive for the window is what lets you clear a whole stretch in one go.
entries.mechanismConnection: Acrocephalus schoenobaenus hyperphagously feeds on swarming plum-reed aphids at specific reedbeds, nearly doubling body mass to fuel a single trans-Saharan flight.

entries.title: Down Behind the Backwash
entries.objective: A sanderling feeds in one narrow band: the wet sand uncovered as each wave drains back, where crabs and worms are briefly near the surface. It runs down behind the backwash, probes fast, and sprints up ahead of the next wave, and because every wave resets the zone the whole thing becomes a series of timed dashes. The window is seconds and it repeats endlessly. Its principle is Wave-Line Timing. The metaphor? Work the seconds-long window immediately behind the thing that just passed, and be out before the next.
entries.animalRule: The work must begin immediately after the thing passes during the attempt, and you have to be clear before the next one rather than caught in it.
entries.userBenefit: Waiting for a calm moment that never comes means the window behind each disruption goes unused. Moving in right after one passes gets you the whole band nobody else works.
entries.mechanismConnection: Calidris alba forages in the swash zone immediately behind each receding wave, probing exposed invertebrates and retreating ahead of the next breaker.

entries.title: Down the Trunk Head-First
entries.objective: Neofelis nebulosa has ankle joints that rotate far beyond any other cat's, which lets it come down a trunk head-first, move along the underside of a branch and hang by its hind feet alone. With short legs, a very long counterweight tail and a body of only fifteen to twenty kilograms, that is what makes a genuinely arboreal predator possible at a size where most cats are stuck on the ground. Its principle is Canopy Range. The metaphor? Change the joint, not the strength.
entries.animalRule: The stairs are descended facing upwards with a hand on the rail each time, and the task is genuinely begun from its far end.
entries.userBenefit: Approaching everything from the same end is why some tasks have stayed impossible for you for years. Reversing the direction often turns out to cost nothing and removes the blockage entirely.
entries.mechanismConnection: Neofelis nebulosa has exceptionally rotatable ankle joints letting it descend trunks head-first and hang by its hind feet, with a long tail acting as counterweight.

entries.title: Downward, Not Sideways
entries.objective: Several wading birds find food by touch in shallow water, and the difference here is the axis. An avocet sweeps sideways through the water column and a spoonbill snaps on contact, while an ibis goes downward: the bill is driven into soft sediment and worked below the surface, hunting things that are buried rather than suspended. The curve is what lets it work at depth. Its principle is Crimson Utility. The metaphor? Change the axis of your search and you are hunting a different population entirely.
entries.animalRule: The axis must genuinely change during the attempt, and the different population reached has to be named.
entries.userBenefit: Searching along the same axis as everyone else means you compete for the same population. Turning it ninety degrees finds one nobody is working.
entries.mechanismConnection: Eudocimus ruber probes its decurved bill vertically into soft sediment to take buried infauna, rather than sweeping laterally through the water column.

entries.title: Dozens of Species, One Warning
entries.objective: A velvet ant is a wingless female wasp that must cross open ground in daylight, so being not worth eating is the only option. The defences stack: a cuticle far harder to puncture than other insects her size, a long mobile sting, a squeak, an odour. What makes it cheap is the colouring, shared by dozens of related species, so any predator's bad experience protects all of them. Its principle is Aposematism. The metaphor? Join a warning people already recognise.
entries.animalRule: The signal must be one already widely recognised rather than newly created, and it has to be actually adopted during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Inventing your own signal means teaching everyone what it means first. Adopting one people already recognise works for you from the first moment.
entries.mechanismConnection: Dasymutilla species participate in a large Mullerian mimicry ring sharing a common aposematic colour pattern, so predator learning from any member confers protection on all.

entries.title: Dozens Together, Motionless
entries.objective: By day a coelacanth rests in volcanic caves along the steep slopes of the Comoros coast, sometimes dozens of individuals together, motionless in cold water. There is no territoriality and no competition for the space, because the resting state costs nothing and the caves are not a contested resource for animals that are not feeding. Its principle is Living Relic. The metaphor? Where the activity costs nothing, sharing the space costs nothing either, so stop defending it.
entries.animalRule: The defence must actually stop during the attempt, and others have to be permitted into the space.
entries.userBenefit: Defending a space your activity does not actually consume costs you attention for nothing. Letting others in loses you nothing and buys goodwill.
entries.mechanismConnection: Latimeria chalumnae aggregates non-territorially in volcanic cave refuges by day, dozens of individuals resting motionless without competition.

entries.title: Drag the Wing, Lead Them Off
entries.objective: Charadrius melodus nests on open sand in a scrape with no cover, and the eggs are speckled so exactly like the surrounding shell and pebble that they are effectively invisible until stepped on. That half works against eyes. Against a predator already too close, the bird switches: it runs from the nest dragging one wing as though broken, calling, staying just within reach, and leads the intruder away before flying off unharmed. The calibration is what keeps it alive. Its principle is Beach Discretion. The metaphor? When hiding fails, draw them off yourself.
entries.animalRule: What you offer has to be genuinely real rather than a lie, and you stay with it until attention has moved away from the protected thing.
entries.userBenefit: Denying or deflecting makes people more curious about the thing you were protecting. Offering something real and nearby instead moves attention away without anyone noticing that a defence happened at all.
entries.mechanismConnection: Charadrius melodus abandons its cryptic sand scrape when a predator comes too close and performs a broken-wing distraction display, staying within reach to lead the intruder away.

entries.title: Drain One Glass Through a Coffee Stirrer
entries.objective: Finish a whole glass of water through the thinnest straw you have, drawing slowly and steadily without moving from your seat.
entries.animalRule: The glass stays on the table and your elbows stay planted until the last drop is gone.
entries.userBenefit: A slow, full glass of water you would otherwise not have drunk.
entries.mechanismConnection: Northern Flatid Planthopper — Still • Pale • Sap-feeding: Adults and waxy nymphs of Flatormenis proxima settle on a single twig for long spells, drawing plant sap through fine piercing mouthparts while staying motionless, so their pale, flattened bodies draw no attention. This Trial translates that long, still feeding through a fine tube into draining a glass through a coffee stirrer without moving.

entries.title: Draw One Shell With a Band Per Year
entries.objective: Draw a clam shell with one growth band for every year of a real span of at least ten years, wide in the early years and tightly packed later.
entries.animalRule: One band per year of your chosen span, the spacing shrinking steadily, and every fifth band numbered.
entries.userBenefit: A calm drawing that turns your own years into something you can see at a glance.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ocean Quahog — Filtering • Burrowed • Slow-growing: Arctica islandica lays down one growth band in its shell each year, growing quickly in its first years and then almost stopping, which is how ages of several centuries have been read from its shells. This Trial translates that annual banding, wide early and tightly packed later, into a drawn shell with one band for every year of a real span you choose.

entries.title: Draw One Sock Ball Round a Hose S-Bend
entries.objective: Show that only a curved probe can reach round an S-bend by failing with a straight one, then drawing a sock ball out with a bent wire.
entries.animalRule: The hose stays in its S on the floor: no lifting, tipping or shaking, and only the curved probe may bring the sock out.
entries.userBenefit: A gentle dexterity puzzle that rewards patience over force.
entries.mechanismConnection: Brown Sicklebill — Cryptic • Curved • Concealed: Epimachus meyeri uses its long, strongly curved bill to probe into bark crevices, moss and epiphytes for insects while its dark plumage blends into the dense forest around it. This Trial translates that curved probe reaching into bent, hidden spaces into drawing a sock ball round a hose's S-bend with a curved wire after a straight tool fails.

entries.title: Draw Six Yellow Dots in Six Marking Morphs
entries.objective: Mark six yellow paper dots with six different spider-style marking patterns so that no two look alike.
entries.animalRule: Every dot must carry a different marking pattern: variety is the defence.
entries.userBenefit: A playful bit of design that shows how variety can hide a whole group.
entries.mechanismConnection: Happy-face Spider — Subtle • Persistent • Noticed: Theridion grallator has a translucent yellow body whose dark and red markings vary strongly between individuals, a polymorphism thought to stop birds forming a single search image for the spider. This Trial translates that inherited variety of body markings that defeats a predator's search image into six yellow dots marked in six different patterns.

entries.title: Draw the Head Into a Cone
entries.objective: An insect resting on a grass blade has the wrong shape. The head is a blunt block at right angles to the body, which reads as an animal however well the colour matches. In the slant-faced grasshoppers the head is drawn out into a cone with the face sloping back, so head and body form one continuous line along the blade. The outline, not the colour, was the problem. Its principle is Starlit Crossing. The metaphor? One part sticking out at the wrong angle gives the whole thing away. Line it up.
entries.animalRule: Only the misaligned element may change and everything else must stay as it is, with the alignment completed during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: One element at the wrong angle makes your whole thing look careless however good the rest is. Bringing just that into line takes minutes and changes how all of it reads.
entries.mechanismConnection: Slant-faced acridids have an elongated conical head with an obliquely sloping face, producing a continuous linear outline with the body that matches the grass blades they rest on.

entries.title: Drift Head-Down on the Current
entries.objective: A coelacanth runs one of the lowest metabolic rates measured in a fish of its size, and both of its states are built around spending nothing. By day it rests in volcanic caves along steep slopes, sometimes dozens together, motionless in cold water. By night it does not swim but drifts, carried head-down along the slope by the current, using a rostral organ to detect prey. Its principle is Living Relic. The metaphor? Let the current move you and spend your attention on detection instead.
entries.animalRule: No self-propulsion may be used during the attempt, and effort has to go into detection instead.
entries.userBenefit: Spending your effort on movement means arriving with nothing left to notice anything. Letting the current carry you puts all of it into detection.
entries.mechanismConnection: Latimeria chalumnae drifts passively head-down on slope currents at night while using an electroreceptive rostral organ to detect prey, with an exceptionally low metabolic rate.

entries.title: Drift Thousands of Kilometres
entries.objective: A loggerhead runs on a timescale almost nothing else in the ocean uses. Hatchlings enter the gyre system and spend years drifting with currents that carry them thousands of kilometres for very little swimming effort, feeding on what the same currents concentrate. Navigation comes from a magnetic sense precise enough to encode position, letting an adult return to its natal region decades later. Its principle is Ocean Continuance. The metaphor? Let the current carry you for years while you keep an exact record of where you are.
entries.animalRule: No steering may occur during the attempt, and a precise record of position has to be maintained.
entries.userBenefit: Steering a process you could drift with costs you effort for the same destination. Keeping the record is what lets you come back to the right place.
entries.mechanismConnection: Caretta caretta juveniles drift passively in oceanic gyres for years at minimal locomotor cost while a magnetic positional sense permits natal homing decades later.

entries.title: Drink Without Lifting Your Head
entries.objective: Almost every bird drinks by taking water in the bill and tipping the head back to let gravity carry it down, which means repeatedly breaking off to look up. Pigeons and doves do not: they immerse the bill and pump, drawing a continuous draught in a few seconds without raising the head at all. The whole act is finished before most birds have taken their second sip. Its principle is Soft Collar Calm. The metaphor? Stop breaking off every few seconds. Take it in one continuous draw and be finished.
entries.animalRule: The thing must be completed in one continuous unbroken run with no checking or breaking off, and it has to be something you normally do in pieces.
entries.userBenefit: Doing something in interrupted sips means you pay the re-entry cost every time and it stretches across your day. One continuous draw finishes it in a fraction of the total.
entries.mechanismConnection: Columbidae drink by immersing the bill and using pharyngeal pumping to draw a continuous draught, uniquely among birds not requiring head elevation and gravity between mouthfuls.

entries.title: Drive It With the Neck
entries.objective: A pig's snout disc is stiffened by a small separate bone found in no other mammal group, and behind it sits a neck heavy enough to drive that disc under roots and stones and lever them up. The tool at the end is useless without the mass behind it. The Red River Hog does not pry with its face; it pushes with its whole body through a hardened tip. Its principle is Rooting Confidence. The metaphor? A sharp point with nothing behind it bounces off. Put your weight behind the tool.
entries.animalRule: The tool or approach must stay the same and only the weight behind it may increase, which has to be a real resource rather than more intention.
entries.userBenefit: Nudging at something repeatedly with small efforts is why it has not moved and you think the approach is wrong. The same approach with real weight behind it usually shifts it first try.
entries.mechanismConnection: Potamochoerus porcus has a rostral bone supporting a hardened snout disc and heavy cervical musculature that drives it beneath roots and stones, levering material up by body mass rather than by jaw force.

entries.title: Drive Them Into the Shallows
entries.objective: A pelican's pouch is a volume scoop, and a volume scoop is nearly useless on scattered fish because it takes whatever happens to be in the water it closes on. So Great White Pelicans form lines and horseshoes and swim forward together, pushing fish ahead of them into the shallows until the water is crowded enough that one scoop pays. The concentration is made, not found. Its principle is Scoop Strategy. The metaphor? Stop scooping at scattered things. Herd them together first.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be actioned until everything has been gathered into a single place, and the work must then happen in one pass rather than being spread out again.
entries.userBenefit: Doing scattered things where they lie means you pay the setup cost over and over. Herding them into one place first feels like a delay and then the whole job takes a fraction of the time.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pelecanus onocrotalus feeds by engulfing a volume of water in its gular pouch, which is only productive on concentrated prey, so groups swim in coordinated lines and horseshoes herding fish into shallow water before scooping.

entries.title: Drive Them Under the Layer
entries.objective: A murre hunts by wing-propelled diving, pursuing fish underwater rather than waiting for them, and it works below the layer where surface feeders operate, reaching prey that has already been driven down by everything hunting from above. The pressure others create is what puts the fish where it can take them. Its principle is Two-World Discipline. The metaphor? Work the level everyone else's activity drives things down into.
entries.animalRule: The level must be one that other activity drives things into, and it has to be named before working there during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Competing at the surface puts you against everyone. Working the level their activity pushes things into gives you what they displaced for free.
entries.mechanismConnection: Uria aalge pursues fish by wing-propelled diving well below the depths worked by surface-feeding seabirds, exploiting prey displaced downward by that surface pressure.

entries.title: Drop From the Perch, Take Anything
entries.objective: A Galapagos hawk hunts from perches and on the soar over open lava, dropping onto lava lizards, centipedes, young iguanas and rats, and it takes carrion and seabird scraps without hesitation. Nothing is beneath it and nothing is specialised for, because on islands this bare the next opportunity may be very different from the last. Its principle is High Island Watch. The metaphor? From a good vantage, commit to whatever actually appears rather than waiting for the kind you had in mind.
entries.animalRule: The opportunity taken may not be the kind you were expecting during the attempt, and no hesitation may occur once it appears.
entries.userBenefit: Holding out from a good position for the kind of opportunity you pictured means watching real ones go past. Taking what appears is what the vantage was for.
entries.mechanismConnection: Buteo galapagoensis hunts from perches and in soaring flight, taking lava lizards, invertebrates, juvenile iguanas, rodents and carrion opportunistically.

entries.title: Drop the Copy Where It Fails
entries.objective: In the north, where the pipevine swallowtail is absent, this butterfly stops mimicking it entirely and carries a bold white band instead. Copying an absent model protects nothing, so the copy is abandoned rather than carried out of habit. The same species, two completely different presentations, each matched to what the local birds have learned. Its principle is Adaptive Mimicry Strategy. The metaphor? A borrowed form that nobody here recognises is pure cost. Drop it and look like yourself.
entries.animalRule: The convention must be genuinely unrewarded in this specific context rather than merely disliked, and it has to be actually dropped during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Carrying a convention into a context that does not reward it costs you effort and signals that you have not read the room. Dropping it frees the effort and fits better.
entries.mechanismConnection: Limenitis arthemis arthemis loses the Batesian mimicry of Battus philenor in northern parts of its range where the model is absent, displaying a conspicuous white band instead.

entries.title: Drop the Disguise on Time
entries.objective: The Ant Mimic Mantis is a convincing ant only as an early nymph. At later instars it stops: the mimicry is abandoned because size alone now defends it, and continuing to look like an ant would cost without paying. The disguise has an expiry date built in. Its principle is Trail-Worker Disguise. The metaphor? The borrowed identity that protected you early starts to limit you. Drop it when it has done its job.
entries.animalRule: The borrowed framing must be genuinely dropped in a real interaction rather than resolved to drop later, and nothing may be substituted for it.
entries.userBenefit: A borrowed framing that got you taken seriously early starts to cap how people see you. Dropping it once is uncomfortable and usually reveals that you needed it less than you thought.
entries.mechanismConnection: Odontomantis planiceps abandons ant mimicry at later instars once body size itself deters predators, as maintaining the morphology and gait would carry costs without further protective benefit.

entries.title: Drop the Pressure, Not the Distance
entries.objective: A giant grouper can exceed two metres and a quarter of a tonne, and it feeds without chasing anything. Holding position near a cave mouth costs it very little, and capture is hydraulics: the mouth and opercular cavity expand fast enough to drop the pressure inside, so water carrying whatever was in front of it is pulled in before the prey can turn. Its principle is Quiet Mass. The metaphor? Create the conditions that bring it to you rather than closing the distance.
entries.animalRule: No distance may be closed during the attempt, and the pulling condition has to be actually created.
entries.userBenefit: Closing the distance yourself warns whatever you are approaching and it is gone. Creating the pull brings it to you before it can react.
entries.mechanismConnection: Epinephelus lanceolatus feeds by rapid buccal and opercular expansion generating a negative pressure gradient that draws prey in before it can initiate an escape response.

entries.title: Drop the Rate and Wait It Out
entries.objective: A reef flat at low tide is one of the harshest places in the sea: pools isolate, water warms, oxygen falls towards nothing over hours. Most fish leave or die. The Brownbanded Bamboo Shark does neither. It suppresses its metabolic rate dramatically, reduces brain activity to a minimum, and survives hours in water with almost no dissolved oxygen until the tide returns. Its principle is Steady Patience. The metaphor? Some bad stretches cannot be fixed or escaped. Drop your rate and wait them out.
entries.animalRule: The reduction must be deliberate and stated rather than drifting into doing less, and an end point has to be named for when normal rate resumes.
entries.userBenefit: Fighting a stretch you cannot change burns the reserves you will need afterwards. Deliberately dropping your rate with a stated end point gets you through intact instead of wrecked.
entries.mechanismConnection: Chiloscyllium punctatum survives hours of near-anoxia in isolated warm tide pools by profoundly suppressing metabolic rate and reducing neural activity until tidal flow returns.

entries.title: Drop the Stealth You Do Not Need
entries.objective: Most owls pay for silence with comb-like feather serrations that break up the airflow. Fish owls have largely given those up, because a fish under the surface cannot hear an approaching bird anyway. What they carry instead is bare legs and rough spiculed toes that hold a slippery fish. Dropping the useless advantage is what paid for the useful one. Its principle is Waterside Listening. The metaphor? Stop paying for an edge that does nothing here. Drop it.
entries.animalRule: The precaution must be named out loud and genuinely dropped not just skipped quietly, and the task must be completed without it in the same take.
entries.userBenefit: You keep paying for a habit that was useful somewhere else. Naming the one that buys nothing here and dropping it frees up the effort for the thing that actually decides the outcome.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ketupa ketupu has largely lost the flight-feather serrations that silence other owls and has a reduced facial disc, because submerged fish cannot hear an approaching bird; instead it carries bare unfeathered legs and spicule-covered toe undersides that grip slippery prey snatched from the surface.

entries.title: Drop the Temperature and Wait
entries.objective: When Madagascar turns cool and dry a common tenrec does not try to keep going at a lower rate. It buries into leaf litter and enters extended torpor, letting its body temperature and metabolism fall for weeks until the food comes back. The low gear is a genuine shutdown, not a reduced version of normal running. Its principle is Many-Form Survival. The metaphor? When the season is bad, shut it down properly rather than running it badly for months.
entries.animalRule: The shutdown must be complete rather than a reduction during the attempt, and the restart condition has to be stated.
entries.userBenefit: Running something at half capacity through a bad season costs you most of what full running would and returns almost nothing. A real shutdown with a restart condition costs you nothing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Tenrec ecaudatus enters prolonged torpor buried in leaf litter during cool dry periods, substantially lowering body temperature and metabolic rate until food availability returns.

entries.title: Drop Twenty Peas Before the Leaking Cup Drains
entries.objective: Fill a leaking paper cup and drop twenty dried peas into it, one at a time with a croak for each, before the water falls to the leak.
entries.animalRule: The pool opens once: no refilling, and a pea only counts if it lands while the water is still above the hole.
entries.userBenefit: A frantic, noisy twenty-second race that is genuinely hard to win.
entries.mechanismConnection: X-marked Snouted Tree Frog — Chorusing • Spawning • Rain-triggered: Scinax x-signatus waits for heavy rain to fill temporary pools, then males gather and call in chorus and pairs spawn quickly, racing to lay eggs while short-lived water lasts. This Trial translates that rain-triggered rush to call and spawn before a temporary pool dries into a croaking race to lay twenty pea eggs in a leaking cup before it drains.

entries.title: Drought Leaves Only the Hard Seeds
entries.objective: After rain the Galapagos is full of small soft seeds and almost any beak will do. In drought the small seeds are eaten out and what is left is large hard fruit like caltrop, which only the deeper beaks can crack. The same inherited beak that was irrelevant in the good year decides who eats in the bad one. Its principle is Beak-Fit Island Thinking. The metaphor? Know which of your tools cracks hard things.
entries.animalRule: The capability must be one that is irrelevant in good conditions, and it has to be used on something genuinely hard.
entries.userBenefit: Spending good conditions on easy work leaves you unsure which of your abilities actually holds up when things get hard. Testing the hard-conditions one now means you know what you have before you need it.
entries.mechanismConnection: In Geospiza fortis beak depth is highly heritable, and during drought only deeper-beaked birds crack the large hard Tribulus fruits that remain.

entries.title: Drum From the Same Log Every Time
entries.objective: A ruffed grouse lives in thick young forest where sound travels badly and being seen is dangerous. Its solution is not a call: the male stands on a chosen log and beats his wings hard enough to create pressure pulses, starting slowly and accelerating into a very low thumping that passes through vegetation better than song. The same log is used repeatedly. Its principle is Signal. The metaphor? Give your signal a fixed address.
entries.animalRule: The place must be fixed and reusable during the attempt, and people have to be told it is the address.
entries.userBenefit: A signal arriving from somewhere different each time makes people hunt for it and miss some of yours. A fixed address means they always know where to look.
entries.mechanismConnection: Bonasa umbellus males drum by wing-generated pressure pulses from a specific repeatedly used log, producing low-frequency sound that propagates through dense vegetation.

entries.title: Drum One Message Through a Surface
entries.objective: Send an agreed message through a wall or floor by drumming alone.
entries.animalRule: Only the drumming may cross; a word or a glance through the doorway ends the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: You end up with a signal that works through a closed door, which is more useful than it sounds.
entries.mechanismConnection: Greater Mouse-deer — Drumming, rapid and signalling: alarmed or in display it beats its hooves against the ground at several strikes a second, producing a low drumming that carries through vegetation. This Trial translates that transmitted drumming into a message sent through a wall or floor.

entries.title: Duet to Space the Ground
entries.objective: A Red-legged Seriema is a predatory bird that has largely given up flight, walking and running after snakes and lizards across open cerrado. Pairs hold territory by duetting: a loud rising and falling call delivered together, audible for kilometres, which spaces neighbouring pairs across the grassland without any of them meeting. The sound does the surveying. Its principle is Stride Voice. The metaphor? Boundaries nobody announces get tested constantly. Say where yours is, out loud, with your partner.
entries.animalRule: Both people must state it together rather than separately, and it has to be said to the people it applies to.
entries.userBenefit: A boundary mentioned by one of you separately reads as a personal preference and gets tested. Both of you saying it together reads as the rule and it stops being questioned.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cariama cristata pairs perform loud synchronised duets audible over kilometres, which establish and maintain spacing between neighbouring territories in open cerrado without physical encounters.

entries.title: Dust Every Leaf of One Houseplant
entries.objective: Clean every leaf of one houseplant in a single careful circuit around the pot.
entries.animalRule: Stay with the one plant, work around it in order without skipping, and do not damage a single healthy leaf.
entries.userBenefit: A healthier plant and a quietly satisfying bit of care.
entries.mechanismConnection: Red-spotted Guard Crab — Measured • Repeating • Patrol: Trapezia tigrina lives among the branches of one Pocillopora coral, patrolling it in careful, measured steps and clearing sediment and debris from its host while guarding it against coral-eating predators. This Trial translates that deliberate patrol that keeps one living host clean into a full, ordered circuit that dusts every leaf of one plant.

entries.title: Dust, Never Water
entries.objective: Chinchilla lanigera survives the cold arid Andes on a coat with dozens of hairs from each follicle instead of one, so dense that parasites cannot move through it and heat cannot escape. The density creates its own problem: a coat like that cannot dry if it gets wet, and would mat and be colonised. The answer is dust - fine volcanic ash that absorbs oils and lifts moisture out of the fur, substituting entirely for washing. Its principle is Soft Toughness. The metaphor? Dry-clean what water would ruin.
entries.animalRule: Water does not touch the item at any point, and the correct dry method has to be actually completed rather than only looked up.
entries.userBenefit: Cleaning delicate things the way you clean everything else is how you slowly destroy them and then replace them. Ten minutes learning the dry method saves the thing you already own.
entries.mechanismConnection: Chinchilla lanigera grows dozens of hairs per follicle, producing a pelt so dense it cannot dry once wet, so the animal cleans itself by rolling in fine volcanic dust.

entries.title: Each One Is a Whole Animal
entries.objective: This sea squirt, described only in 2024 from reefs off Kume Island, lives as a cluster of small glass-clear zooids joined only at their base. Each zooid is a complete filter-feeding animal in its own right: cilia draw water in through one siphon, a mucus sheet across the perforated pharynx traps plankton, and the water leaves through a second. The colony is a shared footing, not a shared body. Its principle is Patterned Colony. The metaphor? Join at the base, stay complete.
entries.animalRule: Your own version must be complete end to end, and the connection has to be reduced to the shared footing.
entries.userBenefit: Becoming a part rather than a whole in a collaboration means you cannot function if it ends, and everyone knows it. Keeping your own complete version lets you join things without becoming dependent on them.
entries.mechanismConnection: Clavelina ossipandae forms colonies of individually complete filter-feeding zooids united only at their basal stolons.

entries.title: Earn the Trust You Will Spend
entries.objective: A fork-tailed drongo's whole living depends on meerkats and babblers trusting its alarms, and most of what it does is give genuine ones. The occasional false alarm only works because the overwhelming majority were real; the trust is a resource it has to keep topping up or the trick stops paying. Its principle is Mimicry Advantage. The metaphor? Spend trust only from a balance you have actually built, and keep adding to it far more often than you draw.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be drawn during the attempt, and the ratio of additions to withdrawals has to be noted.
entries.userBenefit: Drawing on people's trust more often than you add to it means it is gone precisely when you need it most. Keeping the ratio honest is what keeps it available.
entries.mechanismConnection: Dicrurus adsimilis gives predominantly honest alarm calls that establish host responsiveness, which its occasional deceptive calls exploit without eliminating.

entries.title: Ears at Different Heights
entries.objective: The structure of the hunt here is the same one every sit-and-wait owl uses, and the distinctive part is in the skull. In barn owls and their relatives the two ear openings are not symmetrical: one sits higher than the other, and the surrounding flaps face slightly different directions. That asymmetry matters because two level ears can only tell you left from right, whereas two ears at different heights resolve elevation too. Its principle is Reception. The metaphor? Deliberate asymmetry in your inputs is what gives you the dimension symmetry cannot.
entries.animalRule: The two sources must be deliberately asymmetric, and the difference between them has to be used during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Two matched sources tell you the same thing twice and you still cannot place it. Making them deliberately asymmetric adds a dimension you did not have.
entries.mechanismConnection: Tyto novaehollandiae has vertically asymmetric ear openings with differently oriented preaural flaps, so interaural differences encode elevation in addition to azimuth.

entries.title: Ease One Whole Orange Into a Child's Sock
entries.objective: Stretch a small, stretchy child's sock around a whole orange wider than its opening, then ease the orange back out with nothing torn or bruised.
entries.animalRule: Work slowly: no forcing or cutting, and the sock and orange must both come through unharmed.
entries.userBenefit: A slow, satisfying stretching puzzle with a genuinely surprising result.
entries.mechanismConnection: Black Swallower — Sparse • Opportunistic • All-in: Chiasmodon niger waits in the dark deep sea and can swallow prey more than twice its own length, its jaws, body wall and stomach stretching to hold it for slow digestion, though an oversized meal can also kill it. This Trial translates that careful distension around an oversized meal, with the risk understood, into stretching a small sock around a whole orange without a tear.

entries.title: Eat All Summer for One Winter
entries.objective: A Groundhog is a marmot that lives alone. Through the warm months it grazes almost continuously, and the entire point of that is fat, which by autumn can be a substantial fraction of body weight. Then it seals itself below the frost line and drops its body temperature to within a few degrees of the ground. Everything in the good season exists to fund the one that follows. Its principle is Winter Budget. The metaphor? Good months are not for enjoying. They are for funding the bad one.
entries.animalRule: The thing set aside must be genuinely reserved for a future hard period rather than general saving, and it has to be labelled with what it is for.
entries.userBenefit: Good weeks feel like your reward, so nothing gets stored and the bad week arrives empty. One deliberate reserve put aside while things are fine makes the hard stretch survivable rather than damaging.
entries.mechanismConnection: Marmota monax feeds almost continuously through summer to accumulate fat reserves that can reach a large fraction of body mass, then hibernates below the frost line with body temperature falling to near ambient.

entries.title: Eat Far Past Enough
entries.objective: Autumn hard mast, the acorns and beech nuts of temperate mountain forest, arrives in enormous quantity for a short period, and an Asiatic black bear eats far past what it needs in order to lay down fat. Where winters are severe that fat is the whole winter: the animal dens and runs for months without feeding. The year is loaded entirely at one end. Its principle is Mountain Strength. The metaphor? During the short abundance, deliberately take much more than you need.
entries.animalRule: More than current need must be taken during the attempt, and it has to be stored rather than used immediately.
entries.userBenefit: Taking only what you need during abundance means the lean months come out of your own reserves. Overtaking now is free and covers the whole gap.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ursus thibetanus hyperphagically exploits the brief autumn hard mast pulse to deposit fat reserves that sustain months of winter denning without feeding.

entries.title: Eat From the Web Without Being Caught
entries.objective: Some of the common scorpionfly's best meals hang in spider webs. It climbs into the web, feeds on the insects trapped there, and gets out, taking the product of someone else's trap without being the thing the trap was built for. Walking into a snare on purpose is the hardest part and the whole opportunity. Its principle is Misleading Tail. The metaphor? Take what the trap caught, carefully.
entries.animalRule: An exit condition must be stated before entering, only the stated thing may be taken, and the exit has to happen immediately after.
entries.userBenefit: Avoiding situations entirely because they catch people means you never touch the things they have caught. A stated exit condition lets you go in, take the one thing, and get out intact.
entries.mechanismConnection: Panorpa communis enters spider webs to feed on ensnared insects, exploiting the web's catch while avoiding capture itself.

entries.title: Eat Leaves From One Host Only
entries.objective: Tune a whole meal to a single plant host and work leaf by leaf.
entries.animalRule: No second plant species may enter the plate during the Trial.
entries.userBenefit: You practice specialist focus by finishing one resource fully before switching.
entries.mechanismConnection: Leaf Beetle — Rhythmic • Plant-tuned • Surface-led: Chrysomelids pace daylight foraging and reproduction to host-plant growth, often feeding on one plant or a few related plants leaf by leaf. This Trial locks the meal to a single host plant surface.

entries.title: Eat One Snack Without Any Performance
entries.objective: Eat One Snack Without Any Performance.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be performed, posted or shared; it is just the snack.
entries.userBenefit: You turn courtship precision into one concrete experience with a visible finish.
entries.mechanismConnection: Red-capped Manakin — Feeding • Small • Fruit-eating: Away from the display perch it is an unremarkable small bird taking berries and insects in the understorey. This Trial translates that mechanism into one snack with no display.

entries.title: Eat Past Enough While It Lasts
entries.objective: An Asiatic black bear is built for the canopy as much as the ground: heavy forelimbs, curved claws and a frame light enough to climb well into mature trees, which is where its most important food is. Autumn hard mast, the acorns and chestnuts of mountain forest, arrives in enormous quantity for a short period, and the bear eats far past what it needs to lay down fat. Where winters are severe that fat is what the winter runs on. Its principle is Mountain Strength. The metaphor? Overeat the short season.
entries.animalRule: The taking must happen inside the short window and must exceed immediate need, and afterwards you live off the store rather than topping it up.
entries.userBenefit: Taking a sensible daily amount from something that will not last leaves you short when it ends. Loading up while it is abundant means the lean months cost you nothing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ursus thibetanus is strongly arboreal, climbing to exploit autumn hard mast and hyperphagically accumulating fat reserves that fund months of winter denning.

entries.title: Eat Ten Grapes Without a Single Sound
entries.objective: Take and eat ten grapes from a bowl, one at a time, without making any audible noise.
entries.animalRule: Feed quietly and unseen: no sound from bowl, hand or mouth.
entries.userBenefit: A calm, oddly focusing snack that slows you right down.
entries.mechanismConnection: Bare-necked Umbrellabird — Cryptic • Canopy • Forager: Outside short display bouts, male Cephalopterus glabricollis keep their crest and throat sac folded away and move quietly through dense canopy picking fruit and insects, staying inconspicuous and saving energy. This Trial translates that quiet, inconspicuous fruit foraging with the display packed away into ten grapes eaten without a sound.

entries.title: Eat the Base, Drop the Rest
entries.objective: A takahe lives on alpine tussock grassland so poor that most of each stem is not worth eating. Its solution is selective: it grips a tussock stem in one foot, pulls it out, and eats only the soft nutrient-rich base before dropping the rest, which produces the piles of discarded stems that are the clearest sign of its presence. Its principle is Grounded Thriving. The metaphor? Take only the nutritious part and discard the rest visibly, rather than working through all of it.
entries.animalRule: The discard must happen immediately during the attempt, and no attempt to use the remainder may be made.
entries.userBenefit: Working through all of something low-quality costs you the day for a fraction of the value. Taking the base and dropping the rest gets it in an hour.
entries.mechanismConnection: Porphyrio hochstetteri extracts tussock stems with one foot and consumes only the soft nutrient-rich basal section, discarding the remainder.

entries.title: Eat the Floor Itself
entries.objective: This deep-sea sea cucumber makes its living by eating the seafloor. Settled on soft sediment thousands of metres down, it sweeps the surface layer into its mouth with a ring of short tentacles and digests the organic particles mixed through it, and you can see the gut contents through its translucent body wall. It does not hunt anything. It processes the ground it is sitting on. Its principle is Glass-Bodied Drift. The metaphor? Process what is already underneath you.
entries.animalRule: No new input may be sought, and a measured amount of the existing accumulation has to be processed.
entries.userBenefit: Looking for new input while material piles up where you are means you own a lot and have used none of it. Processing a measured amount of the pile is where the value you already paid for is.
entries.mechanismConnection: Enypniastes eximia ingests surface sediment with oral tentacles and digests its contained organic particles, the gut contents visible through a translucent body wall.

entries.title: Eat the Glass and Poison
entries.objective: Sponges are everywhere on a reef and almost nothing eats them. They are laced with cytotoxic compounds and reinforced with needle-like silica spicules, so a fish taking a bite gets a mouthful of glass and poison. That is exactly why so much sponge biomass sits there available. The Blueface Angelfish is one of the few that can process it. Its principle is Color Signal Strategy. The metaphor? The abundant untouched thing is untouched for a reason. Solve the reason and it is all yours.
entries.animalRule: The specific reason others avoid it must be named and actually solved rather than tolerated, and something has to be taken from the resource during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Abundant things sit untouched because of one specific obstacle, not because they are worthless. Solving that obstacle once gives you a supply nobody is competing for.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pomacanthus xanthometopon is among the few reef fishes able to consume sponges, processing their cytotoxic secondary metabolites and siliceous spicules, giving access to an abundant and largely uncontested food source.

entries.title: Eat the One You Skip
entries.objective: On a floodplain the crab-eating fox works the shallows for crabs and amphibians in the wet season; when the water goes, more than half the diet can become fruit, alongside rodents, insects and carrion. Pairs hunt together and hold a shared range. The switch is not a fallback, it is the method, which is why the same pair holds ground from forest to savanna. Its principle is Generalism. The metaphor? Widen the list before you need it.
entries.animalRule: The ingredient must be one you normally ignore completely, it has to be a real portion rather than a taste, and it is eaten as part of a meal.
entries.userBenefit: Ignoring most of what is available means your options collapse whenever the usual thing is gone. Actually eating one of them widens what you can live on.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cerdocyon thous is an opportunistic omnivore whose diet shifts seasonally between crustaceans, amphibians, fruit, rodents and carrion across flooded and dry phases.

entries.title: Eat the Part Everyone Discards
entries.objective: A Spotted Hyena eats the part of a carcass worthless to everything else. Conical premolars behind enormous jaw muscles, on a skull built around a tall bony crest, crack limb bones nothing else on the savanna can open, and behind them sits a gut acid enough to break down the collagen inside, which is where most of the food in a bone actually is. Its principle is Bone Economy. The metaphor? The leftovers everyone walks past still contain most of the value. Get the equipment to open them.
entries.animalRule: The source must be something others have already finished with and discarded, and something genuinely useful has to come out of it rather than a confirmation that it was empty.
entries.userBenefit: What everyone else discarded is the only material nobody is competing over, and it usually still holds most of the value. Learning to open it gives you findings other people cannot get.
entries.mechanismConnection: Crocuta crocuta cracks long bones with conical premolars powered by massive jaw musculature on a sagittally crested skull, and digests the collagen within using exceptionally acidic gastric secretions.

entries.title: Eat the Part Nobody Else Can
entries.objective: What a greater honeyguide most wants from a bees' nest is the wax, a food almost no other bird can digest at all. It is not competing for the honey; it is taking the part everyone else leaves behind, which is why honey-hunters and the bird can share the same nest without either losing anything. Its principle is Guided Resource Call. The metaphor? Build yourself around the part of a resource nobody else can use, and the competition disappears.
entries.animalRule: The part taken must be one others discard during the attempt, and the contested part has to be left alone.
entries.userBenefit: Competing for the part everyone wants means paying the full price for a share. Taking what they throw away gets you something free and nobody notices you have it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Indicator indicator digests beeswax, a substrate almost no other bird can metabolise, so it consumes the comb that human honey-hunters discard.

entries.title: Eat the Poisonous Plant
entries.objective: Oleander is among the most poisonous garden plants in the world, carrying cardiac glycosides that are dangerous to a person and lethal to livestock. The Oleander Hawk-moth caterpillar eats it. Having solved that one chemical problem, it has access to an abundant ornamental plant growing everywhere that essentially nothing else will touch. Its principle is Night Garden. The metaphor? The abundant thing everyone avoids has one obstacle. Solve that and it is all yours.
entries.animalRule: The specific obstacle must be named and solved rather than worked around, and something has to be taken from the resource during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: An abundant resource nobody uses usually has exactly one obstacle in front of it, not many. Solving that single thing gives you a supply with no competition at all.
entries.mechanismConnection: Daphnis nerii larvae feed on Nerium oleander, tolerating its cardiac glycosides, which gives them near-exclusive access to an abundant ornamental host plant that almost no other herbivore can use.

entries.title: Eat the Thing Nobody Can Digest
entries.objective: Polystyrene resists breakdown for centuries. In 2015 researchers showed Mealworm Beetle larvae fed nothing but polystyrene foam survived, and isotope labelling proved the polymer was genuinely being broken down rather than passing through, by gut bacteria rather than the insect itself. A supply nothing else can use is uncontested forever. Its principle is Resourcefulness. The metaphor? The input everyone writes off is the one nobody is competing for. Digest it.
entries.animalRule: The input must be something genuinely treated as unusable by others, and the result has to be real value rather than the waste merely being disposed of neatly.
entries.userBenefit: You compete for inputs everyone wants and ignore the pile nobody will touch. Learning to get value from the written-off supply gives you a cheap source with no competition for it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Tenebrio molitor larvae degrade polystyrene via gut microbiota, with isotope labelling confirming the polymer carbon is mineralised to carbon dioxide and incorporated into biomass rather than passing through the gut unaltered.

entries.title: Eat the Tough Regrowth
entries.objective: Most reef herbivores take the soft turf algae. A handful handle the tough leathery brown weeds that grow back after a reef is damaged, and the Bluespine Unicornfish is one of them. That makes it structurally important out of all proportion to its numbers, because a reef losing its browsers is one where Sargassum takes hold and coral cannot recruit. Its principle is Reef Navigation. The metaphor? Everyone handles the easy regrowth. Take on the tough stuff that otherwise takes over.
entries.animalRule: The thing must be something regrowing after a previous problem rather than a fresh issue, and it has to be dealt with rather than tidied around.
entries.userBenefit: Everyone handles the easy regrowth and steps around the tough bit, which is the bit that eventually takes over your whole week. Dealing with that one thing is what stops it coming back.
entries.mechanismConnection: Naso unicornis browses tough leathery macroalgae including Sargassum and Turbinaria that most reef herbivores avoid, suppressing the algal regrowth that otherwise prevents coral recruitment after disturbance.

entries.title: Eat the Toxin and Wear It
entries.objective: A flamingo tongue snail grazes gorgonian coral tissue with a rasping radula, and the same meal does two things: it takes in the coral's chemical defences and it supplies the pigments that make the mantle's bright spots. The mantle flows over a plain shell and advertises a toxicity it acquired by eating. One act feeds, arms and signals. Its principle is Borrowed Mantle. The metaphor? Take your protection from what you already consume, and advertise it.
entries.animalRule: The protection must come from an existing activity during the attempt, and it has to be made visible rather than kept internal.
entries.userBenefit: Adding a separate safeguard for everything means more to maintain than the thing itself. Taking it from what you already do and showing it costs you nothing extra.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cyphoma gibbosum sequesters defensive compounds from the gorgonian tissue it grazes and advertises them through the bright spotted mantle covering its shell.

entries.title: Eat Things Built Not to Be Eaten
entries.objective: A wolffish eats things built not to be eaten. The jaws carry heavy conical teeth at the front and rounded molars behind, the roof of the mouth is paved with more of them, and the whole apparatus reduces sea urchins, whelks and scallops to fragments. That gives the fish access to a food supply that is abundant precisely because it is armoured. Its principle is Crushing Bite. The metaphor? Abundance and armour are the same fact; build for the armour and the abundance is yours.
entries.animalRule: The link between the abundance and the difficulty must be named during the attempt, and the capability has to be built or borrowed.
entries.userBenefit: Supplies that look abundant to you are usually abundant because they are hard to handle. Building for the difficulty is what makes the abundance real.
entries.mechanismConnection: Anarhichas lupus has heavy conical anterior teeth, posterior molars and a palate paved with crushing dentition, reducing armoured echinoderms and molluscs to fragments.

entries.title: Eat What Is Not Open Yet
entries.objective: Late winter is the hard season for a seed eater: last autumn's crop is gone and the next is months away. A bullfinch's answer is to eat the thing nobody is eating because it is not ready, working along fruit-tree branches shearing dormant flower buds with a broad rounded bill and taking several hundred a day. The nutrients were laid down last season and nobody else is competing. Its principle is Budchoice. The metaphor? Take the version of the resource that is not ready yet, while nobody else will.
entries.animalRule: The resource must be used in its unready state during the attempt, and the cost of having waited has to be stated.
entries.userBenefit: Waiting for the ready version means you compete for it with everyone and go without until then. The unready version is uncontested and usually does the job.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pyrrhula pyrrhula shears dormant flower buds from fruit trees and hawthorn with a broad rounded bill during late winter when seed crops are exhausted.

entries.title: Eat What Nobody Fights For
entries.objective: An Aardwolf licks harvester termites straight off open ground, and those termites spray a chemical that puts off nearly every other insect-eater alive. So it eats alone, from something abundant and completely uncontested, and never even breaks the mound. That is why it never has to fight. Its principle is Specialized Humility. The metaphor? Stop queueing for the crowded prize. Take the thing nobody wants.
entries.animalRule: It must be something genuinely avoided by others and named as such and you take it without displacing anyone. Nothing is broken open or taken from another person.
entries.userBenefit: Competing for the crowded prize costs you the most for the least. Taking what other people find distasteful gets you an abundant supply that nobody will fight you over.
entries.mechanismConnection: Proteles cristata feeds almost exclusively on harvester termites, which deter most insectivores with terpene secretions it is unaffected by, so it licks them from the surface of abundant, predictable and effectively uncontested colonies without breaking the mound.

entries.title: Eat What Nothing Else Will Touch
entries.objective: South America's only bear lives almost entirely on plants, and specifically on the ones nothing else will attempt: bromeliad hearts, palm growing points, cactus, bark and hard unripe fruit. Processing them needs force, so the skull is short and deep with heavy jaw muscles and broad grinding molars. Nothing about the diet is rich, which is exactly why it is uncontested. Its principle is Cloud-forest Resilience. The metaphor? The poor resource nobody fights over can be enough, if you build the equipment for it.
entries.animalRule: The thing taken on must be genuinely uncontested, and a specific capability for it has to be built or borrowed during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Competing for the rich resources means your result depends on beating better-equipped people. A poor one with no queue is yours, and the equipment is cheap.
entries.mechanismConnection: Tremarctos ornatus has a short deep skull with heavy masticatory musculature and broad molars for processing bromeliad hearts, palm meristems, bark and unripe fruit that other frugivores cannot use.

entries.title: Eat What the Reef Refuses
entries.objective: Sponges are packed with glass-like spicules and defensive chemicals, and most reef fish will not touch them. Adult French angelfish make them the largest part of their diet, grazing steadily across the reef all day on a food supply that is everywhere precisely because nothing else wants it. The difficulty is what keeps it available. Its principle is Reef Pair Patrol. The metaphor? Take the thing nobody is competing for.
entries.animalRule: The thing taken must be one others genuinely avoid, and the popular work has to be left alone while you do it.
entries.userBenefit: Competing for the work everyone wants means you fight hard for a normal share. Taking the thing nobody will touch gives you the whole supply and almost no competition for it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pomacanthus paru specialises on sponges defended by siliceous spicules and noxious chemistry, exploiting an abundant resource most reef fishes cannot process.

entries.title: Eat Where You Are Already Hidden
entries.objective: A great tinamou gathers fallen fruit, seeds and invertebrates from the leaf litter it is already camouflaged against, so feeding never requires exposing itself in open space. It steps slowly and freezes often, and because the food and the concealment are in the same place, the two needs never compete. Its principle is Forest-Floor Secrecy. The metaphor? Take what you need from the place you are already safe in, rather than leaving it to get supplies.
entries.animalRule: The need must be met from within the safe place during the attempt, and the trip out has to be refused rather than postponed.
entries.userBenefit: Leaving your safe setup to get something means the trip is where things go wrong, every time. Meeting the need from inside it costs you a smaller version and nothing else.
entries.mechanismConnection: Tinamus major forages for fallen fruit, seeds and invertebrates directly within the leaf litter against which its mottled plumage is cryptic, avoiding exposure in open ground.

entries.title: Eat Yesterday's Web
entries.objective: An orb web is expensive protein and it stops working fast: ultraviolet light degrades the silk, dust kills the stickiness, and every insect tears something. A web more than a day old catches far less. So the spider takes it down and eats it, recovering most of the protein within hours, and spins a fresh one from the recovered material. Recycling is what makes daily rebuilding affordable. Its principle is Rebuilt Daily. The metaphor? Do not abandon it. Reclaim the parts.
entries.animalRule: The old thing must be fully dismantled and its parts kept, and the replacement must be built mainly from those recovered parts rather than new ones.
entries.userBenefit: You either keep limping along with the broken version or start from nothing. Stripping it for parts first means the rebuild is cheap, which is what makes rebuilding often rather than rarely possible.
