entries.objective: Reptiles are supposed to take their temperature from their surroundings, and for most of the year a tegu does. Then through the breeding season it does something almost no other lizard does: it generates heat internally and holds its body several degrees, sometimes ten, above the night-time air, sustaining activity when the environment would otherwise shut it down. That is what lets it work hours its own physiology forbids. Its principle is Robust Adaptation. The metaphor? Supply the conditions rather than waiting for them.
entries.animalRule: The warm-up happens before the focused work rather than during it, it lasts ten minutes, and the focused stretch must follow immediately.
entries.userBenefit: Waiting to feel ready means most of your good hours are spent not working. Generating the state yourself first means the work starts when you decide it does.
entries.mechanismConnection: Salvator merianae achieves facultative endothermy in the reproductive season, maintaining body temperature up to ten degrees above ambient overnight.

entries.title: Geometry Instead of Strength
entries.objective: Venus' flower basket is made of glass and lives under crushing deep-sea pressure. It survives because the silica spicules are fused into a precise interlocking lattice reinforced with organic layers, so the tower flexes slightly under current and pressure instead of resisting rigidly. The material is brittle; the arrangement is not. Its principle is Glass Architecture. The metaphor? When you cannot make the material stronger, change the arrangement so it bends instead of breaking.
entries.animalRule: No material may be added or strengthened during the attempt, and the rearranged thing has to be able to give under load rather than hold rigid.
entries.userBenefit: Trying to make something strong enough to resist everything means it holds until it shatters without warning. Rearranging it to give a little costs you nothing and it stops failing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Euplectella aspergillum builds a rigid tubular lattice of fused siliceous spicules layered with organic material, allowing slight flexure under deep-sea pressure and current rather than brittle failure.

entries.title: Get Close Enough to Copy
entries.objective: Most macaques run steep hierarchies where a subordinate approaching a dominant animal is taking a risk. The Celebes Crested Macaque sits at the tolerant end: rank exists but is loosely enforced, reconciliation after conflict is frequent, and the bared-teeth display that means submission elsewhere is used here as a friendly signal. Tolerance is what lets a young animal get close enough to watch properly. Its principle is Bold Social Learning. The metaphor? You cannot learn from someone you are too careful around. Get close enough to watch.
entries.animalRule: You must observe the process rather than the finished output, and it has to be a real session of watching rather than a conversation about how they do it.
entries.userBenefit: Studying someone's finished work teaches you almost nothing about how they got there. Watching the actual process for twenty minutes usually shows you the thing nobody writes down.
entries.mechanismConnection: Macaca nigra exhibits unusually tolerant social organisation with weakly enforced dominance, frequent post-conflict reconciliation and affiliative use of the bared-teeth display, permitting close proximity and observational learning between ranks.

entries.title: Get Down and Run
entries.objective: Little Owls do not look like owls doing owl things. They are active in daylight as well as dusk, perch low and in the open on posts and walls, and do much of their hunting on the ground: the bird drops down and then runs, on legs noticeably long for an owl, after beetles, worms and crickets. Abandoning the aerial method is what lets a small owl live on small things. Its principle is Night Focus Strategy. The metaphor? Stop hovering above the problem. Get down into it.
entries.animalRule: The distant method must be set aside entirely for the attempt, and you have to physically handle the real thing or speak directly to the real person.
entries.userBenefit: Managing from a distance gives you a tidy version of a messy situation, which is why your fixes keep missing. An hour at ground level usually shows you the thing no report was ever going to contain.
entries.mechanismConnection: Athene noctua hunts substantially terrestrially, dropping from low open perches and pursuing invertebrates and small mammals on foot using proportionally long legs, and is active in daylight as well as at dusk.

entries.title: Get Into the Crack and Inflate
entries.objective: A chuckwalla is a slow plant-eating lizard with no speed to rely on, so its defence is positional: it runs for the nearest rock crevice, gets in, and then inflates its lungs so the body wedges against the walls and cannot be pulled out. The protection is not the running; it is what happens once it is inside. Its principle is Rock-Wedge Confidence. The metaphor? Get into the narrow place and then make yourself impossible to extract.
entries.animalRule: The difficulty of removal must be created after arriving during the attempt, and arriving quickly may not be the protection relied on.
entries.userBenefit: Relying on getting somewhere first means being found there with nothing holding you. Making yourself hard to remove once you arrive is the part that actually protects you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Sauromalus ater retreats into rock crevices and inflates its lungs to wedge its body against the walls, making extraction mechanically impossible.

entries.title: Get It Out of Where It Is Hidden
entries.objective: The tufted capuchin's system is extractive foraging: getting food out of places where it is hidden or protected. It eats a great deal of fruit, but much of its skill goes on harder targets, with strong hands and a powerful jaw letting it rip open dead branches, palm leaf bases and bamboo stems to reach insect larvae. The food is not found; it is extracted. Its principle is Tool-Hand Curiosity. The metaphor? Build for extraction rather than for finding, and the hidden supply becomes available.
entries.animalRule: At least five containers or structures must be opened during the attempt, and nothing may be taken from the open.
entries.userBenefit: Looking for things in the open means you compete for a small visible fraction. Extracting from inside structures reaches the part nobody else gets to.
entries.mechanismConnection: Sapajus apella practises extractive foraging, using powerful hands and jaws to open dead branches, palm petioles and bamboo to reach concealed invertebrate larvae.

entries.title: Gills for Ordinary, Lungs for the Rest
entries.objective: A greater siren keeps external gills into adulthood and also carries lungs, and the split is deliberate: the water it occupies is warm, still and often nearly anoxic, so gills handle the ordinary case cheaply and lungs cover everything the gills cannot. Neither system is redundant and neither is the primary one. Its principle is Aquatic Simplicity. The metaphor? Run a cheap method for the ordinary case and keep an expensive one for the rest, rather than one method for both.
entries.animalRule: Both methods must be defined separately, and the cheap one has to be used by default during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Using one method for both ordinary and exceptional cases means paying the expensive price every time. Splitting them means most of your day runs cheap.
entries.mechanismConnection: Siren lacertina retains functional external gills for normal aquatic respiration while also using lungs for air breathing when the warm still water it occupies becomes hypoxic.

entries.title: Gills Reduced, Mouth Does the Work
entries.objective: Gills are for water that has oxygen in it. This eel mostly does without them: the gill arches are reduced and gas exchange happens across the lining of the mouth and throat, which is densely supplied with blood vessels and functions as a lung. It can therefore live in stagnant paddy water where dissolved oxygen is effectively nil, and survive out of water in damp conditions. Its principle is Adaptive Movement. The metaphor? Reduce the standard organ and move its job somewhere that works in the conditions you actually face.
entries.animalRule: The standard version must be genuinely reduced during the attempt, and the function has to work in the real conditions.
entries.userBenefit: Keeping a function in the standard place means it fails in the conditions you actually work in. Moving it somewhere that works is the whole fix.
entries.mechanismConnection: Monopterus albus has reduced gill arches with gas exchange occurring across a highly vascularised buccopharyngeal lining, permitting survival in anoxic water and damp air.

entries.title: Girdle One Paper Pupa Upright to a Twig
entries.objective: Fasten a paper pupa upright against a twig with a thread loop so it reads as a stub of the plant.
entries.animalRule: It must stand upright against the stem held by a tail pad and a girdle, never hanging from a single point.
entries.userBenefit: A small, careful make that shows how hiding can be about posture, not colour.
entries.mechanismConnection: Black Swallowtail — A silk pad spun at the tail end and gripped by the cremaster, holding the base of the pupa to a stem • A loop of silk spun across the thorax and anchored at both ends, forming a girdle • The pupa held upright against the stem rather than hanging, so it sits in the posture and position of a broken twig or a leaf base: Papilio polyxenes pupates upright against a stem, gripping a silk pad at the tail and slinging a silk girdle across the thorax, so the chrysalis sits in the posture of a broken twig or leaf base instead of hanging as an obvious object. This Trial translates that silk-girdled upright pupa posed as part of the plant into a paper pupa tied upright to a twig with a tail pad and a thread girdle.

entries.title: Give Every Part One Job
entries.objective: The blue button is not a jellyfish but a floating colony whose parts divide the work completely. A flat gas-filled disc holds it at the surface, a single central mouth sits beneath with the reproductive structures around it, and the blue tentacle-like parts at the rim carry the stinging cells that catch copepods and larval fish and pass them inward. No part does two jobs, and that is what lets it feed with no brain and no muscle. Its principle is Colonial Drift. The metaphor? Give each part one job only.
entries.animalRule: No part may keep two jobs, and the split has to be run once rather than only written down.
entries.userBenefit: Holding several roles at once in the same task means each one gets done at half quality and you cannot tell which part failed. One job per part makes the weak link visible immediately.
entries.mechanismConnection: Porpita porpita is a colonial hydrozoan in which a gas-filled float, a single central mouth and peripheral stinging zooids each perform one specialised function.

entries.title: Give It Room and It Grows First
entries.objective: The same tilapia that stunts in a crowded tank grows large before breeding when it has open water, food and space, digging and holding a nest pit and mouthbrooding the fry. The rule is conditional in both directions: give it room and it invests in size first, crowd it and it skips straight to output. Its principle is Adaptive Hardiness. The metaphor? Give something genuine room and it will build before it produces, which is what you wanted.
entries.animalRule: The additional room must be genuine during the attempt, and no early output may be extracted.
entries.userBenefit: Extracting output early from something cramped means it stays small forever. Giving it room and waiting is what gets you the large version.
entries.mechanismConnection: Oreochromis niloticus in uncrowded conditions delays maturity to attain larger body size, establishing and defending a nest pit before mouthbrooding.

entries.title: Give One Useful Thing To Someone
entries.objective: Give or lend one small useful item to someone who needs it and explain in one sentence why you chose it.
entries.animalRule: Each eyeball is about the size of the animal's own brain and completely fills its socket, so it cannot rotate and the head turns instead, while the body hangs motionless on a vertical sapling for long stretches at almost no cost. Keep that true for the whole attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Strengthens practical generosity and turns an ordinary possession into immediate social value.
entries.mechanismConnection: Philippine Tarsier expresses Tarsier Focus through this mode: Philippine Tarsier — Eyes Too Big to Move — Clinging • Turning • Waiting: Each eyeball is about the size of the animal's own brain and completely fills its socket, so it cannot rotate and the head turns instead, while the body hangs motionless on a vertical sapling for long stretches at almost no cost. The Trial carries that same limiting structure into one concrete human action.

entries.title: Give Them the Tail
entries.objective: A Comet Moth cannot eat and has four or five days to find a mate on what the caterpillar stored. Its most expensive feature is a pair of long trailing tails, and they are a decoy: a hunting bat gets its strongest echo off the twisting tail tip, strikes that, and the moth flies on without it. Paying for something losable is what keeps it alive. Its principle is Soft Drama. The metaphor? Give the hit somewhere cheap to land.
entries.animalRule: The decoy must be genuinely detachable and cheaper than the thing it protects, and you show it taking a real pull or snag rather than describing one.
entries.userBenefit: You protect valuable things by being careful, which fails the moment you are tired. Building in a cheap part that takes the damage means the loss lands somewhere you do not mind.
entries.mechanismConnection: Argema mittrei adults have no functional mouthparts and live days on larval reserves, and their long hindwing streamers return a stronger echolocation signal than the body, so bats strike the expendable tail and the moth escapes with its thorax intact.

entries.title: Give Up on Lungs
entries.objective: A Titicaca water frog lives at nearly four thousand metres where the water is cold and holds less dissolved oxygen than at sea level, and it has essentially given up on lungs. Its skin hangs in extravagant loose folds multiplying the surface available for gas exchange, and its red blood cells are unusually small and numerous, raising the surface available to carry oxygen. Both changes are about surface area. Its principle is Folded-Skin Breathing. The metaphor? When the input is thin, multiply your surface rather than your effort.
entries.animalRule: The surface area must genuinely increase during the attempt, and no increase in effort may be used.
entries.userBenefit: Working harder to pull in a thin input exhausts you and barely changes the total. Multiplying the surface it arrives through does it passively.
entries.mechanismConnection: Telmatobius culeus has extensive cutaneous folds greatly increasing respiratory surface area plus unusually small numerous erythrocytes, compensating for low dissolved oxygen at altitude.

entries.title: Give Up the Arm, Keep the Animal
entries.objective: Grabbed by an arm, a brittle star does not resist. It sheds the limb deliberately, leaving a wriggling piece behind to hold the predator's attention while the disc and remaining arms pull it deeper into cover, and internal growth zones rebuild the arm over the following months. The loss was designed to be payable. Its principle is Breakable Reach. The metaphor? Decide in advance what you will give up without a fight, and make sure it is the regrowable part.
entries.animalRule: The part to be given up must be decided before the pressure during the attempt, and it has to be the recoverable part rather than the core.
entries.userBenefit: Resisting every loss means you fight hardest over whatever is grabbed first, which is rarely what matters. Deciding beforehand what you will drop keeps the core intact.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ophiothrix fragilis autotomises arms at a predetermined fracture plane, leaving the writhing limb as a distraction while regenerating it from basal growth zones over months.

entries.title: Give Up the Glide for the Depth
entries.objective: A razorbill resolves every auk's problem toward depth. A wing must be small and stiff to work as a paddle underwater, and a wing that small keeps the bird airborne only with continuous rapid beating and no glide at all. What it gets is exceptional diving: a dense body and stiff wings carry it past a hundred metres, into a layer the rest of the colony cannot reach. Its principle is Dual Mastery. The metaphor? Give up coasting and go where nobody does.
entries.animalRule: The coasting must be genuinely given up during the attempt, and what it buys access to has to be named.
entries.userBenefit: Keeping the ability to coast caps how deep you can go in anything. Giving it up is uncomfortable and puts you somewhere with no competition.
entries.mechanismConnection: Alca torda has small stiff wings optimised for underwater propulsion at the cost of gliding flight, enabling dives beyond 100 metres into a prey layer inaccessible to shallower-diving relatives.

entries.title: Give Up the Station to Roam
entries.objective: An adult gray angelfish abandons the cleaning station entirely. The bright juvenile pattern goes, the clients stop coming, and the fish becomes a wide-ranging sponge grazer taking food almost nothing else can process. Keeping the station would have meant staying small. Its principle is Sponge-Reef Roaming. The metaphor? The thing that got you noticed is now holding you in place. Give it up and go wider.
entries.animalRule: The role must actually be handed to a named person rather than simply declined, and you have to tell the people who normally come to you.
entries.userBenefit: Staying available for the thing people already associate with you is comfortable and quietly caps what you do next. Handing it on properly frees the time and nobody is left stuck.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pomacanthus arcuatus abandons juvenile cleaning behaviour and its associated conspicuous pattern on maturing, becoming a wide-ranging adult grazer specialising on sponges that most reef fishes cannot process.

entries.title: Give Up the Wings, Make the Eggs
entries.objective: Male and female Cocoa Tussock Moths are not two versions of the same insect. The male is a normal winged moth that flies at night tracking pheromone. The female has vestigial wings and cannot fly at all: she emerges from her cocoon, stays on it, signals until a male finds her, and lays her entire clutch there. Everything that would have gone into flight went into eggs instead. Its principle is Stay Put. The metaphor? Mobility is expensive. Spend it on output and let them come to you.
entries.animalRule: The cancelled movement must be real and the recovered time has to go into producing something tangible rather than into other admin, with your availability stated clearly.
entries.userBenefit: Travel and meetings quietly consume the hours you would have made something in. One cancellation put straight into output usually produces more than the trip would have.
entries.mechanismConnection: Female Orgyia postica are brachypterous and flightless, remaining on the cocoon and emitting pheromone until a winged male locates them, reallocating the resources of flight musculature into egg production.

entries.title: Glands That Excrete Salt
entries.objective: The American crocodile lives where fresh water meets the sea, and the reason it can is a pair of glands on the tongue that excrete salt at a concentration higher than seawater. That removes the constraint keeping most crocodilians in fresh water and opens estuaries and coastal lagoons where prey concentrates and competition is thinner. One physiological fix, one whole habitat. Its principle is Brackish Stillness. The metaphor? Solve the one constraint that keeps everyone out and the uncontested ground is yours.
entries.animalRule: Exactly one constraint may be addressed during the attempt, and entry into the previously excluded place has to follow.
entries.userBenefit: Avoiding places because of one constraint means competing where everyone else is. Solving just that one puts you somewhere with nobody in it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Crocodylus acutus has lingual salt glands excreting sodium chloride at above-seawater concentration, permitting occupation of hypersaline estuarine habitat closed to most crocodilians.

entries.title: Glide a Tissue Membrane Model Down to Books
entries.objective: Build a small glider with a tissue membrane stretched across four straw limbs and glide it from a table top down to a low book stack.
entries.animalRule: The model must stay a stretched membrane between four limbs and fly on its own: no paper-dart wings and no throwing.
entries.userBenefit: A tiny engineering project that makes gliding physics make sense.
entries.mechanismConnection: Southern Flying Squirrel — Rhythmic • Corridor • Forager: Glaucomys volans commutes each night between known trees by gliding on a patagium stretched between its wrists and ankles, launching from high on one trunk, steering by changing limb tension and landing lower on the next trunk to forage. This Trial translates that downhill tree-to-tree glide on a limb-stretched membrane into one tissue-and-straw membrane model released from a table to land on a lower book stack.

entries.title: Glide While You Wait
entries.objective: Carcharhinus longimanus lives in the open ocean, which is mostly empty, and its answer is to make being there almost free. Its pectoral fins are extraordinarily long, broad and rounded - proportionally the largest of any requiem shark - and they work as lifting surfaces, generating enough lift at slow speed that it cruises indefinitely without sinking and without burning energy on active swimming. That is what lets it cover vast distances between widely separated food. Its principle is Open-Ocean Persistence. The metaphor? Make the waiting cost nothing.
entries.animalRule: All checking mechanisms are removed rather than merely reduced, and exactly one future date to look is set and written down.
entries.userBenefit: Waiting with the checking switched on costs you more than the thing is worth, every day, and changes nothing. Cutting the cost to zero gives you the same outcome and your attention back.
entries.mechanismConnection: Carcharhinus longimanus uses exceptionally long broad pectoral fins as lifting surfaces, generating lift at low speed so it cruises the open ocean at almost no energetic cost.

entries.title: Glint One Foil Shield Ten Times in Torchlight
entries.objective: In a dark room lit by one torch, make a foil breast-shield catch the beam ten times in ten seconds.
entries.animalRule: Stay on one spot, and each glint must be a clear flash of light from the foil, not just movement.
entries.userBenefit: A dramatic, funny burst of dance that feels like a stage moment.
entries.mechanismConnection: Magnificent Riflebird — Focused • Display • Burst: Ptiloris magnificus males display from a chosen perch by raising their wings into a black circle and swinging their head, so their light-absorbing velvet plumage makes the iridescent breast shield flash sharply as it catches the light. This Trial translates that dark stage making each iridescent flash stand out into ten torchlit glints from a foil shield framed by dark clothing.

entries.title: Go Closer to the Strange Thing
entries.objective: A Javan Myna approaches what other birds avoid, and that single disposition explains almost everything about it. A novel object, an unfamiliar food, a machine, a person eating: the response is to move closer and test rather than withdraw. That is the opposite of the caution governing most urban animals, and it is why a city that is a wall of unfamiliar things to everything else is an open larder to this one. Its principle is Urban Cleverness. The metaphor? Your caution is costing you the city. Go closer.
entries.animalRule: It must be something you have genuinely avoided out of unfamiliarity rather than dislike, and you have to actually use or open it rather than observing it.
entries.userBenefit: The unfamiliar things you walk past every day are mostly free and useful, and the only thing keeping you out is that you have never looked. One investigation usually opens something you will use for years.
entries.mechanismConnection: Acridotheres javanicus is markedly neophilic, approaching and investigating novel objects, foods and human activity rather than avoiding them, which gives it access to urban food sources most birds will not exploit.

entries.title: Go Dark to Warm Faster
entries.objective: A desert lizard emerging at dawn faces a plain physical problem: it is cold, it cannot generate heat, and every minute warming is a minute not feeding. Uromastyx geyri solves part of it with pigment, darkening its skin in the early morning so it absorbs solar radiation faster, then paling through the day as it needs to shed heat instead. The surface changes to suit the hour. Its principle is Heat Regulation. The metaphor? The same setting cannot serve the whole day. Change your surface by the hour.
entries.animalRule: The same setting must be changed at least twice in opposite directions during the day, each time to suit the current conditions.
entries.userBenefit: A setting fixed for the whole day is wrong for most of it and you stop noticing. Two deliberate changes cost seconds and the day stops working against you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Uromastyx geyri darkens its dorsal skin in the cool early morning to increase solar absorptance and pales as body temperature rises, using physiological colour change for thermoregulation.

entries.title: Go Down to Where It Already Is
entries.objective: Scoliid wasps invert the arrangement their relatives use. A mud dauber builds a nest and carries prey to it; this one burrows down through soil hunting the larva of a scarab beetle, and when it finds one it stings it into permanent paralysis where it lies and lays the egg there. No transport, no construction. It goes to the resource rather than bringing the resource home. Its principle is Wrinkled Wingtips. The metaphor? Stop hauling things back to your setup. Go and work where the thing already is.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be transported back to your own setup, and the work has to be completed where the thing already is.
entries.userBenefit: Bringing things back to your own setup adds a round trip and a translation step to every job. Going to where it lives usually halves the time and removes the misunderstandings.
entries.mechanismConnection: Scoliid females burrow through soil to locate scarab larvae, paralyse them permanently in situ with a sting and oviposit on them underground, without constructing a nest or transporting prey.

entries.title: Go Down, Not Away
entries.objective: The sulcata tortoise lives at the southern edge of the Sahara, where the problem is not heat alone but months without water, and it solves both by going down. Powerful flattened forelimbs dig burrows running several metres into soil holding cool humid air regardless of conditions above, and through the long dry season it retreats into that space and slows almost everything down. Its principle is Desert Refuge. The metaphor? When conditions above are impossible for months, go downward rather than travelling.
entries.animalRule: No travel may be attempted during the attempt, and the depth has to be genuinely increased.
entries.userBenefit: Travelling to find better conditions when the whole surface is bad means arriving somewhere equally bad, tired. Going deeper where you are costs one day.
entries.mechanismConnection: Centrochelys sulcata excavates burrows several metres deep with flattened forelimbs into soil retaining cool humid air, aestivating there through prolonged Sahelian drought.

entries.title: Go Into the Ground, Not Across It
entries.objective: A shrimp on open sand in daylight is food for everything. Crangon crangon does not flee across the seabed; it goes into it. The pleopods beat to drive water and grains backwards, the body works downward, and within a few seconds the animal has vanished with only its eyes and antennae clear. Its speckled colour matches whatever sand it is on, adjusting over hours. Its principle is Sand Flicker. The metaphor? Go down into it instead of running.
entries.animalRule: No relocation of any kind may happen, and the response has to be going further into the existing situation.
entries.userBenefit: Responding to pressure by moving somewhere else means you arrive with the same problem and no accumulated ground. Going deeper where you are is the only move that also makes you harder to reach.
entries.mechanismConnection: Crangon crangon buries into sediment within seconds using pleopod-driven excavation, leaving only eyes and antennae exposed, and adjusts its speckling to the substrate over hours.

entries.title: Go Quiet for a Day and Lose It
entries.objective: A European robin holds its feeding patch by being constantly audible rather than by fighting, singing right through the year including the winter when most songbirds fall silent. The orange breast is the close-range version of the same claim. Both are cheap compared with combat and both only work because they repeat: a patch goes quiet for a day and a neighbour moves in. Its principle is Territory. The metaphor? What you hold, you hold by being heard continuously, not by defending it once.
entries.animalRule: The claim must be made at least twice during the attempt, and no reference to a previous claim may be substituted.
entries.userBenefit: Assuming people remember your claim is how you find someone else in your space. Two cheap repetitions cost you minutes and that never happens.
entries.mechanismConnection: Erithacus rubecula advertises territory by near-continuous year-round song including in winter, supplemented by the orange breast at close range, a low-cost signal that requires constant repetition.

entries.title: Go Quiet for Twenty Minutes
entries.objective: Withdraw from optional social output for one finite restorative period.
entries.animalRule: The withdrawal must be temporary and low-output, echoing Purple Frog spending almost all of its life underground before a brief emergence.
entries.userBenefit: You create a short recovery period from social output and notice what your attention does when you stop broadcasting.
entries.mechanismConnection: Purple Frog — Subterranean Year and Two-Week Surface — Buried • Termite-fed • All year: Lives metres underground eating termites through a narrow snout and a grooved tongue, appearing nowhere at all for most of its life This Trial translates that species-specific mechanism into one twenty-minute quiet period.

entries.title: Go Where the Water Is
entries.objective: A glossy ibis does not have a migration so much as a habit of going where the water is. Wetlands flood and dry on no fixed schedule, so the flock travels in long lines between them, settling wherever shallow water and soft mud have appeared and probing entirely by touch. The species spread across continents on exactly this behaviour. Its principle is Flock Passage. The metaphor? Drop the fixed route and go wherever the conditions have appeared; that is what lets you spread.
entries.animalRule: The fixed route must be actually abandoned during the attempt, and current conditions have to be checked before moving.
entries.userBenefit: A fixed route takes you where conditions were last year. Checking and going where they actually are is why you end up with ground nobody else worked.
entries.mechanismConnection: Plegadis falcinellus is nomadic rather than route-faithful, relocating to wherever ephemeral shallow wetland has formed and foraging by tactile probing.

entries.title: Go Where the Water Is Failing
entries.objective: A jabiru is built around a season rather than a place. When a floodplain is full, fish are spread through an enormous volume and almost nothing wading can reach them; as the dry season advances the water withdraws into shrinking pools and the same fish become packed into a fraction of the space. The worse the drought, the better the feeding. Its principle is Measured Strike. The metaphor? Go where something failing is concentrating it.
entries.animalRule: The contraction that is concentrating it must be named, and the move has to go there rather than to the larger volume during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Going where there is most of something means it is spread too thin for you to reach. Where it is being squeezed into less space is where you can take it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Jabiru mycteria tracks seasonal drawdown on Neotropical floodplains, where receding water concentrates fish into shrinking pools and raises capture rates as drought intensifies.

entries.title: Go Where the Wind Keeps It Bare
entries.objective: In winter deep snow buries the alpine meadows the Siberian ibex grazed all summer, and the herds do not dig. They shift to steep slopes and exposed ridges where the wind strips the ground bare, feeding on far poorer forage in far more dangerous terrain, because that is where food is reachable at all. Exposure is the price of access. Its principle is High-Ridge Endurance. The metaphor? Move to where it is already clear.
entries.animalRule: No digging at the buried version is allowed, and the exposed alternative has to be worked today.
entries.userBenefit: Digging at the buried version of something costs you the whole winter and usually fails. Taking the harsher, exposed version gets you less of it and gets it now, which is the difference between eating and not.
entries.mechanismConnection: Capra sibirica abandons snow-buried alpine meadows in winter for wind-scoured steep slopes and ridges where sparse forage remains exposed.

entries.title: Grab and Eat One Mandarin Mid-Stroll
entries.objective: Complete a whole snack cycle, from catching an easy-peel mandarin to the last segment, without ever stopping or setting anything down.
entries.animalRule: The whole cycle happens on the move at a slow walk: the mandarin is taken without stopping, and there is no stopping, sitting or setting anything down until the last segment is eaten.
entries.userBenefit: A calm, unhurried snack and a short walk in the same few minutes.
entries.mechanismConnection: Mississippi Kite — Soaring • Catching • Consuming aloft: It takes large insects in flight with a foot and brings them to its bill to eat on the wing, so a complete catch-and-consume cycle happens without ever landing. This Trial translates that catch-and-consume cycle completed aloft into grabbing and eating one mandarin mid-stroll.

entries.title: Grab One Rolling Ball From Behind Cover
entries.objective: Wait still behind cover and then lunge once to clamp a ball as it rolls past within reach.
entries.animalRule: Only one lunge per roll: no creeping forward first, the gap is closed in a single burst.
entries.userBenefit: A sharp jolt of reaction speed and a lot of laughter.
entries.mechanismConnection: Mugger Crocodile — Explosive • Closing • Clamp: Crocodylus palustris waits almost motionless at the bank and, when prey comes within range, drives a sudden lunge with its tail and clamps its jaws, using the short distance to turn stored stillness into a decisive capture. This Trial translates that single explosive lunge from cover and clamp into grabbing a rolling ball with one burst from behind furniture.

entries.title: Grab One Target After Ten Silent Seconds
entries.objective: Choose one soft target object, stand still for exactly ten seconds, then grab it in one sudden committed movement.
entries.animalRule: Converts the approach into one bite delivered to the skull or shell rather than the throat. Keep that true for the whole attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Trains the contrast between patience and decisive action instead of constant half-commitment.
entries.mechanismConnection: Jaguar expresses Stealth through this mode: Jaguar — Skull-Piercing Ambush Bite — Crushing • Committed • Seconds: Converts the approach into one bite delivered to the skull or shell rather than the throat. The Trial carries that same limiting structure into one concrete human action.

entries.title: Grab One Target in the Dark
entries.objective: Locate something in a darkened room and take it as fast as you can.
entries.animalRule: No light of any kind, and the room must be cleared of trip hazards first.
entries.userBenefit: A short sharp burst that shows how quickly your eyes actually adapt.
entries.mechanismConnection: Swordfish — Heated Eyes in Cold Water — Descending • Resolving • Slashing: A block of muscle behind the eye has stopped contracting and become a heater, holding the eyes and brain far above the surrounding water so that vision stays fast enough to track prey during dives into cold dark layers This Trial translates that heater organ keeping vision working in the cold dark into a target found and taken without light.

entries.title: Grab One Token From Behind a Door
entries.objective: Grab One Token From Behind a Door.
entries.animalRule: Your hand may cross the flap only once and may not pursue the token beyond one hand-length.
entries.userBenefit: You turn hidden strategy into one concrete, visible experience instead of an abstract idea.
entries.mechanismConnection: Trapdoor Spider — Lifting • Seizing • Withdrawing: The strike is a fraction of a second in which the door swings, the spider comes half out, takes whatever crossed the threshold and is back inside, with no pursuit available beyond a body length. This Trial translates that high-frequency mechanism into one token from behind a hinged flap.

entries.title: Graze Beans Along a Moving Flood Edge
entries.objective: Gather beans only from the thin strip along a moving waterline, following it as it floods forward and draws back.
entries.animalRule: You may take beans only within a hand-width of the moving edge: never from under the towel and never from the dry ground farther off.
entries.userBenefit: A quick, surprisingly absorbing game about keeping up with a boundary that will not stay still.
entries.mechanismConnection: Puku — Grazing • Lifting • Following water: A Puku herd works the narrow productive strip where the floodplain meets dry ground, and because that edge advances and retreats through the year, its territory is a position relative to the water rather than a fixed piece of land. This Trial translates that grazing band that moves with the flood edge into gathering beans only from a hand-width strip beside a towel waterline that a helper slides forward and back.

entries.title: Graze Far From the Water
entries.objective: An onager lives in desert steppe where forage is spread thin and water is concentrated at a few points, and its system is built on the tension between those facts. A horse-like gut processes coarse dry grass quickly and inefficiently, so large volumes must be taken and grazing has to happen far from water, which is only possible because of dehydration tolerance and fast sustained travel. Its principle is Open-Range Freedom. The metaphor? If the resource and the supply are in different places, build tolerance for the distance between them.
entries.animalRule: No attempt to move the two closer may be made during the attempt, and the tolerance has to be concretely increased.
entries.userBenefit: Trying to move your work and your resupply closer together usually fails and costs the attempt. Building tolerance for the gap makes both usable as they are.
entries.mechanismConnection: Equus hemionus combines rapid inefficient hindgut processing of coarse grass with high dehydration tolerance and sustained travel speed, permitting grazing far from scarce water points.

entries.title: Graze Hard While the Meadow Floats
entries.objective: When the Amazon rises, the floodplain becomes a network of lakes and flooded forest, and floating meadows of grasses, water hyacinth and water lettuce spread across all of it. The manatee moves in and grazes heavily, gathering plants with a muscular bristled upper lip, and lays down fat as fast as it can. The meadow will be gone, and the eating has to be done now. Its principle is Rivergentle. The metaphor? Eat hard while the abundance lasts.
entries.animalRule: A large amount must actually be used rather than rationed, and the quantity has to be recorded.
entries.userBenefit: Rationing an abundance that is going to disappear means you lose most of it unused and still feel short. Taking a large amount now converts it into something that lasts past the window.
entries.mechanismConnection: Trichechus inunguis grazes floating macrophyte meadows intensively during the flood pulse, accumulating fat reserves with a muscular bristled upper lip.

entries.title: Graze One Bowl of Young Shoots Through Dusk
entries.objective: Eat a small bowl of young shoots slowly, alone, by a window as the light fades after sunset.
entries.animalRule: Start after sunset and eat only while the light is fading, slowly and alone, one small mouthful at a time.
entries.userBenefit: A calm, green meal that slows the end of the day down.
entries.mechanismConnection: Tamaraw — Grazing • Nocturnal • Solitary: Bubalus mindorensis grazes grasses and young bamboo shoots in open grassland mainly at night and around dawn and dusk, a timing attributed to hunting pressure, and adults are mostly solitary and wary. This Trial translates that solitary grazing on young shoots in the dim hours into a bowl of young shoots eaten slowly and alone through the fading light.

entries.title: Graze One Meadow Platter in Three Bouts
entries.objective: Share one platter of fresh greens with at least two others on a blanket, clearing it in three short feeding bouts with a rest between each.
entries.animalRule: Everyone feeds from the one shared platter on the blanket, eating only during a bout and resting without food between bouts.
entries.userBenefit: A shared plate of greens and a funny, relaxed rhythm of eating and resting together.
entries.mechanismConnection: Hoary Marmot — Feeding • Colonial • Watchful: In its few snow-free months Marmota caligata lives in family colonies near its burrows, feeding heavily on alpine grasses, herbs and flowers in bouts broken by rests basking on warm rocks, fattening for a winter hibernation of about eight months. This Trial translates that colony's rhythm of heavy feeding bouts and basking rests in a short season into a shared platter of greens cleared in three timed bouts with rests between.

entries.title: Graze One Shared Bowl in a Marked Square
entries.objective: With two or three others, share one bowl of raw greens inside a marked square of grass in a cool hour, timed around a rest together in shade.
entries.animalRule: Everyone eats only inside the square and from the one bowl, in a cool hour, and the group moves between shade and square together.
entries.userBenefit: A slow shared snack outdoors at the gentlest time of day, and a lie-down together afterwards.
entries.mechanismConnection: Mountain Reedbuck — Grazing • Small-group • Hillside: Redunca fulvorufula grazes grassy hillsides in small groups of females and young within a single male's territory, feeding in the cool of morning and from late afternoon into the night and lying up in the shade of bushes and boulders through the midday heat. This Trial translates that small group feeding together on one patch in the cool hours and lying up in shade around the heat of the day into a shared bowl of greens eaten inside one marked square, with a rest together in shade after a morning feed or before an evening one.

entries.title: Graze One Snack From Your Screening Shrub
entries.objective: Sit tucked against an edible plant that screens you and make a slow snack only from what you can pick within arm's reach of it.
entries.animalRule: The plant that hides you is the plant you eat: stay seated within arm's reach of it, facing out, from the first pick to the last bite.
entries.userBenefit: A calm, sheltered snack straight from the plant, eaten where no one can see you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Greater Sage-Grouse — Covered • Cautious • Foraging: Centrocercus urophasianus depends on sagebrush for both food and shelter, feeding almost entirely on sagebrush leaves in winter and staying low beside the same shrubs to avoid eagles and other predators outside the lekking season. This Trial translates that feeding on the very shrub that gives cover into a snack picked only from the edible plant that screens you.

entries.title: Graze the Clearing to Keep It Open
entries.objective: The African forest buffalo is small enough to move through dense rainforest but still eats mostly grass and sedge, so it depends entirely on openings: grassy clearings, marshy glades, riverbanks and old logging roads. A herd stays in a small home range centred on a few favoured clearings and grazes them in the cooler hours, and that grazing is what keeps them open. Use is what maintains the thing it needs. Its principle is Forest Herd Weight. The metaphor? Use it or it closes over.
entries.animalRule: The use must be ordinary rather than ceremonial, and it has to happen today rather than be scheduled.
entries.userBenefit: Things you value but leave alone close over, and by the time you want them back the cost of reopening is far higher than using them would have been. Ordinary use is the whole maintenance.
entries.mechanismConnection: Syncerus caffer nanus depends on forest clearings for its grass and sedge diet, and its own repeated grazing maintains those clearings against regrowth.

entries.title: Graze the Film Nobody Else Can
entries.objective: Australia's largest native land slug lives on a food almost nothing else can use: the thin film of microscopic algae, fungi and bacteria coating tree trunks, rocks and logs in damp forest. It rasps that film off with a ribbon of tiny teeth, leaving visible grazing tracks on smooth bark. The resource is everywhere and unexploited because processing it needs equipment nothing else has. Its principle is Slow Warning. The metaphor? Harvest the layer everyone walks past.
entries.animalRule: The resource must be one others genuinely ignore, and a real quantified amount has to be harvested.
entries.userBenefit: Looking for resources that look like resources puts you in competition for all of them. The thin layer everyone walks past is unclaimed, and the only cost to you is the equipment to use it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Triboniophorus graeffei rasps epilithic and corticolous biofilm of algae, fungi and bacteria with its radula, exploiting a resource few animals can process.

entries.title: Graze to the Budget, Then Bask
entries.objective: Amblyrhynchus cristatus is the only lizard that feeds in the sea, and its limit is temperature, not food. Algae are abundant, but Galapagos water drains body heat steadily, and a reptile below working temperature can neither swim properly nor digest what it just ate. So the day divides strictly: graze until the thermal budget runs out, then press flat on black lava and reload heat before anything else happens. Its principle is Sea Adaptation. The metaphor? Stop at the budget, not the appetite.
entries.animalRule: The stop is written before you begin and honoured exactly, and the twenty recovery minutes carry no task of any kind.
entries.userBenefit: Pushing a good session until you are empty costs you the next day, and you never get that back cheaply. Stopping on a written limit and actually recovering means tomorrow starts at full capacity.
entries.mechanismConnection: Amblyrhynchus cristatus grazes submerged algae only until cold water drains its body heat, then basks on lava to restore the temperature that both digestion and swimming require.

entries.title: Green Against Sunlit Leaves
entries.objective: An emerald tree skink is a daytime lizard on the vertical surfaces of palms and forest trees, and its brilliant green is the point: against sunlit foliage it is hard to pick out at any distance, so it can forage in the open on a trunk rather than in cover. Several individuals will often work the same tree without much conflict, unusual among skinks. Its principle is Invitation. The metaphor? Match your background and you can work in the open, alongside others, without contest.
entries.animalRule: The match to the setting must be deliberate rather than incidental, and the work has to be done openly alongside others during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Standing out in a setting means every move you make is examined. Matching it lets you work openly in the same space without any of that.
entries.mechanismConnection: Lamprolepis smaragdina is cryptic against sunlit foliage, permitting open diurnal foraging on exposed trunks and tolerance of conspecifics working the same tree.

entries.title: Grind It Instead of Passing It
entries.objective: Fruit-eating birds are usually seed dispersers, and green pigeons are a conspicuous exception. The Pink-necked Green Pigeon swallows fruit whole like other frugivores, but behind the crop sits a heavily muscled gizzard containing grit that destroys the seeds rather than passing them intact. It extracts far more from each fruit and plants nothing. Its principle is Canopy Colour. The metaphor? Passing things along intact is generous and cheap. Grinding them properly gets you what is inside.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be forwarded on during the attempt, and the content has to be genuinely extracted rather than skimmed.
entries.userBenefit: Forwarding things unread makes you a relay and you get nothing from anything passing through. Grinding one properly gives you the content and usually means you never need to forward it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Treron vernans possesses a heavily muscularised gizzard containing grit that mechanically destroys ingested seeds, extracting their contents rather than passing them intact as other frugivores do.

entries.title: Grip Beats Speed on a Struggling Thing
entries.objective: This assassin bug is not fast, and it does not need to be, because it hunts caterpillars and soft larvae that do not run. What it does need is to hold something that struggles, so its forelegs carry dense pads of fine hairs that grip a thrashing body far better than any smooth surface could, and then the rostrum goes in. Grip, not pursuit. Its principle is Sticky Patience. The metaphor? You do not need to be quicker. You need to not lose hold once you have it.
entries.animalRule: The mechanism must make losing hold structurally harder rather than relying on your own diligence, and it has to be in place during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Things you lose hold of halfway are not a speed problem, and trying harder has not worked. One gripping mechanism means it finishes without your diligence.
entries.mechanismConnection: Zelus and related reduviids bear fore-tibial pads of dense adhesive setae that secure struggling soft-bodied prey, compensating for slow locomotion with retention rather than pursuit.

entries.title: Grip Behind the Head
entries.objective: Taking snakes is a specialist problem because the prey is armed and strikes from something that does not have to turn to face you. The Crested Serpent Eagle's answer is in the legs: short, thick, covered in large overlapping scales that work as armour so a bite cannot reach skin. The grip goes behind the head, controlling the only part that matters. Its principle is Serpent Focus. The metaphor? Stop wrestling the whole problem. Armour up and grip the part that does the damage.
entries.animalRule: Only one specific part may be acted on, named out loud before you start, and the rest of the problem has to be deliberately left untouched.
entries.userBenefit: Tackling a problem as a whole is how it stays unsolved for months. Finding the one part that actually does the damage usually takes you an afternoon to control, and the rest stops mattering.
entries.mechanismConnection: Spilornis cheela has short thick tarsi covered in large overlapping scales that armour the legs against snake bites, and seizes prey immediately behind the head to control the strike.

entries.title: Groan Continuously for Weeks
entries.objective: In autumn the fallow deer system inverts. Bucks take small heavily trampled patches of ground, groan almost continuously for weeks, fight when challenged, and eat so little that they lose a large share of their body weight. Females move between stands and choose, which means a buck's whole reproductive return rests on sustaining an output he cannot sustain for long. Its principle is Elegance. The metaphor? Some returns only come from an output you cannot keep up, so start it at the right moment.
entries.animalRule: The window must be confirmed open before starting during the attempt, and the push has to be genuinely unsustainable.
entries.userBenefit: Starting an unsustainable push before the window opens means you are spent when it does. Confirming it first is the difference between everything and nothing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Dama dama bucks maintain near-continuous groaning and stand defence through a weeks-long rut while losing a substantial proportion of body mass.

entries.title: Groom One Night Path From Bed to Door
entries.objective: Clear every trip hazard from the route between your bed and bedroom door.
entries.animalRule: Items come off the path one at a time and nothing new may be placed on it afterwards.
entries.userBenefit: A safer walk to the door in the dark, tonight and after.
entries.mechanismConnection: Rufous Elephant Shrew — Hidden • Mapping • Maintenance: Elephantulus rufescens quietly grooms its runways, removing twigs and leaves one by one so each route stays memorised and clear between nest, food and shelter. This Trial translates that patient one-item-at-a-time runway grooming into clearing your own night path.

entries.title: Groom Your Favourite Jacket Until It Looks Pristine
entries.objective: Restore one favourite jacket or coat to pristine condition by de-fuzzing, brushing, re-shaping and fixing every small flaw.
entries.animalRule: Maintenance only: nothing new may be added, just the care that keeps it at its best.
entries.userBenefit: A calm, satisfying care routine that leaves you with a ready-to-wear favourite.
entries.mechanismConnection: Lesser Bird-of-paradise — Quiet • Hidden • Preparing: Paradisaea minor spends long quiet periods preening between displays, keeping its flank plumes and tail feathers immaculate so they are ready when a display is needed. This Trial translates that quiet preening that keeps plumes ready for display into a slow, careful grooming of one favourite jacket.

entries.title: Grooves That Read the Water
entries.objective: A common fangtooth lives in black midwater where prey is scattered and nothing is visible. Deep grooves across its oversized head carry lateral-line canals that detect water movement from nearby animals, and the dark skin absorbs what little light there is. It senses disturbance rather than objects, because disturbance is what the water will actually give it. Its principle is Abyss Teeth. The metaphor? Build your sensing around the signal the environment actually carries, not the one you wish it did.
entries.animalRule: The direct looking must stop during the attempt, and the detection has to be of the disturbance rather than the thing.
entries.userBenefit: Watching for the thing itself in conditions that will never show it means you find out afterwards, every time. Watching for the disturbance it causes tells you now.
entries.mechanismConnection: Anoplogaster cornuta detects prey by water displacement through deep lateral-line canals grooved across its enlarged head, in the absence of usable light.

entries.title: Ground Feeding Needs Ground Cover
entries.objective: The Socorro dove walked the shaded forest floor picking up seeds and fallen fruit, in a system built for an island with no ground-hunting mammals. Sheep stripped the understorey and feral cats found birds that had never needed wariness. The method was sound and depended entirely on a condition that was removed. Its principle is Lost-Island Gentleness. The metaphor? Name the condition your method depends on, because when it goes the method goes with it.
entries.animalRule: The depended-on condition must be named explicitly during the attempt, and the response to its loss has to be stated rather than assumed.
entries.userBenefit: Not knowing what your way of working quietly depends on means you discover it the week the thing disappears. Naming it now costs you ten minutes.
entries.mechanismConnection: Zenaida graysoni fed on the ground in the absence of terrestrial mammalian predators, a dependency exposed when feral cats and grazing sheep were introduced.

entries.title: Groups That Choose Their Neighbours
entries.objective: Vulturine guineafowl groups do not merely coexist; particular groups associate preferentially with particular neighbours, sharing space and roosts with some and not others. That multilevel structure, once thought to need a large mammalian brain, gives them the predator detection of a big aggregation while keeping the familiarity of a small one. Its principle is Armored Elegance. The metaphor? Choose which groups you associate with, and you get the size without losing the familiarity.
entries.animalRule: The choice must be deliberate during the attempt, and the reason for that group rather than another has to be named.
entries.userBenefit: Joining whatever group is biggest means you get the numbers and know nobody in them. Choosing which to associate with gets you the same reach with people who know you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Acryllium vulturinum social groups show stable preferential inter-group associations, producing a multilevel society that combines large-aggregation vigilance with small-group familiarity.

entries.title: Grow Deeper When Pike Are Near
entries.objective: A pike swallows prey whole and can only take what fits its mouth, so for a roach it is body depth rather than length that matters. Roach raised where predators are abundant develop measurably deeper bodies, triggered by chemical cues from predators and injured fish during development. The depth is not free, since it is slower and costs more to move, which is exactly why it appears only in response to the cue. Its principle is Quiet Abundance. The metaphor? Grow the costly defence only when the signal says you need it, not permanently.
entries.animalRule: The signal must be identified before the protection is added during the attempt, and it has to be left off where the signal is absent.
entries.userBenefit: Protecting against everything everywhere costs you speed on all of it for a risk that is mostly absent. Adding it where the signal appears keeps you quick elsewhere.
entries.mechanismConnection: Rutilus rutilus develops a deeper body morphology in response to chemical cues from predators and damaged conspecifics, a gape-limitation defence carrying locomotor costs.

entries.title: Grow Fast Without Holding Ground
entries.objective: Among this prawn's three male forms, the orange-claw males grow fast without holding territory at all, while the blue-claws defend space and guard females and the small males sneak matings. Growth and territory are separate investments here, and one form deliberately takes the first and skips the second. Its principle is Adaptive Versatility. The metaphor? Growing and holding ground are separate investments; you are allowed to take one and skip the other.
entries.animalRule: Exactly one of growth or territory may be invested in during the attempt, and the other has to be explicitly skipped.
entries.userBenefit: Trying to grow and hold ground at once means doing both slowly and losing the ground anyway. Choosing one gets you much further on it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Macrobrachium rosenbergii orange-claw males allocate to rapid somatic growth without territorial defence, while blue-claw males allocate to territory and mate guarding.

entries.title: Grow in Any Salinity
entries.objective: An estuary is difficult because the salinity will not hold still: rain, river flow and tide swing it between nearly fresh and fully marine within hours, and a fish tuned to one end spends energy it cannot afford. The Snubnose Pompano is euryhaline, regulating across the whole range so it grows normally wherever the water happens to sit that day. It did not pick a point on the gradient. Its principle is Coastal Adjustment. The metaphor? Tuning yourself to one condition makes every other day expensive. Widen the range you work in.
entries.animalRule: The condition must not be corrected or escaped during the attempt, and something real has to be completed inside it.
entries.userBenefit: Needing your conditions to be right means most days are spent fixing conditions rather than working. Widening what you can work in gets those days back.
entries.mechanismConnection: Trachinotus blochii is strongly euryhaline, osmoregulating effectively across the full estuarine salinity range so growth is maintained despite rapid tidal and rainfall-driven fluctuation.

entries.title: Grow It, Shake It, Shed It
entries.objective: A peacock's train is not part of the wing and does nothing for flight. It is grown fresh each breeding season, carried at real cost for months, spread and rapidly vibrated so the eyespots shimmer and the shafts rattle, and then moulted away entirely. Only a bird in good condition could do it, which is exactly what makes it informative. Its principle is Magnificence. The metaphor? Build it for the season, use it fully, then let it go.
entries.animalRule: Either full use or deliberate shedding must actually happen during the attempt, and continuing to carry it unused is not permitted.
entries.userBenefit: Carrying something impressive past its season costs you upkeep for no return and you keep hoping it comes back. Using it fully or shedding it both end that.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pavo cristatus grows its ornamental train anew each breeding season, displays it by fanning and rapid train-rattling vibration, and moults it entirely afterwards.

entries.title: Grow the Brain for the Season
entries.objective: Canaries overturned an assumption about vertebrate brains. Work in the 1980s showed the forebrain nuclei controlling song add new neurons in adulthood, expanding substantially as daylength increases and the bird comes into song, then shrinking again afterwards. It was among the first clear proof that adult brains grow new cells at all. Capacity is built for the season that needs it. Its principle is Vocal Mastery Strategy. The metaphor? You are not fixed. Grow the part this season needs.
entries.animalRule: The fifteen minutes must be spent practising rather than reading about it, and the bad first attempt has to be kept rather than discarded.
entries.userBenefit: Deciding you are not a person who can do something closes it permanently on no evidence. Fifteen bad minutes is enough to find out, and the capacity genuinely builds when you use it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Serinus canaria shows seasonal adult neurogenesis in the song control nuclei HVC and RA, which add neurons and increase in volume as photoperiod lengthens and song develops, then regress outside the season.

entries.title: Grow the Claw in Autumn
entries.objective: The northern collared lemming turns white in winter, and the change goes further than colour. In autumn the claws on its two middle front toes grow into enlarged double tips, which are the tool for digging through hard packed snow, and after the melt it moults back to grey-brown. The equipment for the hard season is grown before the hard season, not during it. Its principle is Wintercoat. The metaphor? Grow the tool before you need it.
entries.animalRule: The acquisition must begin before the hard season arrives, and nothing unrelated to it may be started today.
entries.userBenefit: Acquiring a tool during the season that needs it means learning while failing, which is the most expensive way to learn anything. Starting now costs you the same effort at none of the pressure.
entries.mechanismConnection: Dicrostonyx groenlandicus grows enlarged bifid claws on the middle forefoot digits each autumn for excavating hard snow, moulting them after snowmelt.

entries.title: Grow the Crest, Then Reabsorb It
entries.objective: A smooth newt spends most of its life on land under logs, hunting slugs in plain velvety skin. Then in spring it returns to a pond and rebuilds itself for the occasion: the male grows a wavy crest along back and tail and a finned swimming tail, and courtship is chemical and visual. When breeding ends the crest is reabsorbed and the animal walks back out. Its principle is Transition. The metaphor? Grow the equipment for the season, then take it back into yourself rather than carrying it.
entries.animalRule: Both the building and the dismantling plan must be stated before starting during the attempt, and the equipment has to be genuinely temporary.
entries.userBenefit: Equipment built for one season and never dismantled becomes upkeep you pay forever. Naming the dismantling first means you get the season and not the bill.
entries.mechanismConnection: Lissotriton vulgaris males develop a dorsal crest and finned tail for the aquatic breeding phase and resorb these structures when they return to terrestrial life.

entries.title: Grow the Fungus, Then Eat the Comb
entries.objective: This is a fungus-growing termite, and the distinction matters. It does not digest wood itself in any complete sense; workers collect plant material, pass it through the gut once, and deposit it as a sponge-like comb inside the mound, where a cultivated fungus grows through it and breaks down the lignin no animal enzyme handles well. The termites then eat the comb. Its principle is Synchronized Launch. The metaphor? Pass the material through once, hand it to something that can finish it, and come back for the result.
entries.animalRule: Only your own step may be performed during the attempt, and the finishing has to be handed to something else.
entries.userBenefit: Trying to finish material your own enzymes cannot handle wastes the whole batch. Handing it on and returning for the result gets you all of it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Macrotermes workers pass plant material through the gut once and deposit it as fungus comb, where cultivated Termitomyces degrades lignin before the comb is consumed.

entries.title: Grow the Helmet on the Rumour
entries.objective: A water flea can detect a predator it has never met. Chemical traces released by fish diffuse through the water, and a Daphnia that detects them changes what it builds: within a moult or two it grows a helmet, neck teeth and a longer tail spine. It never waited to be attacked. Its principle is Clone Until Crisis. The metaphor? You do not need the incident. The signal that one is coming is enough to start building.
entries.animalRule: The protection must be built on a signal rather than an incident that has already happened, and it has to be concrete rather than heightened vigilance.
entries.userBenefit: You wait for the problem to actually happen before preparing, which means you prepare under pressure and badly. Building on the early signal costs you one calm afternoon instead of one bad week.
entries.mechanismConnection: Daphnia pulex detects predator kairomones in the water and undergoes inducible morphological defence within one or two moults, growing a helmet, neck teeth and an elongated tail spine without ever encountering the predator.

entries.title: Grow Up in the Safe River
entries.objective: The Largetooth Sawfish differs from its relatives in where it spends its youth. Females give birth in estuaries and the young then move far upriver, occupying fresh water for several years, historically hundreds of kilometres up the Fitzroy and the Amazon. The adults return to the sea. The vulnerable years are spent somewhere the adult predators are not. Its principle is Heavy Saw. The metaphor? Do the fragile early part somewhere the pressure cannot follow. Come out when you are big enough.
entries.animalRule: The thing must be moved out of public or semi-public view during the attempt, and a specific condition or date for bringing it out has to be stated.
entries.userBenefit: Exposing something before it can survive scrutiny usually kills it outright, and you conclude the idea was bad. Protecting it until it is sized to take the pressure is the difference between surviving and not.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pristis pristis pups are born in estuaries and spend several years in fresh water far upriver before returning to marine habitat as adults, segregating the vulnerable juvenile phase from adult predators.

entries.title: Grow Wings or Grow Eggs
entries.objective: A rice planthopper decides, in effect, whether to stay or to leave, and it does so by growing a different body. Nymphs developing at low density on a healthy crop become short-winged adults that cannot fly, have small flight muscles and put everything into eggs, building the population explosively where it already is. Nymphs developing under crowding or on a deteriorating crop become long-winged and leave. Its principle is Rice-Stem Cling. The metaphor? Decide early whether you are building here or leaving, because the body for each is different.
entries.animalRule: Exactly one of the two must be configured for during the attempt, and no hedging between them is permitted.
entries.userBenefit: Hedging between building here and preparing to leave gives you a body suited to neither. Choosing one early is what makes either work.
entries.mechanismConnection: Sogatella furcifera develops brachypterous flightless high-fecundity adults at low density and macropterous migratory adults under crowding or host deterioration.

entries.title: Grow Wings When It Gets Crowded
entries.objective: A rice planthopper decides whether to stay or leave by growing a different body. Nymphs developing at low density on a healthy crop become short-winged adults that cannot fly and put everything into eggs; nymphs developing in crowded deteriorating conditions become long-winged adults with full flight muscles and fewer eggs. The crowding itself determines which body is built. Its principle is Rice-Stem Cling. The metaphor? Conditions should change what you build, not just how you feel. Let crowding trigger the wings.
entries.animalRule: A specific numeric threshold must be written down, and the change of approach it triggers has to be stated rather than left vague.
entries.userBenefit: Absorbing more until something breaks means the change happens at the worst moment and not by choice. A written threshold makes the switch automatic and you decide it in advance.
entries.mechanismConnection: Sogatella furcifera exhibits wing dimorphism determined by nymphal density: low density produces brachypterous high-fecundity adults, crowding produces macropterous dispersing adults with reduced fecundity.

entries.title: Guard a Cup From Freezing by Water Jacket
entries.objective: Show that a cup of water sitting inside a larger bowl of water stays liquid in the freezer after a bare cup beside it has frozen.
entries.animalRule: Both cups hold the same water and go in the freezer together, and only the surrounding water differs.
entries.userBenefit: A simple kitchen experiment that shows why water buffers the cold.
entries.mechanismConnection: Bog Turtle — Hibernating • Buried • Spring-fed: From about October to April Glyptemys muhlenbergii hibernates in spring-fed muck, root tangles or old muskrat burrows, where flowing groundwater brings a steady supply of above-freezing water that keeps the ground around it from freezing solid. This Trial translates that shelter kept unfrozen by surrounding groundwater into a cup kept liquid by a jacket of water in the freezer.

entries.title: Guard One Chair Perch From Five Rolled Balls
entries.objective: Defend a small floor zone from five balls rolled in by a helper, returning to the same chair after every chase.
entries.animalRule: You must be seated on the same chair each time a ball is rolled.
entries.userBenefit: A lively five-minute game with bursts of movement and a steady rhythm.
entries.mechanismConnection: Two-tailed Pasha — Rhythmic • Patrol • Hold: Charaxes jasius males hold a favoured perch with a clear view near their host plants, launch short powerful flights to chase off intruding butterflies and return to the same perch. This Trial translates that watch, dash and return from a defended perch into five defensive dashes from one chair to keep rolled balls out of a floor square.

entries.title: Guard One Orange-Taped Square From Intruders
entries.objective: Keep a taped square at your work spot clear of five items a helper tries to sneak into it.
entries.animalRule: Only objects inside the tape count, and each must be returned outside the border within five seconds of landing.
entries.userBenefit: A playful test of focus and boundaries while you actually get some work done.
entries.mechanismConnection: Garibaldi Fish — Visible • Patrolling • Defensive: Hypsypops rubicundus males clear and tend a nest patch of red algae on the reef and patrol a territory around it, advertised by their vivid orange colour, charging and making thumping sounds at any fish that crosses the border. This Trial translates that clearly signalled territory with steady patrols and quick local responses into a bright taped square kept clear of sneaked-in items.

entries.title: Guide a Coin Blindfolded Through Standing Cups
entries.objective: Blindfolded, steer a coin across a tabletop forest of standing cups to a target without knocking any over.
entries.animalRule: Stay blindfolded throughout, move slowly, and no cup may fall over; if one falls, stand it back and restart from the edge.
entries.userBenefit: A slow, absorbing puzzle that sharpens touch and spatial sense.
entries.mechanismConnection: Amazon River Dolphin — Weaving • Flooded-forest • Probing: Inia geoffrensis swims slowly into flooded forest, bending its unfused neck sideways and twisting between submerged trunks and roots while it echolocates and probes with its bristled beak, because in murky water sight is of little use. This Trial translates that slow probing weave between drowned trunks without sight into a blindfolded, feel-ahead coin route through a random cluster of standing cups.

entries.title: Guide One Ball Into a Partner's Catch
entries.objective: Guide One Ball Into a Partner's Catch.
entries.animalRule: The ball must change direction off the guide; your partner stays in one place.
entries.userBenefit: You turn thermal command into one concrete experience with a visible finish.
entries.mechanismConnection: Wedge-tailed Eagle — Paired • Driving • Coordinated: A pair hunts together on prey no single eagle could take, one bird flushing and pressing a kangaroo while the other strikes from the direction it is driven toward. This Trial translates that mechanism into one rolling ball into a partner catch.

entries.title: Guide One Long Streamer Round the Furniture
entries.objective: Walk a slow route around the furniture with a two-metre streamer trailing behind, without it snagging once.
entries.animalRule: If the streamer catches on anything, go back to the start: slow and wide is the whole trick.
entries.userBenefit: A slow, surprisingly absorbing lesson in how much room you really take up.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ribbon-tailed Astrapia — Burdened • Careful • Conserving: Astrapia mayeri males spend most of their time moving cautiously through the forest carrying metre-long tail ribbons that can snag and break, so everyday movement is shaped around protecting and conserving an expensive ornament. This Trial translates that careful, burdened movement into a slow route around furniture with a long streamer that must never catch.

entries.title: Gulp Air in the Dead Backwater
entries.objective: A gar's swim bladder is lined with blood vessels and connected to the throat, so it can rise, gulp air and extract oxygen directly. That means warm stagnant backwaters which kill most fish are perfectly habitable and largely free of competitors. The capability did not make it faster or stronger; it made a dead place into its own. Its principle is Surface Ambush. The metaphor? One independent supply turns a place nobody can work into a place with no competition.
entries.animalRule: The supply must be independent of the place during the attempt, and the place has to be one others avoid for that reason.
entries.userBenefit: Avoiding places that lack what you need means you are always where everyone else is. Bringing your own supply makes those places yours alone.
entries.mechanismConnection: Lepisosteus osseus has a vascularised physostomous gas bladder permitting direct aerial respiration, so it occupies hypoxic stagnant backwaters largely free of competing fish.

entries.title: Gulp Five Floating Paper Dots With a Baster
entries.objective: Hold a squeezed turkey baster still just above a basin of water and, with one release each, suck in hole-punch paper dots a helper drops near it at random.
entries.animalRule: One lunge per dot: no second tries, no moving before the dot lands, and it must be taken by suction alone.
entries.userBenefit: A quick, competitive table game that sharpens timing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Bowfin — Explosive • Short • Precise: Amia calva waits in weedy cover and makes short, precise lunges, rapidly expanding its mouth to suck prey in the moment it comes within range rather than chasing it. This Trial translates that short, exact suction lunge from rest into sucking floating paper dots into a baster with a single release of its bulb.

entries.title: Gulp Ten Cereal Rings by Bottle Squeeze
entries.objective: Suck ten floating cereal rings out of a bowl of water with a squeezed plastic bottle in sixty seconds.
entries.animalRule: One sudden release per ring, and the bottle mouth may not scoop or touch the ring before the gulp.
entries.userBenefit: A fast, splashy physics game that makes suction feeding click.
entries.mechanismConnection: Painted Frogfish — Gape • Suction • Swallow: When prey comes within reach, Antennarius pictus opens its very wide mouth in a few thousandths of a second, expanding the mouth cavity so that water and prey are sucked in whole. This Trial translates that sudden cavity expansion that sucks prey inside into releasing a squeezed bottle so fast that floating rings are gulped in.

entries.title: Gum Up the Jaws
entries.objective: A tomato frog is bright orange-red and makes no attempt to hide, which for an amphibian requires a defence that works at contact. Seized, it inflates to become hard to swallow and exudes a thick white secretion from skin glands; the material is gummy enough to bind a predator's jaws and mucous membranes and provoke release, and it irritates rather than poisons. Its principle is Visibility. The metaphor? A defence that works at contact lets you stop hiding entirely.
entries.animalRule: The defence must act at contact rather than deter in advance, and the concealment has to actually stop during the attempt.
