entries.title: Look Like a Leaf Until Touched
entries.objective: At rest an Io Moth is a plain yellow or brown shape that reads as a dead leaf, and that costs it nothing at all, which matters for an animal that cannot eat. The eyespots exist but are completely hidden under the forewings until something actually makes contact. Nothing is spent on looking impressive while nothing is happening. Its principle is Illusion Defense. The metaphor? Looking impressive all the time is expensive and buys nothing. Stay plain until contact.
entries.animalRule: Only the presentation may be removed and the underlying capability must be fully intact, demonstrated once during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Maintaining polish on things nobody is looking at costs you hours every week and changes nothing. Stripping it where it is unobserved frees that time and the capability is still there when needed.
entries.mechanismConnection: Automeris io rests with cryptic forewings fully covering the hindwing ocelli, maintaining a leaf-like appearance at no energetic cost, and reveals the eyespots only on tactile stimulus.

entries.title: Look Like the Furniture
entries.objective: The lure only works because nothing else about the Alligator Snapping Turtle reads as an animal. Algae-covered, ridged, motionless, it is indistinguishable from rock on the river bottom, and a fish inspecting the worm never registers what the worm is attached to. The disguise is what makes the bait credible. Its principle is Attraction. The metaphor? An offer only works if you are not visibly waiting for it to work. Go still.
entries.animalRule: No follow-up, reminder or mention may happen after it goes out, and the quiet has to hold for the rest of the day rather than a few minutes.
entries.userBenefit: Chasing a response after you have asked is what makes people wary of answering. Going quiet costs you nothing and the reply you get back is the honest one rather than the pressured one.
entries.mechanismConnection: Macrochelys temminckii remains entirely motionless with an algae-covered, ridged carapace resembling riverbed rock, so only the lure appendage moves and approaching prey does not recognise the surrounding animal.

entries.title: Look Like What They Are Looking For
entries.objective: A spiny flower mantis is not camouflaged into the background; it is disguised as the thing its prey actively wants. Its colours and spiralled markings read as a blossom, so insects searching for flowers steer towards it, and it spends almost nothing while they do the travelling. Resembling the target of a search is better than being invisible. Its principle is Beautiful Trap. The metaphor? Look like what the people you want are already searching for, rather than trying to be noticed.
entries.animalRule: The resemblance must be to something already being searched for during the attempt, and the attention-drawing effort has to stop.
entries.userBenefit: Pushing something at people who were not looking for it costs you constant effort for almost nothing. Making it look like what they already want means they come to you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pseudocreobotra wahlbergii bears floral-mimicking coloration and a spiral discal marking that actively attracts flower-seeking pollinators rather than merely concealing the mantis.

entries.title: Look Up Less Because Others Do
entries.objective: A monkey feeding on the ground cannot watch for leopards at the same time, and every second scanning is a second not eating. In a group the arithmetic changes: if each animal looks up at intervals, the probability that nobody is looking at any moment falls fast with group size, so each individual can scan less and still be covered. Vigilance per animal drops as the group grows. Its principle is Shared Watch. The metaphor? You are watching everything because you do not trust anyone else to. Share it and each of you watches less.
entries.animalRule: The alternation must be explicitly agreed with a real person, and your own checking frequency has to actually reduce rather than staying the same.
entries.userBenefit: Monitoring something constantly because nobody else will means you never fully disengage from it. Alternating with one person halves your load and nothing is less covered.
entries.mechanismConnection: Semnopithecus priam shows the standard group-size effect on vigilance: individual scanning rate declines as group size increases because collective detection probability rises.

entries.title: Loop Five Seed Bowls Back to One Waterhole
entries.objective: Forage from five snack bowls, returning to a single glass of water between every bowl.
entries.animalRule: You eat and drink only at the waterhole, and you must come back to it after every single bowl.
entries.userBenefit: A playful snack break that also gets a full glass of water into you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Peach-faced Lovebird — Flocking • Drinking • Seed-eating: Flocks of Agapornis roseicollis feed on seeds and berries across dry savanna, but they must drink every day, so they are rarely far from permanent pools and return to the same waterholes in large numbers. This Trial translates that water-tethered seed foraging into five snack loops that each end at one glass of water.

entries.title: Loop Ten Floor Items Onto a Table Nonstop
entries.objective: Clear ten numbered items from the floor onto matching numbered spots on a table at the far end of the room, in number order and without ever standing still.
entries.animalRule: Never stop: no pausing, sitting or standing still between laps, and hunt for the next number while you keep walking.
entries.userBenefit: A brisk loop of movement and searching that also leaves the floor tidy.
entries.mechanismConnection: Salmon Shark — Cruising • Diving • Migratory: Lamna ditropis swims continuously through the cold North Pacific day and night, diving repeatedly between the surface and a few hundred metres without ever settling. This Trial translates that continuous swimming with repeated dives into ten nonstop walking laps that each dip to the floor and rise to a table.

entries.title: Loop the Dense Patch Again
entries.objective: Plankton is not spread evenly; tides, currents and upwelling gather it into particular bays and channels. Reef mantas do not graze across the ocean, they concentrate exactly where and when it is dense, looping repeatedly through the same patch and sometimes feeding in chains and spirals until it thins. Returning to the same small place is what makes filter feeding affordable at that size. Its principle is Reef Wing Trust. The metaphor? Go back through the same rich patch.
entries.animalRule: The patch must be chosen from real past results, and it has to be worked at least twice more today.
entries.userBenefit: Moving on to somewhere new after one good result leaves most of the value sitting in the place you just left. Looping the rich patch again is the cheapest return available to you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Mobula alfredi aggregates at tidally concentrated zooplankton patches and loops repeatedly through them, often in feeding chains, rather than searching broadly.

entries.title: Lose the Gut, Keep the Bacteria
entries.objective: An adult giant tube worm has no mouth and no gut at all. It houses dense chemosynthetic bacteria in an internal organ and uses its red plume to circulate vent chemicals and oxygen to them, letting the microbes do all the feeding while the worm stays cemented in its tube beside the vent. It gave up eating to be fed. Its principle is Vent-Rooted Continuance. The metaphor? Host the thing that produces, and you no longer have to go and get.
entries.animalRule: The fetching must stop during the attempt, and the arrangement has to be supplied with its inputs rather than left to run alone.
entries.userBenefit: Going out for something every time you need it ties the supply to your effort and it fails the week you are stretched. Hosting what produces it ends the trips.
entries.mechanismConnection: Riftia pachyptila lacks a mouth and gut as an adult, housing chemosynthetic symbionts in a trophosome and supplying them with vent sulphides and oxygen via its branchial plume.

entries.title: Lose the Scales
entries.objective: A moth's wings are opaque because they are covered in scales, and a wasp's are transparent. To mimic one, the Wasp Moth gives the scales up almost entirely. It is a real loss, of waterproofing and of the pattern most moths depend on, accepted because the resemblance is worth more. Its principle is Hornet Costume. The metaphor? Becoming the new thing means giving up something real from the old one. Lose the scales.
entries.animalRule: The thing given up must be genuinely useful rather than obviously obsolete, and it has to be actually relinquished during the attempt rather than resolved to drop later.
entries.userBenefit: Carrying the old version alongside the new one is why the new one never quite lands for you. Giving up one genuinely useful thing from before is uncomfortable for a day and settles the question.
entries.mechanismConnection: Arctiine wasp moths lose most wing scales to achieve transparency, forfeiting the water repellency and patterning that scales provide, as the cost of resembling a stinging wasp.

entries.title: Lose the Scales on the First Flight
entries.objective: The narrow-bordered bee hawkmoth emerges with fully scaled wings and loses most of those scales within its first few flights, leaving clear panels edged with a narrow dark border. Combined with a furry buff and dark body, that makes it look like a bumblebee. The finish it was born with had to come off before the resemblance worked at all. Its principle is Glasswing. The metaphor? Shed the finish on the first outing.
entries.animalRule: The thing must be used hard enough to visibly wear, and the worn state has to be kept rather than restored.
entries.userBenefit: Keeping something of yours in pristine condition means it never reaches the state where it actually works, and you protect it instead of using it. The wear is usually the part that makes it effective.
entries.mechanismConnection: Hemaris tityus emerges fully scaled and sheds most wing scales within its first flights, producing the transparent panels of its bumblebee resemblance.

entries.title: Loud From Inside the Cover
entries.objective: A bird that hides perfectly has a problem: nothing knows it is there, and a territory nobody knows about is not held. Cetti's warbler never leaves the reeds. Instead it solves presence with volume, delivering a song so abrupt and loud that it carries right out of the vegetation while the bird itself stays completely hidden. It never trades cover for recognition. Its principle is Hidden Voice. The metaphor? Be unmistakable without becoming visible.
entries.animalRule: You must not be physically present in the room during the attempt, and the contribution has to be unmistakably attributed to you.
entries.userBenefit: Being in the room is not what makes your work count, and it costs you hours. Something unmistakable sent from outside it gets you the same credit for far less.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cettia cetti sings an explosive high-amplitude song from deep within dense reedbed cover, achieving territorial advertisement without the exposure that visual display would require.

entries.title: Loud Where You Cannot Be Strong
entries.objective: A lapwing nests on bare open ground in a scrape with no cover, and the first defence is that the eggs look like stones and the sitting bird does not move. The second is the opposite of concealment. The wings are unusually broad and round, poor for efficient flight and excellent for display: rolling and diving in a way that produces an audible throbbing beat, which is what drives crows and foxes off a nest it could never defend directly. Its principle is Display Flight. The metaphor? Noise does what force cannot.
entries.animalRule: The display lasts a full thirty seconds, is aimed at the specific thing you cannot beat by force, and uses noise and movement rather than contact.
entries.userBenefit: Trying to win on strength against something stronger ends one way. Thirty seconds of noise and movement can drive it off without you ever making contact.
entries.mechanismConnection: Vanellus vanellus has broad rounded wings optimised for an acoustically throbbing display and dive flight used in territorial claim and persistent predator mobbing.

entries.title: Lunge From Prone to Clamp One Sliding Sock
entries.objective: Lie flat and still, then lunge to clamp a sock between your forearms as a helper slides it past.
entries.animalRule: Stay flat and still until the sock moves, and clamp with forearms only, no grabbing with the hands.
entries.userBenefit: A short, explosive reaction game that is hilarious to watch.
entries.mechanismConnection: Spectacled Caiman — Explosive • Short • Capture: Caiman crocodilus waits almost motionless in the shallows, then drives a sudden forward surge with tail and limbs and snaps its jaws shut when prey comes within range, returning to stillness if it misses. This Trial translates that explosive lunge and jaw clamp from motionless waiting into a lunge from lying flat that clamps a sliding sock between the forearms.

entries.title: Lunge Only at the Dense Patch
entries.objective: Balaenoptera musculus is the largest animal that has ever existed and it eats one of the smallest. That only works through lunge feeding: it accelerates into a dense krill patch, opens its jaws to nearly ninety degrees, and the pleated throat takes in more water than the whale's own mass before squeezing it out through baleen. It is the most expensive single action measured in any animal, affordable only where krill are concentrated. Its principle is Magnitude. The metaphor? Only lunge at dense patches.
entries.animalRule: No more than two items survive the cut, and nothing from the cut list gets any effort for the rest of the day.
entries.userBenefit: Spreading big effort across thin opportunities is how you end a week exhausted with nothing to show. Reserving your heavy effort for the few dense ones means the same energy actually returns something.
entries.mechanismConnection: Balaenoptera musculus engulfs a volume of water exceeding its own body mass in a single lunge, an action so energetically costly that it pays only on densely aggregated krill.

entries.title: Lunge When It Is Fish
entries.objective: The sei whale can do two completely different things with its mouth. Its baleen has the finest softest fringes of any rorqual, which it uses to skim millimetre-long copepods, but when the prey in front of it is krill or small schooling fish it lunges like its larger relatives, accelerating and engulfing the patch in one gulp. Which method it uses is decided by what is there. Its principle is Filterpace. The metaphor? Let the prey choose the method.
entries.animalRule: The method must be chosen from the task's actual nature and stated before starting, and your default may not be used by habit.
entries.userBenefit: Using your default method on everything means roughly half of what you do takes twice as long as it should. Naming the match before you start is a few seconds that changes the whole task.
entries.mechanismConnection: Balaenoptera borealis switches between continuous ram skim filtering of copepods and engulfment lunge feeding on krill and schooling fish.

entries.title: Lurk Still Until a Creeping Toy Stops
entries.objective: Lie motionless under a blanket watching the room until a toy slowly drawn across the floor stops, then say 'stop' without moving.
entries.animalRule: Nothing moves but your eyes and your voice, and your nose and mouth stay uncovered the whole time.
entries.userBenefit: Ten warm, still minutes with a small moment of pay-off that sharpens attention.
entries.mechanismConnection: Spectacled Caiman — Still • Hidden • Tracking: Caiman crocodilus spends much of the night almost motionless at the water's edge with only its eyes and nostrils above the surface, conserving energy while it tracks prey moving nearby. This Trial translates that motionless lurking while tracking movement into a still watch under a blanket that follows a slowly drawn toy and calls the moment it stops.

entries.title: Maintain the Coat That Buys You In
entries.objective: A clownfish is slow, small and brightly coloured, which on an open reef would be fatal. It survives inside a sea anemone whose stinging cells kill most fish, protected by a mucus coat acquired and maintained through careful repeated contact so the anemone does not recognise it as prey. In return it drives off polyp-eaters and improves water movement. The protection is conditional on maintenance. Its principle is Symbiosis. The metaphor? The thing that lets you live inside someone else's defence needs maintaining, continuously.
entries.animalRule: The maintained thing must be named during the attempt, and the maintenance has to be actually performed.
entries.userBenefit: Access to someone else's protection quietly lapses when you stop maintaining whatever earned it. Doing the maintenance keeps it indefinitely.
entries.mechanismConnection: Amphiprion ocellaris acquires and continuously maintains a mucus coat through graded contact that prevents the host anemone's nematocysts from discharging.

entries.title: Make a Chain to Span It
entries.objective: Adult weaver ants cannot make silk, so the colony uses its own larvae as tools, squeezing them to extrude silk and running them along a seam like a shuttle while others hold the leaf edges together. Getting those edges within reach is a separate problem, solved by workers gripping each other into living chains that span gaps no individual could cross, then contracting. The chain is what closes the distance. Its principle is Collective Construction. The metaphor? Stop stretching alone. Make a chain.
entries.animalRule: At least three consenting people must be physically linked or passing hand to hand, and the task has to be one genuinely impossible for a single person from one position.
entries.userBenefit: You treat a job that is out of reach as needing more strength, so it stays undone. Linking a few people turns an impossible span into a short reach for each of them.
entries.mechanismConnection: Oecophylla smaragdina workers carry larvae in their mandibles and squeeze them to extrude silk, using them as shuttles to stitch leaf nests, and form living chains by gripping one another to bridge and contract gaps far wider than a single ant can span.

entries.title: Make a Wing From Ribs
entries.objective: A snake has no limbs to make a wing out of, so this one makes a wing out of its ribs. Launching from a branch, it rotates the ribs forward and pulls the belly in until the round body becomes a wide concave roughly semicircular section, which is an aerofoil that generates real lift rather than merely slowing a fall, and the glide covers a surprising horizontal distance for the height lost. Its principle is Shape Shift. The metaphor? Reshape what you already have into the thing you lack rather than acquiring it.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be acquired during the attempt, and the existing thing has to be genuinely reconfigured rather than repurposed as-is.
entries.userBenefit: Acquiring something for a function you lack takes weeks and money. Reshaping what you have gets you the function the same afternoon.
entries.mechanismConnection: Chrysopelea paradisi rotates its ribs forward and flattens the ventral surface into a concave semicircular aerofoil cross-section that generates lift, converting the body itself into a wing.

entries.title: Make Being Taken a Mistake
entries.objective: An Asian Common Toad cannot outrun anything, so it makes being eaten the wrong decision. Paired glands behind the eyes hold a secretion that attacks heart muscle directly, and when seized it does not struggle: it inflates and tilts the glands toward whatever has hold of it. A dog that mouths one drops it. That chemistry is what lets a slow animal sit in the open. Its principle is Streetlamp Larder. The metaphor? Stop trying to be faster. Make the grab not worth it.
entries.animalRule: The deterrent must attach a real cost to taking it rather than hiding or locking the thing away, and it has to be in place before anyone next reaches for it.
entries.userBenefit: Guarding something harder costs you attention every day and still fails. Attaching a visible cost to taking it does the work once, and people stop reaching for it without you having to say anything.
entries.mechanismConnection: Duttaphrynus melanostictus carries paired parotoid glands whose bufadienolide secretion disrupts the sodium-potassium pump in cardiac muscle, and when seized it inflates and angles the glands toward the attacker rather than fleeing.

entries.title: Make It Twitch First
entries.objective: The famous shock is the second move. Hunting in mud where it can see nothing, an Electric Eel fires two quick pulses that reach into a hidden fish's nerves and force an involuntary twitch, which gives away exactly where it is. Only then comes the full volley. That probe is what makes the power land. Its principle is Voltage. The metaphor? Do not swing blind. Make it move. Then commit everything.
entries.animalRule: Exactly two taps before you commit, and you may not feel around or lift the cover to search. You go in once, at the spot the movement revealed, with no second attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Committing hard in the wrong place wastes your whole effort. Two cheap probes to find where the thing actually is turn one big push from a gamble into a hit.
entries.mechanismConnection: Electrophorus electricus runs a constant stream of weak pulses to read the water, then fires a doublet of high-voltage pulses that activate a hidden fish's motor neurons from outside its body, forcing a twitch that reveals its position before the full volley locks it rigid.

entries.title: Make One Angle-Stable Blue
entries.objective: Create or find a non-iridescent blue object and photograph it from three viewing angles in one collage to show the colour staying stable.
entries.animalRule: Use one blue surface only; it must remain recognisably the same colour from all three angles rather than relying on a changing reflective effect.
entries.userBenefit: You can tell structural colour from pigment on sight, which changes how you look at everything iridescent.
entries.mechanismConnection: Asian Fairy-bluebird uses this mode by produces blue from a spongy disordered nanostructure rather than from stacked layers, so the colour is the same from every direction instead of flashing and shifting as iridescent colour does

entries.title: Make One Compact Day Shelter
entries.objective: Build a small closed retreat you can return to between active stretches.
entries.animalRule: The shelter must be closed or closable; an open blanket pile does not count.
entries.userBenefit: You create a reliable reset space so the next bout of activity starts from rest.
entries.mechanismConnection: Sac Spider — Sheltering • Moulting • Guarding: By day it rests in a closed tubular silk sac inside a rolled or folded leaf, under bark or beneath stones, and similar sacs serve for moulting, mating and for females guarding their eggs. Clubionid sac spiders roam to hunt, then spin compact silk shelters under leaves, bark, or stones for rest, molting, and egg protection. This Trial translates that mechanism into build a small closed retreat you can return to between active stretches.

entries.title: Make One Family Shelf From Shared Objects
entries.objective: Make One Family Shelf From Shared Objects.
entries.animalRule: Every object must belong to the same household group and stay together in one boundary.
entries.userBenefit: You turn crevice kinship into one concrete experience with a visible finish.
entries.mechanismConnection: Gidgee Skink — Grouped • Related • Resident: Stable family groups of parents and successive offspring occupy one rock crevice system across years, recognising relatives individually and returning to shared latrine sites. This Trial translates that mechanism into one shared shelf of related household objects.

entries.title: Make One Hidden Compartment
entries.objective: Turn an ordinary object into something with a concealed space inside it.
entries.animalRule: Finish it in one sitting, and it must look like nothing from the outside — never label it or leave an obvious edge.
entries.userBenefit: You end up with one genuinely safe place for the two or three things you would hate to lose, which almost nobody actually has.
entries.mechanismConnection: A trapdoor spider digs one silk-lined shaft and closes it with a thick bevelled door faced with soil and moss so it disappears into the bank it was cut from. Building it costs a great deal and is done once; the same burrow is then held for years.

entries.title: Make One Meal Entirely From Fruit
entries.objective: Prepare and eat one complete meal made only from fruit.
entries.animalRule: The feeding event must remain entirely fruit-based while drawing from several fruit sources.
entries.userBenefit: Turns specialized fruit feeding into one bounded, visible meal rather than an all-day diet rule.
entries.mechanismConnection: Jambu Fruit Dove expresses Canopy-Green Stillness through this mode: Swallows fruit whole and voids the seeds intact elsewhere, so the width of its gape determines which tree species are dispersed at all and which are left to drop beneath their parent. The Trial carries that same limiting structure into one concrete human action.

entries.title: Make One Paper Parachute Work
entries.objective: Build one simple paper parachute and adjust it until it falls noticeably slower than the first attempt.
entries.animalRule: Moves between and down from canopy trees on spread webbing rather than by climbing or hopping. Keep that true for the whole attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Teaches rapid prototyping through an obvious physical before-and-after result.
entries.mechanismConnection: Wallace's Flying Frog expresses Parachute through this mode: Wallace's Flying Frog — Webbed-Foot Glide Descent — Arboreal • Gliding • Cheap: Moves between and down from canopy trees on spread webbing rather than by climbing or hopping. The Trial carries that same limiting structure into one concrete human action.

entries.title: Make One Scraps-Only Snack
entries.objective: Make One Scraps-Only Snack.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be bought, and every component must already have been destined for the bin.
entries.userBenefit: You extract value from food that would otherwise be ignored.
entries.mechanismConnection: Processes sediment and detritus with a muscular grinding stomach and an extremely long gut, which lets a large fish live on material with almost no nutritional value that nothing else is competing for

entries.title: Make One Small Object Look Twice Bigger
entries.objective: Make One Small Object Look Twice Bigger.
entries.animalRule: Only folding, spacing or angle may be used; adding a second copy ends the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: You learn how presentation can change perceived size without changing the thing itself.
entries.mechanismConnection: Doubles its apparent size instantly by erecting oversized dorsal and anal fins and turning side-on, so the display uses surface area rather than growth and can be switched on and off in a moment

entries.title: Make One Snack From Three Oldest Dry Stores
entries.objective: Stay in and make one snack from the three dry, shelf-stable foods in your cupboard with the earliest best-before dates.
entries.animalRule: Nothing fresh, nothing from the fridge and nothing bought today: the snack uses only the three oldest of the five stored packets.
entries.userBenefit: A calm, no-shopping snack that uses up what is already in the cupboard.
entries.mechanismConnection: Magnetic Termite — Enclosed • Stored-food • Waterlogged: Amitermes meridionalis stays inside its mound above the waterlogged floodplain clay when wet-season rain makes foraging difficult, and is thought to live partly on grass it stored during the dry season. This Trial translates that shut-in season on older stored grass into one snack built only from the oldest dry stores already in the cupboard.

entries.title: Make One Startling Rattle Fast
entries.objective: Build and perform a harmless sound warning.
entries.animalRule: The container has to stay closed during the performance; one five-second burst only.
entries.userBenefit: You get a ridiculous miniature performance and a homemade sound object worth replaying.
entries.mechanismConnection: California Spiny Lobster — Produces sound by drawing a soft tissue plectrum across a ridged file, a stick-slip mechanism that needs no hard rubbing surfaces, so the animal can still deter and startle a predator during the days after moulting when everything else about it is soft. The Trial compresses that mechanism into one immediate, proofable human session.

entries.title: Make Part of It Visible on Purpose
entries.objective: An orb web is expensive: silk is protein and building one takes an hour or more. It is also almost invisible, which is the point for insects and a serious problem when a bird flies through it. This spider's answer is to make part of the web visible on purpose, adding conspicuous tufts of white silk along the frame and anchor lines where they do not interfere with the catching spiral. Its principle is Spined Web Signature. The metaphor? Mark the structural parts visibly so they are not destroyed, and leave the working parts invisible.
entries.animalRule: Only the structural parts may be marked during the attempt, and the working parts have to stay unmarked.
entries.userBenefit: An entirely invisible structure gets walked through and destroyed by people who meant you no harm. Marking just the frame prevents that without losing the function.
entries.mechanismConnection: Gasteracantha adds conspicuous silk tufts to frame and anchor lines, reducing bird strike damage without compromising the invisibility of the capture spiral.

entries.title: Make Rank and Intent Visible
entries.objective: Hamadryas baboons live in large multi-level societies that must move together between open savanna feeding grounds and steep cliff sleeping sites. Bright skin patches, manes and postures make rank and intent highly visible, and ritualised interactions keep relationships predictable, so a troop of that size can move without constant negotiation. Visibility is what prevents conflict. Its principle is Cliff-troop Discipline. The metaphor? Ambiguity about who does what is where the friction comes from. Make it visible.
entries.animalRule: The arrangement must be written somewhere the whole group can see rather than communicated individually, and it has to state who does what plainly.
entries.userBenefit: Implicit arrangements get remembered differently by everyone, and the friction lands on you at the worst moment. Writing one where the whole group sees it takes two minutes and ends the ambiguity.
entries.mechanismConnection: Papio hamadryas societies use conspicuous visual signals of rank and intent, including skin colouration, mane development and ritualised postures, to maintain predictable relationships in large multi-level troops that move cohesively between feeding and sleeping sites.

entries.title: Make the Bite Fail
entries.objective: A sailfin catfish is slow and makes no attempt to escape. Its answer to predation is that the attack should fail after it has already succeeded: overlapping bony plates instead of scales, a solid head, and stiff leading fin rays that lock outward when it is seized, turning it into something that cannot be swallowed or folded. Where it has been introduced, native predators attack and fail. Surviving the bite is the whole strategy. Its principle is Endurance Claim. The metaphor? You will get caught. Be unswallowable.
entries.animalRule: The armour must go on the specific point that actually fails, and you must give it a genuine real-world knock and show it holding.
entries.userBenefit: Trying to never knock the thing is a plan that fails the first busy day. Armouring the one point that always breaks means the knock stops mattering and you can stop being careful.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pterygoplichthys pardalis is covered in overlapping dermal bony plates with a solid skull, and the leading pectoral and dorsal fin rays lock outward when the fish is seized, making it difficult to swallow or manipulate so that predation attempts fail after capture.

entries.title: Make the Current, Do Not Chase the Food
entries.objective: A rotifer never pursues anything. Bands of cilia around its mouth beat in a steady rotating rhythm that pulls water towards it, so suspended algae arrive on a current it generated itself while the animal stays where it is. The cost is a constant small rhythm instead of travel. Its principle is Wheel-Mouth Renewal. The metaphor? Set up a steady pull that brings things to you, rather than going out after each one.
entries.animalRule: The pull must be steady and repeating during the attempt, and the individual trips have to stop rather than be batched.
entries.userBenefit: Making a separate trip for each thing you need means the travelling is most of your day. One steady pull gathers them while you get on with something else.
entries.mechanismConnection: Philodina roseola generates a feeding current with metachronal beating of its coronal cilia, drawing suspended particles to a stationary body rather than pursuing prey.

entries.title: Make the First Cut, Then Everyone Eats
entries.objective: A carcass with intact hide is closed to most scavengers, whose bills cannot cut it. The lappet-faced vulture has a massive bill and heavy skull built for exactly that step, and it is usually the bird that makes the first opening, after which everything else present can feed. It owns one step in a shared process, and that step is why it is there. Its principle is Heavy Opening. The metaphor? Own the step everyone is stuck behind and you never have to compete for the rest.
entries.animalRule: Only the blocking step may be done during the attempt, and the rest has to be deliberately left to others.
entries.userBenefit: Doing the whole job means competing with everyone and being thanked for none of it. Doing only the blocking step makes you the one they cannot start without.
entries.mechanismConnection: Torgos tracheliotos has a massive bill and robust skull enabling it to open intact carcass hide, the limiting step that subsequently permits other scavenger species to feed.

entries.title: Make the Fish Come to You
entries.objective: An Alligator Snapping Turtle has moved the effort of hunting from the predator onto the prey. It settles on the river bottom looking like algae-covered rock, holds its mouth open, and wriggles a small pink appendage on the floor of its tongue that moves convincingly like a worm. Fish come to inspect it. The turtle spends almost nothing and the fish does all the travelling. Its principle is Attraction. The metaphor? Stop going out to get it. Put out the thing that makes it come.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be pursued once the bait is set, and the bait has to be something genuinely attractive to the thing you want rather than an announcement about yourself.
entries.userBenefit: Chasing costs you energy on every single attempt and most of them miss. One good piece of bait put out and left works while you do other things, and the ones that come to you were already interested.
entries.mechanismConnection: Macrochelys temminckii lies camouflaged on the riverbed with its jaws open, luring fish by wriggling a pink vermiform appendage on the floor of its tongue, so prey approaches the ambush rather than being pursued.

entries.title: Make the Food You Cannot Find
entries.objective: A seed is a poor thing to raise a chick on, so a mourning dove manufactures something better: both parents produce crop milk, a secretion of sloughed crop lining far richer in protein and fat than anything they eat. The consequence is scheduling. Other small birds must breed when insects peak; a dove is decoupled from that and raises broods from early spring into autumn. Its principle is Soft Mourning. The metaphor? Make the input yourself and you stop being governed by when it is available.
entries.animalRule: The version must be genuinely produced by you rather than sourced elsewhere, and you have to proceed without the original supply during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Waiting on someone else's supply means your whole schedule is theirs. Making a rough version yourself means you go when you decide to.
entries.mechanismConnection: Zenaida macroura parents secrete protein- and lipid-rich crop milk from sloughed crop epithelium, decoupling breeding from invertebrate availability and extending the nesting season.

entries.title: Make the Group Audible
entries.objective: A kookaburra holds territory as a family, not a pair, and the call is how that becomes legible. When one bird starts, the rest join, so a neighbouring territory hears a chorus whose size tells it exactly how many birds it would have to displace. Between calls they hunt silently. The group is only a deterrent while it can be heard. Its principle is Chorus. The metaphor? Support that nobody can hear counts for nothing.
entries.animalRule: The existing support must be made publicly audible during the attempt, and no new support may be recruited.
entries.userBenefit: People who back you privately may as well not, because nobody deciding about you knows. Getting it said out loud changes how you are treated immediately.
entries.mechanismConnection: Dacelo novaeguineae gives chorused territorial calls in which family group members join in, so call volume and composition advertise group size to neighbouring territories.

entries.title: Make the Invisible Readable
entries.objective: Fruit flies became the foundation of genetics because of one visible thing. Cells in their salivary glands copy their DNA repeatedly without dividing, so each chromosome becomes a bundle of a thousand identical strands lying in register, thick enough to see under an ordinary microscope, with a fixed pattern of bands as landmarks. Stacking the copies is what made genes readable at all. Its principle is Rapid Adaptation Strategy. The metaphor? Stop guessing at the invisible. Stack it until you can see it.
entries.animalRule: The record must be physically visible in frame, on paper or as objects rather than in an app, and you must say out loud the pattern you can now see that you could not before.
entries.userBenefit: A vague sense of how often something happens is almost always wrong, and you cannot argue with it. Making it physically visible settles it in ten minutes and usually surprises you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Drosophila melanogaster salivary gland cells undergo endoreduplication, producing polytene chromosomes of around a thousand aligned identical strands with a fixed reproducible banding pattern visible under light microscopy, which made physical gene mapping possible.

entries.title: Make the Pass Slow and Laboured
entries.objective: A breeding male long-tailed widowbird grows a tail about half a metre long, several times his own length, and advertises his territory with slow, laboured display flights low over the grass with the tail spread and hanging beneath him. He could fly better without it. The point is that the flight is visibly hard and visible from right across open country. Its principle is Tail-Weight Performance. The metaphor? Let the effort be seen.
entries.animalRule: The work must be done in view of the people it is for, and the effort has to remain visible rather than compressed.
entries.userBenefit: Doing hard work quickly and out of sight means people price your effort as easy and ask for more of it for nothing. Letting the effort be seen once resets what they think it costs.
entries.mechanismConnection: Euplectes progne males perform slow, laboured low display flights with a half-metre tail that measurably increases mating success when experimentally lengthened.

entries.title: Make the Return Stroke Work
entries.objective: Almost every bird makes lift on the downstroke and recovers on the upstroke, so half of each wingbeat is wasted and true hovering is impossible. Hummingbirds do not work that way: the shoulder rotates nearly a full turn, so at the end of the forward stroke the wing inverts and sweeps backwards leading edge first, generating lift in both directions. Nothing in the cycle is dead. Its principle is Precision Hovering. The metaphor? Half your cycle is currently recovery. Make the way back do work too.
entries.animalRule: The return leg must do genuinely useful work rather than being merely pleasant, and the outbound leg has to stay unchanged.
entries.userBenefit: Half your repeated motions produce nothing because you treat them as recovery. Loading the return leg once gets you a free second output from a trip you were making anyway.
entries.mechanismConnection: Trochilid shoulder joints permit near-complete wing rotation so the wing inverts and generates lift on the backstroke as well as the forward stroke, producing sustained hovering impossible for other birds.

entries.title: Make the Rim Hostile
entries.objective: A nuthatch nests in a cavity and cannot make the hole much smaller, so this one makes the rim hostile instead. It collects globules of conifer resin, carries them in its bill and sometimes uses a flake of bark as a tool to apply them, smearing the entrance until anything crossing gets stuck. The opening stays the same size and becomes unusable to everything else. Its principle is Vertical Foraging. The metaphor? You cannot make the entrance smaller. Make crossing it unpleasant.
entries.animalRule: The opening must stay the same size and the friction has to be at the threshold rather than inside, applied during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: You cannot close the opening without cutting off the people you actually want, so it stays wide open. Friction at the threshold filters it without closing anything.
entries.mechanismConnection: Sitta canadensis smears conifer resin around its nest cavity entrance, sometimes applying it with a bark flake held in the bill, deterring predators and competitors without altering the hole's dimensions.

entries.title: Make the Signal Expensive
entries.objective: A springbok grazes in open country where there is nowhere to hide. When a predator is spotted it does not run first: it bounces stiff-legged with its back arched, opening a fold of skin that fans a crest of white hair along the spine. The leap is expensive and difficult, and that is the point, because an animal fit enough to waste energy so visibly is not worth chasing, which is why the chase is often called off before it starts. Its principle is Assertion. The metaphor? A cheap claim is never believed.
entries.animalRule: The display must be genuinely costly to perform and visible to whoever applied the pressure, and no explanation may accompany it.
entries.userBenefit: Explaining that you can handle pressure invites argument, because talk is cheap and everyone can do it. One visibly costly display settles the question without you saying anything.
entries.mechanismConnection: Antidorcas marsupialis stots on stiff legs with an erected dorsal crest of white hair, an energetically expensive and therefore unfakeable advertisement of condition to pursuing predators.

entries.title: Make the Waiting Cost Nothing
entries.objective: The heron's strike takes a fraction of a second; the waiting takes most of the day. Standing in shallow water costs the bird almost nothing, and that cheapness is what lets it keep waiting rather than switching to hunting methods that spend energy for the same fish. The wait is not wasted time, it is the affordable part. Its principle is Poise. The metaphor? You quit because waiting costs too much.
entries.animalRule: The fifteen minutes must cost you almost nothing, with nothing else running alongside, and the wait has to continue to the end rather than being converted into action.
entries.userBenefit: Making waiting expensive is why you give up on things just before they arrive. A wait that costs you almost nothing can be held long enough to actually pay off.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ardea herodias uses a near-zero-cost standing wait in shallow water, which makes prolonged ambush energetically sustainable compared with active pursuit.

entries.title: Make the Water Move
entries.objective: Hunting cloudy shallows is a detection problem: the prey is there and invisible. A snowy egret does not wait for information, it creates it, dragging and vibrating a bright yellow foot through mud so shrimp and small fish bolt, then striking as they move. It generates exactly the movement it needs in order to see. Its principle is Provocation. The metaphor? When nothing is visible, stop looking harder. Do something that makes things move.
entries.animalRule: The disturbance must be small and deliberate rather than disruptive, and what moved has to be observed and named during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Staring harder at a situation nobody is explaining tells you nothing and wastes your week. One small deliberate disturbance makes the real positions show themselves.
entries.mechanismConnection: Egretta thula performs foot-stirring and foot-raking with its bright yellow feet in turbid shallows, flushing concealed prey into motion and converting an undetectable target into a visible one.

entries.title: Make the Whole Head the Tool
entries.objective: Carpenter ant colonies sit inside dead trunks, beyond almost every other bird. A pileated woodpecker reaches them by turning its whole body into one tool: a chisel bill, a skull braced to absorb repeated impact, stiff tail feathers bracing against the trunk, and a long barbed tongue that follows the galleries once the wood is open. The work is slow and repeated, and the rectangular holes it leaves become other species' nests. Its principle is Excavation. The metaphor? For deep work, every part of the setup has to serve the one task.
entries.animalRule: Every part of the setup must serve the single task during the attempt, and anything serving something else has to be removed.
entries.userBenefit: Deep work in a setup that serves four purposes is why it never goes deep. Arranging everything for one task gets you further in an hour than a day of that.
entries.mechanismConnection: Dryocopus pileatus combines a chisel bill, impact-bracing skull architecture, stiffened rectrices for trunk bracing and a long barbed tongue into an integrated excavation and extraction system.

entries.title: Make Them Take Off First
entries.objective: A fantail almost never stops moving, and the movement is the hunting method. Insects resting on foliage are cryptic and hard to find, but they respond to sudden high-contrast movement by taking off, and a fantail working through vegetation with its tail fanned and swung from side to side triggers exactly that, then catches the insect in the air where it is conspicuous and slow. Its principle is Adaptive Flow Pattern. The metaphor? Make the hidden thing move first, and then take it where it is easy to see.
entries.animalRule: The thing must be made to move before any attempt during the attempt, and action has to wait until it is exposed.
entries.userBenefit: Searching for something cryptic means you find a fraction of it after a long time. Making it move first puts it in the open where it is easy for you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Rhipidura javanica flushes cryptic foliage-resting insects using high-contrast tail fanning movement and captures them in flight where they are conspicuous.

entries.title: Make Three Passes Around Four Obstacles
entries.objective: Dash One Zigzag Course.
entries.animalRule: All three passes must stay on your feet with no gliding stops between obstacles.
entries.userBenefit: Three fast controlled passes, and a clear sense of where your balance actually gives out.
entries.mechanismConnection: Carries a heavy body on small wings, which makes gliding impossible and forces continuous rapid beating, producing a flight too fast and too abrupt for a bird to intercept

entries.title: Make Your Own Non-Stick
entries.objective: A leafhopper feeds on sap and excretes a large volume of sugary liquid, which is a problem because a sticky insect on a wet leaf is a fouled insect. The Candy-striped Leafhopper manufactures its own powder: specialised cells produce brochosomes, hollow protein granules a few hundred nanometres across, which it spreads over itself so nothing adheres. It makes the solution to its own by-product. Its principle is Vibrant Communication Pattern. The metaphor? Your own output is what fouls you. Make the thing that keeps it off.
entries.animalRule: The routine must handle the by-product as part of the work rather than as a separate cleanup, and it has to run at least once during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Your own by-product is what makes your workspace unusable by Thursday. A routine that disposes of it as you go means you never have to spend a session cleaning up after yourself.
entries.mechanismConnection: Graphocephala coccinea secretes brochosomes, hollow proteinaceous nanostructures produced in the Malpighian tubules, and spreads them over the cuticle to create a superhydrophobic anti-wetting coating against its own honeydew.

entries.title: Manage It by Posture Afterwards
entries.objective: A dragonfly's flight muscles only work in a narrow temperature band, and a darter is too small to hold shivering-generated heat for long, so the sun does the work. It basks flat against a warm stone until the thorax is warm enough to fly, then hunts in short sorties from a perch, returning between them, and manages temperature afterwards through posture rather than by generating more heat. Its principle is Warm Perch Return. The metaphor? Get into the band externally, then hold it by posture rather than by effort.
entries.animalRule: The condition must be reached externally during the attempt, and it has to be held by posture rather than effort.
entries.userBenefit: Generating your own working condition and then maintaining it by effort exhausts you by midday. Reaching it externally and holding it by position costs nothing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Sympetrum basks to raise thoracic temperature into the flight range and subsequently regulates it by postural adjustment of the angle presented to the sun.

entries.title: Manage the Lighting
entries.objective: Wilson's bird-of-paradise does something very few animals do: it manages the lighting. A male clears a patch of forest floor of debris and then removes foliage from the branches above it, so daylight reaches the court directly rather than being filtered by canopy, which matters because the display depends on colour that only reads properly in direct light. He prepares the room before performing. Its principle is Stagecraft. The metaphor? Fix the lighting before the performance, because the content only works under the right conditions.
entries.animalRule: The conditions must be prepared before presenting during the attempt, and the content may not be changed.
entries.userBenefit: Improving your content while the conditions obscure it means nobody sees the improvement. Clearing the view first makes the same content land.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cicinnurus respublica males clear both the forest floor court and the overhanging foliage so direct sunlight illuminates the display, which depends on colours that fail under filtered light.

entries.title: Many Burrows, Rotated
entries.objective: A greater bilby makes its living by moving soil. Powerful foreclaws dig out bulbs, seeds and fungi invisible from the surface, and the same tools produce spiralling burrows up to three metres long, of which an individual maintains many and rotates between them rather than occupying one. A single bilby turns over several tonnes of soil a year. Its principle is Desert Provision. The metaphor? Maintain many shelters and rotate, rather than depending on one.
entries.animalRule: At least two must be maintained and the rotation has to actually happen during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Settling into your best fallback means the others decay and you have one left. Rotating keeps all of them usable for the week you need a different one.
entries.mechanismConnection: Macrotis lagotis excavates and maintains multiple spiral burrows up to three metres long, rotating occupancy rather than depending on a single refuge.

entries.title: Many Eyes and Water Within Reach
entries.objective: A capybara is a very large rodent on a very poor diet, coarse grass handled with continuously growing teeth and by re-ingesting its own droppings to pass material through twice. Nothing about that supports a fast or defensive animal, so safety comes from two things instead: a group in which many animals are watching at once, and water always within reach. Its principle is Social Calm. The metaphor? If you cannot be fast or armed, keep many eyes around you and an exit always in reach.
entries.animalRule: Both the shared watching and the reachable exit must be in place during the attempt, and no personal defence may be relied on.
entries.userBenefit: Relying on your own alertness and defence means both fail at once when you are tired. Many eyes and a near exit hold without you doing anything.
entries.mechanismConnection: Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris relies on group vigilance and immediate water access rather than speed or defence, with hypsodont teeth and caecotrophy handling coarse forage.

entries.title: Many Noses, One Front
entries.objective: A coati band moves through forest as a loose sweeping front, every animal nose-down, turning over leaf litter at once. The band is the search: many noses covering ground simultaneously find far more than one could, and constant chittering holds the line together in cover where nobody can see anybody. The method is width, not cleverness. Its principle is Exploration. The metaphor? Searching alone is the slow version. Spread a line across it and keep talking.
entries.animalRule: At least two others must cover different parts simultaneously, and a running channel between searchers has to be kept open during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Searching something wide on your own takes days and you still miss parts. A spread line with people talking finds it in an afternoon.
entries.mechanismConnection: Nasua nasua forages in bands that advance as a broad front, each individual probing leaf litter with its flexible snout while continuous chittering maintains group cohesion in dense cover.

entries.title: Many Ordinary Trips, One Large Cache
entries.objective: Red harvester ants live where seed falls in pulses and lean stretches last months. No single trip matters: workers leave, take a few small seeds, come back, and the colony's traffic management and sorting turn thousands of unremarkable outings into one reliable underground store. The cache is an accumulation, never an achievement. Its principle is Seed Discipline. The metaphor? Make the trips small enough to repeat, because the store is built from their number and not their size.
entries.animalRule: Each contribution must be small enough to repeat during the attempt, and the running total has to be recorded rather than the individual amounts.
entries.userBenefit: Making contributions large enough to feel significant means you do it twice and stop. Small ones you would repeat tomorrow are what the store is actually built from.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pogonomyrmex barbatus accumulates large granaries through numerous short individual foraging trips, with trail traffic regulation and seed sorting converting small loads into a durable cache.

entries.title: Many Small Fast Decisions
entries.objective: Mosquitoes operate through rapid sensing, frequent flight corrections and repeated approach-withdraw cycles. The advantage comes from many small fast decisions rather than one large durable action, and no single approach has to succeed because another follows immediately. Nothing is committed to for long. Its principle is Needle Persistence. The metaphor? Make many small fast attempts with immediate withdrawal, rather than one carefully committed one.
entries.animalRule: Withdrawal must be immediate on each failure during the attempt, and no single attempt may be committed to.
entries.userBenefit: Committing to one careful attempt means one result and no information. Many fast attempts with instant withdrawal costs you the same time and finds the way in.
entries.mechanismConnection: Culicid host-seeking proceeds through rapid repeated approach and withdrawal cycles driven by fast sensory sampling rather than sustained committed approach.

entries.title: Many Small Power Strokes
entries.objective: A giant millipede is a burrowing machine rather than a walking one. Two pairs of legs on each body segment give an enormous number of small power strokes pushing against soil, which is what drives a rigid body through packed litter a longer-legged animal could not enter. It breaks dead plant material into fragments bacteria can then work on. Its principle is Decomposition. The metaphor? Many small simultaneous pushes get you through packed material that no single large push would.
entries.animalRule: The pushes must be many and small during the attempt, and no single large effort may be used.
entries.userBenefit: One large push against packed material just stops you and tires you out. Many small simultaneous ones move you through steadily.
entries.mechanismConnection: Diplopod diplosegments provide two leg pairs per segment, generating a high number of small simultaneous power strokes that drive a rigid body through compacted litter.

entries.title: Many Small Stores, Used This Week
entries.objective: When a black-billed magpie finds more than it can eat, it does not build one hoard. It pushes the surplus into many small caches, each covered over in soil or grass, and it digs most of them up again within days. The storage is short term and spread wide, so no single loss matters and nothing sits long enough to spoil. That is what makes a patchy food supply survivable. Its principle is Black-Billed Cachecraft. The metaphor? Store small, spend soon.
entries.animalRule: The surplus must be split into at least three stores, and each one needs a use date inside the week.
entries.userBenefit: One big store feels safe and quietly rots, because you never touch it and you lose it all at once if it goes. Several small stores you spend this week keep the surplus actually useful to you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pica hudsonia scatter-hoards surplus food into many small covered caches and recovers most of them within a few days.

entries.title: Map One Human-Made Habitat
entries.objective: Find three human-made features in one area that an animal could plausibly use for shelter, perching, or nesting, without disturbing wildlife.
entries.animalRule: Observe only: do not touch nests, animals, or occupied shelter; all three features must be human-made structures.
entries.userBenefit: You start seeing the built world the way something living in it would, which you cannot really switch off afterwards.
entries.mechanismConnection: Common Pheasant uses this mode by exists in the countryside as an annually released population rather than a self-sustaining wild one, so its numbers, timing and ecological effects are set by rearing and release decisions rather than by anything the species does

entries.title: Map One Quiet Route Through Cover
entries.objective: Map One Quiet Route Through Cover.
entries.animalRule: The route must connect both points without using the most direct open line.
entries.userBenefit: You turn range stealth into one concrete, visible experience instead of an abstract idea.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cougar — Solitary • Ranging • Reading cover: Most of the animal's life is quiet travel across a home range far larger than its body needs, choosing broken ground and vegetation because closing the distance unseen is what makes a kill possible at all. This Trial translates that mid-frequency mechanism into one quiet route through cover.

entries.title: Mark A Bright Warning Boundary
entries.objective: Keep a costly shield visible so others stop before contact.
entries.animalRule: Do not touch or move the guarded object once the boundary is set.
entries.userBenefit: You make limits obvious early so you spend less energy on last-second defense.
entries.mechanismConnection: Blister Beetle — Armored • Signaled • Costly: Meloid beetles keep a persistent defensive shield and warning colors instead of constant high-speed escapes. This Trial sets a bright no-touch boundary and holds it without crossing.

entries.title: Mark It Until the Boundary Is Obvious
entries.objective: The impressive part about a Japanese serow is not that it can stand on a cliff but how small its world is. It occupies a fixed territory it rarely leaves and marks it heavily, using preorbital glands proportionally among the largest of any bovid, wiping them on rocks until the boundary is chemically obvious. Its principle is Forest Footing. The metaphor? If you are staying put for years, make the boundary unmistakable.
entries.animalRule: The boundary must be marked at more than one point during the attempt, and it may not simply be stated once.
entries.userBenefit: Assuming your boundary is understood means discovering it is not at the worst moment. Marking it repeatedly is cheap and the question stops arising.
entries.mechanismConnection: Capricornis crispus has proportionally among the largest preorbital glands of any bovid and marks rocks and vegetation repeatedly to make the boundary of its small permanent territory chemically explicit.

entries.title: Marrow in a Sealed Container
entries.objective: A picked-over carcass looks finished and is not. Inside the long bones sits marrow, sealed in a rigid container that keeps it edible for days after the rest has gone, and almost nothing on an African or Asian dry landscape can open it. A striped hyena can: its jaw muscles and blunt conical premolars generate enough force to crack a femur, so it arrives after everyone else has left. Its principle is Useful Power. The metaphor? Build the capability to open the sealed part, and arrive after the crowd.
entries.animalRule: The thing must already have been abandoned by others, and the sealed part has to be genuinely opened during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Arriving with the crowd means competing for what is easy to reach. Arriving late with the right capability gets you something nobody else could open.
entries.mechanismConnection: Hyaena hyaena has heavy jaw musculature and blunt conical premolars capable of fracturing long bones, accessing marrow that remains edible for days after other scavengers have finished.

entries.title: Mass Per Unit Length Sets the Reach
entries.objective: The reputation is of a fast aggressive snake; the reality is a shy animal whose first response is to disappear upward into leaves. What the body is actually optimised for is reach, because a snake crossing between branches must hold part of itself out over nothing, and the limit on that is mass per unit length. Its principle is Green Velocity. The metaphor? How far you extend unsupported is set by weight, not strength.
entries.animalRule: The weight per unit must be genuinely reduced during the attempt, and no additional support may be added.
entries.userBenefit: Strengthening supports so you can extend further means adding structure everywhere and carrying it. Reducing your weight per unit extends the same reach for nothing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Dendroaspis angusticeps has exceptionally low mass per unit length, maximising the unsupported cantilever span it can hold while bridging between branches.

entries.title: Match a Supply People Make Constantly
entries.objective: The collared dove crossed Europe in a few decades without any special ability to fly, fight or hide. What it has is a match to a food supply people create constantly: spilled grain around farms, feed yards and gardens, available in winter when wild seed is not. A bird that does not need to migrate and raises brood after brood converts that steady surplus into more doves. Its principle is Urban Adaptation. The metaphor? Match a supply that is continuously produced as a by-product, and you need no other advantage.
entries.animalRule: The supply must be a by-product of another activity during the attempt, and no primary resource may be competed for.
entries.userBenefit: Competing for a primary resource means competing with everyone who wants it. A by-product nobody is counting is continuously available to you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Streptopelia decaocto exploits anthropogenic spilled grain available year-round, enabling non-migratory residency and repeated brooding through a long season.

entries.title: Match One Moving Background
entries.objective: Stand near moving curtains, leaves, or another harmless moving background and gently match its rhythm for 20 seconds.
entries.animalRule: You must move only when the background moves and freeze when it settles; do not create the background movement yourself.
entries.userBenefit: Sharpens environmental timing by matching surrounding motion rather than treating stillness as the only form of concealment.
entries.mechanismConnection: Stick Mantis uses this mode by rocks gently while stationary so that its movement matches the vegetation around it, because in air that is moving everything else, holding perfectly still is what a searching predator would notice

entries.title: Match One Object to a Background
entries.objective: Match One Object to a Background.
entries.animalRule: The object stays fully visible; nothing may cover it.
entries.userBenefit: You turn branch illusion into one concrete, visible experience instead of an abstract idea.
entries.mechanismConnection: Great Potoo — Rigid • Bill-up • Unmoving: The entire daylight period is spent upright and motionless on an exposed snag with bark-patterned plumage, monitoring the surroundings through small notches in the closed eyelids because any movement would end the imitation. This Trial translates that low-frequency mechanism into one object against a background.

entries.title: Match One Outfit to Today's Ground
entries.objective: Choose clothes whose colours blend with whatever the ground outside looks like today.
entries.animalRule: The colours come from today's actual ground, not from your favourite clothes: the outfit has to fit the current backdrop.
entries.userBenefit: A slow, playful look at the colours around you that may change what you reach for next season.
entries.mechanismConnection: Arctic Fox — Blended • Careful • Concealing: Vulpes lagopus moults between a white winter coat and a brown or grey summer coat so that its colour tracks the tundra as it changes between snow and bare ground, keeping it concealed without having to outrun predators. This Trial translates that coat matched to the current season's ground into an outfit chosen to blend with today's ground.

entries.title: Match the Depth Exactly
entries.objective: A flower with a long tube has made a choice: it excludes almost every insect in order to be visited by the few that can reach the bottom. This hawkmoth is one of those, with a proboscis longer than its body, carried coiled and extended while hovering. The relationship works both ways, because the moth gets a reliable supply and the flower gets a reliable carrier. Its principle is Green-streak Rest. The metaphor? Matching exactly what something needs is worth more than being generally capable.
entries.animalRule: The requirement must be found by asking rather than inferred, and what you provide has to match it exactly without extras or substitutions.
entries.userBenefit: Providing roughly what someone needs plus extras means they still have to do the matching themselves. Asking and providing exactly that makes you the one they come back to.
entries.mechanismConnection: Theretra nessus carries a proboscis longer than its body and hovers to feed from deep-corolla flowers inaccessible to short-tongued insects, forming a reciprocal specialised pollination relationship.

entries.title: Match the Form to the Lake
entries.objective: Salvelinus alpinus has the widest latitudinal range of any freshwater fish, and it manages that by refusing to commit to one life history. Where there is access to the sea it runs to salt water each summer and returns to spawn, reaching several kilograms. Landlocked, the same species matures at a fraction of that size on invertebrates. In some lakes several forms coexist at once, differing in head shape and size. That flexibility is what keeps it everywhere. Its principle is Cold Versatility. The metaphor? Set the form to the lake you are in.
entries.animalRule: Three physical changes are made before the hour starts, and nothing is changed back during it.
entries.userBenefit: Working in a space set up for a different life is why everything takes effort you cannot account for. Three physical changes matched to what you actually do there removes that drag permanently.
entries.mechanismConnection: Salvelinus alpinus expresses anadromous, landlocked and multiple coexisting morphs of differing size and head shape depending on the lake it occupies.

entries.title: Match the Grain, Not the Colour
entries.objective: A brill on the bottom does not simply turn sand-coloured. It adjusts the pattern of its upper surface to the substrate's grain: fine sand gives a fine speckle, coarse gravel a coarser mottling, and a chequerboard laid on an aquarium floor produces a rough chequerboard on the fish. The control is nervous rather than hormonal, so it takes minutes, and it works from what the fish sees. Its principle is Seabed Subtlety. The metaphor? Match the texture, not the shade.
entries.animalRule: What is matched must be a texture such as pace or formality rather than an appearance, and one thing has to be done at that grain.
entries.userBenefit: Matching how a place looks while getting its pace and formality wrong is exactly what marks you as new there. Matching the grain is invisible and does far more for how you are received.
entries.mechanismConnection: Scophthalmus rhombus adjusts dermal chromatophore patterning to substrate grain under visual and neural control, matching scale as well as hue within minutes.

entries.title: Match the Ground, Build Nothing
entries.objective: A snowy plover nests on open beach and salt flat where there is nowhere to hide and makes only a shallow scrape, sometimes lined with shell fragments. The protection is entirely colour: speckled buff eggs that match the sand and a pale adult that is hard to pick out sitting on them. Nothing was constructed, because construction would be the thing that showed. Its principle is Sand-Nest Caution. The metaphor? Match the ground exactly and build nothing, because what you build is what gets noticed.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be built during the attempt, and anything previously added that stands out has to be removed.
entries.userBenefit: Building something to protect what you have is itself the signal that there is something there. Matching the surroundings and adding nothing is what keeps it unnoticed.
entries.mechanismConnection: Charadrius nivosus nests in an unlined shallow scrape on open substrate, relying entirely on cryptic egg and adult plumage rather than any structure.

entries.title: Match the Host's Rhythm Exactly
entries.objective: A pin-tailed whydah raises nothing itself. Its eggs, its chicks' calls and their begging patterns are tuned to match a specific host species closely enough that the host's own parenting cycle absorbs them without disruption. The young develop entirely inside somebody else's stable repeated routine, and the whole thing depends on fitting that routine rather than being better than it. Its principle is Foster-Nest Egg. The metaphor? Match an existing routine's shape precisely, and it will carry your work without noticing.
entries.animalRule: The routine may not be changed during the attempt, and your piece has to match its existing shape rather than approximate it.
entries.userBenefit: Asking an existing routine to change for your work means it is resisted and nothing gets carried. Matching its shape exactly means it absorbs your piece for free.
entries.mechanismConnection: Vidua macroura eggs, nestling calls and begging displays closely mimic those of its specific estrildid finch hosts, integrating into the host's unaltered provisioning cycle.

entries.title: Match the Lines You Live Among
entries.objective: A razorfish does not swim the way a fish swims. It holds its body vertical with the snout pointing at the seabed and moves in that posture permanently, because what it shelters among is the long spines of sea urchins. Head-down among vertical spines, it reads as another spine. The permanent discomfort of the posture is the entire defence. Its principle is Vertical Movement. The metaphor? Match the orientation of what surrounds you, even when it is awkward.
entries.animalRule: Their rhythm must be adopted rather than negotiated, and it has to be held for the whole session even where it is uncomfortable.
entries.userBenefit: Importing your own rhythm into a group marks you as outside it and everyone works around you. Adopting theirs for one session is awkward and gets you treated as inside almost immediately.
entries.mechanismConnection: Aeoliscus strigatus swims permanently head-down in a vertical posture, aligning with the long spines of Diadema urchins among which it shelters so its outline matches the surrounding structure.

entries.title: Match the Shape of the Room
entries.objective: A tawny frogmouth's defence is a posture. Through daylight it sits along a branch rather than across it, tilts its bill upward into a line, narrows its eyes to slits so no reflection gives it away, and stiffens, and mottled grey plumage completes the impression of a broken stub of wood. That is what keeps it unseen in plain sight. At night it drops from a low perch onto insects and frogs, taking them with an enormous wide bill rather than talons. Its principle is Disguise. The metaphor? Alignment hides better than colour.
entries.animalRule: Posture, pace and register all have to match the room, and the alignment is held for the whole interaction without exception.
entries.userBenefit: Standing out by habit means every room costs you energy to be in. Matching its shape for one interaction lets you stay as long as you want unnoticed.
entries.mechanismConnection: Podargus strigoides adopts a cryptic branch-aligned posture with bill elevated and eyes slitted, its mottled plumage completing the resemblance to a broken limb.

entries.title: Match This Stone, Not Stone
entries.objective: A wall lizard on granite is not generically camouflaged, it is matched to that granite. The reticulated green, brown and black on a Bocage's Wall Lizard corresponds closely to the lichen mottling of weathered outcrops in northwestern Iberia, and populations on different rock differ measurably in ground colour. General resemblance would not work. Its principle is Lichened-Granite Mottle. The metaphor? Fitting the category is not fitting the place. Match this one exactly.
entries.animalRule: At least three details must be changed to fit this specific case rather than the general category, and the generic version must not go out.
entries.userBenefit: A generic version signals that you did not look at their situation, which is what gets it ignored. Three specific details costs five minutes and completely changes the response rate.
entries.mechanismConnection: Podarcis bocagei populations show dorsal reticulation closely matching the lichen patterning of their local granite substrate, with measurable differences in ground colour between populations on different rock types.

entries.title: Match Three Fabrics to One Hedge's Greens
entries.objective: Test green and brown fabrics against a leafy hedge and keep the three whose colours best match its leaves.
entries.animalRule: Colour decides: an item stays only if its shade blends with the leaves around it.
entries.userBenefit: A closer look at colour and a clear idea of which of your fabrics blend in outdoors.
entries.mechanismConnection: Common Green Forest Lizard — Blended • Background • Idle: Calotes calotes spends most of its time still or slow among foliage, its green body and patterning matching the leaves so it stays visually quiet to predators and prey alike. This Trial translates that colour match to foliage into choosing the three fabrics whose greens and browns match one hedge.

entries.title: Matching Is an Escalation
entries.objective: A song sparrow does not have a song; it has eight or so, learned in its first year from nearby adults, which is why the local population shares a dialect. What is unusual is that which type it sings is itself the message: singing back the exact type a neighbour just used is matching, an escalation, while switching types de-escalates. Its principle is Small Song. The metaphor? Which response you choose is itself the message.
entries.animalRule: The choice must be deliberate during the attempt, and the message it sends has to be stated.
entries.userBenefit: Replying in whatever form comes naturally sends a message you did not intend and often escalates. Choosing deliberately keeps the exchange where you want it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Melospiza melodia song type matching during territorial disputes constitutes escalation, while switching to a non-matching type signals de-escalation.

entries.title: Melt One Ice Cube Faster on Dark Cloth
entries.objective: Show how a dark surface soaks up radiant heat by setting two equal ice chips to bask, one on dark cloth and one on white.
entries.animalRule: Only radiant light does the warming: no touching, breathing on or moving the chips.
entries.userBenefit: A quiet sit in the sun with a neat bit of physics to show for it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pond Slider — Grounded • Warming • Watchful: Trachemys scripta hauls out onto logs and basks with its dark shell and skin angled to the sun, absorbing radiant heat to raise its body temperature for digestion and activity. This Trial translates that dark shell soaking up radiant heat while basking into two ice cubes basking on dark and white cloth.

entries.title: Memorise the Route Instead
entries.objective: A bushbaby's eyes are so large relative to the skull that they barely move in their sockets, so the head and ears do the looking. Even with a reflective layer behind the retina, a small primate moving fast through thorn scrub at night cannot see a branch well enough to decide anything in mid-air. The answer is to know the route already, which is why it uses the same pathways repeatedly. Its principle is Night Reading. The metaphor? Where you cannot see well enough to decide in motion, memorise the route in advance.
entries.animalRule: The route must be memorised before moving during the attempt, and no mid-route assessment may be required.
entries.userBenefit: Assessing as you go in poor conditions means moving slowly or getting it wrong. Memorising the route first lets you move fast without looking.
