entries.userBenefit: Travelling to every opportunity yourself means you reach a handful. Sending what you made means it goes further than you ever would.
entries.mechanismConnection: Trichonephila clavata adults are sedentary orb-web occupants for weeks, while spiderlings disperse by ballooning on silk into rising air over distances of kilometres.

entries.title: Stay Through the Winter and Start First
entries.objective: The stonechat and the whinchat hunt the same way from the same perches over the same rough ground. The difference is the calendar. The whinchat winters in Africa and cannot arrive until late spring; the stonechat stays, holds its territory through the winter, and begins breeding several weeks earlier. That head start is worth two or three broods against the migrant's one. Its principle is Perchwatch. The metaphor? Hold the ground through the cold.
entries.animalRule: The act must happen during the quiet season rather than at the restart, and the thing held has to be one you normally step away from.
entries.userBenefit: Leaving something during its quiet months means you spend the first weeks of every busy season just getting back to where you were. Holding it through the cold is what puts you ahead when it matters.
entries.mechanismConnection: Saxicola rubicola is resident and holds its territory through winter, so it begins breeding weeks before the migratory Saxicola rubetra and raises more broods per season.

entries.title: Staying Beats Dispersing
entries.objective: Grey-crowned babbler helpers are grown birds that do not breed, and they work hard: building domed stick nests, feeding nestlings, mobbing predators, defending territory, and groups with more of them fledge more young. They stay because the woodland is saturated and a young bird dispersing alone into it usually dies. Staying and contributing to relatives is simply the better return. Its principle is Cooperative Nesting. The metaphor? When the outside is saturated, contribute where you already are instead of leaving to start alone.
entries.animalRule: The contribution must go to an effort that already exists during the attempt, and no parallel version may be started.
entries.userBenefit: Leaving to start your own version when there is nowhere to put it means years of effort and nothing standing. Contributing where you already are gets you a share of something working.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pomatostomus temporalis non-breeding helpers assist with nest construction, nestling provisioning and territory defence, raising group fledging success where suitable territory is saturated.

entries.title: Steep One Jar of Weeds Into Plant Feed
entries.objective: Pack a jar with green leaves and water to start a slow, microbe-driven plant feed.
entries.animalRule: The leaves stay under water and the lid stays loose; then the jar is left alone to do its slow work.
entries.userBenefit: A free liquid feed for houseplants or a garden in a few weeks.
entries.mechanismConnection: Gee's Golden Langur — Leaf-eating • Resting • Arboreal: Trachypithecus geei eats mainly leaves, and microbes in its chambered stomach ferment that tough plant material slowly, so its days are built around feeding bouts separated by long rests in the canopy while the fermentation runs. This Trial translates that slow microbial fermentation of leaves in a chambered stomach into a jar of leaves left to ferment into plant feed.

entries.title: Steer One Blindfolded Friend to Fruit by Clicks
entries.objective: Using only a click-and-call code, steer a blindfolded partner across a room to a fruit bowl a helper has hidden.
entries.animalRule: No words, touching or leading by hand: only clicks and the stop call, and the blindfold stays on until a piece of fruit is in hand.
entries.userBenefit: A funny trust game that shows how precise your instructions really are.
entries.mechanismConnection: Egyptian Fruit Bat — Rhythmic • Coordinated • Vocal: Rousettus aegyptiacus leaves its cave roosts at night in groups that keep in contact with a rich repertoire of social calls while moving between fruiting trees and the roost, so travel through the dark is coordinated by sound rather than sight. This Trial translates that call-coordinated movement through the dark to fruit into a blindfolded partner steered to hidden fruit by a click-and-call code.

entries.title: Steer to the Interception Point
entries.objective: A slender skimmer catches other flying insects mid-air, which is a problem of prediction rather than speed. Compound eyes cover nearly the whole visual field and the four wings are driven independently, so the animal holds a target in one part of its vision and steers to an interception point instead of chasing from behind. Attacks are frequent, short and mostly successful. Its principle is Aim. The metaphor? Go to where it will be, not to where it is.
entries.animalRule: The interception point must be worked out before moving during the attempt, and no pursuit from behind is permitted.
entries.userBenefit: Chasing where something currently is means always arriving behind it. Working out where it will be gets you there first with less effort.
entries.mechanismConnection: Orthetrum sabina fixates prey on a specific retinal region and steers an interception course using independently actuated wings rather than pursuing from behind.

entries.title: Step Over Rather Than Plough Through
entries.objective: Legs that long let a moose step over deep snow and fallen timber rather than ploughing through them, which opens boreal forest in winter to an animal that would otherwise be trapped in it. The obstruction is not removed or pushed aside; it simply passes beneath. Everything about the animal's winter range follows from that one proportion. Its principle is Heavy Passage. The metaphor? Build the clearance to step over obstructions rather than the force to push through them.
entries.animalRule: The solution must increase clearance rather than force during the attempt, and no obstruction may be pushed through.
entries.userBenefit: Pushing through obstructions costs you energy at every one of them. Clearance means they stop being obstructions at all for you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Alces alces limb length permits stepping over deep snow and deadfall rather than displacing it, making boreal forest traversable in winter.

entries.title: Step Two Fingers Across a Tray of Rice
entries.objective: Walk two fingers step by step across a tray of rice and pick up five dried beans without the hand ever lifting away.
entries.animalRule: The fingers step, never slide or hop: at least one walking fingertip is touching the rice at every moment, even during a pinch.
entries.userBenefit: A slow, absorbing hand-control exercise that calms busy thoughts.
entries.mechanismConnection: Little Dragonfish — Cautious • Terrain-led • Walker: Eurypegasus draconis walks slowly over sand and rubble on its stiff, modified pelvic fins, staying in constant contact with the bottom while it sucks tiny invertebrates from the sediment with its small tubular mouth. This Trial translates that slow pelvic-fin walking in constant contact with the seafloor into two fingers stepping across rice, never lifting both at once, to take beans from its surface.

entries.title: Stick Because It Is Wet
entries.objective: A gecko sticks by dry adhesion and fails on wet leaves. A tree frog lives on wet leaves, and its toe pads work the opposite way: broad, soft, covered in a pattern of hexagonal cells separated by channels that drain water away, leaving a thin film that holds by surface tension. Wetness is not the obstacle; it is the mechanism. Its principle is Grip Then Leap. The metaphor? The condition defeating everyone else may be exactly what your method needs. Build for it rather than against it.
entries.animalRule: The approach must actively use the troublesome condition rather than tolerate or exclude it, and work has to be completed under that condition.
entries.userBenefit: Designing around a condition that is always present means your method only works on rare good days. Designing to use it means every day is a working day.
entries.mechanismConnection: Tree frog toe pads bear hexagonal epidermal cells separated by drainage channels that remove excess water, leaving a thin fluid layer that generates wet adhesion through capillarity and surface tension.

entries.title: Stiff Enough and Jointed Enough
entries.objective: This fish belongs to a lineage already old when the dinosaurs were new, and the reason it is still here is a coat rather than a behaviour. Its scales are ganoid, thick rhomboid plates interlocking into a continuous jointed sheet, each carrying an outer layer harder than most bone. The arrangement is stiff enough to resist penetration and articulated enough to let the body still bend. Its principle is Ancient Strength. The metaphor? Make it stiff enough to resist and jointed enough to still move; either alone fails.
entries.animalRule: Both rigidity and articulation must be present during the attempt, and both have to be actually tested.
entries.userBenefit: Rigid without joints means you cannot move, and jointed without rigidity means you are not protected. Both together is the only version that works for you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Atractosteus spatula bears interlocking ganoid scales with a ganoine surface harder than bone, forming an articulated armour sheet that resists penetration while permitting body flexion.

entries.title: Stiff Wings, Not Flexible Ones
entries.objective: A Magellanic penguin flies underwater. Its wings are not folding feathered wings at all but stiff flippers, rigid along their length, and that rigidity is what lets them drive the bird after anchovies, sprats, squid and crustaceans on trip after trip out from the burrow. A flexible wing would spill the force. The loss of flight is the price of the stiffness. Its principle is Burrow-Colony Loyalty. The metaphor? Stiffen it so it transmits force.
entries.animalRule: The give must be genuinely removed rather than reduced, and the stiffened version has to be used once today.
entries.userBenefit: A request or a rule with give in it absorbs all your force and moves nothing, and you repeat it until you give up. Removing the give is what makes the same words do something.
entries.mechanismConnection: Spheniscus magellanicus propels itself underwater with rigid, fused flippers that transmit force efficiently at the cost of aerial flight.

entries.title: Still Above the Water
entries.objective: Shinisaurus crocodilurus arranges its whole life around one escape route. It perches on branches overhanging slow forest streams in southern China and northern Vietnam, often in the same spot for days, entering a motionless state so complete that early observers named it the lizard of great sleep. The point of the perch is the water beneath: disturbed, it does not run or fight but releases its grip and drops, which is what keeps it alive. Its principle is Stream Stillness. The metaphor? Hold still above one exit.
entries.animalRule: The exit is arranged before you settle, you stay completely still until something requires leaving, and then you leave immediately by that exit.
entries.userBenefit: Without a decided exit you argue yourself into staying in situations that have already gone wrong. One arranged escape lets you hold still much longer, because leaving costs you no thought.
entries.mechanismConnection: Shinisaurus crocodilurus holds a motionless perch over slow forest streams for days and, when disturbed, releases its grip and drops into water rather than fleeing or fighting.

entries.title: Still Until You Move
entries.objective: A Javan Pond Heron is easy to overlook standing still and unmistakable the moment it moves, because the wings are white all year while the body is not. A brown shape on a paddy bund becomes a white flash the instant it lifts. The contrast between the two states is the whole effect, and it costs nothing to maintain. Its principle is Wetland Timing. The metaphor? You do not need to be visible while you work. Be unremarkable until the moment you move.
entries.animalRule: No progress updates of any kind may be given during the work, and exactly one announcement goes out at completion.
entries.userBenefit: Narrating progress invites opinions while the thing is still soft and costs you the time you were reporting on. Silence then one clear announcement gets a cleaner reaction and more work done.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ardeola speciosa has permanently white remiges concealed under cryptic folded plumage, so a motionless bird is inconspicuous on a paddy bund and becomes a conspicuous white flash on taking flight.

entries.title: Stillness Comes Before the Zigzag
entries.objective: A cottontail's famous zigzag is the second option, not the first. Almost everything that hunts it is triggered by movement, so it flattens and holds absolutely still, and a motionless rabbit in cover is genuinely hard to find. Only when that fails does it bolt, in sharp turns aimed at a burrow it already knows. Its principle is Zigzag Escape. The metaphor? Moving is what reveals you. Hold still first and most things pass.
entries.animalRule: No action at all may be taken until the situation actually reaches you, and the stillness has to be genuine rather than a delay before the same reaction.
entries.userBenefit: Reacting straight away is what pulls you into things that would have passed you by. Holding still costs nothing and removes most of them.
entries.mechanismConnection: Sylvilagus floridanus relies first on immobility, since most predators detect prey by motion, and resorts to erratic zigzag flight toward a known refuge only when concealment fails.

entries.title: Stir It and Take What Touches
entries.objective: A yellow-billed stork does not look for fish. It wades with its bill held partly open below the surface, sweeping it slowly from side to side while one foot paddles and stirs the mud in front, flushing whatever is hiding into contact with the bill. The instant something touches it the bill snaps shut, in a reflex faster than deciding. This is what lets it feed in water too muddy to hunt by sight. Its principle is Tactile Search. The metaphor? Stir it up. Trust the reflex.
entries.animalRule: You may not search for anything specific, the stirring has to be continuous, and whatever surfaces is taken immediately rather than assessed first.
entries.userBenefit: Scanning a backlog for the item you expect means you keep missing what is actually in there. Stirring blind and taking what surfaces clears it far faster for you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Mycteria ibis forages tactilely with a partly open submerged bill swept side to side while foot-stirring, closing on contact in a reflex of a few tens of milliseconds.

entries.title: Stitch Two Leaves Into One Hanging Pocket
entries.objective: Join two large leaves or paper leaves into a hanging pocket using separate short fibre stitches.
entries.animalRule: Every stitch is its own short fibre plug with fluffed ends: no continuous seam, knots, tape or glue.
entries.userBenefit: A delicate craft challenge that makes a real little hanging pocket.
entries.mechanismConnection: Common Tailorbird — Rhythmic • Site-bound • Craft: Orthotomus sutorius pierces holes along the edges of living leaves and pushes plant fibre or spider silk through each one, where the fluffed ends swell like rivets, drawing the leaves into a cup for its nest. This Trial translates that riveted, hole-by-hole leaf sewing into a pocket joined with separate fluffed wool stitches.

entries.title: Stock One Rest Spot and Stay Put
entries.objective: Stock one comfortable spot with everything you need, then rest there for fifteen minutes without getting up.
entries.animalRule: Once you sit down you may not leave the spot or fetch anything new; only what you stocked beforehand may be used.
entries.userBenefit: A properly uninterrupted rest, because nothing needs fetching halfway through.
entries.mechanismConnection: Northern Elephant Seal — Stored • Fasting • Shorebound: Mirounga angustirostris hauls out on beaches for weeks at a time, moving very little and running on the blubber it stored at sea while it breeds or moults. This Trial translates that haul-out on stored reserves into a stocked rest spot you do not leave for fifteen minutes.

entries.title: Stock One Shared Snack Plate in Swapped Trips
entries.objective: With a partner, build one shared snack plate by alternating fetching trips, so one of you always stays at the nest.
entries.animalRule: The nest is never left empty: one person always stays with the plate while the other fetches, and roles swap every trip.
entries.userBenefit: A shared snack that doubles as a small practice in covering for each other.
entries.mechanismConnection: Prairie Vole — Rhythmic • Shared • Patrol: Prairie Vole pairs share one nest and take turns, one adult making short foraging trips along covered runways while the other stays to warm, groom and guard the young, then swapping. This Trial translates that shared nest duty traded between partners into six snack trips taken in turn while one person always holds the nest.

entries.title: Stolen and Reburied, Dozens of Times
entries.objective: An agouti is one of very few animals able to open the largest rainforest seeds, and what it does next matters more. Surplus seeds are buried singly across the forest floor, and other agoutis then find and steal them and bury them again somewhere else, repeatedly. Tracked seeds have moved dozens of times and hundreds of metres by a chain of thieves. Its principle is Seed Stewardship. The metaphor? Let it be taken; the chain carries it further than you could.
entries.animalRule: The thing must be released in a form others can take freely, and no tracking or control may be exercised during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Controlling where your work goes next caps it at how far you can personally carry it. Letting it be taken moves it further than you ever would.
entries.mechanismConnection: Dasyprocta punctata scatter-hoards large seeds that are repeatedly pilfered and re-cached by conspecifics, producing cumulative dispersal distances far exceeding any individual's movement.

entries.title: Stones First, Then the Throbbing Dive
entries.objective: A lapwing nests on bare open ground in a scrape with no cover, and the first defence is that the eggs look like stones and the sitting bird does not move. The second is the opposite of concealment: broad round wings, poor for efficient flight and excellent for climbing, rolling and diving with an audible throbbing beat, used to mob crows and foxes away with real persistence. Its principle is Display Flight. The metaphor? Be invisible first, and loud only once invisibility has failed.
entries.animalRule: The quiet approach must be tried first during the attempt, and the loud response may only follow actual discovery.
entries.userBenefit: Going loud first means you create attention you then have to manage. Staying quiet usually ends it, and the loud option is still there if it does not.
entries.mechanismConnection: Vanellus vanellus relies first on egg and incubating-bird crypsis on open ground, and only on discovery switches to a broad-winged throbbing display flight used to mob predators.

entries.title: Stop at a Clean Point
entries.objective: A cat's routines are controlled rather than interrupted: resting, grooming, watching and patrolling each end at a point the animal chose, which is what keeps the baseline cheap. Nothing is abandoned half-finished to be picked up at extra cost later. The rhythm is self-chosen rather than imposed by events. Its principle is Self-chosen Rhythm. The metaphor? End each stretch at a clean point you chose, because resuming from a ragged one costs more than the break saved.
entries.animalRule: Each stop must be at a chosen clean point during the attempt, and no stretch may end mid-task.
entries.userBenefit: Stopping wherever you were interrupted means paying a reorientation cost every time you come back. Choosing the point costs you one minute.
entries.mechanismConnection: Felis catus maintenance behaviours terminate at self-determined points rather than external interruption, preserving the low cost of the baseline rhythm.

entries.title: Stop Completely, Not Partly
entries.objective: Wood frogs breed in northern forests where the ground freezes hard, and they do not dig below the frost line. When ice begins to form in the leaf litter around them, the liver floods the body with glucose that protects the cells while ice forms in the spaces between them; breathing stops, the heart stops, and much of the body's water becomes solid. Nothing about this is a gradual slowdown, which is what makes the thaw a clean restart. Its principle is Revival. The metaphor? A partial stop rests nothing.
entries.animalRule: The stop has to be total with nothing running in the background, it lasts five minutes, and the restart resumes the same task rather than a different one.
entries.userBenefit: Taking a half-break with a screen still running means you neither rest nor work and the task feels worse afterwards. A total stop gives you the restart back.
entries.mechanismConnection: Rana sylvatica tolerates freezing by flooding tissues with hepatic glucose cryoprotectant and permitting extracellular ice formation while cardiac and respiratory function cease entirely.

entries.title: Stop Eating and Go Home
entries.objective: After two or three years at sea the sockeye stops eating entirely and turns for the river and lake system it came from. There is no feeding on the way and no option to refuel, so the whole journey runs on what is already stored, and the body reddens and reshapes as it burns down. Everything after that decision is paid for in advance. Its principle is Red Return Instinct. The metaphor? Close the intake and commit the journey.
entries.animalRule: The intake must be fully closed for the stretch, and the work has to proceed on existing resources only.
entries.userBenefit: Taking in more as preparation feels like progress and is usually the thing stopping you from starting. Closing the intake forces you to find out that what you already have is enough.
entries.mechanismConnection: Oncorhynchus nerka ceases feeding on entering fresh water and completes its upstream spawning migration entirely on stored energy reserves.

entries.title: Stop Every Few Steps and Push In
entries.objective: The common treeshrew moves in quick bursts across leaf litter, fallen logs and low branches and pauses constantly to investigate, pushing its long pointed snout into litter, bark and crevices after insects. The pausing is not hesitation; the food is hidden and only found by stopping to look inside things. Covering ground without the pauses would find nothing. Its principle is Small-Branch Curiosity. The metaphor? Stop and look inside things.
entries.animalRule: There must be at least five genuine stops, each one looking into something rather than at it, and the findings have to be stated.
entries.userBenefit: Covering ground at speed means you pass the same hidden things every day without ever opening one. Five real stops on a route you already walk show you what has been sitting there unnoticed.
entries.mechanismConnection: Tupaia glis forages in short bursts interspersed with frequent investigative pauses, probing litter, bark and crevices with its elongated snout for concealed invertebrates.

entries.title: Stop Feeding Before the Cold
entries.objective: Before it freezes, a woolly bear caterpillar stops feeding entirely and shelters under leaf litter. It does not try to keep eating through the cold. Stopping intake is part of the preparation, not a failure of it, because a gut full of food is a liability once ice forms. Its principle is Winter Coat. The metaphor? Taking more in right before a hard stretch does not help you. Stop intake and get under cover.
entries.animalRule: Something genuinely incoming must be declined or deferred during the attempt, said to the person rather than silently ignored, and no new commitment may be accepted.
entries.userBenefit: Saying yes right before a hard stretch is how it becomes an impossible one. One declined thing now is the cheapest protection you will get, and nobody minds being told early.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pyrrharctia isabella larvae cease feeding entirely before overwintering, clearing the gut and sheltering under leaf litter prior to cryoprotectant accumulation and freezing.

entries.title: Stop Feeding It for the Winter
entries.objective: Below a temperature threshold a Koi's digestive enzymes simply stop working, so it cannot process food even if food is there, and feeding it then does harm rather than good. Growth resumes when the water warms, and because it never truly stops these fish reach great age and size. Knowing when the system is closed is what keeps it alive. Its principle is Ornamental Perseverance. The metaphor? Some seasons cannot digest input. Stop feeding it.
entries.animalRule: You must name the thing that is not processing and then stop adding to it. Nothing new may be queued up for it during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Pushing more in while nothing is being processed makes the backlog worse and reads to everyone as pressure from you. Recognising a closed season and stopping input is what lets the thing clear and start again.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cyprinus carpio digestive enzyme activity falls below a temperature threshold so the fish cannot process food in cold water, and because growth is indeterminate and resumes when water warms, koi continue growing and reach great age rather than feeding year-round.

entries.title: Stop Halfway and Moult There
entries.objective: Replacing every feather is one of the most expensive things a small bird does, and the usual options are to do it before leaving or after arriving. Western painted buntings do neither. They fly part of the way, stop in the north-west Mexican monsoon belt where late rains have produced a flush of seed, moult completely there, then finish. Its principle is Painted Utility. The metaphor? Do the expensive part at the stopover.
entries.animalRule: The intermediate point must have genuinely better resources than either end, and the step has to happen there during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Doing the expensive step at either end means doing it where resources are thin. One stop where they are abundant makes it cost you far less.
entries.mechanismConnection: Western Passerina ciris interrupt migration to undergo complete moult in the north-west Mexican monsoon region, where late-summer rainfall produces a seed and insect flush, before completing the journey.

entries.title: Stop Rather Than Fly
entries.objective: A ruddy ground dove feeds by walking slowly over bare and disturbed ground, picking up small seeds, and its rufous and grey plumage matches exactly that substrate. So its first response to danger is to stop moving rather than to fly, and a motionless bird on matching soil is genuinely hard to find. Flight is short, explosive and used only once concealment has already failed. Its principle is Grounded Camouflage. The metaphor? If you match the ground you work on, stopping beats moving.
entries.animalRule: The match to the surroundings must be confirmed first, and the first response has to be stopping during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Moving first makes you the thing that moved, which is what gets noticed. Stopping, when you match the ground, usually ends it without anything happening.
entries.mechanismConnection: Columbina talpacoti has rufous-grey plumage matching bare disturbed ground, so freezing is the primary antipredator response and explosive flight only secondary.

entries.title: Stop to See Again
entries.objective: A six-spotted tiger beetle runs so fast that its own vision cannot keep up and the prey it is chasing blurs out of existence. So it does not run further. It sprints, stops dead to let its visual system settle and relocate the insect, then sprints again. The stops are not fatigue; they are the only way the chase stays aimed. Its principle is Flash Chase. The metaphor? Build full stops into fast work, because past a certain speed you stop being able to see the target.
entries.animalRule: Each stop must be complete rather than a slowdown during the attempt, and the target has to be relocated before the next burst begins.
entries.userBenefit: Pushing through fast work without stopping means you lose the target and finish something that was not the thing. Complete stops to re-aim cost seconds and keep it accurate.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cicindela sexguttata runs faster than its visual system can integrate, so it pursues prey in sprint-and-stop bouts, halting to reacquire the target before resuming.

entries.title: Stop, Plant, Assess
entries.objective: The donkey's reputation for stubbornness is a misread of a desert adaptation. Horses evolved on grassland where bolting across open country works; the wild asses this animal descends from lived in arid rocky terrain where bolting spends water that may not be replaceable. What was selected instead was to stop, plant the feet and assess. It is not refusing. It is costing the option. Its principle is Steady Burden. The metaphor? Where the resource is irreplaceable, stopping to assess is the correct response, not the slow one.
entries.animalRule: The stop must happen before any response during the attempt, and the assessment has to be explicit rather than a hesitation.
entries.userBenefit: Reacting at the pace you are handed spends the resource you cannot get back. Stopping to assess looks slow and is why you still have anything left.
entries.mechanismConnection: Equus asinus descends from arid-land asses in which flight responses were selected against because evaporative water loss may be unreplaceable, favouring a stop-and-assess reaction instead.

entries.title: Stopping Is the Thing That Kills It
entries.objective: A mackerel has no swim bladder, so it is denser than seawater and sinks the instant it stops, and it is a ram ventilator, driving water over its gills by swimming forward rather than pumping. Stopping means sinking and suffocating at once, so it swims continuously from the moment it can until it dies. Its whole body is built around never pausing. Its principle is Flank-Flash Shoal. The metaphor? Some things only work while moving.
entries.animalRule: The thing chosen must genuinely degrade when paused, and real movement has to be given to it today.
entries.userBenefit: Treating a pause as neutral is what kills the things that only exist in motion, and you only notice once restarting costs more than continuing would have. A small move today keeps it alive cheaply.
entries.mechanismConnection: Scomber scombrus lacks a swim bladder and ventilates by ram, so it must swim continuously to avoid both sinking and asphyxiation.

entries.title: Store It Against a Landmark
entries.objective: A Clark's nutcracker buries tens of thousands of pine seeds in small scattered caches, then digs them up months later under snow. It does not search; it remembers, because each cache was placed in relation to rocks and trunks rather than simply put somewhere. The landmark is what makes the storing worth doing at all. Its principle is Pine-Cache Memory. The metaphor? Store things against a fixed reference, or you have not stored them, you have lost them neatly.
entries.animalRule: The fixed reference must be stated at the moment of placing during the attempt, and no placement may be made merely because space was free.
entries.userBenefit: Putting something wherever there is room means you will search for it when you need it, which is as good as not having it. One stated reference makes it retrievable.
entries.mechanismConnection: Nucifraga columbiana caches thousands of pine seeds individually and relocates them months later using spatial memory encoded relative to terrain landmarks.

entries.title: Store It Where You Can See It
entries.objective: When food is plentiful the fat-tailed dunnart lays fat down in the base of its tail, which visibly thickens, and the tail thins again as the reserve is spent. The store is not hidden anywhere internal; it is on the outside where its size is obvious at a glance. A margin you can see is a margin you can manage. Its principle is Tail-Stored Margin. The metaphor? Keep the reserve visible.
entries.animalRule: The reserve's level must become visible without any checking step, and it has to be looked at once today.
entries.userBenefit: A reserve whose level you must look up is a reserve you find out about too late, usually when it is already gone. Making the level visible means you adjust early instead of reacting.
entries.mechanismConnection: Sminthopsis crassicaudata stores lipid in the base of its tail, which visibly thickens when prey is abundant and thins as reserves are mobilised.

entries.title: Store One Backup Where It Can Wait
entries.objective: Store One Backup Where It Can Wait.
entries.animalRule: It must stay dry and reachable, and the label must say why it is there.
entries.userBenefit: A quiet reserve is ready before conditions turn bad.
entries.mechanismConnection: Operates as a durable benthic stage that survives poor conditions indefinitely, holding the population in place on rock, shell and increasingly on harbour walls and artificial structures

entries.title: Store the Heat Instead of Spending Water
entries.objective: The Arabian oryx lives where surface water is rare and rain is unpredictable, and it handles the heat by not fighting it. Through the day it rests in shade or a shallow scrape and lets its own body temperature climb, storing the heat rather than sweating it away, then sheds it at night for free. Moisture from plants and dew lets it go weeks without drinking. Its principle is Rewilding. The metaphor? Store the discomfort, spend it when it is free.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be discharged in the moment, and the holding has to end with the thing actually dealt with later the same day.
entries.userBenefit: Discharging every irritation the moment it arrives costs you credibility and relationships at the most expensive possible time. Carrying it to the evening deals with the same thing for almost nothing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Oryx leucoryx tolerates a rising daytime body temperature, storing heat for passive nocturnal dissipation instead of losing water to evaporative cooling.

entries.title: Store the Heat, Radiate It at Night
entries.objective: Mammals normally hold body temperature nearly constant, and in a hot dry country that is expensive, because the only way to shed heat is to evaporate water the animal cannot spare. An oryx changes the rule, letting its core climb several degrees through the day, storing the heat in its own mass, and radiating it back out during the cold desert night for nothing. Its principle is Heat Endurance. The metaphor? Release the stress when releasing is free.
entries.animalRule: No discharge may happen during the expensive hours, and the release has to actually occur in the cheap ones during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Discharging stress during the costly hours spends the resource you cannot replace. Holding it until release is free costs you nothing at all.
entries.mechanismConnection: Oryx beisa permits adaptive heterothermy, storing metabolic and environmental heat as a several-degree core temperature rise by day and radiating it passively during cold desert nights.

entries.title: Store the Version That Will Not Spoil
entries.objective: A cicada killer solves a storage problem, not a hunting one. Meat rots, and a larva sealed in an underground cell needs food for weeks, so the female stings a cicada in a way that paralyses it permanently without killing it, drags prey heavier than herself into a burrow, lays an egg on it and seals the cell. The larva eats a living, non-decaying store, which is what makes the whole cycle possible. Its principle is Provision. The metaphor? Store it alive.
entries.animalRule: The stored form must be one that does not degrade over weeks, and it has to be put somewhere you cannot casually draw on it.
entries.userBenefit: Storing things in a form that spoils means you either use them now or lose them. Keeping the durable version instead means the reserve is still there when you actually need it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Sphecius speciosus paralyses cicadas with a sting that preserves them alive, provisioning a sealed burrow cell so the larva feeds on non-decaying tissue.

entries.title: Store What the Source Defended With
entries.objective: Passion vines defend themselves with cyanogenic glycosides that release cyanide when tissue is damaged, and most insects cannot eat them. Leopard Lacewing larvae can, and rather than excreting the compounds they sequester them, storing them in their own tissues so the adult is unpalatable for life. The plant's defence becomes the butterfly's. Its principle is Bitter-Orange Wings. The metaphor? Whatever made the source hard to use is exactly what you keep once you can.
entries.animalRule: The capability must be one that comes specifically from handling something others avoid, and it has to be stated somewhere other people will see rather than just noted.
entries.userBenefit: The hard thing you learned to handle feels ordinary to you and is invisible to everyone else. Stating it once is what turns a private tolerance into something people come to you for.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cethosia cyane larvae feed on cyanogenic Passiflora and sequester the glycosides rather than excreting them, retaining them into adulthood so the butterfly is chemically defended throughout life.

entries.title: Strain the Mud, Not the Water
entries.objective: Every other baleen whale feeds in the water column. The gray whale rolls onto its side, presses the side of its head to the seabed and sucks in mouthfuls of sediment, then forces the mud out through short coarse baleen that holds back amphipods. Its baleen is the shortest and coarsest of any whale because it is straining sand, and most individuals wear one side of the head down doing it. Its principle is Benthicturn. The metaphor? Work the substrate everyone swims over.
entries.animalRule: The base layer must be worked directly rather than summarised, and a measured amount has to be got through.
entries.userBenefit: Working from the summarised version of your situation means you only ever see what someone else already noticed. Going through the base layer yourself is where things nobody has seen actually are.
entries.mechanismConnection: Eschrichtius robustus suction-feeds benthic sediment and strains amphipods through unusually short coarse baleen, with asymmetric head and baleen wear.

entries.title: Strain the Volume, Do Not Pick
entries.objective: A shoveler eats animals too small to pick up one at a time. Its oversized spatulate bill is lined with fine comb-like lamellae; water is drawn in at the tip and pushed out at the sides so crustaceans, larvae and seeds are strained out and swallowed. It swims in slow circles, sometimes in a line with others, to keep stirring food into suspension, and feeding is continuous rather than event-based. Its principle is Marsh Sifting. The metaphor? Stop picking individual items. Run the volume through a filter.
entries.animalRule: No individual items may be assessed during the attempt, and the entire volume has to pass through a single filter.
entries.userBenefit: Handling things one at a time means you process a fraction and the rest piles up. One filter run through the whole volume clears it in an hour.
entries.mechanismConnection: Spatula clypeata draws water through an oversized spatulate bill lined with fine lamellae, straining small crustaceans, larvae and seeds continuously rather than capturing individual prey.

entries.title: Stream a Dye Plume Downwind Across a Tray
entries.objective: Release one signal from a fixed point and let the moving air carry it all the way across.
entries.animalRule: The source stays still and does nothing after the drop: no stirring, tilting or blowing.
entries.userBenefit: A calm, mesmerising way to see how a signal can drift a long way from a still source.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cecropia Moth — Calling • Stationary • Female: a newly emerged female sits still and releases pheromone into the night air, and the moving air draws it out into a long plume that a male can detect a kilometre or more downwind. This Trial translates that still source and wind-stretched plume into a single spoonful of warm tinted water that floats on the cold surface and is carried downwind across the tray by the fan-driven surface current.

entries.title: Streetlights Removed the Search Problem
entries.objective: A bat hunting by echolocation has a search problem: calls are expensive, the range is short, and insects are scattered. Streetlights removed the problem. Moths and midges accumulate around a lamp in numbers no natural situation produces, and a pipistrelle flying circuits around one is working a concentration rather than searching a landscape. The echolocation did not change; the distribution did. Its principle is Echolocation Mastery. The metaphor? Find the artificial concentration and your expensive search method becomes cheap.
entries.animalRule: The concentration must be artificial or externally created during the attempt, and no wider-area searching may happen.
entries.userBenefit: An expensive search across a wide area means most of your attempts return nothing. One artificial concentration makes the same method pay every pass.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pipistrellus kuhlii forages in circuits around artificial lighting where phototactic insect aggregations exceed natural densities, reducing echolocation search cost.

entries.title: Strike One Dragged Sock From Behind a Doorframe
entries.objective: Wait hidden behind a doorframe and seize a sock lure as a helper drags it past.
entries.animalRule: One strike per pass and three passes only; once gripped, the sock must not slip free.
entries.userBenefit: A jolt of fast reaction and grip strength, and a great game to play in turns.
entries.mechanismConnection: Dragon Moray — Striking • Seizing • Explosive: Enchelycore pardalis lunges from its reef hole to seize passing fish, crustaceans or octopus with long, backward-curving fangs that make escape difficult, and as in other morays a second set of jaws in the throat pulls the prey inside. This Trial translates that lunge from cover and backward-hooked grip into a doorway strike on a dragged sock held against a tug and reeled in.

entries.title: Strike One Joint Hole, Then Haul the Box
entries.objective: Hit a coin-sized joint hole in a heavy box with a straw, then drag the box to a doorway and cover it, all inside twenty seconds.
entries.animalRule: Only a clean straw strike through the hole counts: if the straw touches the cardboard first, the timer restarts before you may haul.
entries.userBenefit: A sharp twenty-second burst of precision followed by honest pulling effort.
entries.mechanismConnection: Tarantula Hawk Wasp — Provoking • Stinging • Hauling: A female Tarantula Hawk Wasp stings a tarantula through the soft membrane at a leg joint into the nerve mass, paralysing it without killing it, then drags a body several times her weight to a burrow and seals an egg in with it. This Trial translates that one precise sting at the joint followed by hauling a load many times her size into a clean straw strike through a small joint hole and a book-loaded box dragged and covered inside twenty seconds.

entries.title: Strike One Warm Target You Cannot See
entries.objective: Find something by its warmth alone and hit it first time.
entries.animalRule: Eyes stay shut and you get one attempt; groping around ends it.
entries.userBenefit: You find out you have a heat sense you have never once deliberately used.
entries.mechanismConnection: Mangshan Pit Viper — Pit Organ Thermal Targeting — Struck • Aimed • Instant: Delivers a strike guided by that thermal image, reaching prey it has never seen in any visible sense This Trial translates that thermally guided strike at unseen prey into one committed reach at a warm object found blind.

entries.title: Strike to Anchor, Then Coil
entries.objective: A Madagascar ground boa's capture is a two-part event: a fast strike that anchors the prey, followed by coils that do the actual work. Nothing about the strike is meant to finish anything; it exists only to establish contact, and everything after it is slow and inexorable. Its principle is Grounded Force. The metaphor? Use your fast move only to establish contact, and let the slow part finish it.
entries.animalRule: The fast action must only establish contact during the attempt, and the finishing has to be done slowly.
entries.userBenefit: Trying to finish something with your fast move means missing or doing it badly. Using it only for contact and finishing slowly works nearly every time for you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Acrantophis madagascariensis strikes rapidly to secure a hold and then applies constriction, with the strike functioning solely to establish contact rather than to subdue.

entries.title: Striking at Three Metres, Nothing at Fifty
entries.objective: A striking face and a wish not to be seen look contradictory, and they are resolved here by range. The white beard and orange brow sit on a small area of the head, work at conversational distance in thick riverine vegetation, and say exactly who this is to another monkey a few metres away. The body is grizzled grey-olive with no strong contrast anywhere, which at fifty metres through leaves resolves into nothing. Its principle is Quiet Distinction. The metaphor? Be unmistakable close up and invisible at distance.
entries.animalRule: The distinctive element must be visible only at close range during the attempt, and distance-visible markers have to be removed.
entries.userBenefit: Being identifiable from a distance means people decide about you before meeting you. Keeping it close up means they only form a view in conversation.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cercopithecus neglectus confines high-contrast white beard and orange brow markings to a small facial area effective at short range, with uniformly grizzled body pelage offering no distance cue.

entries.title: Strip the Stage First
entries.objective: A Raggiana display site is not just a branch the bird happens to use; the male works on it, and the surrounding clutter matters because the plumes only read against a clear background. Most days follow a rhythm of moving through fruiting trees and returning to maintain and occupy the same site. Preparation and occupation are the ordinary work. Its principle is Red-plume Ceremony. The metaphor? Clear the background before you present anything, because clutter costs more than content gains.
entries.animalRule: Only the background may be changed during the attempt, and the thing itself has to stay as it is.
entries.userBenefit: Improving the thing while the background is cluttered means nobody sees the improvement. Clearing the background costs you minutes and changes everything.
entries.mechanismConnection: Paradisaea raggiana males clear and maintain display perches, with plume contrast depending on an uncluttered visual background.

entries.title: Stripe Across the Pseudopupil
entries.objective: An insect can match bark closely and still be given away by its eyes. A compound eye shows a pseudopupil, a dark spot formed by the ommatidia pointing directly at the observer, and because it moves as the observer moves it is a strong high-contrast cue on an otherwise camouflaged animal. This grasshopper carries vertical dark stripes running across the eye that break the pseudopupil up. Its principle is Hind-Leg Catapult. The metaphor? Find the one feature that gives you away no matter how good the rest is, and run the pattern through it.
entries.animalRule: The giveaway feature must be identified during the attempt, and the disruption has to be applied to it rather than elsewhere.
entries.userBenefit: Improving everything else while one feature gives you away means all that work is wasted. Disrupting that one feature is where the whole gain is.
entries.mechanismConnection: Anacridium aegyptium bears vertical dark banding across the compound eye that disrupts the pseudopupil, the high-contrast cue that otherwise reveals a camouflaged insect.

entries.title: Stripes Legible in Almost No Light
entries.objective: A zorilla's chemical defence is among the most effective in Africa, enough to make lions back off, but the spray is finite and expensive, so almost all the work is done by advertisement. Bold white stripes on black remain legible at very low light levels, which is the only pattern that carries information to a nocturnal predator. Before spraying it raises its fur and presents itself. Its principle is Warning. The metaphor? Make the warning readable in the conditions it will actually be read in.
entries.animalRule: The real conditions must be established before changing it, and the change has to be tested in those conditions during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: A warning readable only in ideal conditions is one nobody reads, and you will blame them for it. Testing it where it is actually seen fixes that.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ictonyx striatus relies primarily on high-contrast black and white aposematic striping that remains visible at nocturnal light levels, reserving its finite anal gland secretion as a last resort.

entries.title: Stripes Only Where It Looks
entries.objective: Okapia johnstoni lives alone in the dense Ituri understorey, where light arrives in hard bars through canopy gaps. Its horizontal white stripes sit only on the hindquarters and upper legs, and against that broken light they dissolve the animal's outline at exactly the angle a leopard following from behind would see. The rest is deep oiled brown that sheds rain and reads as shadow. That is what keeps it unseen. Its principle is Forest Mystery. The metaphor? Hide where you are actually looked at.
entries.animalRule: Both cloths go in the same bars from the same five paces, and the result is noted before either of them is moved.
entries.userBenefit: You spend effort hiding things from angles nobody views them from, and leave the one angle that matters wide open. Seeing which pattern vanishes from one viewpoint tells you where protection is worth putting.
entries.mechanismConnection: Okapia johnstoni carries horizontal white striping only on its hindquarters, which disrupts its outline against the barred understorey light a following leopard would see it in.

entries.title: Structure Lasts, Pigment Fades
entries.objective: Bird colour comes from two sources and green birds usually combine them. The Common Green Magpie makes blue structurally, from the microscopic architecture of the feather, and overlays a yellow carotenoid pigment, and the two together read as brilliant green. The structure is permanent because it is architecture. The pigment is not, and birds cannot synthesise carotenoids, so a captive one on the wrong diet fades to turquoise. Its principle is Vocal Adaptability Strategy. The metaphor? Part of what you are rests on structure and part on continuous intake. Know which is which.
entries.animalRule: The strengths must be sorted into structural and input-dependent explicitly, and one input-dependent one has to be actually topped up during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: You assume all your strengths persist, so the input-dependent ones quietly fade and you cannot work out what changed. Sorting them once tells you exactly which need feeding.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cissa chinensis produces green by overlaying dietary carotenoid pigment on structurally generated blue; carotenoids cannot be synthesised de novo, so captive birds on deficient diets fade to turquoise while the structural blue persists.

entries.title: Strut for One Hen's Pick With Cheek Pops
entries.objective: With at least two other displayers, hold your own spot and compete with strut-and-pop displays until a watching 'hen' picks a winner.
entries.animalRule: Everyone stays on their own spot and displays at their own rhythm, competing rather than keeping time; only the hen chooses the winner.
entries.userBenefit: A ridiculous, joyful group performance that gets everyone laughing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Greater Sage-Grouse — Rhythmic • Collective • Display: Centrocercus urophasianus males gather on open leks at dawn in spring, each holding a small spot and competing with strut displays in which they fan spiky tail feathers and inflate two bare yellow air sacs on the chest that collapse with loud pops, while females walk among them and choose a mate. This Trial translates that lek of rival strutting displays judged by visiting hens into a line of competing strut-and-pop displays with one hen picking a winner.

entries.title: Subsidised to High Numbers
entries.objective: Gulls are generalists that eat whatever is briefly abundant, and this one shares that. Where it differs is what happens when a large gull is subsidised to high numbers next to a seabird colony: yellow-legged gulls take eggs and chicks from shearwaters and terns, kill adults of smaller species outright, and chase returning birds until they drop food. The subsidy produced the predation. Its principle is Trawler-wake Pickings. The metaphor? A subsidy that lifts one group's numbers changes what it does to everyone nearby; look at the second-order effect.
entries.animalRule: The second-order effect must be named explicitly during the attempt, rather than only the direct effect.
entries.userBenefit: Looking only at the direct effect of a subsidy means you miss what it does to everyone next to it. Naming the second-order effect is where the real cost sits.
entries.mechanismConnection: Larus michahellis populations subsidised by fishery discards and refuse reach densities at which they predate eggs, chicks and adults of sympatric seabirds.

entries.title: Sugar Straight Into Flight
entries.objective: Rivoli's hummingbird holds itself still in thin turbulent highland air with wingbeats generating lift in every direction, which costs so much fuel that it converts the sugar it drinks almost directly into the flight that is drinking it. There is no storing and no slack; intake and expenditure are the same loop running at full rate. Its principle is Highland Hover. The metaphor? When the burn rate is that high, put what comes in straight back out and do not try to bank it.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be banked during the attempt, and the yield has to be reinvested within the same session rather than later.
entries.userBenefit: Banking what something yields while the activity stalls means you lose the momentum and the stored amount was never enough anyway. Putting it straight back keeps it running.
entries.mechanismConnection: Eugenes fulgens sustains hovering in thin highland air at a metabolic rate that converts ingested nectar into flight energy almost immediately, with negligible storage capacity.

entries.title: Surface One Stored Thing and Return It
entries.objective: Bring one buried thing up, actually use it, and put it straight back.
entries.animalRule: It must be used, not merely inspected, and it must go back the same session.
entries.userBenefit: You find out whether the thing is worth keeping, instead of storing it for another year unexamined.
entries.mechanismConnection: Purple Frog — Subterranean Year and Two-Week Surface — Surfaced • Breeding • Two weeks: Comes up for a fortnight at the start of the monsoon, breeds in swollen streams and goes back down This Trial translates that single fortnight of surfacing into one stored thing used and returned in a session.

entries.title: Surprise One Person With A Detour
entries.objective: While walking with someone, confidently suggest one harmless unexpected detour to see something nearby, then lead it without overexplaining.
entries.animalRule: Heavy rain drumming through the soil brings the whole population up at once to breed in pools that will be gone in a fortnight, feeding enough in a few nights to fund the following year underground. Keep that true for the whole attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Practises decisive redirection and turns an ordinary journey into a small shared discovery.
entries.mechanismConnection: Couch's Spadefoot expresses Spadefoot Timing through this mode: Couch's Spadefoot — Years Underground, Days in Water — Emerged • Calling • Racing: Heavy rain drumming through the soil brings the whole population up at once to breed in pools that will be gone in a fortnight, feeding enough in a few nights to fund the following year underground. The Trial carries that same limiting structure into one concrete human action.

entries.title: Surprise One Person With a Sudden Character
entries.objective: Begin one ordinary interaction normally, then switch into a completely different harmless character or voice for one sentence.
entries.animalRule: Fires raptorial forelegs at an arriving insect, or throws the whole body open in a startle display. Keep that true for the whole attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Five seconds that a room genuinely does not expect, and everyone gets to carry on immediately afterwards.
entries.mechanismConnection: Devil's Flower Mantis expresses Deceptive Beauty through this mode: Devil's Flower Mantis — Petal-Mimic Strike Perch — Snatching • Flaring • Instant: Fires raptorial forelegs at an arriving insect, or throws the whole body open in a startle display. The Trial carries that same limiting structure into one concrete human action.

entries.title: Survey One Room From a High Seat
entries.objective: Survey One Room From a High Seat.
entries.animalRule: Use only furniture designed for sitting; no climbing, stools on furniture or elevated ledges.
entries.userBenefit: You turn thermal command into one concrete experience with a visible finish.
entries.mechanismConnection: Wedge-tailed Eagle — Soaring • Very high • Patient: It circles at heights where it is barely visible from the ground, using a long wedge tail as a rudder to hold a tight thermal for hours at almost no cost. This Trial translates that mechanism into one room from its highest normal seat.

entries.title: Suspend the Egg Before the Prey Goes In
entries.objective: The potter wasp builds a small clay vessel and stocks it with paralysed caterpillars, which it shares with the mud daubers. What is specific is the order of operations: before any prey goes in, the female lays a single egg and suspends it from the ceiling of the cell on a short thread, so the larva hatches above the mass rather than inside it and is never crushed by shifting prey. Its principle is Clay Chamber Care. The metaphor? Place the fragile thing first, and suspended, before anything heavy goes in around it.
entries.animalRule: The fragile part must be placed before the bulk during the attempt, and it has to be suspended clear of it.
entries.userBenefit: Putting the fragile part in after the bulk means it is crushed or lost among it and you rebuild. Placing it first and clear means nothing reaches it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Eumenes females suspend the egg from the cell ceiling on a filament before provisioning with paralysed caterpillars, preventing crushing by the prey mass.

entries.title: Swallow It Whole and Walk
entries.objective: The Western Crowned Pigeon is the largest pigeon alive and has given up almost everything that makes pigeons quick. It walks the floor of New Guinea's lowland forest at a deliberate pace, swallowing fallen fruit whole including seeds too large for most birds, and passing them intact, which makes it one of the forest's significant large-seed dispersers. Slow and whole, rather than fast and picked apart. Its principle is Quiet Regality. The metaphor? Stop breaking it into pieces you can manage quickly. Take it whole and go slowly.
entries.animalRule: The thing must be handled as one unbroken whole with no chunking, and the pace has to be deliberately slower than your usual rather than rushed to finish.
entries.userBenefit: Chunking something into fragments means you never hold the whole shape of it and the joins stay broken. Taking it whole once, slowly, is usually faster in total and the result hangs together.
entries.mechanismConnection: Goura cristata forages on the forest floor at a deliberate walking pace, swallowing fallen fruit whole including large seeds that pass through the gut intact, making it a key disperser of large-seeded trees.

entries.title: Swallow It Whole, Drop the Seed Elsewhere
entries.objective: A resplendent quetzal makes its living from wild avocados and their relatives, and the mechanism is the swallowing. The bird hovers to pluck a fruit and takes it whole, a fruit far larger relative to its gape than most birds attempt, digests the fleshy layer and passes the large seed intact, usually well away from the parent tree. The gape is what gives it the supply. Its principle is Resplendence. The metaphor? Take it whole rather than processing it on the spot, and deal with the remainder later and elsewhere.
entries.animalRule: No processing may happen at the source during the attempt, and the remainder has to be dealt with elsewhere.
entries.userBenefit: Processing something where you found it means standing exposed while you do it. Taking it whole and dealing with the rest elsewhere is faster and safer.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pharomachrus mocinno swallows large lauraceous fruit whole, digests the pulp and defecates or regurgitates the intact seed away from the parent tree.

entries.title: Swallow It Whole, Drop the Seeds Elsewhere
entries.objective: A superb fruit dove does not crush or husk anything. Fruit goes down entire, the pulp is digested and the seeds pass through undamaged and are dropped somewhere else in the forest, which makes the bird a disperser rather than a seed predator. Because each tree ripens on its own schedule, the bird works steadily between them and carries the trees outward as it goes. Its principle is Quiet Radiance. The metaphor? Take only what you need and pass the rest on intact, somewhere it can be used.
entries.animalRule: The remainder must be passed on intact during the attempt, and it has to go somewhere it can actually be used rather than merely elsewhere.
entries.userBenefit: Consuming or binning everything you touch means nothing you handle leaves any value behind you. Passing the remainder on intact costs nothing and compounds somewhere else.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ptilinopus superbus swallows fruit whole and defecates seeds undamaged away from the parent tree, functioning as a seed disperser rather than a granivore.

entries.title: Swallow It Whole, Mill It Later
entries.objective: Most shellfish eaters have to open the shell, and opening a shell takes time and a tool. This duck skips that step. It dives to the seabed, often well beyond twenty metres, swallows molluscs whole, and breaks them apart afterwards in a gizzard so muscular and so loaded with swallowed grit that it functions as a mill. The dive is spent collecting rather than processing. Its principle is Arctic Style. The metaphor? Collect at the expensive site and process somewhere the time is cheap.
entries.animalRule: No processing may happen at the expensive site during the attempt, and all of it has to happen afterwards elsewhere.
entries.userBenefit: Processing on site means spending your scarcest minutes on work that could happen anywhere. Collecting only is how you get twice as much.
entries.mechanismConnection: Somateria spectabilis swallows molluscs whole during deep benthic dives and crushes them subsequently in a heavily muscular grit-loaded gizzard, maximising collection time underwater.

entries.title: Swallow Water, Not Air
entries.objective: A porcupinefish's defence runs on water rather than air. A highly distensible stomach with a folded wall lets it swallow water in rapid gulps until the body is nearly spherical, and because the skin carries spines that lie flat, inflation stands them all upright at once. Using the medium it is already in costs it nothing to carry. Its principle is Inflated Defense. The metaphor? Stop importing what you need. Take in what is already around you.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be bought, ordered or fetched from elsewhere, and the need has to be genuinely met rather than postponed.
entries.userBenefit: Ordering what you need means the task waits days for delivery and you lose the thread. Meeting it from the room usually works and the thing gets finished today.
entries.mechanismConnection: Diodon holocanthus inflates by gulping water into a highly distensible folded stomach, and the resulting expansion erects the scaleless skin's spines, which lie flat when the fish is deflated.

entries.title: Swap One Drawer Over to Next Season
entries.objective: Switch one drawer or shelf of clothes to the coming season before the weather turns.
entries.animalRule: Switch before the weather does: the change is made ahead of the season, not after it arrives.
entries.userBenefit: The first cold or hot morning of the new season finds you ready.
entries.mechanismConnection: Snowshoe Hare — Rhythmic • Seasonal • Fitting: Lepus americanus moults from brown to white and back ahead of the snow, and shifts its diet from green plants to twigs and bark as the season turns, keeping itself matched to conditions before predators can exploit a mismatch. This Trial translates that seasonal switch made ahead of time into one drawer switched over to next season's clothes.

entries.title: Swap Teeth for Plates
entries.objective: Morays are built around backward-pointing teeth: a fish seized cannot be pulled free, and pharyngeal jaws in the throat come forward to drag it down. The zebra moray has none of it. Its teeth are blunt pebble-like plates for crushing crabs and urchins, so it gave up the entire holding apparatus that defines its family in exchange for access to hard-shelled prey nothing else in the genus can take. Its principle is Striped Blending. The metaphor? The equipment that defines your group may be the wrong equipment for your食. Swap it.
entries.animalRule: The standard tool must be genuinely set aside rather than supplemented, and a real task has to be completed with the replacement.
entries.userBenefit: Using your field's standard tool when your work is different means fighting it daily and assuming that is normal. One swap usually makes the work straightforward.
entries.mechanismConnection: Gymnomuraena zebra has blunt molariform crushing dentition rather than the recurved holding teeth typical of muraenids, specialising on hard-shelled crustaceans and echinoderms.

entries.title: Swap the Kit, Not the Compromise
entries.objective: Reindeer make the longest overland migrations of any land mammal, and the equipment changes with the season rather than being a compromise between seasons. In summer the hoof pads are soft and spongy and grip wet tundra; in winter they shrink and harden so the rim of the hoof cuts into ice and digs through snow. Two specialised configurations instead of one adequate one. Its principle is Road Fit. The metaphor? A setup that works adequately all year works well in none of them. Swap it with the season.
entries.animalRule: The change must be a genuine swap to suit current conditions rather than a general improvement, and you have to name the conditions it is now tuned for.
entries.userBenefit: A setup tuned for the average of all seasons is wrong in every one of them. One seasonal swap takes an hour and the conditions stop fighting you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Rangifer tarandus hoof pads are soft and spongy in summer for traction on wet tundra and contract and harden in winter so the exposed rim cuts into ice and excavates snow.

entries.title: Swap the Nutcracker for a Brush
entries.objective: Almost every parrot is built around a seed: the bill is a nutcracker and the tongue a thick muscular pad for handling kernels. Lorikeets abandoned all of it. The tongue carries a fringe of fine papillae that stand erect when extended, forming a brush that mops nectar and sweeps pollen, with a short gut to match. Giving up the general tool is what opened a food nothing else was taking. Its principle is Vibrant Communication. The metaphor? Stop carrying the all-purpose tool. Build the brush.
entries.animalRule: The dedicated tool must be purpose-built or purpose-configured for that one task, not a general tool used carefully, and the task has to be completed with it.
entries.userBenefit: A general tool used carefully still costs you setup every single time. Building the dedicated version takes twenty minutes once and the task stops being a task.
entries.mechanismConnection: Trichoglossus haematodus has a brush-tipped tongue whose papillae erect on extension to collect nectar and pollen, paired with a short simple gut adapted to a liquid diet, replacing the seed-cracking apparatus of typical parrots.

entries.title: Swat Ten Crinkled Packets Located by Ear
entries.objective: Blindfolded, locate a crinkling packet by sound alone and tap it with an open hand before it goes quiet, ten times.
entries.animalRule: The blindfold stays on, the helper keeps the packet at arm's length away from their face, and each round allows one tap only.
entries.userBenefit: A fast, surprising test of how well your ears can aim your hands.
entries.mechanismConnection: Long-eared Jerboa — Hopping • Listening • Insect-catching: Euchoreutes naso hunts at night on open Gobi ground, using ears enormous in proportion to its head to locate moving insects, which make up most of its diet and are snapped up on the ground or in flight. This Trial translates that ear-guided strike at an insect in the dark into ten blindfolded taps at a packet located only by its crinkle.

entries.title: Swathe a Landed Sock Prey in Ten Seconds
entries.objective: Dash to a rolled sock the moment it lands and wrap it in at least ten full turns of yarn within ten seconds.
entries.animalRule: Nothing moves until the sock lands, and a round counts only if ten full turns are on the sock within ten seconds.
entries.userBenefit: A quick, frantic burst of hand speed with a ridiculous-looking result.
entries.mechanismConnection: Silver Argiope — Wrapping • Shaking • Explosive: When an insect strikes its web, the silver argiope runs out from the hub and wraps the prey in swathes of silk before biting, subduing it in seconds. This Trial translates that explosive run-and-wrap attack into three timed wraps of a tossed sock in yarn.

entries.title: Sway Like a Leaf, Hours at a Time
entries.objective: A rufous potoo perches alone low in shaded understorey for the whole of daylight, eyes nearly closed, almost motionless except for a slight sway exactly like a dead leaf in moving air. The crypsis depends on doing nothing, and on the one small motion being the right one. Hours of that is the survival strategy. Its principle is Disappearing Posture. The metaphor? Hold the inactive position long enough to be boring, and add only the small motion the setting would have.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be done for the duration during the attempt, and only the motion natural to the setting may be added.
entries.userBenefit: Breaking your stillness every few minutes to do something small means you were never actually out of sight. Holding it long enough to become boring is what works.
entries.mechanismConnection: Nyctibius bracteatus remains near-motionless for hours in shaded understorey with eyes nearly closed, swaying slightly in the manner of a suspended dead leaf.

entries.title: Sway So the Breeze Does Not Expose You
entries.objective: A Eurasian bittern solved concealment with posture rather than colour alone. Its buff streaked plumage runs in vertical lines matching standing reeds, and when alarmed it points its bill straight up, compresses its body and sways gently in time with the reeds moving in the wind, so the disguise survives the one thing static camouflage cannot, which is a breeze. Its principle is Reed Disguise. The metaphor? Build the disturbance into your disguise, because the disturbance is what exposes a static one.
entries.animalRule: The disturbance must be identified first and incorporated rather than resisted during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Arrangements built for still conditions get exposed the moment anything moves. Building the disturbance in is what makes yours hold through it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Botaurus stellaris adopts a vertical bill-up compressed posture with vertically streaked plumage and sways in phase with wind-driven reed movement, maintaining crypsis in moving vegetation.

entries.title: Sweep a Long Tube to Find a Toy
entries.objective: Blindfolded and kneeling, sweep a long cardboard tube across the floor to locate a toy a helper has placed, then take it.
entries.animalRule: Your hands stay on the tube until it has found the toy, and you remain kneeling in one spot while sweeping.
entries.userBenefit: A calm, absorbing game that shows how much a long reach can tell you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Tailless Whip Scorpion — Sweeping • Waiting • Grabbing: A Tailless Whip Scorpion sweeps two enormously long, thread-thin front legs covered in receptors over the surfaces around it instead of walking on them, mapping a space several body lengths across in darkness at almost no energy cost, then grabs with its spiny pedipalps. This Trial translates that long sensory legs swept over surfaces to map the dark into a blindfolded search in which a long tube sweeps the floor until it finds a toy.

entries.title: Sweep for the Swarm, Not the Item
entries.objective: The American Paddlefish feeds on zooplankton in Mississippi water where visibility is centimetres and each food item is almost invisible. Its paddle-shaped rostrum, up to a third of its length, carries tens of thousands of electroreceptors that detect the faint fields produced by swarms of small crustaceans. It does not find individuals. It finds the cloud and swims through it. Its principle is Paddle Sense. The metaphor? Stop hunting for the single item. Detect where the density is and go there.
entries.animalRule: You may not search for a single named item, and the attempt has to work a whole dense area rather than extracting one thing from it.
entries.userBenefit: Hunting for one specific item in a big mess is slow and often fails. Finding where they cluster and working the whole patch gets you that item and several others you had forgotten about.
entries.mechanismConnection: Polyodon spathula detects zooplankton aggregations using tens of thousands of ampullary electroreceptors on its elongated rostrum, filter-feeding through swarms rather than locating individual prey in near-zero visibility.

entries.title: Sweep Once Then Collect What Fell
entries.objective: One big sideways sweep, then gather whatever it brought down.
entries.animalRule: One sweep only; anything left standing stays standing.
entries.userBenefit: Five seconds that are far more satisfying than they have any right to be.
entries.mechanismConnection: Smalltooth Sawfish — Electro-Sensing Rostral Slash — Slashed • Sideways • Instant: Swings the saw laterally through a school with enough speed to stun or cut, then returns to take what has fallen This Trial translates that single lateral saw stroke followed by return into one sweep and the collection after it.

entries.title: Sweep One Charged Balloon Through Falling Confetti
entries.objective: Release a cloud of tiny paper bits and see how many a single passing balloon can pick up.
entries.animalRule: All the bits go out in one release, and only the pieces that cling to the passing balloon count; the rest are lost.
entries.userBenefit: A burst of static-electricity magic that also explains a very strange life cycle.
entries.mechanismConnection: Freshwater Pearl Mussel — Releasing • Host-attached • Seasonal: Each summer a female pearl mussel releases millions of tiny glochidia larvae into the current, and only the few inhaled by a young salmon or trout survive, clamping onto its gills and riding there through the winter. This Trial translates that mass release where only host-attached larvae survive into one burst of confetti and a single balloon pass.

entries.title: Sweep One Magnet Wand for Five Hidden Clips
entries.objective: Find five paper clips hidden under a flat sheet of card or newspaper by sweeping a magnet on a ruler side to side and feeling for the tug.
entries.animalRule: The sheet stays in place and you may only reach under it where the wand has found a clip.
entries.userBenefit: A clever little detection game that makes an invisible force easy to feel.
entries.mechanismConnection: Common Sawshark — Rhythmic • Sweeping • Bottom-hunting: Pristiophorus cirratus sweeps its long toothed rostrum over the seabed, where sensory pores that detect weak electric fields and a pair of barbels let it find prey buried in sand, then slashes sideways to disable it. This Trial translates that low side-to-side sweep of a sensing tool into finding hidden clips with a magnet wand.

entries.title: Sweep One Room for Ten Hidden Tokens
entries.objective: As a small team, check every nook of one bounded room and pool what you find.
entries.animalRule: The search never leaves the room, and every token goes into the shared bowl rather than anyone's pocket.
entries.userBenefit: A short cooperative game that rewards patience over speed.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cozumel Coati — Nosing • Turning over • Remembering: A band forages together over the same bounded island ground again and again, pushing flexible snouts into soil, logs and litter to check a huge number of small scattered parcels. This Trial translates that band search of bounded ground into sweeping one room for ten hidden tokens.

entries.title: Sweep One Room Together With Three Different Jobs
entries.objective: Tidy one room in a single pass with at least two other people, each gathering a different kind of thing.
entries.animalRule: The group moves together from spot to spot, and each person takes only their own kind of item into their own basket.
entries.userBenefit: A tidy room in a quarter of the time, and a cheerful shared job.
entries.mechanismConnection: Paradise Tanager — Flocking • Fruit-eating • Canopy-gleaning: Tangara chilensis travels in small, chattering parties at the core of mixed-species flocks in the Amazon canopy, moving from tree to tree while each species searches in its own way, some for fruit and some for insects on twigs and foliage. This Trial translates that flock moving together while each member forages differently into a group tidy where each person takes a different kind of item.

entries.title: Sweep One Wide Area From One Spot
entries.objective: Sweep One Wide Area From One Spot.
entries.animalRule: Both feet must stay inside the marked spot; only the tool may leave it.
entries.userBenefit: You extend your effective reach without chasing every target.
entries.mechanismConnection: Feeds by trailing a curtain of tentacles many times its own length behind a slowly pulsing bell, so the animal sweeps a large volume of water without pursuing anything in it

entries.title: Sweep Ten Floating Pieces Into One Catch
entries.objective: Sweep Ten Floating Pieces Into One Catch.
