entries.animalRule: Do not pick pieces individually; one final scoop only after the sweep groups them.
entries.userBenefit: You turn sifting into one concrete experience with a visible finish.
entries.mechanismConnection: Eurasian Spoonbill — Sweeping • Flattened • Snapping: The flattened bill tip is swung through shallow water with the mandibles slightly apart, pushing a volume of water through the gap so anything solid in it touches the sensory lining and triggers a snap. This Trial translates that mechanism into ten floating pieces into one catch.

entries.title: Sweep the Surface Film
entries.objective: A spoon-billed sandpiper carries a bill unlike any other wader's, flattened into a spatula at the tip, which it sweeps side to side through the surface film of soft intertidal mud. That is a different technique from the probing most sandpipers use, and it takes invertebrates from the top layer rather than from within it, which restricts the bird to very particular mudflats of exactly the right softness. Its principle is Spoon Precision. The metaphor? A technique that takes only the top layer commits you to very specific ground.
entries.animalRule: Only the surface layer may be worked during the attempt, and the restriction to specific ground has to be accepted explicitly.
entries.userBenefit: A surface technique is fast and only works on exactly the right ground, which you will not notice until it fails. Accepting the restriction keeps you where it works.
entries.mechanismConnection: Calidris pygmaea sweeps its spatulate bill tip laterally through the surface film of soft intertidal mud, taking surface invertebrates and restricting it to specific substrate conditions.

entries.title: Sweep the Trails, Then Memorise Them
entries.objective: A black-and-rufous elephant shrew spends much of each day cleaning. It sweeps leaf litter aside with its snout and feet to keep a network of narrow trails clear across its territory, and it commits that network to memory. The trails are not shortcuts to food; they are the escape system, because a known swept surface lets a disturbed animal accelerate immediately. Its principle is Route Memory. The metaphor? Spend your time clearing and memorising the escape routes, not the routes to the reward.
entries.animalRule: The routes cleared must be exits rather than routes to a reward, and one has to be actually tested during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Knowing the routes to the reward and not the exits means one disturbance leaves you stuck. Clearing the exits costs an hour and you never think about it again.
entries.mechanismConnection: Rhynchocyon petersi maintains and memorises a swept network of trails across its territory which function as high-speed escape routes rather than foraging paths.

entries.title: Sweep Three Dry Bins for Three Reusable Finds
entries.objective: Wearing gloves, check the recycling bin and two other dry-waste containers in one circuit and rescue three items that can be reused.
entries.animalRule: Check each container once in a single circuit and rescue exactly three items, each with a named new use.
entries.userBenefit: Three free useful things and a little less rubbish.
entries.mechanismConnection: Yellow Dung Fly — Circuit • Cue-led • Repeating: Scathophaga stercoraria shuttles between fresh dung pats, nearby cover and hunting perches, drawn by smell to each new pat while it is still useful and leaving as it crusts over. This Trial translates that repeating circuit of waste patches that finds value others overlook into one gloved loop through three dry bins that rescues three reusable finds.

entries.title: Swing Below the Branch and Shout
entries.objective: A male Montezuma oropendola displays by swinging his whole body below the branch at the exposed colony edge while delivering a loud bubbling call that carries across canopy gaps to females that cannot see him properly. The posture and the sound are one act: hanging upside down is what projects the voice outward rather than into the leaves. Its principle is Hanging Voice. The metaphor? Change your position so the signal goes where it needs to, not just louder.
entries.animalRule: The position must change during the attempt, and the signal may not simply be repeated louder from the original place.
entries.userBenefit: Repeating something louder from the same place means the people who could not hear you still cannot. Moving so it carries reaches them the first time.
entries.mechanismConnection: Psarocolius montezuma males invert below the nest branch while delivering a loud gurgling song, a posture that projects the call across open canopy gaps.

entries.title: Swing It Once as They Arrive
entries.objective: A bolas spider builds no web. She hangs from a line holding a short thread tipped with a sticky globule, and when a male moth arrives following a pheromone she faked, she swings the globule at him. The glue holds through the loose scales that normally let moths slide off silk. One swing, one target, nothing standing to catch anything else. Its principle is Scented Snare. The metaphor? Hold one tool ready and use it on the thing you called in, rather than building something to catch whatever comes.
entries.animalRule: Nothing general may be built during the attempt, and the tool has to be used on the specific thing that was invited.
entries.userBenefit: Building something general to catch whatever turns up means maintaining it constantly for things you did not want. One tool for the thing you invited costs nothing to keep.
entries.mechanismConnection: Mastophora hutchinsoni swings a single adhesive globule on a short thread at moths drawn in by her emitted pheromone mimic, the glue penetrating their detachable scales.

entries.title: Swing It Sideways, Not Forward
entries.objective: A gar's snout is long and very narrow, and that shape lets it be swung sideways through water at speed because it presents almost no frontal area. A lunge with a broad head would push a wall of water ahead of it and warn the prey. The gar does not strike forward at all; it slashes across, and the geometry is the whole reason it works. Its principle is Surface Ambush. The metaphor? Come across it rather than at it, so nothing is pushed ahead of you.
entries.animalRule: The approach must be lateral rather than frontal, and nothing may be announced ahead of it during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: A head-on approach pushes a warning ahead of you and the thing is gone. Coming across it means you arrive before anyone has reacted.
entries.mechanismConnection: Lepisosteus osseus has a narrow elongated rostrum presenting minimal frontal area, permitting rapid lateral head sweeps that avoid the bow wave a broad-headed forward lunge would generate.

entries.title: Swing the Pendulum at the Predator
entries.objective: A motmot's two central tail feathers lose their barbs along part of the shaft, leaving a bare stem with a paddle at the end, and the bird swings it slowly side to side. It does this most when a predator is present, and both sexes do it, which points away from courtship and toward a message aimed at the predator: I have seen you. Its principle is Racket-Tail Poise. The metaphor? Let them know you noticed and the attempt stops being worth making.
entries.animalRule: The signal must convey only that you have noticed during the attempt, with no accusation and no action taken on it.
entries.userBenefit: Saying nothing means they assume you have not noticed and continue. Signalling that you have, without accusing anyone, usually ends it with no confrontation.
entries.mechanismConnection: Eumomota superciliosa performs racket-tail wagging predominantly in the presence of predators and in both sexes, functioning as a pursuit-deterrent signal of detection rather than courtship.

entries.title: Swipe Five Red Beads Out of a Heap
entries.objective: Pick five target beads out of a packed mixed heap with a single straight stick, fast.
entries.animalRule: The cupped hand only corrals and the stick only swipes: no picking up with fingers, and no more than five non-red beads may leave the heap.
entries.userBenefit: Thirty seconds of fine, fast hand control that is much harder than it looks.
entries.mechanismConnection: Atlantic Sailfish — Explosive • Slashing • Short-window: Sailfish close on a bait ball, often hunting in groups that keep the school crowded, and slash their bills through it to injure and separate single fish, turning a mass with no target into individual catchable prey. This Trial translates that crowding of the school and the bill-slash that knocks single fish loose into a thirty-second race to swipe five targets out of one cupped heap.

entries.title: Switch It Off, Do Not Slow It
entries.objective: Boxelder Bug diapause is not cold slowing the animal down. It is a hormonally distinct programme in which reproduction is switched off and feeding stops completely. The difference matters: a slowed animal still spends, a switched-off one does not. Its principle is Seasonal Gathering. The metaphor? Running everything at reduced speed is how you run out. Switch one thing fully off.
entries.animalRule: The thing must be fully stopped rather than reduced, with a stated end date, and anyone relying on it must be told during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Half-doing five things costs nearly as much as doing them properly and gets you none of the benefit. Switching one fully off for a set period gives the others enough to actually work.
entries.mechanismConnection: Boisea trivittata enters a hormonally distinct diapause rather than simple cold torpor, with reproduction suppressed and feeding ceasing entirely, conserving reserves rather than merely slowing expenditure.

entries.title: Switch Off Every Standby Light in One Room
entries.objective: Stop one room paying to keep idle devices warm and ready overnight.
entries.animalRule: Leave fridges, freezers, medical devices, alarms and anything that must stay on; everything else stops paying for readiness.
entries.userBenefit: A slightly lower electricity bill and a properly dark room tonight.
entries.mechanismConnection: Lesser Hedgehog Tenrec — Searching leaf litter • Curling up • Shutting down for months: Rather than defending a fixed body temperature at great cost, the tenrec lets its body drift with the air and drops into torpor, so the cost of existing falls to almost nothing through the unproductive dry season. This Trial translates that refusal to pay for staying warm and ready when nothing is happening into switching one room's idle devices fully off overnight.

entries.title: Switch the Whole System Off
entries.objective: The hummingbird's famous day is only half the system. At night no flowers are open and nothing it earned in daylight can be carried, so instead of defending its temperature it abandons it: the bird drops into torpor, body temperature and heart rate falling steeply, spending a fraction of what an alert bird would. Shutting down is what makes the next expensive day affordable. Its principle is Control. The metaphor? Strip it back to nothing.
entries.animalRule: Everything not strictly required leaves the space, the bare state has to be used for a full hour, and nothing goes back before then.
entries.userBenefit: Keeping everything within reach because you might need it means you pay for all of it daily. An hour stripped bare shows you how little you actually use.
entries.mechanismConnection: Archilochus colubris enters nightly torpor, allowing body temperature and heart rate to fall far below normothermic levels to conserve energy when nectar is unavailable.

entries.title: Switch to Leaves When the Grass Fails
entries.objective: A banteng's diet is not fixed. When dry-season grass is poor it shifts towards leaves, shoots and bamboo at the forest edge, and where hunting pressure is heavy whole herds move their feeding into the night. The animal does not defend a preference; it tracks what the season and the risk actually allow. Its principle is Tropical Wild Strength. The metaphor? Shift what you take and when you take it as conditions change, instead of holding a pattern that stopped working.
entries.animalRule: Either what is taken or when must change during the attempt, and the condition that prompted it has to be named.
entries.userBenefit: Holding a routine after the conditions it suited have gone means working harder for less and calling it discipline. One deliberate shift gets you back to the same return.
entries.mechanismConnection: Bos javanicus shifts seasonally from grazing to browsing leaves and bamboo as dry-season grass quality declines, and becomes nocturnal under heavy hunting pressure.

entries.title: Switch to Lichen in Winter
entries.objective: A golden snub-nosed monkey lives higher and colder than almost any other primate, and its system is not one strategy but a switch between two. Through the growing season the animals work leaves, buds and fruit across a wide area in semi-independent units. When winter closes that supply the diet shifts onto lichen, a food nothing else wants and which is available when nothing else is. Its principle is Cold Togetherness. The metaphor? Keep a second food nobody wants, for the season when the good one closes.
entries.animalRule: The fallback must be genuinely unwanted by others and available out of season, and access has to be secured during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Having only the good resource means every closed season empties you out. One unwanted fallback nobody competes for carries you through all of them.
entries.mechanismConnection: Rhinopithecus roxellana switches from a wide-ranging foliage and fruit diet in the growing season to lichen through montane winters when other resources are unavailable.

entries.title: Switch While It Still Works
entries.objective: An impala herd lives on the edge between open grass and thicket, and it does not pick one. It grazes fresh grass while the rains hold and switches to browsing leaves and shoots when the grass dries, which is why it can hold ground that grazing specialists and browsing specialists both lose. The switch happens mid-season, not after a failure. Its principle is Elastic Escape. The metaphor? Switch food before the first one runs out.
entries.animalRule: The switch happens while the first approach is still working, at the halfway point, and the second approach must carry the task to the end.
entries.userBenefit: Waiting until something stops working before changing means you spend weeks in the failing version. Switching while it still works keeps you productive through the change itself.
entries.mechanismConnection: Aepyceros melampus is a mixed feeder, shifting between grazing and browsing as seasonal grass quality changes rather than specialising on either resource.

entries.title: Swivel a Paperclip-Clawed Figure to Hang Head-Down
entries.objective: Build a card figure whose hind claws swivel, and show it slipping off a towel head-down until the claws are turned, then holding.
entries.animalRule: The claws must not be re-bent between the two tries: only the half-turn swivel changes whether they catch.
entries.userBenefit: A clever little model that explains a rare piece of anatomy better than any diagram.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cacomistle — Climbing after dark • Reversing the ankles • Coming down head first: A Cacomistle can rotate its hind feet about half a turn at the ankle, so when it faces down a trunk its rear claws still point upward into the bark and it can descend head first at speed instead of slipping. This Trial translates that hind-foot reversal that keeps the claws hooked while facing downward into a card figure that slips off a towel head-down until its paperclip claws are swivelled half a turn, and then holds.

entries.title: Sync One Six-Move Perch Display in Fifteen Seconds
entries.objective: With a partner, perform a fast six-move display side by side on two taped floor perches, perfectly in time, within fifteen seconds, ending with both ribbons brushing a judge's card.
entries.animalRule: Both performers must hit every move at the same time without leaving their squares, and each performer's ribbon must brush the judge's card on the final move.
entries.userBenefit: A burst of laughter and teamwork that is harder than it looks.
entries.mechanismConnection: Wire-tailed Manakin — Displaying • Cooperative • Tactile: Male Pipra filicauda perform fast, stereotyped displays on set perches at leks, often with a partner male, and during courtship brush the female's chin with their wire-like tail filaments. This Trial translates that fast, stereotyped two-male display finished with a filament brush into a synchronised six-move duo display on two set floor perches ending in a ribbon brush.

entries.title: Sync Torch Blinks With a Partner
entries.objective: Keep two torches blinking in the same rhythm with a partner for ninety seconds without counting aloud.
entries.animalRule: No counting aloud, music or tapping: the light pattern is the only signal you share.
entries.userBenefit: A calm, quiet coordination game that builds a sense of connection.
entries.mechanismConnection: Flashlight Fish — Rhythmic • Guided • Patrol: Anomalops katoptron schools at night using steady rhythms of blinks from its bacterial light organs, which let the fish see one another and keep formation in dark water. This Trial translates that shared blink rhythm that keeps a school together into two torches kept blinking together by watching each other's light.

entries.title: Synchronise One Two-Minute Window
entries.objective: Choose a partner or two devices and coordinate one useful action to happen inside the same two-minute window. Capture a timestamped screenshot or photo.
entries.animalRule: Both parts have to occur inside the same two-minute window; if one misses it, restart with a new window.
entries.userBenefit: You find out how hard exact simultaneity is, and how satisfying it is when it lands.
entries.mechanismConnection: St Mark's Fly uses this mode by emerges synchronously in a window of about two weeks each spring, which concentrates mating into a period short enough that predators cannot build up in response and every individual finds others of its kind

entries.title: Tactile Stimulation Changes the Animal
entries.objective: Desert locusts are one of the clearest biological examples of density-driven phase change. At low density individuals develop a solitary form: cryptic colouring, less robust hind legs, smaller brains, cautious dispersive behaviour. When crowding increases and tactile stimulation from other locusts rises past a threshold, the same genotype develops into something different in colour, shape and behaviour. Contact with others changes the animal. Its principle is Changed By Company. The metaphor? Who you are around past a certain density changes what you become, not just what you do.
entries.animalRule: The contact must genuinely exceed your usual level during the attempt, and the change in you has to be noted rather than in output.
entries.userBenefit: Assuming company only changes what you produce means missing that it changes what you are. Noticing that is how you choose your density deliberately.
entries.mechanismConnection: Schistocerca gregaria undergoes density-dependent phase transformation in colouration, morphology, brain size and behaviour, triggered by tactile stimulation from conspecifics.

entries.title: Tag One Bottle With a Curled Foil Signature
entries.objective: Fix ten tight glossy foil curls to one everyday item so it can be picked out at a glance among look-alikes.
entries.animalRule: The curls are a constant signature: every strip holds a tight, shiny curl, and only your item wears them.
entries.userBenefit: Your bottle or mug will never be mixed up again.
entries.mechanismConnection: Curl-crested Aracari — Ongoing • Signalling • Presence: Pteroglossus beauharnaisii has crown feathers whose shafts end in flattened, glossy, curled plates like shavings of black plastic, a unique texture worn every day that makes the bird instantly recognisable in the canopy. This Trial translates that constant curled-feather signature into ten foil curls that make one bottle instantly recognisable among look-alikes.

entries.title: Tag One Partner Mid-Crossing From Behind Cover
entries.objective: Wait hidden beside a crossing zone and burst out to tag a partner before they reach safety.
entries.animalRule: Launch only from cover and only once the partner is in the open zone: no tags on the mats and no chasing past the zone.
entries.userBenefit: A fast, funny game of timing that gets both of you moving.
entries.mechanismConnection: Leopard Seal — Explosive • Ambush • Capture: Hydrurga leptonyx waits at the ice edge, often just beneath it, where penguins must cross open water, then accelerates explosively to seize one before it reaches the safety of the ice. This Trial translates that ambush at the boundary crossing into a burst from cover to tag a partner inside a two-metre crossing zone.

entries.title: Tails In, Heads Out
entries.objective: A ground-nesting bird sleeping in open country has no cover and no height. Bobwhites solve it as a group: at dusk a covey of ten to fifteen settles into a tight disc with tails pointed inward and heads facing out, so every direction is watched by somebody and the whole group explodes outward in all directions if something comes. No individual watches everything. Its principle is Teamwork. The metaphor? Nobody can cover every direction. Sit back to back and each take one.
entries.animalRule: Each person must own exactly one area with no overlap, and the assignment has to be stated so everyone knows who covers what.
entries.userBenefit: Everyone half-watching everything means nobody is actually watching anything and all of you are tired. One direction each costs less attention and covers more.
entries.mechanismConnection: Colinus virginianus roosts in a tight outward-facing disc with tails inward, giving the covey full peripheral surveillance and enabling simultaneous explosive flush in all directions.

entries.title: Take It and Resume the Pose
entries.objective: A rufous potoo spends the day as a clump of dead leaves and hunts at night by sitting still until an insect is close, taking it in a short sally, and returning to exactly the same perch and the same posture. The crypsis is only intact if the position is resumed; a bird that stayed where the catch happened would have stopped being a dead leaf. Its principle is Disappearing Posture. The metaphor? After the brief action, return to the exact position you left, not somewhere near it.
entries.animalRule: The return must be to the exact position during the attempt, and the posture has to be matched rather than approximated.
entries.userBenefit: Settling somewhere near where you were after each interruption means your setup degrades all day and you never notice. Returning exactly costs seconds and preserves it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Nyctibius bracteatus sallies briefly for insects from a cryptic perch and returns to the identical position and dead-leaf posture that maintains its concealment.

entries.title: Take It at the Angle, Not the Moment
entries.objective: A bee-eater does not launch at every bee that passes. It sits and lets most of them go, and goes only when one crosses at the particular angle and distance that makes the intercept cheap, catching it in the air and dealing with the sting on the way back. Selectivity is what makes the whole method affordable. Its principle is Aerial Snatch. The metaphor? Let the badly angled ones pass; go when the geometry is already in your favour.
entries.animalRule: At least one badly angled opportunity must be let go during the attempt, and the favourable angle has to be named before the commitment.
entries.userBenefit: Chasing every opportunity means most of your effort goes into the badly angled ones and fails. Letting those pass leaves you able to take the one that works.
entries.mechanismConnection: Merops apiaster sallies from an exposed perch only at insects passing within a favourable interception angle and range, handling and de-stinging the prey in flight or on return.

entries.title: Take It In From Above
entries.objective: A shark takes water in through its mouth and pushes it over the gills, which works when the mouth is at the front. A ray's mouth is on the underside pressed against the seabed, and in a fish lying flat under sand that route would draw in sediment. The answer is spiracles on top of the head: intake moved to the clean side while the working side stays buried. Its principle is Flat Patience. The metaphor? Your intake is in the dirty place. Move it to the clean side and keep working where you are.
entries.animalRule: Only the intake may move and the work has to stay where it was, with the new intake channel genuinely cleaner rather than merely different.
entries.userBenefit: Moving your whole operation to escape a noisy channel costs you everything you had set up. Moving only the intake is quick and the noise stops reaching you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Batoid rays draw respiratory water through dorsal spiracles rather than the ventrally positioned mouth, allowing them to remain buried in sediment without ingesting substrate.

entries.title: Take It In Solid
entries.objective: Almost everything people believe about harvestmen is wrong, including the famous claim about venom: they have no venom glands at all. What they do have is a gut that handles solids. Every spider and scorpion must liquefy its food outside the body and drink the result; a harvestman simply takes particles in. Skipping the pre-processing is what lets it eat what others cannot. Its principle is Adaptable Movement. The metaphor? Stop breaking things down before you can start. Take it in whole.
entries.animalRule: No planning, sorting or restructuring may happen first, and the ten minutes must go on the actual work in its raw state.
entries.userBenefit: Insisting on tidy steps before you begin is how things stay unstarted for months. Working on the mess as it is gets you ten real minutes in, and the structure usually appears once you are moving.
entries.mechanismConnection: Opiliones lack venom glands entirely and, unlike spiders and scorpions which must digest prey externally and ingest liquid, possess a gut capable of processing solid food particles directly.

entries.title: Take On the Local Call
entries.objective: Budgerigar mimicry is membership, not performance. These birds change their own contact calls to match whoever they are currently with, and one moved to a new group converges on that group's call within weeks, so the call reports present company rather than origin. In flocks of thousands chasing rain, a signal fixed at hatching would mark you a stranger forever. Updating is what keeps you in. Its principle is Social Mimicry. The metaphor? Learn the local words. Use them.
entries.animalRule: The three terms must be genuinely from that group rather than invented, and at least one must be used in a real exchange with them.
entries.userBenefit: Sounding like an outsider keeps you treated as one, however good your work is. Picking up the handful of words a group actually uses closes that gap faster than any amount of proving yourself.
entries.mechanismConnection: Melopsittacus undulatus modifies its contact calls to converge on those of its current social group within weeks of joining it, so call similarity tracks present flock membership rather than natal origin, allowing groups to re-form continuously as they move.

entries.title: Take One Fast Opportunity Immediately
entries.objective: When one small useful opportunity appears today—an open seat, easy task, good photo, or helpful opening—act on it immediately instead of debating.
entries.animalRule: Repeated passage wears a private network of tunnels through dense undergrowth, so the animal feeds at the open edge of the forest and can re-enter thick cover at speed along routes nothing chasing it has learned. Keep that true for the whole attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Trains rapid commitment when a short-lived opportunity appears and reduces hesitation.
entries.mechanismConnection: Dusky Pademelon expresses Edge Discretion through this mode: Dusky Pademelon — Runways Only It Knows — Tunnelling • Feeding out • Slipping back: Repeated passage wears a private network of tunnels through dense undergrowth, so the animal feeds at the open edge of the forest and can re-enter thick cover at speed along routes nothing chasing it has learned. The Trial carries that same limiting structure into one concrete human action.

entries.title: Take One Floating Thing Without Stopping
entries.objective: Lift something off a surface while moving past, in one pass.
entries.animalRule: Your feet may not stop or change pace; a second pass ends the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: A quick burst that is far harder than it looks and improves every time you try it.
entries.mechanismConnection: African Fish Eagle — Swooping, gripping and brief: it drops to take fish from just below the surface with spicules on the feet gripping the scales, a few seconds of effort perhaps once or twice a day. This Trial translates that grab taken in passing into an object lifted without breaking stride.

entries.title: Take One Ready-Made Slot Fairly
entries.objective: Use an existing opening instead of building a new structure.
entries.animalRule: Use only an actually available opening; moving somebody else's claim does not count.
entries.userBenefit: You notice how much effort disappears when you use capacity that already exists.
entries.mechanismConnection: Egyptian Goose — Acquires nest sites by evicting the occupants of tree holes, cliff ledges and other birds' nests rather than constructing anything, using persistent direct aggression that larger birds including raptors frequently give way to. The Trial compresses that mechanism into one immediate, proofable human session.

entries.title: Take One Target From Ten Centimetres
entries.objective: Start so close there is no room to adjust, and take it anyway.
entries.animalRule: Your hand must start within about ten centimetres and may not draw back before moving.
entries.userBenefit: A burst that trains the reach you actually use for dropped things, at the distance you actually have.
entries.mechanismConnection: Malachite Kingfisher — Dropping, short and shallow: the dive is very short because the perch is low, which means almost no time to correct and a target only centimetres below the surface. This Trial translates that near-zero correction distance into a take made from ten centimetres with no wind-up.

entries.title: Take the Growth Others Leave
entries.objective: A Siamese Algae Eater makes its living on surfaces rather than in water. A modified lower lip with a hardened rasping edge is drawn across rock, wood and leaves, taking the film that grows on anything left still, and it is one of very few fish that will keep eating the tough red algae most grazers refuse. The specificity is the whole value. Its principle is Persistent Cleaning. The metaphor? The easy growth is already taken. Learn to eat the tough stuff nobody else will.
entries.animalRule: The job must be one avoided for tedium rather than difficulty, done fully rather than sampled, and the knowledge gained has to be named out loud.
entries.userBenefit: Everyone skips the tedious job, which is why it holds information nobody has. Doing it fully once makes you the person who knows how the thing actually works.
entries.mechanismConnection: Crossocheilus oblongus grazes attached biofilm with a hardened rasping lower lip and is one of few fishes that consumes tough filamentous red algae which most grazers avoid.

entries.title: Take the Heat Already There
entries.objective: A rock hyrax regulates its temperature badly for a mammal, and the whole social structure follows. Colonies spend long periods piled on top of each other on sunlit rock, taking heat from the stone and from each other rather than generating it, which is why a group is visible for hours doing apparently nothing. The stone does the work. Its principle is Rock Communion. The metaphor? Borrowed warmth costs nothing to make.
entries.animalRule: The warmth has to be already there rather than generated by you, you stay ten minutes, and nothing else is done in that time.
entries.userBenefit: Generating your own warmth and energy for everything means you burn through what you have by midday. Ten minutes of taking what is already there costs you nothing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Procavia capensis has poor thermoregulation and relies on huddling and conductive heat uptake from sun-warmed rock rather than metabolic heat production.

entries.title: Take the Heat From the Patch of Sun
entries.objective: Simalia boeleni lives in montane New Guinea forest where the air is persistently cool and sunlight arrives in broken patches, so being an ectotherm there is a heat problem before it is a food problem. Its answer is its surface: deep black iridescent scales that absorb radiant heat wherever direct sun reaches a mossy limb. Because temperature comes from absorption rather than metabolism, the animal can run slowly, which is what makes long gaps between meals survivable. Its principle is Black Sheen. The metaphor? Take heat from outside. Spend less.
entries.animalRule: You generate none of it during the twenty minutes, and the place has to already be producing it before you arrive.
entries.userBenefit: Manufacturing your own motivation and structure every day is the most expensive thing you do, and it is why you run out by mid-afternoon. Taking it from a place that already has it costs you nothing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Simalia boeleni raises body temperature by absorbing radiant heat through highly iridescent black scales in cool montane forest, rather than by generating it metabolically.

entries.title: Take the Help Without Evicting
entries.objective: The common cuckoo's chick heaves the host's eggs over the rim within hours of hatching. The Pied Cuckoo does not. Its egg closely matches the babbler's own, the chick hatches earlier and grows faster and simply outcompetes for food, but the host's chicks are usually raised alongside it. It takes a large share of the help without destroying the brood providing it. Its principle is Babbler-Raised Chick. The metaphor? Taking help does not require taking everything. Leave the nest working.
entries.animalRule: What you take must leave the shared resource functional for others, and you have to restore or replace what you consumed during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Taking everything available from a shared resource gets you one good week and closes it to you afterwards. Taking your share and leaving it working means you can come back.
entries.mechanismConnection: Clamator jacobinus lays a mimetic egg in babbler nests and its chick outcompetes host young for provisioning without ejecting them, so host offspring are commonly fledged alongside the parasite.

entries.title: Take the Hit Head-On
entries.objective: In the late-autumn rut argali rams rear up and crash their massive spiralled horns together, and those horns can be a substantial share of body weight. The thickened skull and the structure behind it exist to absorb impacts the animal will deliberately seek out. It is not avoiding the collision; it is built to receive it squarely. Its principle is Highhorn. The metaphor? Meet it head-on with the part built for it.
entries.animalRule: The approach must be direct rather than angled, and nothing may be softened to avoid the impact.
entries.userBenefit: Handling a confrontation sideways means you have it repeatedly and never settle it, and the cost accumulates quietly. Meeting it head-on once hurts more in the moment and ends it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ovis ammon rams engage in frontal horn clashes absorbed by a thickened cranium and massive spiralled horns forming a large fraction of body mass.

entries.title: Take the Hole That Exists
entries.objective: Nesting cavities are the scarcest thing in most bird communities, because almost nothing can make one. The Common Myna does not wait for a vacancy: it finds occupied holes and takes them. Combined with eating insects, fruit, grain and refuse alike, and a positive preference for towns, that is why it is everywhere. Taking what exists beats waiting for what is free. Its principle is Pavement Pickings. The metaphor? Stop waiting for a clean slot to open. Use what is already built.
entries.animalRule: Nothing new may be created, and you must not displace anyone who is already using it. The existing structure has to carry your purpose at least once.
entries.userBenefit: Creating a new channel means recruiting everyone into it before it does anything. Running your thing through a structure that already has attention works immediately and costs nobody anything new.
entries.mechanismConnection: Acridotheres tristis is an aggressive secondary cavity nester that evicts existing occupants from tree hollows and building cavities, and its broad omnivorous diet and tolerance of urban habitat let it exploit human-made structures throughout its range.

entries.title: Take the Hours Nobody Wants
entries.objective: A squirrelfish does its work after dark. Its eyes are disproportionately large, built for gathering what little light exists at night, and it leaves the crevice to hunt crustaceans over reef and sand when nothing is competing for them. Sharp spines and a grunting sound made with the swim bladder cover the rest. Working the hours nobody else wants is what makes a slow fish viable. Its principle is Night Vision. The metaphor? Competition is a choice of timing.
entries.animalRule: The task must be done after sunset in a genuinely quiet period, and no additional lighting may be switched on for it.
entries.userBenefit: Working only the hours everyone else works means you compete for everything you get. Shifting even part of it to the quiet hours gives you the place to yourself.
entries.mechanismConnection: Holocentrus adscensionis has enlarged light-gathering eyes for nocturnal foraging over reef and sand, with defensive spines and swim-bladder stridulation covering its slowness.

entries.title: Take the Most Exposed Seat
entries.objective: A lilac-breasted roller hunts by sitting still somewhere deliberately conspicuous, a dead branch or a wire, where open ground is clearly visible, then dropping steeply onto insects, scorpions and lizards. Sitting in the open would be reckless for most birds its size, but it buys a field of view no concealed perch offers. Being seen is part of the design, which is what makes the exposure worth its risk. Its principle is Flourish. The metaphor? Hiding costs you everything you cannot see.
entries.animalRule: The seat has to be the most exposed one available, you stay for the full ten minutes, and you act on only the first thing that qualifies.
entries.userBenefit: Choosing the hidden corner means you see a fraction of what is happening and get asked for nothing. The exposed seat costs you comfort and gives you the whole room.
entries.mechanismConnection: Coracias caudatus hunts from deliberately conspicuous exposed perches, trading concealment for an unobstructed field of view over open ground before a steep drop onto prey.

entries.title: Take the Part Nobody Wants
entries.objective: A marabou stork feeds where almost nothing else will. A head and neck largely free of feathers stay workable when pushed inside a carcass, a massive bill handles bone and hide, and soaring on thermals covers huge areas for almost no effort. It hunts nothing and rejects very little, so it is almost never in competition for anything. Its principle is Acceptance. The metaphor? The part of the work nobody wants is the part with no queue.
entries.animalRule: The part taken must be one nobody else wanted, and it has to be done properly rather than minimally during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Competing for the parts everyone wants means your result depends on beating people. The part nobody wants is yours immediately and people remember who took it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Leptoptilos crumenifer has reduced head and neck feathering suited to carcass feeding, a massive bill for processing bone and hide, and thermal soaring for low-cost wide-area search of carrion.

entries.title: Take the Part That Grows Back
entries.objective: Most predators consume the animal they catch, so a hunted patch is an empty patch. The Leopard Shark feeds differently over soft-sediment flats: it hovers close to the bottom and applies suction to draw out what is buried, and much of what it takes is the siphons of clams and the tails of innkeeper worms, parts the prey regenerates. The same patch stays productive. Its principle is Steady Movement Strategy. The metaphor? Taking the whole thing empties the source. Take the part that grows back.
entries.animalRule: What you take must be something the source genuinely regenerates, and the larger non-renewing ask has to be deliberately declined during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Taking the big thing once gets you more today and closes the source for good. Taking only the part that regrows means you can come back indefinitely, which is worth far more.
entries.mechanismConnection: Triakis semifasciata feeds by suction over soft sediment, frequently taking regenerating structures such as clam siphons and innkeeper worm tails rather than whole prey, allowing repeated exploitation of the same area.

entries.title: Take the Poison, Make the Perfume
entries.objective: Danaine butterflies cannot make pyrrolizidine alkaloids and cannot do without them. Adults seek out withered or damaged plants containing the compounds, sometimes scratching the tissue to release more, and store what they take. The alkaloids make the butterfly genuinely unpalatable, and males also convert them into the pheromone used in courtship. One intake, two completely different jobs. Its principle is Toxic-Twin Wings. The metaphor? Make the same input do two jobs before you go looking for another.
entries.animalRule: The second use must be genuinely different from the first rather than a variation, and both uses have to be real rather than hypothetical.
entries.userBenefit: Everything you gather costs the same effort whether it does one job or two. Finding a real second use is free output, and it usually takes minutes to spot.
entries.mechanismConnection: Euploea adults sequester pyrrolizidine alkaloids from withered plant tissue, which render them unpalatable to predators and are also biosynthetically converted by males into courtship pheromone components.

entries.title: Take the Root, Not the Blade
entries.objective: The Dugong is the only strictly marine mammal that eats plants, and its whole head is built for one job: the muzzle is turned sharply downward with a broad muscular upper lip that ploughs shallow sediment and takes whole seagrass plants including the starchy rhizomes, rather than cropping blades from above. A far richer return from the same patch. Its principle is Gentle Grazing. The metaphor? You keep taking the visible part. The value is in the root.
entries.animalRule: You must obtain the underlying thing rather than a better summary of it, and the surface version has to be set aside during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Taking the summary means you inherit someone else's reading of it and cannot check anything. Going for the underlying thing takes longer once and you stop being dependent on their interpretation.
entries.mechanismConnection: Dugong dugon has a sharply downturned muzzle with a broad muscular upper lip used to plough sediment and extract entire seagrass plants including starch-rich rhizomes, rather than cropping leaf blades.

entries.title: Take the Shift Nobody Works
entries.objective: Unusually among wasps, the European Hornet forages after dark and is readily drawn to lit windows. That shift gives it insects that are active at night and unavailable to every day-flying wasp competing for the same ground, and the competition on that shift is close to zero. Its principle is Night Navigation. The metaphor? The hours everyone works are the contested ones. Take the shift nobody wants.
entries.animalRule: The hours must be ones genuinely nobody around you works rather than merely quieter, and you have to name what was available then that is not normally.
entries.userBenefit: Working the same hours as everyone means competing for the same rooms, people and attention. One session on the uncontested shift usually gets you more than three on the busy one.
entries.mechanismConnection: Vespa crabro forages nocturnally as well as by day, exploiting night-flying insects unavailable to diurnal wasps and reducing competition for the same prey base.

entries.title: Take the Sunlit Log
entries.objective: A freshwater turtle cannot make its own heat, so digestion, growth, immunity and egg development all depend on getting warm, which makes a log in the sun a genuine resource and there are never enough. The Red-eared Slider does not outcompete native turtles for food. It takes the basking sites: hauls out earlier, stays longer, grows faster, displaces residents. Holding the warm spot is the whole advantage. Its principle is Patient Browsing Strategy. The metaphor? Stop competing on effort. Take the good seat early.
entries.animalRule: You must arrive before anyone else and still be in the spot when others turn up, and nobody may be moved or asked to shift for you.
entries.userBenefit: You compete by working harder in worse conditions. Claiming the genuinely better spot early costs you fifteen minutes once and improves everything you do in it afterwards.
entries.mechanismConnection: Trachemys scripta elegans is ectothermic and depends on basking for digestion, growth and reproduction; where introduced it displaces native turtles by monopolising limited basking sites, hauling out earlier and remaining longer rather than by competing for food.

entries.title: Take the Unclaimed Hours
entries.objective: Almost every other small cat in the Americas works at night. The jaguarundi does not. It is regularly active through the middle of the day, which is strange for an animal its size and probably not a preference so much as an occupancy decision: the ocelot and margay are out after dark, the ocelot will kill a smaller cat that crosses it, and the daylight hours are unclaimed. Its principle is Streamlining. The metaphor? Take the hours nobody has claimed, even if they are the wrong hours for your kind.
entries.animalRule: The hours must be genuinely unclaimed by others, and that has to be verified before working them during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Working the natural hours for what you do means sharing them with everyone who does it. Unclaimed hours are awkward and nobody is competing with you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Herpailurus yagouaroundi is substantially diurnal, unusual among small Neotropical felids, likely an avoidance response to nocturnal ocelots that kill smaller sympatric cats.

entries.title: Take the Water From the Plants
entries.objective: The Barbary sheep grazes grasses, shrubs and herbs in the cooler hours and takes much of its water from the plants themselves and from dew, which lets it range far from any spring. It drinks when water is available and it is not tied to it. Getting what it needs from what it is already doing removes the thing that would otherwise chain it to one place. Its principle is Cliffbalance. The metaphor? Get it from what you already do.
entries.animalRule: The need must be met from an existing activity rather than a new one, and the usual return may not happen today.
entries.userBenefit: Having one need that only one place can meet means your whole range is set by how far you can get from it. Meeting it out of something you already do widens everything at once.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ammotragus lervia obtains most of its water from plant moisture and dew, allowing it to range far from permanent water sources.

entries.title: Take the Water With You
entries.objective: A mudskipper is a fish that works on land, and it does it by taking its medium along. Enlarged gill chambers are filled with water before it emerges and closed to hold that charge, while wet skin and mouth lining take up oxygen from the air as long as they stay moist. It props itself forward on muscular pectoral fins like crutches. Its principle is Threshold. The metaphor? You can work outside your element if you carry a charge of it.
entries.animalRule: The charge must be prepared before entering, and it has to be sufficient for the whole time spent there during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Going somewhere unsupported and expecting to find what you need is how you come back with nothing. Carrying the charge means the environment stops mattering.
entries.mechanismConnection: Periophthalmus fills and seals enlarged branchial chambers with water before emerging, supplementing with cutaneous and buccal respiration while the surfaces remain moist.

entries.title: Take Three From Air, Three From Ground
entries.objective: Catch out of the air and snatch off the floor in the same round.
entries.animalRule: The two kinds must alternate strictly; taking two of the same in a row ends the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: A short burst that trains two completely different reaches in the same minute.
entries.mechanismConnection: Boobook Owl — Sallying, catching and agile: it takes moths and beetles out of the air as readily as mice off the ground, which is a hawk-like way of hunting rather than an owl-like one. This Trial translates that dual hunting style into six takes alternating between air and floor.

entries.title: Take What Is Already Being Carried
entries.objective: A great skua does not really have a diet so much as a position in a flow. It catches very little for itself, and instead takes what is already being carried: gannets are chased and struck until they disgorge, smaller seabirds are killed directly, and anything a trawler throws overboard is taken from the water. The bird is a reading of whatever the system happens to be generating. Its principle is Kleptoparasitism. The metaphor? Position yourself in a flow that is already carrying things rather than producing anything.
entries.animalRule: Nothing may be produced during the attempt, and what is taken has to come from something already in motion.
entries.userBenefit: Producing everything yourself means competing with the flow already carrying it past you. Standing in that flow gets you the same thing for nothing.
entries.mechanismConnection: Stercorarius skua obtains most food by kleptoparasitism of gannets and other seabirds and by scavenging fishery discards, producing almost nothing by its own foraging.

entries.title: Take Whatever the Night Offers
entries.objective: In a good season a common tenrec runs a steady nocturnal rhythm and is almost indifferent to what it eats: insects, fruit, small vertebrates, whatever the night and the cover provide. It does not hold out for a preferred food, because on a seasonal island the flexibility is what keeps the middle gear running at all. Its principle is Many-Form Survival. The metaphor? In the ordinary gear, take what is actually available rather than holding out for the preferred version.
entries.animalRule: The preferred version must be given up during the attempt, and the cost of having waited for it has to be named in time.
entries.userBenefit: Holding out for the preferred version means long stretches with nothing while it stays unavailable. Taking what is there keeps you moving and the difference is usually small.
entries.mechanismConnection: Tenrec ecaudatus forages nocturnally as a generalist omnivore, taking insects, fruit and small vertebrates interchangeably according to seasonal availability.

entries.title: Take Whatever the Surface Offers
entries.objective: A skeleton shrimp will filter particles with bristly antennae, scrape diatoms and detritus off surfaces, or catch and scavenge small animals, switching freely between all of it. That opportunism is why it can live on practically any fouled rope, buoy or hydroid rather than needing a particular habitat. The generalism is what makes the minimal body enough. Its principle is Minimal Frame. The metaphor? Keep the body simple and the diet broad, and almost any surface becomes somewhere you can live.
entries.animalRule: The setup must stay simple during the attempt, and at least two different kinds of input have to be taken with it.
entries.userBenefit: A setup specialised for one kind of input leaves you stuck everywhere it is unavailable. A simple one that takes several means almost anywhere works for you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Caprella mutica feeds by antennal filter-feeding, surface scraping of diatoms and detritus, and predation or scavenging, allowing colonisation of almost any fouled substrate.

entries.title: Take Your Own Tail in Your Mouth
entries.objective: An armadillo girdled lizard is built like a tool rather than a hunter. Heavy keeled scales armour the back and tail, and it spends most of its life wedged into horizontal sandstone cracks where the spines make it almost impossible to extract. Caught in the open, it takes its own tail in its mouth and curls into a ring, presenting nothing but spines on every side and protecting the soft belly. Its principle is Self-Armor. The metaphor? Have a form you can close into when caught outside your usual position.
entries.animalRule: The closed form must leave nothing soft exposed, and it has to be actually entered once during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Being caught outside your usual position with no closed form means improvising badly under pressure. One practised form takes seconds and always works.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ouroborus cataphractus bites its own tail and curls into a spined ring when caught in the open, enclosing the unarmoured ventral surface entirely.

entries.title: Tap Five Buried Beans Up Through Rice
entries.objective: Bring five large dried beans buried in a bowl of rice to the surface by tapping the bowl alone.
entries.animalRule: No fingers, spoons or tools may go into the rice: only vibration from outside the bowl.
entries.userBenefit: A surprising bit of real physics you can show anyone in two minutes.
entries.mechanismConnection: Wood Turtle — Wandering • Foraging • Stamping: Glyptemys insculpta forages on land for worms, slugs, berries and mushrooms, and sometimes stamps the ground with its forefeet, a vibration that appears to bring earthworms up to the surface where it can take them. This Trial translates that rhythmic surface drumming which brings hidden food upward into tapping a bowl until buried beans rise through the rice.

entries.title: Tape One Zigzag Band Across a Glass Door
entries.objective: Make a clear glass door or window visible with a bright zigzag band of tape so people notice it before walking into it.
entries.animalRule: The band must zigzag across the pane, not just mark a corner, so the whole structure reads as solid.
entries.userBenefit: One easy-to-miss pane that people now see before they walk into it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Black-and-yellow Garden Spider — Rhythmic • Signaled • Operational: Argiope aurantia builds a large orb web crossed by a bright zigzag silk band, the stabilimentum, which reflects ultraviolet and makes the web conspicuous, and one strong explanation is that it warns birds and larger animals away so the working web is not blundered through. This Trial translates that visible zigzag warning band on a working structure into one zigzag of bright tape across a clear glass door.

entries.title: Taste It, Then Wait
entries.objective: A Brown Rat cannot vomit. With no way to correct a bad meal, it meets anything new by avoiding it for days, then taking a trace amount and leaving, and returning for more only once nothing has happened. Bait shyness is not cunning, it is that arithmetic running correctly. Sampling small is what makes it almost impossible to poison. Its principle is Urban Survivability. The metaphor? Do not commit on the first bite. Trace it. Wait.
entries.animalRule: The test must be the smallest usable amount and you must visibly wait before deciding, with the timer or clock in frame. No committing to the full version inside the same attempt.
entries.userBenefit: You commit fully to new things and then cannot undo them. Taking a trace and deliberately waiting costs you a day and removes nearly all of the downside you would otherwise be stuck with.
entries.mechanismConnection: Rattus norvegicus has no functioning emetic reflex and cannot expel anything harmful it has eaten, so it avoids novel items in familiar territory for days, then ingests only a trace and withdraws, returning for a full meal only after a delay with no ill effect.

entries.title: Teach a Partner Your Nut-Cracking Trick
entries.objective: Find a bare-hands way to crack a nut, pass it on in one silent demonstration, and see whether it survives the copy.
entries.animalRule: The technique travels by copying alone: one silent demonstration, no verbal explanation and no tools or stones.
entries.userBenefit: You find out whether your trick is actually teachable, and someone ends up with a new skill and a snack.
entries.mechanismConnection: White-faced Capuchin — Handling • Testing • Transmitted: Capuchins work hard foods with their hands, pounding them against anvils, and a technique invented by one animal is copied by others and persists as a group tradition. This Trial translates that one hand-invented nut-cracking technique passed on in a single silent demonstration and raced into teach a partner your nut-cracking trick.

entries.title: Tear One Old Magazine Into Strips
entries.objective: Steadily tear an old magazine into strips and store them for a later papier-mache build.
entries.animalRule: This stage only gathers and stores: no gluing or building yet, just steady tearing until the whole magazine is in the bowl.
entries.userBenefit: A calming, repetitive quarter hour that leaves a ready stock of craft material.
entries.mechanismConnection: Eupterote Fabia Moth — Growing • Accumulating • Sheltered: Eupterote fabia spends its long larval stage crawling on host plants and steadily eating leaves, building mass and reserves that the pupa later reorganises into an entirely different adult body. This Trial translates that slow, steady leaf-by-leaf intake stored for a later form into one magazine torn page by page into a bowl of strips for a future build.

entries.title: Teeth Even on the Tongue
entries.objective: A lizardfish spends almost all its time doing nothing, lying partly buried on rubble with only the eyes showing. The strike is vertical and fast, and what makes it final is that the teeth are everywhere: on the jaws, on the roof of the mouth, and on the tongue itself, all pointing backwards. Anything taken cannot work its way out in any direction. Its principle is Sand Ambush. The metaphor? One grip point can be slipped. Make every surface hold.
entries.animalRule: A hold must exist at every stage rather than at one point, and the single-checkpoint version has to be replaced during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: One checkpoint means anything slipping past it is gone and you find out much later. A hold at every stage catches it where it happened and costs you seconds each time.
entries.mechanismConnection: Synodus variegatus bears recurved teeth on the jaws, palate and tongue, so prey seized in the vertical ambush strike cannot be dislodged in any direction.

entries.title: Teeth on a Pigeon's Bill
entries.objective: A tooth-billed pigeon carries a bill unlike any other pigeon's: heavy, strongly hooked, with several tooth-like projections along the cutting edge of the lower mandible. It uses them to saw into the hard fruit of Dysoxylum trees and reach the seed inside, a food supply closed to almost every other bird in Samoa. The bill is also why the species matters beyond itself, as the closest living relative of the dodo. Its principle is Toothed Design. The metaphor? One structure your category does not have opens a supply closed to all of them.
entries.animalRule: The capability must be atypical for your category during the attempt, and the supply has to be genuinely closed without it.
entries.userBenefit: Carrying only your category's standard capabilities means eating only what all of them can eat. One atypical addition opens a supply with no competition.
entries.mechanismConnection: Didunculus strigirostris has a heavy hooked bill with mandibular tooth-like projections used to saw open hard Dysoxylum fruit inaccessible to other Samoan birds.

entries.title: Tell One Boundary Before It Is Needed
entries.objective: State one real preference or boundary early in a normal interaction instead of waiting for friction.
entries.animalRule: Hunts other snakes by scent trail across large areas and subdues them with a large venom delivery. Keep that true for the whole attempt.
entries.userBenefit: The boundary lands as information rather than as a complaint, because it arrived before the friction.
entries.mechanismConnection: King Cobra expresses Crowned Warning through this mode: King Cobra — Snake-Tracking Venom Dose — Searching • Tracking • Deliberate: Hunts other snakes by scent trail across large areas and subdues them with a large venom delivery. The Trial carries that same limiting structure into one concrete human action.

entries.title: Tell One Long Story Without Notes
entries.objective: Tell one coherent story aloud for at least five minutes without reading or using notes.
entries.animalRule: Sustain one continuous line of movement for the whole telling instead of relying on short bursts or resets.
entries.userBenefit: Builds sustained verbal endurance and narrative continuity.
entries.mechanismConnection: Red Hartebeest — Long-strided • Economical • Unstopping: High shoulders, long legs and a narrow track produce a gait that holds a fast pace for a very long way instead of producing a violent one briefly, and the same proportions carry the animal between grazing that is far apart. This Trial translates that mid-frequency mechanism into one light load for ten minutes.

entries.title: Ten Metres Into Sandy Soil
entries.objective: A gopher tortoise digs a tunnel that can run ten metres or more into sandy soil, and the significance extends far beyond the tortoise. Inside, temperature and humidity stay close to constant while the surface above swings between heat, frost and fire, so the burrow is where it spends most of its life and survives events that kill anything left outside. Many other species shelter there too. Its principle is Keystone Shelter. The metaphor? Build one deep stable place and it carries you through events that destroy everything on the surface.
entries.animalRule: The refuge must be built for conditions worse than current ones during the attempt, and the overbuilding has to be deliberate.
entries.userBenefit: A refuge built for current conditions fails in the event that actually matters. Overbuilding it costs you a day and it carries you through anything.
entries.mechanismConnection: Gopherus polyphemus excavates burrows exceeding ten metres in which temperature and humidity remain near-constant, allowing survival of surface fire, frost and heat extremes.

entries.title: Ten Minutes Reading, One Small Tap
entries.objective: Prionailurus viverrinus has been recorded lightly tapping the water with a paw, in a rhythm that draws fish upward toward what looks like a fallen insect. Before that it does nothing but read the surface from the bank, learning where movement is. The tap is cheap and the fish comes to it, which is what makes the whole hunt affordable. Its principle is Water Stalking. The metaphor? Read first, then make a small invitation.
entries.animalRule: The ten minutes of watching come first with no phone and no interruption, and only one small invitation is made afterwards.
entries.userBenefit: Leading with a big ask to someone you have not actually watched is why you get refused and never learn why. Ten minutes of reading first makes a tiny invitation land instead.
entries.mechanismConnection: Prionailurus viverrinus reads the water surface from the bank and taps it with a forepaw, mimicking a fallen insect to bring fish within reach rather than chasing them.

entries.title: Ten Quiet Minutes at Dusk
entries.objective: A night heron's build is for a short accurate strike rather than a long reach: proportionally very large eyes for low light, and a short thick neck with a heavy bill. It takes the same fish from the same shallows when nothing else is there, which is what makes a modest reach enough. Nothing is wasted on competing. Its principle is Nocturnal Timing. The metaphor? An empty room forgives a short reach.
entries.animalRule: The walk happens at dusk, nothing is played and nothing is held, and it lasts ten unbroken minutes.
entries.userBenefit: Filling every walk with audio means you arrive with nothing you did not bring. Ten quiet minutes at dusk gives you a version of the place you never see.
entries.mechanismConnection: Nycticorax nycticorax has enlarged low-light eyes and a short heavy bill suited to close-range strikes in darkness rather than long-reach diurnal foraging.

entries.title: Ten Still Minutes of Gathering
entries.objective: Harpia harpyja cannot see far inside closed rainforest, so it hears instead. A ruff of stiff feathers around the face works like an owl's disc, gathering the sound of an animal shifting in the canopy, and the bird holds still on a perch while it collects that information. The grip is famous, but it is the listening that makes the grip possible. Its principle is Canopy Grip. The metaphor? Gather the sound before you move.
entries.animalRule: You move nothing for the full ten minutes, each sound is written with a direction, and no action is taken until the list is complete.
entries.userBenefit: Moving before you have gathered information is why you keep acting on the wrong thing and having to redo it. Ten still minutes of listening usually changes what you do next.
entries.mechanismConnection: Harpia harpyja uses a ruff of stiff facial feathers as a sound-gathering disc, locating prey moving in dense canopy it cannot see through, from a motionless perch.

entries.title: Tend One Ridged Sand Circle Three Times
entries.objective: Revisit one ridged sand circle three times, clearing the scattered food from its valleys and adding a shell to every ridge each visit.
entries.animalRule: Every visit follows the same order, lentils out first and then one decoration per ridge, and no ridge may be flattened while you work.
entries.userBenefit: A calm, pleasing rhythm of small returns that trains patience and precision.
entries.mechanismConnection: White-spotted Pufferfish — Rhythmic • Site-bound • Forager: Torquigener albomaculosus picks small invertebrates from the sand while revisiting the same familiar patch of seafloor, and breeding males keep returning to one circular nest to tend it and set shell fragments along its structure. This Trial translates that repeated, site-bound feeding and tending of one patch into three scheduled visits that clear food from and decorate the same sand circle.

entries.title: Tens of Thousands Through One Gap
entries.objective: Because thermals do not form over open sea, every soaring stork crossing between Europe and Africa funnels through the same two narrow land bridges, and tens of thousands pass over them in a season. The constraint does not just shape one bird's route; it concentrates the entire population into a handful of places at a handful of moments. Its principle is Return. The metaphor? Where a shared constraint exists, everyone will be in the same few places at the same time. Plan for the crowd.
entries.animalRule: The shared constraint and the concentration point must both be named during the attempt, and a concrete plan for the crowd has to be made.
entries.userBenefit: Being surprised by a crowd at a chokepoint costs you the whole trip. Working out where the shared constraint puts everyone lets you plan around it.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ciconia ciconia populations concentrate at Gibraltar and the Bosphorus because thermal soaring prohibits open-sea crossing, producing seasonal passages of tens of thousands.

entries.title: Tension on One Side
entries.objective: The membrane is the animal. A fold of skin runs from the fifth finger to the ankle on each side, loose when the limbs are folded and taut when spread, turning what would be a fall into a glide of up to fifty metres. The Sugar Glider steers by changing tension on one side and using the tail as a rudder, then rotates to land head-up. Small asymmetries, not effort, decide where it ends up. Its principle is Bonded Glide. The metaphor? You cannot add power mid-fall. Steer with small differences instead.
entries.animalRule: Only one small adjustment may be made, the thing must not be stopped or restarted, and the adjustment has to be asymmetric rather than an across-the-board change.
entries.userBenefit: Trying to take control of something already moving usually breaks it. One small asymmetric nudge changes where it lands without stopping anything, and you can do it today.
entries.mechanismConnection: Petaurus breviceps glides on a patagium running from the fifth digit to the ankle, controlling direction by altering tension asymmetrically between the two membranes and using the tail as a rudder before rotating to land.

entries.title: Tent and Probe Eight Tubes for Hidden Balls
entries.objective: Work through eight cardboard tubes that a helper has secretly loaded, tenting every one before probing it, so that each hidden ball is flushed into a towel.
entries.animalRule: You cannot know which tubes hold prey, so every tube is tented before it is probed; no hands inside the tubes, and no ball may escape the towel.
entries.userBenefit: A clever, playful puzzle that makes a two-part hunting trick click.
entries.mechanismConnection: Wonderpus Octopus — Web-casting • Probing • Crawling: Wunderpus photogenicus crawls over open sand checking holes and crevices it cannot see into, spreading the web between its arms over each opening like a tent and pushing long, slender arm tips inside to flush any hidden fish, shrimps and crabs out into the web. This Trial translates that tent-then-probe routine over unknown holes into tenting and probing eight secretly loaded tubes so that every hidden ball lands in the towel.

entries.title: Tenure Spent From What You Brought
entries.objective: A central kob territory contains no grazing worth taking and cannot be left, so tenure is spent entirely from condition the male brought onto it, and lasts days before he is displaced and rejoins the herd. Nothing is replenished while he holds it. Everything depends on arriving already loaded. Its principle is Display Ground. The metaphor? If the position allows no resupply, the whole outcome was decided by what you arrived with.
entries.animalRule: The reserves must be loaded before taking the position, and the number of days they cover has to be stated during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Taking a no-resupply position without loading first means you lose it in days and cannot say why. Stating the number tells you whether to go at all.
entries.mechanismConnection: Kobus kob thomasi central territory holders cannot graze or leave, so tenure duration is determined entirely by body condition at arrival and typically lasts only days.

entries.title: Test Five Objects on One Floating Leaf
entries.objective: Find out which small objects one floating leaf can hold and which it cannot.
entries.animalRule: Each object is set down gently and lifted off before the next, so only weight decides.
entries.userBenefit: A calm little experiment that shows how weight, not size, decides what a surface holds.
entries.mechanismConnection: Cotton Pygmy Goose — Resting • Perching • Cavity-nesting: Nettapus coromandelianus is one of the smallest waterfowl, and through the hottest hours it rests on floating mats of vegetation or a low branch, where its low weight lets it sit without breaking through. This Trial translates that low weight that lets it rest on floating plants into a gentle weight test of five objects on one floating leaf.

entries.title: Test How the Branch Bends First
entries.objective: A Bornean orangutan builds a new sleeping platform almost every night, and the construction is more considered than the word nest suggests: branches are selected by testing how they bend, the main ones are broken part-way and woven into a rim, smaller leafy twigs are laid inside as a mattress, and in wet weather a cover is added above. Young animals take years of watching before they can do it. Its principle is Nestcraft. The metaphor? Test the material before you build with it, every time, even on something you build nightly.
entries.animalRule: Each piece must be tested before use during the attempt, and failures have to be actually rejected.
entries.userBenefit: Building with untested material on something routine is where the failure comes from, and you will blame the design. Testing each piece costs seconds.
entries.mechanismConnection: Pongo pygmaeus selects nest branches by flexion testing, part-fractures and weaves structural members into a rim, and adds leafy lining and weather covers.

entries.title: Test One Unsolved Glow
entries.objective: Use a UV-safe household fluorescence example if already available, or a phone-screen simulation if not, and document two plausible functions the glow could serve without declaring either proven.
entries.animalRule: Treat both explanations as hypotheses only; do not use UV sources outside normal consumer-safe use and do not claim the function is settled.
entries.userBenefit: Practises scientific restraint by exploring multiple plausible explanations for a striking trait while preserving genuine uncertainty.
entries.mechanismConnection: Malaysian Forest Scorpion's relevant mechanism is: Fluoresces under ultraviolet light through compounds in its cuticle, a property universal in scorpions whose function remains genuinely unresolved despite decades of investigation and several plausible proposals

entries.title: Tethered to the Water
entries.objective: The four-horned antelope is the only bovid that grows four horns, but the feature that governs how it lives is its dependence on drinking. It needs water frequently and cannot go long without it, so its whole range is drawn as a short radius around a reliable source and it visits several times a day. That tether shapes everything else about it. Its principle is Rare Signature. The metaphor? Your distinctive feature is not what constrains you; find the dependency that actually sets your radius.
entries.animalRule: The limiting dependency must be identified rather than the distinctive feature, and the radius has to be stated during the attempt.
entries.userBenefit: Your distinctive feature gets all the attention while an unnoticed dependency sets how far you can go. Naming the radius tells you what to plan inside.
entries.mechanismConnection: Tetracerus quadricornis requires frequent drinking and cannot tolerate water deprivation, confining its range to a short radius around permanent water visited several times daily.

entries.title: Thatch One Cardboard Frame With Three Builders
entries.objective: Build a shared thatched canopy with at least two other people, each weaving ten strips into one frame.
entries.animalRule: Each builder adds exactly ten strips, fixed only by weaving them through the frame and the other strips: no tape or glue.
entries.userBenefit: A shared making task that gets a household working with their hands together.
entries.mechanismConnection: Sociable Weaver — Rhythmic • Cooperative • Site‑fixed: Philetairus socius colonies build one huge communal nest, with many birds weaving dry grass stems into a shared thatched canopy that no single pair could make, and they keep adding to it together. This Trial translates that cooperative thatching of one shared structure into three builders weaving strips into a single frame.

entries.title: The Action Is the Warning
entries.objective: A crested pigeon has no alarm call. It has a narrowed eighth primary feather that sounds a sharp high note on every downstroke, and because a frightened bird beats faster and harder than one leaving casually, an alarmed takeoff sounds audibly different. The flock flushes on hearing it. The signal is produced by the escape itself, which is why it cannot be faked and costs nothing to maintain. Its principle is Alarm. The metaphor? Let the act do the signalling.
entries.animalRule: No separate announcement is allowed; the warning has to be carried by the visible action itself, and it happens the moment the problem appears.
entries.userBenefit: Announcing a problem before acting on it wastes the minutes that mattered and makes people doubt you the next time. Acting visibly warns them and fixes it at once.
entries.mechanismConnection: Ocyphaps lophotes produces an acoustic alarm mechanically, through a modified narrow eighth primary that sounds on each wingbeat, so alarm tempo encodes genuine flight.

entries.title: The Adult Only Finds the Colony
entries.objective: A green lacewing is effectively two animals sharing one life cycle. The adult is not a predator at all: it feeds on nectar and honeydew, and its entire work is to find aphid colonies and lay eggs on them. The larva that emerges is the feeding stage, flat and sickle-jawed, capable of draining several hundred soft-bodied insects. The finding and the doing are done by different stages. Its principle is Guardianship. The metaphor? Your job may be to find the site and place the thing, not to do the work there.
entries.animalRule: No work may be done at the site during the attempt, and the placement has to be accurate.
entries.userBenefit: Doing the work at every site you find means you only ever cover a few. Finding and placing means far more of them get worked without you.
entries.mechanismConnection: Chrysoperla carnea adults are nectarivorous and locate aphid colonies for oviposition, while the predatory larval stage performs all consumption.

entries.title: The Average of the Gazes
entries.objective: A herd of Cape buffalo can number in the hundreds and it has no leader. Observations recorded what happens before a move: during the resting period individual adult females stand up, hold a gaze in a particular direction for a while, and lie down again, and when the herd eventually moves it goes in roughly the average of the directions that were gazed in. Nobody decides and everybody votes. Its principle is Herdline. The metaphor? Collect everyone's direction without debate and go in the average of them.
entries.animalRule: The directions must be collected without discussion during the attempt, and the outcome has to be their average.
entries.userBenefit: Discussing a direction means the loudest person decides and you get resentment either way. Collecting and averaging silently gets a better answer and no argument.
entries.mechanismConnection: Syncerus caffer herds perform a pre-departure voting behaviour in which adult females signal direction by standing and gazing, with the eventual movement approximating the mean bearing.

entries.title: The Bacteria Make What the Sap Lacks
